[Exodus] [17]:[1] Then all the Israelis moved on from Sin in the wilderness, travelling following Yahweh’s instructions. They camped at Refidim but there was no water for the people to drink.
[Exodus] [17]:[2] So the people argued with Mosheh (Moses) again, saying, “Give us water to drink!” “Why are you all quarrelling with me?” Mosheh answered. “Why are you all testing Yahweh?”
[Exodus] [17]:[3] But the people were very thirsty there and they murmured against Mosheh, so he demanded, “Is this why you brought us out of Mitsrayim (Egypt)? To kill me and my sons and my cattle with thirst?” ???
[Exodus] [17]:[4] Mosheh cried out to Yahweh, asking, “What should I do for these people? It won’t take much more and they’ll kill me.”
[Exodus] [17]:[5] “Walk on ahead of the people,” Yahweh told Mosheh, “and take some of the Israeli elders with you, and your staff—the one which you struck the river with. Take it in your hand and go.
[Exodus] [17]:[6] Watch me. I will stand in front of you there on the rock at Horev. Then you will strike the rock and water will come out of it, and the people will drink.” So Mosheh did that while the Israeli elders watched.
[Exodus] [17]:[7] Mosheh named that place both ‘Masah’ (which means ‘testing’) and ‘Merivah’ (which means ‘complaining’), because of the conflict among the Israelis and because of how they tested Yahweh by saying, ‘Is Yahweh among us or not?’
[Exodus] [17]:[8] Then the Amalek army came and attacked Yisrael (Israel) at Refidim,
[Exodus] [17]:[9] and Mosheh (Moses) instructed Yehoshua (Joshua), “Choose men for us and go out and fight with Amalek. Tomorrow I’ll be stationed on top of the hill with the staff of God in my hand.”
[Exodus] [17]:[10] So Yehoshua prepared to fight Amalek as Mosheh had told him, and Mosheh, Aharon (Aaron), and Hur climbed up to the top of the hill.
[Exodus] [17]:[11] And so it happened that when Mosheh raised his arm, then Yisrael would be winning, but when he lowered his arm, then Amalek would start winning.
[Exodus] [17]:[12] However, Mosheh’s arms got tired, so they got a large stone and sat him on it, and Aharon and Hur stood on each side of him holding up his arms, and holding him steady in that position until the sun went down.
[Exodus] [17]:[13] So this was how Yehoshua defeated Amalek and his army with their swords.
[Exodus] [17]:[14] Then Yahweh told Mosheh, “Write this event in the book and read it aloud to Yehoshua, because I will certainly blot out the memory of Amalek from off the earth.”
[Exodus] [17]:[15] Then Mosheh built an altar and he named it ‘Yahweh-nissi’ (which means ‘Yahweh is my banner’),
[Exodus] [17]:[16] saying, “Because they battled against Yah’s throne, then Yahweh will battle against Amalek throughout the generations.”
[Exodus] [18]:[1] Now Yitro (Jethro), the priest at Midyan and Mosheh’s (Moses) father-in-law, heard about everything that God had done for Mosheh and for his people the Israelis—that Yahweh had brought the Israelis out of Mitsrayim (Egypt).
[Exodus] [18]:[2] (Yitro had been looking after Mosheh’s wife Tsiporah and their two sons after he had sent her back
[Exodus] [18]:[3] along with their two sons. One was named ‘Gereshom’ (which sounds like the Hebrew word for ‘foreigner’) because Mosheh had said, “I’ve been a foreigner living in another country.”
[Exodus] [18]:[4] Their other son’s name was ‘Eliezer’ (which sounds like the Hebrew word that means ‘God helps me’, because Mosheh had said, “God, who my father worshipped, has helped me and stopped the Mitsri (Egyptian) king Par’oh (Pharaoh) from killing me.”))
[Exodus] [18]:[5] So now Mosheh’s father-in-law brought Mosheh’s wife and sons to the wilderness where the people were camping near the mountain of God.
[Exodus] [18]:[6] He had sent a message ahead saying, “I, your father-in-law Yitro, am coming to you, as well as your wife and your two sons.”
[Exodus] [18]:[7] So Mosheh went out to meet his father-in-law, and he bowed down and kissed him. They asked each other about their welfare, then they went into the tent,
[Exodus] [18]:[8] and Mosheh related to his father-in-law all that Yahweh had done to Par’oh and to Mitsrayim on account of Yisrael (Israel), all the hardship that found them along the way, and about how Yahweh had rescued them.
[Exodus] [18]:[9] Yitro was very happy to hear about all the good things that Yahweh had done for Yisrael when he had rescued them out from Mitsri control,
[Exodus] [18]:[10] and he said, “Bless Yahweh, who rescued you from slavery in Mitsrayim, and from Par’oh’s power.
[Exodus] [18]:[11] Now I can see that Yahweh is greater than all the other gods because of the this result after the Mitsrim (Egyptians) had acted proudly against you all.”
[Exodus] [18]:[12] Then Mosheh’s father-in-law Yitro made a burnt offering as well as sacrifices to God, and Aharon (Aaron) and all of the Israeli elders came to eat bread with Mosheh’s father-in-law in God’s presence.
[Exodus] [18]:[13] The following day, Mosheh (Moses) sat down to judge the people, and the people stood around him from morning until evening.
[Exodus] [18]:[14] When his father-in-law noticed everything that he personally did for the people, he asked, “What’s this that you’re doing with the people? Why do you sit there alone, and all the people position themselves around you from morning until evening?”
[Exodus] [18]:[15] “Because the people come to me to find out what God wants for them,” Mosheh replied to Yitro (Jethro).
[Exodus] [18]:[16] “When a difficult situation comes up among them, someone comes to me and I make the judgement between a man and his neighbour. In addition, I help them understand the god’s statutes and laws.”
[Exodus] [18]:[17] “It’s not a good idea what you’re doing,” said Yitro.
[Exodus] [18]:[18] “You’re definitely on the road to wear yourself out, plus you’ll also wear out these people who are with you, because the responsibility is too heavy for you—you can’t just do it alone.
[Exodus] [18]:[19] Now, listen to this: I’ll advise you and God will be with you. You be before God for the people, and you should bring their disputes to God yourself.
[Exodus] [18]:[20] You should also teach them the statutes and the laws, and you should teach them the way they should live and the work that they should do.
[Exodus] [18]:[21] But you yourself should search through all the people to find capable men who are godly and faithful, and not greedy for dishonest profit. Then appoint the best of them to be over a thousand households, and then others to be over groups of one hundred, fifty, and ten households.
[Exodus] [18]:[22] They’ll be the ones to judge the people, except that every serious situation they’ll bring to you—they’ll judge every minor situation themselves. Yes, you must lighten this load off yourself, and they’ll share the load with you.
[Exodus] [18]:[23] If you do that, and if God tells you to proceed, then you’ll be able to endure in the long term, plus all of these people standing around will be able to return to their tents peacefully.”
[Exodus] [18]:[24] So Mosheh (Moses) took his father-in-law’s advice and implemented all of his suggestions.
[Exodus] [18]:[25] He chose capable men from among all the Israelis, and he appointed them as heads over the people: leaders of thousands, leaders of hundreds, leaders of fifties, and leaders of tens of households.
[Exodus] [18]:[26] They became the ones who settled most disputes for the people. They brought the difficult cases to Mosheh, but they judged each minor situation themselves.
[Exodus] [18]:[27] Then Mosheh bid farewell to Yitro (Jethro) and he returned to his own home.
[Exodus] [19]:[1] The Israelis entered the Sinay wilderness in the third month after exiting Mitsrayim (Egypt).
[Exodus] [19]:[2] After they had departed from Refidim, they had entered the Sinay wilderness and camped there at the base of the mountain.
[Exodus] [19]:[3] Yahweh called Mosheh (Moses) from the mountain, so he climbed up and God gave him this message and asked him to pass it on to Ya’akov’s (Jacob) descendants, the Israelis:
[Exodus] [19]:[4] “You yourselves saw what I did to the Mitsrim (Egyptians)—how I carried you on eagles’ wings and brought you all here to myself.
[Exodus] [19]:[5] And now, if you all carefully listen to my words and keep my agreement, then your nation will be my possession, separate from all the others, because all the earth is mine,
[Exodus] [19]:[6] So you all will be my kingdom of priests and a nation dedicated to me.” (That’s the message to pass on to the Israelis.)
[Exodus] [19]:[7] So Mosheh descended again and summoned the Israeli elders, then he passed on that message just as Yahweh had commanded him,
[Exodus] [19]:[8] and all the people responded together, agreeing, “We’ll do everything that Yahweh has said.” Then Mosheh took the people’s response back to Yahweh
[Exodus] [19]:[9] and Yahweh told him, “Look, I’ll come to you in a thick cloud so that the people will be able to hear when I speak with you so they’ll also continue to trust you.” Then Mosheh told Yahweh the people’s words
[Exodus] [19]:[10] and Yahweh responded, “Go down to the people and purify them today and tomorrow. Have them wash their clothes
[Exodus] [19]:[11] and be prepared for the third day, because on the third day I will come down to Mt. Sinay while all the people watch.
[Exodus] [19]:[12] Set boundaries for the people all around, and tell them, ‘Don’t climb on the mountain or touch its edge, because anyone who does will definitely be executed.
[Exodus] [19]:[13] Anyone who touches the mountain mustn’t be touched by anyone else—they must be executed by throwing rocks at them or shooting them with a bow. No person or animal who touches the mountain can stay alive.’ Only after a long trumpet blast should they start to climb the mountain.”
[Exodus] [19]:[14] So Mosheh went down the mountain to the people. He purified them and they all washed their clothes,
[Exodus] [19]:[15] and he told them, “Abstain from sexual relations, and be ready by the third day.”
[Exodus] [19]:[16] So on the morning of the third day, there was thunder and lightning and a thick cloud on the mountain, and an extremely loud horn blast, and all the people in the camp were trembling.
[Exodus] [19]:[17] Then Mosheh led the people out of the camp to go and meet God, and they stationed themselves at the foot of the mountain.
[Exodus] [19]:[18] Yahweh descended onto Mt. Sinay surrounded by fire and the entire mountain smoked. Its smoke went up like the smoke from a furnace, and the whole mountain trembled violently.
[Exodus] [19]:[19] Then it happened after the sound of the horn got extremely loud, that Mosheh was speaking and God was answering him in a voice.
[Exodus] [19]:[20] Yahweh had descended onto the top of Mt. Sinay, and he called Mosheh up to the top of the mountain, so Mosheh ascended.
[Exodus] [19]:[21] But Yahweh told him, “Go back down and warn the people in case they force their way through to look at me and many of them perish.
[Exodus] [19]:[22] Also, the priests who come nearer to me, they must be very careful to purify themselves in case I suddenly punish them.”
[Exodus] [19]:[23] But Mosheh questioned Yahweh, “The people aren’t able to come up on Mt. Sinay, because you yourself warned us, ‘Set boundaries all around the mountain to keep it sacred.’ ”
[Exodus] [19]:[24] “Go back down,” Yahweh responded, “and bring Aharon (Aaron) back up with you. However, the priests and the people must not cross the boundary to come up to me, in case I suddenly punish them.”
[Exodus] [19]:[25] So Mosheh went down and spoke to the people.
[Exodus] [20]:[1] Then God gave these instructions to the Israelis:
[Exodus] [20]:[2] I’m your god Yahweh, who rescued you from where you were enslaved in Mitsrayim (Egypt).
[Exodus] [20]:[3] You mustn’t own any other gods in my sight.
[Exodus] [20]:[4] You mustn’t make a carved figure for yourself, nor carve a copy of anything in the sky above or in the earth below, or that’s in the water under the earth.
[Exodus] [20]:[5] Don’t bow down to idols and don’t serve them, because I, your god Yahweh, am a jealous God. I remember the sins of the fathers and punish the children of even the third and fourth generation of those who hate me,

[Exodus] [20]:[7] You mustn’t wrongly promote the name of Yahweh your god, because I won’t leave anyone unpunished who does that.

[Exodus] [20]:[9] there’s six days every week for working.
[Exodus] [20]:[10] The seventh day is a rest day for Yahweh your god: you mustn’t do any work—not you, or your children, or your male or female servants, or your cattle, or the foreigners living among you—
[Exodus] [20]:[11] because Yahweh made the heavens and earth, the sea, and everything that’s in them in six days. Then he rested on the seventh day, so that’s why he blessed the rest day and made it sacred.
[Exodus] [20]:[12] Honour your father and your mother, so that you’ll have a long life on the land that your god Yahweh is about to give you.

[Exodus] [20]:[15] You mustn’t steal.

[Exodus] [20]:[17] You mustn’t covet your neighbour’s house or spouse, or their male or female servants, or their animals, or anything else they own.

[Exodus] [21]:[1] These are the rules that you must present to them:
[Exodus] [21]:[2] If you buy a Ivri (Hebrew) slave, he should serve for six years, then in the seventh year he must be set free without having to pay you anything.
[Exodus] [21]:[3] If he came by himself, he can go free by himself. If he’s married with a wife, then his wife must be set free with him.
[Exodus] [21]:[4] If his master gave him a wife and she bore him sons or daughters, then the wife and her children are her master’s, and only the husband must be set free.
[Exodus] [21]:[5] But if he plainly says, “I love my master, my wife, and my children so I voluntarily choose not to be set free,”
[Exodus] [21]:[6] then his master must take him to the place of worship. He must bring him to a door or to a doorpost, and his master must bore a hole his ear with an awl. Then he must serve him for life.
[Exodus] [21]:[7] And if a man sells his daughter as a female slave, she won’t be sent away after six years like the male slaves.
[Exodus] [21]:[8] If the man who bought her wanted her to become his slave-wife, but later he isn’t pleased with her behaviour, he must allow her to be bought back by her relatives. He has no authority to sell her on to outsiders, because that would break the understanding of proper treatment of her.
[Exodus] [21]:[9] Or if he selected her to become his son’s slave-wife, then he must treat her like a daughter would expect to be treated.
[Exodus] [21]:[10] If he go on to take another slave-wife, he mustn’t reduce the first one’s food or clothing, or her marital rights,
[Exodus] [21]:[11] but if he doesn’t provide these three things to her, then she can go free without having to pay anything.
[Exodus] [21]:[12] Anyone who strikes someone and that person dies, must definitely be put to death.
[Exodus] [21]:[13] But if it wasn’t premeditated—if God had let it happen as an accident—then I’ll assign a place where the one who hit them can flee to.
[Exodus] [21]:[14] However, if someone had schemed to trap and kill their neighbour, then even if the killer clings to my altar, you must take them for execution.
[Exodus] [21]:[15] Anyone who strikes their father or mother must certainly be put to death.
[Exodus] [21]:[16] Anyone who abducts another person—either to sell or to keep as a slave—that person must certainly be put to death.
[Exodus] [21]:[17] Anyone who curses their father or mother must certainly be put to death.
[Exodus] [21]:[18] If two people fight and one hits their neighbour with a stone or with their fist, and the injured one doesn’t die but is bedridden,
[Exodus] [21]:[19] if that person eventually rises and can walk about outside using a staff, then the person who struck them is free, other than reimbursing the costs of their lost work and their medical expenses.
[Exodus] [21]:[20] If a master hits their male or female slave with a staff and the slave dies, then the death must certainly be avenged.
[Exodus] [21]:[21] However, if the slave is able to stand within a couple of days, then the owner won’t be punished because the slave is their property.
[Exodus] [21]:[22] If two people fight together and strike a pregnant woman and cause her to deliver the baby, if there’s no serious injury, then he must certainly be fined whatever the husband of the woman demands and the judges allow.
[Exodus] [21]:[23] But if there’s serious injury, then you must give a life for a life,
[Exodus] [21]:[24] an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth, a hand for a hand, a foot for a foot,
[Exodus] [21]:[25] a burn for a burn, a wound for a wound, and a bruise for a bruise.
[Exodus] [21]:[26] If a master hits their male or female slave’s eye and damages it, they must let the slave go free in compensation for the eye.
[Exodus] [21]:[27] Or if the master knocks out a tooth of a male or female slave, they must let the slave go free in compensation for the tooth.
[Exodus] [21]:[28] If a bull gores a man or a woman and they die, the bull must certainly be killed by throwing rocks at it. The owner of the animal is to be considered innocent, but its meat mustn’t be eaten.
[Exodus] [21]:[29] But if the bull had a habit of goring in the past and its owner was warned but didn’t keep it fenced in, and it kills a man or a woman, then the bull must be killed by throwing rocks at it and its owner must also be put to death.
[Exodus] [21]:[30] If a ransom payment is demanded instead, the owner may buy back their life by paying the full amount demanded.
[Exodus] [21]:[31] Those rules also apply if the bull gores a person’s son or daughter.
[Exodus] [21]:[32] If the bull gores a male or female slave, its owner must give thirty silver shekels to the slave owner and the bull must be killed by throwing rocks at it.
[Exodus] [21]:[33] If someone uncovers a pit for storage, or digs a new one and leaves it uncovered, and a cow or a donkey falls into it,
[Exodus] [21]:[34] the owner of the pit must pay compensation. The pit owner must pay in cash, but the dead animal will then belong to them.
[Exodus] [21]:[35] If one person’s bull attacks someone else’s bull and it dies, then they should sell the live animal and divide the money as well as dividing up the dead animal.
[Exodus] [21]:[36] But if it was known that the bull had a habit of goring in the past and its owner hadn’t kept it fenced in, then that owner must certainly give a live bull for the dead one, but the dead animal will become theirs.

[Exodus] [22]:[2] (If a thief is discovered at night while breaking in, and is struck and dies, no one should be charged for murder.
[Exodus] [22]:[3] But if it’s daylight already, then that person is guilty of murder.) A thief who’s caught must make restitution, but if they’re unable to pay, then the thief must be sold to cover it.
[Exodus] [22]:[4] If a thief is found in the possession of a stolen animal, be it a cow or a donkey or a sheep, then they must pay back another matching animal as well.
[Exodus] [22]:[5] If a person releases their livestock to graze their own field or vineyard, and it ends up grazing in the someone else’s field, the owner of the animal must compensate from the best of their field and from the best of their vineyard.
