[Ruth] [2]:[11] “People have told me,” Boaz replied, “about everything you’ve done for your mother-in-law since your husband died—how you left your parents and your homeland behind and came here to live with people that you hadn’t even met before.
[Ruth] [2]:[12] May Yahweh reward your hard work. Since you’ve come here for protection under Yisrael’s (Israel) god Yahweh, may he reward you in full.”
[Ruth] [2]:[13] “My lord,” she replied, “I trust that I’ll continue to please you because you’ve comforted me by speaking so kindly to me, your servant, even though I’m not like your servant girls.”
[Ruth] [2]:[14] Then when it was time to eat, Boaz told Ruth, “Come and join us. Take some bread and dip it in the sauce and eat.” So she sat beside the harvesters, and he also offered her some roasted grain. She ate until she was full and even had some left over.
[Ruth] [2]:[15] Then she went back to picking up heads and Boaz ordered his men, “Let her gather grain even among the bundles and don’t shame her.
[Ruth] [2]:[16] Even pull some stalks out from the bundles and drop them for her to pick up, and don’t tell her off.”
[Ruth] [2]:[17] So Ruth picked up grain in the countryside until evening and when she beat the heads and collected the grains, she had a large basket of barley.
[Ruth] [2]:[18] So she picked up the basket and headed back into town and showed her mother-in-law how much she had collected. Ruth also gave No’omi (Naomi) the roasted grain left-over from her lunch.
[Ruth] [2]:[19] “Where did you pick up grain today and where did you work?” asked No’omi. “May the man who took notice of you be blessed.” So she told her mother-in-law where she had worked, “The name of the man I worked with today is Boaz.”
[Ruth] [2]:[20] “May he be blessed by Yahweh,” responded No’omi. “Yahweh hasn’t forgotten his kindness towards us who are still living and to our husbands who’ve died.” And then she added, “That man is a close relative of Elimelek. In fact, he’s one of those responsible for taking care of our family.”
[Ruth] [2]:[21] “He also told me,” said Ruth the Moavit, “to stay with his workers until they finish the harvesting.”
[Ruth] [2]:[22] “It’s good, my daughter,” said No’omi to her daughter-in-law, “for you to stay near his servant girls because you don’t know how people might treat you in another field.”
[Ruth] [2]:[23] So Ruth stayed near Boaz’ servant girls and picked up heads of grain until the end of the barley harvest and then the wheat harvest, and she lived with her mother-in-law.
[Ruth] [3]:[1] One day Ruth’s mother-in-law No’omi (Naomi) said to her, “My daughter, I think I need to be finding a secure living situation for you?
[Ruth] [3]:[2] Now, Boaz whose servant girls you’ve been working with, he’s a relative of ours. In fact, he’ll be on the threshing floor winnowing barley tonight.
[Ruth] [3]:[3] So wash yourself and put on some perfume. Wear your cloak and go out to the threshing floor, but don’t let him know you’re there until he’s finished eating and drinking.
[Ruth] [3]:[4] Then when he lies down to sleep, pay attention to where he lies down. Once he’s asleep, go and lift the blanket near his feet and lie down. Then he’ll tell you what to do next.”
[Ruth] [3]:[5] “I’ll do everything you say,” Ruth answered,
[Ruth] [3]:[6] then she went out to the threshing floor and did everything her mother-in-law had instructed.
[Ruth] [3]:[7] When Boaz had finished eating and drinking and was feeling cheery, he went off to lie down at the end of the pile of grain. Then Ruth quietly followed him, and uncovered his feet and lay down there.
[Ruth] [3]:[8] But Boaz was startled in the middle of the night, and when he turned over he was stunned to find a woman lying at his feet.
[Ruth] [3]:[9] “Who are you?” he asked. “I’m your servant Ruth,” she replied, “Spread your cloak over me because you have a responsibility as our close relative.”
[Ruth] [3]:[10] “My dear girl, may Yahweh bless you.” Boaz replied, “You have shown more kindness now that before, because you haven’t chased after the young men, whether rich or poor.
[Ruth] [3]:[11] So now dear girl, don’t be afraid. I’ll do what you’ve asked for, because the whole town knows that you’re an honourable woman.
[Ruth] [3]:[12] It is true that I have a responsibility towards your family, but there’s another man who’s more closely related to you all than me.
[Ruth] [3]:[13] Stay here for the rest of the night, and then in the morning, if he’ll accept then he can marry you. But if he’s not willing to take care of you, then as Yahweh lives, I’ll do it myself. Now lie down here until morning.”
[Ruth] [3]:[14] So Ruth lay there near his feet until morning, but she got up before it was light enough to be recognised as Boaz had said, “It’s best if no one knows that a woman visited the threshing floor.”
[Ruth] [3]:[15] Then Boaz said, “Bring your cloak here and hold it out.” So she held it while he poured a generous amount of barley into it, and lifted it onto her shoulder. Then he or she went into the town.
[Ruth] [3]:[16] When Ruth got home, her mother-in-law asked her, “My daughter, how did everything go?” So Ruth told her everything that Boaz had said and done for her
[Ruth] [3]:[17] and she also said, “He gave me all this barley because he told me that he didn’t want me to return to my mother-in-law empty-handed.”
[Ruth] [3]:[18] “Okay my daughter,” No’omi (Naomi) responded. “Wait now until we see what happens, because that man won’t rest today until the matter gets settled.”
[Ruth] [4]:[1] Meanwhile, Boaz went to the place inside the town gate (where people conducted their official business) and sat down there. Just as he had hoped, the man responsible for No’omi’s (Naomi) family came along—the man whom Boaz had mentioned earlier—and Boaz called out to him by name and said, “Come over here and sit down.” So the man came over and sat down.
[Ruth] [4]:[2] Then Boaz called over ten of the older, well-respected men from the town and asked them to sit and witness their discussion, so they sat down with them.
[Ruth] [4]:[3] Then Boaz asked the other relative, “The part of the countryside that belonged to our relative Elimelek is for sale. No’omi, who recently returned from Moav (Moab), is selling it.
[Ruth] [4]:[4] I thought that I should tell you about it and in case you buy the land while the people sitting here are listening, including these leaders of our people. If you want to buy it back into the family, then do so. But if you do not want to buy it back, then let me know, because you are the closest relative to Elimelek, and I am next after you.” “I’ll buy it,” the man replied.
[Ruth] [4]:[5] “When you buy the land from No’omi,” Boaz continued, “you will also need to marry Ruth, our deceased relative’s widow from Moav, so that she’ll have a son who will inherit the property and continue Elimelek’s family line.”
[Ruth] [4]:[6] “I can’t buy it back myself, then,” the closer relative answered. “If I did that, I would ruin my own son’s inheritance. You can have the land and the woman instead of me, because I simply can’t take it.”
[Ruth] [4]:[7] (At that time in Yisrael (Israel), people had a different way of buying land or exchanging goods between them. In order to make these matters legally binding, one man would take off one of his sandals and give it to the other party. That was the way people in Yisrael confirmed what they had agreed to do.)
[Ruth] [4]:[8] “You buy it yourself,” the relative said and he took off one of his sandals and gave it to Boaz.
[Ruth] [4]:[9] Then Boaz said to the respected men and to all the other people who were there, “Today you have all witnessed that I’ve bought from No’omi all the property that belonged to Elimelek, Kilyon, and Mahlon.
[Ruth] [4]:[10] I am also taking Ruth, Mahlon’s widow from Moav, to be my wife so that she can have a son. Everyone will consider that son to be Elimelek’s descendant and he will inherit the property and carry on Elimelek’s family name among his relatives and here in his hometown. You’ve seen and heard that today and can tell anyone who asks about it.”
[Ruth] [4]:[11] All the respected men, and the others who were sitting at the town gate, agreed, and they said, “Yes, we are your. We pray that Yahweh will allow this woman who will be coming into your home, to be like Rahel (Rachel) and Le’ah, the two who gave birth to our ancestors and started our people, Yisrael. May you become great in the clan of Efratah and famous here in Beyt-Lehem (Bethlehem)!
[Ruth] [4]:[12] We pray that your family will be like the family of your ancestor Perets, son of Yehudah (Judah) and Tamar, because of the many descendants that Yahweh will give to you and this young woman.”
[Ruth] [4]:[13] So Boaz married Ruth, and when he slept with her, Yahweh enabled her to become pregnant and she gave birth to a son.
[Ruth] [4]:[14] The women in Beyt-Lehem (Bethlehem) said to No’omi (Naomi), “Praise Yahweh for giving you a male descendant to preserve your family today. We pray to Yahweh that people throughout Yisrael (Israel) will greatly respect him.
[Ruth] [4]:[15] Your daughter-in-law, who loves you and who’s been better to you than if you had seven sons, has given birth to him. Now he’ll make you feel young again and he’ll take care of you when you get old.”
[Ruth] [4]:[16] Then No’omi picked up the baby and held him closely and became like second mother to him.
[Ruth] [4]:[17] The women who were living nearby said, “It is as if No’omi now has a son!” They named him Oved. Eventually Oved went on to become the father of Yishay (Jesse), who became the father of King David.
[Ruth] [4]:[18] Here is a list of the descendants of Perets: Perets’s son was Hetsron.
[Ruth] [4]:[19] Hetsron’s son was Ram and Ram’s son was Aminadav.
[Ruth] [4]:[20] Aminadav’s son was Nahshon and Nahshon’s son was Salmon.
[Ruth] [4]:[21] Salmon’s son was Boaz and Boaz’s son was Oved.
[Ruth] [4]:[22] Oved’s son was Yishay and Yishay’s son was King David.
[1 Shmuel] [1]:[1] There was a man named Elkanah from Ramatayim-Tsofim who lived in the Efrati hill country. (He was an Efrati—the son of Yeroham, son of Elihu, son of Tohu, son of Tsuf.)
[1 Shmuel] [1]:[2] He had two wives: Hannah (who had no children) and Peninah (who had several children).
[1 Shmuel] [1]:[3] Every year he would take his family to Shiloh to offer sacrifices to commander Yahweh. Eli was Yahweh’s priest there, and his two sons Hofni and Pinhas also served there.
[1 Shmuel] [1]:[4] on the day that Elkanah made his sacrifice, he would give portions of the cooked meat to Peninah and to all her sons and daughters,
[1 Shmuel] [1]:[5] but he’d give a double portion to Hannah because he loved her, even though Yahweh had not enabled her to have children.
[1 Shmuel] [1]:[6] Then her rival would provoke her and try to make her angry, because Yahweh hadn’t given her children.
[1 Shmuel] [1]:[7] And so it happened every year. Every time they went to Yahweh’s tent, Peninah ridiculed him, and Hannah would weep and wouldn’t eat.
[1 Shmuel] [1]:[8] Then Elkanah would ask her, “Hannah, why are you crying? And why aren’t you eating? And why are you so upset? Isn’t it better having me than having ten sons?”
[1 Shmuel] [1]:[9] One time Hannah got up after eating and drinking at Shiloh. (Eli the priest was sitting on the seat near the entrance of Yahweh’s tent.)
[1 Shmuel] [1]:[10] Hannah was very upset, and she prayed to Yahweh and wept uncontrollably.
[1 Shmuel] [1]:[11] Then she made a vow, saying, “Commander Yahweh, if you would only notice the misery of your female servant and remember me. Don’t ignore me. Help your female servant to give birth to a son, then I’ll give him to you for his entire life, and he’ll never have his hair cut.”
[1 Shmuel] [1]:[12] As she continued praying to Yahweh, Eli was watching her mouth.
[1 Shmuel] [1]:[13] Now Hannah was praying from her heart, and her lips were moving but she wasn’t speaking aloud. Eli thought she must be drunk,
[1 Shmuel] [1]:[14] and scolded her, “You shouldn’t be getting drunk. Get rid of your wine.”
[1 Shmuel] [1]:[15] “No, my master,” Hannah replied, “I’m a woman who’s suffering deep down. I haven’t drunk any wine or intoxicating drink, but rather I’ve been sharing my inner issues with Yahweh.
[1 Shmuel] [1]:[16] Don’t think that your female servant is just a worthless woman, because just now I was praying as a result of my terrible anguish and frustration.”
[1 Shmuel] [1]:[17] “Then go in peace,” Eli replied. “And may Yisrael’s (Israel) god grant your request that you presented to him.”
[1 Shmuel] [1]:[18] “Please assume the best of your female servant,” said Hannah, then she went on her way and had something to eat, and something had changed in her demeanor.
[1 Shmuel] [1]:[19] They all gut up early the next morning and worshipped Yahweh again, then they returned to their home at Ramah. Then Elkanah slept with his wife Hannah, and Yahweh answered her prayer.
[1 Shmuel] [1]:[20] Hannah got pregnant, and in due course, she gave birth to a son. She named him ‘Shmuel’ (Samuel) (meaning ‘heard by God’, usually changed to ‘Shmuel’ in English) because she had requested him from Yahweh.
[1 Shmuel] [1]:[21] At the usual time, Elkanah and all his household went to Shiloh to offer their sacrifices and fulfill their vows to Yahweh.
[1 Shmuel] [1]:[22] But Hannah didn’t accompany them because she’d told her husband, “I’ll come and bring him when he’s weaned. Then he can be taken in to Yahweh and permanently remain there.”
[1 Shmuel] [1]:[23] “Do what you think’s best,” her husband replied. “Stay until you’ve weaned him. May Yahweh do whatever he said to you.” So she stayed behind and breastfed her son until she eventually weaned him.
[1 Shmuel] [1]:[24] The next year, after she’d weaned him, she took the young boy with them, along with three bulls, a sack of flour, and a container of wine. Then she brought him to Yahweh’s tent in Shiloh,
[1 Shmuel] [1]:[25] and after slaughtering the bull, they took the boy in to Eli.
[1 Shmuel] [1]:[26] “Please, my master,” Hannah said. “As your spirit lives, my master, I’m the woman who was standing with you here to pray to Yahweh.
[1 Shmuel] [1]:[27] I prayed that Yahweh would give me a son, and he did, and this is him.
[1 Shmuel] [1]:[28] Also, I dedicated him to Yahweh all his life, so he’s now given to Yahweh.” Then they worshipped Yahweh there.
[1 Shmuel] [2]:[1] Then Hannah prayed, saying, “I’m so happy with Yahweh. My strength comes from Yahweh. I can loudly refute my enemies. Because I’m so pleased that you rescued me.
[1 Shmuel] [2]:[2] No one else is holy like Yahweh. There’s certainly no one else who’s like you. No one else is like a rock to me like our god is.
[1 Shmuel] [2]:[3] You all shouldn’t speak so proudly. Don’t let arrogance come out of your mouths. Because Yahweh is a god of knowledge, and all actions are weighed by him.
[1 Shmuel] [2]:[4] Warriors have their bows shattered, but those who stumbled are given extra strength.
[1 Shmuel] [2]:[5] Those who had been satisfied now hire themselves out for food, but the hungry people no longer lack. The woman who’d been childless, gives birth to seven, but the woman with many sons is depressed.
[1 Shmuel] [2]:[6] Yahweh puts to death and he makes alive. He sends down to the grave and brings up.
[1 Shmuel] [2]:[7] Yahweh makes poor and makes rich. He humbles, and he also honours.
[1 Shmuel] [2]:[8] He lifts the poor up from the dust, and lifts up the needy from the ash heap so they can sit with influential people and be given the seat of honour. The earth’s foundations belong to Yahweh— he was the one who placed the world on top of them.
[1 Shmuel] [2]:[9] He watches over those who are loyal to him, but wicked people will die in the darkness, because we don’t succeed through our own strength.
[1 Shmuel] [2]:[10] It’s Yahweh who shatters our enemies. He thunders against them from the heavens. Yahweh will judge the entire earth, and will give strength to the king, and will give victory to his chosen one.”
[1 Shmuel] [2]:[11] Then Elkanah and his family returned to their home in Ramah, but young Shmuel (Samuel) stayed to help Eli the priest serve Yahweh.
[1 Shmuel] [2]:[12] Now Eli’s sons were worthless scoundrels who didn’t obey Yahweh.
[1 Shmuel] [2]:[13] It was the custom of those priests that when anyone was offering a sacrifice and as soon as the meat was boiling, the priest’s servant would come along holding a three-pronged fork
[1 Shmuel] [2]:[14] and stick it into the pot or pan. The priest would then claim whatever the fork brought up. That’s what they did to all the Israelis who came to Shiloh to offer sacrifices.
[1 Shmuel] [2]:[15] Also, before the fat was removed to burn, the priest’s servant would say to the person sacrificing, “Give some meat to the priest—he doesn’t want just boiled meat all the time—he’ll take some raw meat as well to roast.”
[1 Shmuel] [2]:[16] But if the person tried to say, “Once the fat has all been burnt, then take whatever you want for yourself,” then he’d assert, “No, you’d better give it right now or I’ll take it by force.”
[1 Shmuel] [2]:[17] And so the actions of those young men were very wicked in Yahweh’s mind because they just treated sacrifices to Yahweh with contempt.
[1 Shmuel] [2]:[18] By now Shmuel (Samuel) was serving Yahweh, dressed in a priestly uniform made from linen.
[1 Shmuel] [2]:[19] Each year his mother would make a small robe for him and bring it when she came with her husband to offer their sacrifices.
[1 Shmuel] [2]:[20] Eli would bless Elkanah and his wife and say, “May Yahweh give more children for you through this woman in place of the boy dedicated to Yahweh.” Then they’d return home.
[1 Shmuel] [2]:[21] So Yahweh visited Hannah and she went on to give birth to three other sons and two daughters. Meanwhile, young Shmuel grew up serving Yahweh.
[1 Shmuel] [2]:[22] Now Eli was very old and he had heard all about what his sons were doing to the Israeli people, and also that they were sleeping around with the women who worked at the sacred tent entrance.
[1 Shmuel] [2]:[23] “Why are you two doing all these things that I keep hearing about—these evil things affecting all those people?” he asked them.
[1 Shmuel] [2]:[24] “No, my sons. The reports that I keep hearing Yahweh’s people passing on aren’t good!
[1 Shmuel] [2]:[25] If someone sins against a person, then God will mediate for him, but if someone sins against Yahweh, who will speak up for that person?” But they wouldn’t listen to their father’s advice because Yahweh wanted to put them to death.
[1 Shmuel] [2]:[26] Meanwhile the boy Shmuel (Samuel) was growing up, and his good behaviour pleased both Yahweh and the people.
[1 Shmuel] [2]:[27] One day one of God’s prophets came to Eli and told him, “This is what Yahweh says, ‘Didn’t I clearly reveal myself to your ancestors when they were Par’oh’s (Pharaoh) slaves in Mitsrayim (Egypt)?
[1 Shmuel] [2]:[28] And out of all the Israeli tribes, I chose your ancestor to be a priest to me, to go up on my altar, to burn incense, and to wear the sacred apron in front of me. Plus I gave your ancestors the rights to all the burnt offerings made by the Israelis.
[1 Shmuel] [2]:[29] Why do you disrespect sacrifices and offerings that I commanded the people to bring to me at my residence. And why do you honour your sons more than me by fattening yourselves from the best of every offering of my people Yisrael (Israel)?’
[1 Shmuel] [2]:[30] “Therefore, this is what Yahweh the god of Yisrael declares: ‘I indeed said your ancestors and then your descendants would serve me forever.’ But now I declare this instead: ‘This cannot continue because I will honour those who honour me, but those who despise me will be side-lined.
[1 Shmuel] [2]:[31] Listen, the time is coming when I’ll bring you and your relatives to an end—none of your men will die of old age
[1 Shmuel] [2]:[32] and you’ll see distress in my residence. I’ll do good for the rest of Yisrael, but there’ll never be another old man in your home.
[1 Shmuel] [2]:[33] I won’t finish them off near my altar. Your eyes will fail and you’ll grieve inside, but your adult sons will die.
[1 Shmuel] [2]:[34] This will be the sign: it’ll turn out that your two sons Hofni and Pinhas will both die on the same day.
[1 Shmuel] [2]:[35] Then I’ll select another man to be a faithful priest to me—he’ll follow my desires and do what’s in my mind. I’ll make him and his faithful descendants to continue and to always serve me.
[1 Shmuel] [2]:[36] Any of your descendants who remain alive will have to go to him to request food and money and beg for some priestly work to earn something to eat.’ ”
[1 Shmuel] [3]:[1] Meanwhile young Shmuel (Samuel) was serving Yahweh under Eli. In those days, Yahweh rarely spoke to the people or sent visions.
[1 Shmuel] [3]:[2] By that time, Eli’s sight was very poor—he could barely see. One night when he was sleeping in his place,
[1 Shmuel] [3]:[3] and Shmuel was lying down in Yahweh’s tent (where the box was that contained the stone slabs), but God’s lamp was still burning.
[1 Shmuel] [3]:[4] Yahweh called out to Shmuel, and he called back, “I’m here. Coming.”
[1 Shmuel] [3]:[5] Then he ran to Eli and said, “Here I am, because you called me.” “I didn’t call,” he said. “Go back and lie down.” So he went back and laid down.
[1 Shmuel] [3]:[6] Yahweh called again, “Shmuel.” Shmuel got up and went to Eli and said, “Here I am, because you called me.” “I didn’t call, my son,” he said, “Go back and lie down.”
[1 Shmuel] [3]:[7] (At this point, Shmuel didn’t really know Yahweh, because Yahweh hadn’t revealed himself to him before.)
[1 Shmuel] [3]:[8] Then Yahweh called Shmuel a third time. He got up and went to Eli and said, “Here I am, because you called me.” Then Eli realised that it was Yahweh who was calling the boy
[1 Shmuel] [3]:[9] and he told Shmuel, “Go and lie down. Then if he calls to you again, just answer, ‘Speak, Yahweh, because your servant is listening.’ ” So Shmuel went and laid down again in his place.
[1 Shmuel] [3]:[10] Then Yahweh came and stood nearby and called like he’d done the other times, “Shmuel, Shmuel.” “Speak,” Shmuel said, “because your servant is listening.”
[1 Shmuel] [3]:[11] “Listen,” Yahweh told him, “I’m about to do something in Yisrael (Israel) that will make everyone’s ears tingle when they hear it.
[1 Shmuel] [3]:[12] When it happens, I’ll do everything that I’ve said about Eli and his family, from the beginning to the end.
[1 Shmuel] [3]:[13] I’ve told him already that I’m about to eternally judge his household because he knew about the evil that was being done, because his sons were bringing curses on themselves and he didn’t scold them.
[1 Shmuel] [3]:[14] That’s why I’ve promised Eli’s family that their disobedience can never be forgiven by means of sacrifices or offerings.
[1 Shmuel] [3]:[15] Then Shmuel (Samuel) lay down again until the morning when he opened the doors of Yahweh’s house as usual, but he was scared to tell Eli about the vision.
[1 Shmuel] [3]:[16] But Eli called him, “Shmuel, my son.” “Here I am,” he answered.
[1 Shmuel] [3]:[17] “What did he tell you?” Eli asked. “Don’t hide it from me. May God punish you severely if you hide a single word from everything he told you.”
[1 Shmuel] [3]:[18] So Shmuel told him everything without hiding anything. Then Eli answered, “It’s Yahweh. May he do whatever he thinks best.”
[1 Shmuel] [3]:[19] As Shmuel grew up, Yahweh was with him and nothing he said failed to happen,
[1 Shmuel] [3]:[20] so all Yisrael (Israel) from Dan in the north and as far as Be’er-Sheva (Beersheba) in the south knew that Shmuel was a faithful prophet of Yahweh.
[1 Shmuel] [3]:[21] Over time, Yahweh continued to appear in Shiloh and to reveal his plans through Shmuel
[1 Shmuel] [4]:[1] and Shmuel’s messages went to all Yisrael. At that time, Yisrael (Israel) went to war against the Pelishtim. They camped at Even-Ha’ezer (Ebenezer), and the Pelishtim camped at Afek.
[1 Shmuel] [4]:[2] Then the Pelishtim lined up to meet Yisrael and the battle spread. Yisrael was defeated by the Pelishtim and they killed about 4,000 warriors in the battle line in the countryside.
[1 Shmuel] [4]:[3] As the people came into the camp, the Israeli elders asked themselves, “Why did Yahweh allow the Pelishtim to slaughter us today? Let’s get the box from Shiloh that contains the stone slabs with Yahweh’s agreement on them. Once it’s amongst us, surely it’ll save us from defeat by our enemies.”
[1 Shmuel] [4]:[4] So the people sent men to Shiloh and from there they lifted the box containing Yahweh’s agreement and the sacred platform with the winged creatures. Eli’s two sons, Hofni and Pinhas, were there with the box containing God’s agreement.
[1 Shmuel] [4]:[5] As the box with Yahweh’s agreement was carried into the camp, all the Israelis shouted so loud that the ground shook.
[1 Shmuel] [4]:[6] When the Pelishtim heard the noise, they said, “What’s that loud shout in the Ivrim’ (Hebrews) camp?” Then they realised that the box with Yahweh’s covenant had come into their camp
[1 Shmuel] [4]:[7] and they were afraid saying, “A god has come into the Israeli camp.” Then they said, “This means trouble, because it wasn’t like this yesterday or the previous days.
[1 Shmuel] [4]:[8] Oh dear! Who will rescue us from these mighty gods? Those are the gods who struck the Mitsrim (Egyptians) with every plague in the wilderness.
[1 Shmuel] [4]:[9] Now we Pelishtim really need to fight with passion, because if we don’t, we’ll ending up serving the Ivrim just like they’ve had to serve us. Now, gather your courage and fight for your lives.”
[1 Shmuel] [4]:[10] So the Pelishtim fought hard, and Yisrael (Israel) was defeated. Many warriors fled back to their tents and it was a terrible slaughter—30,000 foot soldiers from Yisrael were killed.
[1 Shmuel] [4]:[11] As well as that, the box with God’s agreement was taken, and Eli’s two sons Hofni and Pinhas were killed.
[1 Shmuel] [4]:[12] A Benyamite man ran from the battle line back to Shiloh that day. His clothes were torn and he was covered in dirt.
[1 Shmuel] [4]:[13] When he arrived there, Eli was sitting on a roadside seat watching, because he was very concerned about the sacred chest. As the man entered the city with the news, all the people started wailing loudly.
[1 Shmuel] [4]:[14] As Eli heard the wailing, he asked, “What’s that big commotion?” So the man ran over to Eli to tell him the news.
[1 Shmuel] [4]:[15] At that time, Eli was ninety-eight years old, and he stared straight ahead because he couldn’t see.
[1 Shmuel] [4]:[16] The man told him, “I’m the one who’s just come from the battle line. I had to fled from the battle line today.” “What was the issue, my son?” Eli asked.
[1 Shmuel] [4]:[17] “Yisrael (Israel) fled defeated from the Pelishtim,” said the messenger. “And also, there has been a terrible slaughter of our people. What’s more, your two sons, Hofni and Pinhas, were killed, and the sacred chest has been captured.”
[1 Shmuel] [4]:[18] The moment he mentioned the capturing of God’s box, Eli fell backwards off the seat beside the city gate. Because he was old and very heavy, his neck broke and he died. Eli had led Yisrael for forty years.
[1 Shmuel] [4]:[19] Now Pinhas’ wife (Eli’s daughter-in-law) was pregnant—about to give birth—when she heard the news about the sacred chest being taken, and that both her father-in-law and her husband had died. At that moment, she knelt down and gave birth because the birth pains suddenly started.
[1 Shmuel] [4]:[20] But she was dying, and the women who stood over her said, “Don’t be afraid, because you’ve given birth to a son.” But she didn’t answer or pay any attention.
[1 Shmuel] [4]:[21] She named the boy ‘I-Kavod’ (which means ‘no glory’), saying, “The glory has departed from Yisrael (Israel),” about the sacred chest being taken, and about the deaths of her father-in-law and her husband.
[1 Shmuel] [4]:[22] Then she said, “The glory has departed from Yisrael, because the sacred chest has been taken.”
[1 Shmuel] [5]:[1] Now the Pelishtim had taken the sacred chest, and they took it from Even-Ha’ezer (Ebenezer) to Ashdod
[1 Shmuel] [5]:[2] where they carried it into the temple of their god Dagon and placed it beside a statue of Dagon.
[1 Shmuel] [5]:[3] Early the next day when the Ashdodim got up, to their horror Dagon had fallen to the ground on its face in front of Yahweh’s box. So they stood it up and returned it to its place.
[1 Shmuel] [5]:[4] But then the next morning, more shock: Dagon had fallen to the ground on its face in front of Yahweh’s box but now its hands and head were cut off, and were lying on the threshold. Only its body remained intact.
[1 Shmuel] [5]:[5] (Because of that, until this day Dagon’s priests and everyone who enters Dagon’s temple in Ashdod won’t tread on the threshold.)
[1 Shmuel] [5]:[6] Yahweh caused a lot of trouble for the people of Ashdod and he terrified them. He caused them and the people in the region to get lumpy growths on their skin.
[1 Shmuel] [5]:[7] When the leaders in Ashdod saw what was happening, they said, “The god of Yisrael’s (Israel) box mustn’t stay with us because he’s punishing both us and our god Dagon.”
[1 Shmuel] [5]:[8] So they sent for all the Pelishti rulers, and when they’d assembled they asked, “What should we do with the god of Yisrael’s box?” “Let the god of Yisrael’s box be taken around to Gat,” they decided. So they moved it there.
[1 Shmuel] [5]:[9] After it arrived, Yahweh started punishing Gat and both young and old men in the city started getting growths on their skin, and it caused a huge panic.
[1 Shmuel] [5]:[10] So they sent God’s box to Ekron, but as soon as it entered the city, the Ekronim cried out, “Hey! They’ve brought the god of Yisrael’s box here to kill us and our people.”
[1 Shmuel] [5]:[11] So they sent for the Pelishti rulers, and when they’d assembled they said, “Send the god of Yisrael’s box away. Send it back to its place so it won’t cause us and our people to die.” Because there was a deadly panic all over the city as God’s punishment there was severe
[1 Shmuel] [5]:[12] and the men who didn’t die suffered with the growths. So the people’s cry went up to the heavens.
[1 Shmuel] [6]:[1] So it was that Yahweh’s box was held in Pelishti territory for seven months,
[1 Shmuel] [6]:[2] then the Pelishtim called their priests and diviners and asked, “What should we do with Yahweh’s box? Show us how we can get it back away to its place.”
[1 Shmuel] [6]:[3] “If you’re going to send the god of Yisrael’s (Israel) box back,” they responded, “don’t send it back by itself, but definitely return it to him with a guilt offering. Then you’ll all be healed, and you’ll all understand why you’ve been suffering.”
[1 Shmuel] [6]:[4] “What guilt offering should we send with it?” they asked. “Five gold replicas of the tumours, and five gold mice,” they said. “That’s the number of our rulers, because the same plague affected both them and the people.
[1 Shmuel] [6]:[5] Make replicas of the tumours and replicas of the mice that have been destroying the land, and it will honour Yisrael’s god. Then perhaps he will less his punishment that’s been on you and on your gods and on your land.
[1 Shmuel] [6]:[6] Why have you all been so stubborn just like the Mitsrim (Egyptians) when Par’oh (Pharaoh) made them stubborn? When Yisrael’s god dealt severely with them, didn’t the Mitsrim send the Israelis away and they went?
[1 Shmuel] [6]:[7] So now, get a brand new cart with two nursing cows which have never had a yoke on their necks. Hitch the cows to the cart but take their calves back to their pen.
[1 Shmuel] [6]:[8] Then pick up Yahweh’s box and put it into the cart along with the gold objects that you are sending with it as a guilt offering put in another container beside the box. Finally, send the cart away and off it will go.
[1 Shmuel] [6]:[9] Then watch it. If it heads towards Beyt-Shemesh (Heliopolis) in Israeli territory, then it’s their god that caused this terrible calamity. But if not, then we’ll know that it wasn’t the Israeli god, and that it all happened to us by chance.”
[1 Shmuel] [6]:[10] So they followed those instructions: they took two cows that had been feeding calves and hitched them to the new cart, but they shut their calves away in the stall.
[1 Shmuel] [6]:[11] Then they put Yahweh’s box into the cart with the other container with the gold mice and the replicas of their tumours.
[1 Shmuel] [6]:[12] Amazingly, the cows went straight down the road going to Beyt-Shemesh. They stayed on that one highway, walking and mooing, and they never once deviated to the left or the right, and the Pelishti rulers followed them as far as the border of Beyt-Shemesh.
[1 Shmuel] [6]:[13] Meanwhile in Beyt-Shemesh, the people were harvesting wheat in the valley, and when they looked up and saw the box, they were very happy.
[1 Shmuel] [6]:[14] The cart came into the field belonging to Yehoshua (Joshua) and then the cows just stood there. There was a large stone there, and the people split the sides of the wooden cart into pieces to start a fire, then offered the cows as a burnt sacrifice to Yahweh.
[1 Shmuel] [6]:[15] Then the Levites lifted down Yahweh’s box and the other container that was with it with the gold objects in it, and they placed them on the large stone. Then the men of Beyt-Shemesh offered up more burnt offerings and sacrificed sacrifices to Yahweh on that day.
[1 Shmuel] [6]:[16] The five Pelishti rulers watched all this from a distance before returning to Ekron that same day.
[1 Shmuel] [6]:[17] The gold replicas of tumours that the Pelishtim sent back as a guilt offering to Yahweh were for the five cities: Ashdod, Azah (Gaza), Ashkelon, Gat, and Ekron.
[1 Shmuel] [6]:[18] And the gold mice were from the number of all the Pelishti cities under the five rulers, including fortified cities as well as the villages in the open country, and as far as the large stone that they sat Yahweh’s box on. (It’s still in Yehoshua’s (Joshua) field in Beyt-Shemesh (Heliopolis) until this day.)
[1 Shmuel] [6]:[19] But some Beyt-Shemesh men looked into Yahweh’s box, and he killed seventy of them. The people mourned because Yahweh had caused such devastation among the people.
[1 Shmuel] [6]:[20] The Beyt-Shemesh (Heliopolis) men said, “Who can stand in front of the face of Yahweh, this holy God? And where should we send the box to from here?”
[1 Shmuel] [6]:[21] So they sent messengers to those living in Kiryat-Yearim, saying, “The Pelishtim have returned Yahweh’s box. Come over here and get it.”
[1 Shmuel] [7]:[1] So the men from Kiryat-Yearim came and lifted up Yahweh’s box and brought it into Avinadav’s house on the hill. They consecrated his son Eleazar to take care of it.
[1 Shmuel] [7]:[2] The sacred chest ended up staying in Kiryat-Yearim for twenty years but the Israelis longed sadly for Yahweh.
[1 Shmuel] [7]:[3] Then Shmuel (Samuel) told all the Israelis, “If you all really want to return to Yahweh, remove the foreign gods and the Ashtarot from among you. Then decide firmly to serve Yahweh and no other, then he’ll rescue you from the Pelishtim’ oppression.”
[1 Shmuel] [7]:[4] So the Israelis removed the Ba’al and Ashtoret idols, and began to serve Yahweh only.
[1 Shmuel] [7]:[5] Then Shmuel called, “Gather all Yisrael (Israel) to Mitspah, and I’ll pray to Yahweh for you all.”
[1 Shmuel] [7]:[6] So they gathered at Mitspah, and drew water and poured it out in front of Yahweh, and they fasted on that day and said there, “We have sinned against Yahweh.” And Shmuel guided the Israelis at Mitspah.
[1 Shmuel] [7]:[7] When the Pelishtim heard that the Israelis had gathered at Mitspah, the Pelishti rulers decided to attack Yisrael. When the Israelis heard that, they were afraid of the Pelishtim
[1 Shmuel] [7]:[8] and begged Shmuel, “Don’t stop crying out to our god Yahweh, so that he’ll rescue us from the Pelishtim.”
[1 Shmuel] [7]:[9] So Shmuel got a young lamb and offered it up—a whole burnt up offering to Yahweh. And he cried out to Yahweh for Yisrael, and Yahweh answered him.
[1 Shmuel] [7]:[10] While Shmuel was offering up that burnt offering, the Pelishtim approached to battle against Yisrael. But that day Yahweh made an intense sound like thunder that confused the Pelishtim and the Israelis were able to defeat them.
[1 Shmuel] [7]:[11] The Israeli men ran out from Mitspah and chased the Pelishtim—killing them all the way to Beyt-Kar.
[1 Shmuel] [7]:[12] Shmuel took a single rock and stood it between Mitspah and Shen. He named it ‘Even-Ha’ezer’ (Ebenezer) (which means ‘stone of help’), saying, “Yahweh helped us all the way up to here.”
[1 Shmuel] [7]:[13] So the Pelishtim ended up being subdued and didn’t invade Yisrael’s border again, and Yahweh worked against the Pelishtim as long as Shmuel lived.
[1 Shmuel] [7]:[14] The cities that the Pelishtim had taken from Ekron and as far as Gat were returned to Yisrael. And so Yisrael rescued their territory from the Pelishtim, and there was peace between Yisrael and the Amorim.
[1 Shmuel] [7]:[15] So Shmuel guided Yisrael while he lived.
[1 Shmuel] [7]:[16] Every year he did the circuit around Beyt-El (Bethel), Gilgal, and Mitspah, and he helped settled disputes for the people in all those places,
[1 Shmuel] [7]:[17] but he always returned to Ramah because his home was there. He would judge disputes there, and built an altar to Yahweh there.
[1 Shmuel] [8]:[1] As Shmuel (Samuel) grew older, he appointed his two sons as judges over Yisrael (Israel).
[1 Shmuel] [8]:[2] The eldest was Yoel (Joel) and his brother was Aviyah. They were based in Be’er-Sheva (Beersheba).
[1 Shmuel] [8]:[3] However, they didn’t take after time, but rather chased dishonest gain—accepting bribes and perverting justice.
[1 Shmuel] [8]:[4] Eventually, the Israeli elders met together with Shmuel at Ramah
[1 Shmuel] [8]:[5] and requested, “Listen, you’re old now, and your sons don’t follow your example. So appoint a king for us now to lead us like all the other nations.”
[1 Shmuel] [8]:[6] But Shmuel thought that their request for a king was an evil request, so he prayed to Yahweh
[1 Shmuel] [8]:[7] who replied, “Listen to everything that the people are saying, because they’re not rejecting you, but they’re rejecting me from reigning over them.
[1 Shmuel] [8]:[8] They’re doing to you just what they’ve done to me every since I rescued them out of Mitsrayim (Egypt) and right up until today: deserting me and serving other gods.
[1 Shmuel] [8]:[9] So listen to what they’re saying now, but certainly warn them about what kings require of their subjects.”
[1 Shmuel] [8]:[10] Then Shmuel (Samuel) passed on everything that Yahweh had said to the people who were requesting a king from him,
[1 Shmuel] [8]:[11] telling them, “If you all have a king reigning over you, this is what he’ll demand: he will conscript your sons and appoint them as his cavalry or charioteers, or they’ll run as foot-soldiers in front, of his chariot.
[1 Shmuel] [8]:[12] Others he’ll appoint a commander of various units. Some will end up ploughing his fields or harvesting his crops, or manufacturing his weapons and chariots.
[1 Shmuel] [8]:[13] He’ll take your daughters to manufacture perfumes, or to be cooks and bakers.
[1 Shmuel] [8]:[14] He’ll confiscate your best fields and vineyards and olive orchards, and give to his servants to control.
[1 Shmuel] [8]:[15] Then he’ll demand a tenth of your seeds and grape harvests for his officials and his servants.
[1 Shmuel] [8]:[16] He’ll commandeer some of your best male and female servants and young men, and he’ll impound some of your donkeys, then he’ll use them all for his projects.
[1 Shmuel] [8]:[17] He’ll expect a tenth of your sheep and goats, and you yourselves will end up being his slaves.
[1 Shmuel] [8]:[18] When that all happens, you’ll all cry out in front of the king who you chose for yourselves, but Yahweh won’t be answering you at that time.”
[1 Shmuel] [8]:[19] However, the people refused to consider Shmuel’s (Samuel) advice and they argued, “No, we want a king over us
[1 Shmuel] [8]:[20] so we’ll be like all the other nations. Our king will judge us, and will lead out our warriors in battle.”
[1 Shmuel] [8]:[21] Shmuel listened to everything the people said, and passed it on to Yahweh,
[1 Shmuel] [8]:[22] and Yahweh told him, “Do what they’re asking and get them a king.” So Shmuel told the people and then sent them all back to their homes.
[1 Shmuel] [9]:[1] Now there was a Benyamite man named Kish (son of Aviel, son of Tseror, son of Bekorat, son of Afiah, the son of a Yemini man) who was strong and wealthy.
[1 Shmuel] [9]:[2] Kish had a son named Sha’ul (Saul) who was a handsome young man and good—in fact there wasn’t any Israeli man better than him, and he was head and shoulders taller than anyone else.
[1 Shmuel] [9]:[3] One time, the female donkeys of Sha’ul’s father Kish had gone missing, and Kish told his son, “Take one of the servants with you, and pack up and go and find those donkeys.”
[1 Shmuel] [9]:[4] So they passed through the Efrati hill country, then through the Shalishah region, but they didn’t find them. Then they went through the Sha’alim region, but there was nothing, so they continued on through the land of the Benyamites, but they didn’t find them.
[1 Shmuel] [9]:[5] Finally, they entered the Tsuf area, and eventually Sha’ul said to his servant, “Come on. Let’s go back home in case my father stops worrying about the donkeys and starts worrying about us.”
[1 Shmuel] [9]:[6] But he replied, “Listen, please. There’s an honoured man of God in this city. Everything he says comes true. Let’s go there now. Perhaps he’ll tell us which way we should have gone.”
[1 Shmuel] [9]:[7] “Okay, then. We can go there,” Sha’ul responded, “but what can we give the man? We don’t have any more food in our bags, and we never brought along a gift. What else do we have?”
[1 Shmuel] [9]:[8] “Look,” answered the servant, “I’ve got a small silver coin. We can give that to the man and he’ll tell us where to go.”
[1 Shmuel] [9]:[9] (In Yisrael (Israel) before then, when people wanted an answer from God, they’d say, “Come and let us go to the ‘seer’,” because the prophet of today was called the ‘seer’ before.)
[1 Shmuel] [9]:[10] “Good idea,” Sha’ul told his servant. “Let’s go then.” So they went to the city there where the man of God was.
[1 Shmuel] [9]:[11] They were climbing up the rise towards the city when they met some young women going out to draw water, and they asked them, “Is the seer in town?”
[1 Shmuel] [9]:[12] “Yes he is,” they answered. “Hurry though, because he’s come to the city today to offer the sacrifice for the people at the high place.
[1 Shmuel] [9]:[13] You’ll find him as soon as you enter the city, before he goes up to the high place to eat. The people won’t eat until he gets there, because he himself will bless the sacrifice. Afterwards, those who’ve been invited will eat together there. So go up there now and you’ll soon find him.”
[1 Shmuel] [9]:[14] So they went on up into the city, and as they were entering, wow, there was Shmuel (Samuel) coming out towards them to go up to the high place.
[1 Shmuel] [9]:[15] On the previous day, Yahweh had quietly told Shmuel,
[1 Shmuel] [9]:[16] “About this time tomorrow, I’ll send a Benyamite man to you, and you should anoint him to be ruler over my people Yisrael. He will rescue my people from the Pelishtim, because I’ve noticed my people because I heard their cries.”
[1 Shmuel] [9]:[17] Then Shmuel saw Sha’ul, and Yahweh told him, “Look, that’s the man that I you about. He will help control my people.”
[1 Shmuel] [9]:[18] As Sha’ul approached Shmuel right there in the middle of the city gateway, he asked, “Please tell me, where’s the seer’s house?”
[1 Shmuel] [9]:[19] “I am the seer,” Shmuel answered, “Now, Go up to the high place ahead of me, and you’ll eat with me today. In the morning, I’ll tell you what you want to know, then I’ll send you off.
[1 Shmuel] [9]:[20] As for your donkeys that were lost three days ago, don’t worry anymore about them because they’ve been found. Now, all of Yisrael is wanting your father’s household, and wanting you in particular.”
[1 Shmuel] [9]:[21] “But I’m a Benyamite,” Sha’ul responded, “That’s the smallest tribe in Yisrael, and my clan’s the lowliest of all the Benyamite clans. So why did you talk to me like that?”
[1 Shmuel] [9]:[22] Then Shmuel took Sha’ul and his servant to the room where the meal had been prepared, and he gave them a place at the head of table—even above the invited guests. (There were about thirty men.)
[1 Shmuel] [9]:[23] And Shmuel told the cook, “Give the special piece of meat that I showed you and said to keep aside.”
[1 Shmuel] [9]:[24] So the cook lifted the cooked leg and placed it in front of Sha’ul. Then Shmuel told Sha’ul, “Look, this has been reserved for you. Eat it, because it’s been kept until the appointed time when I could call these people together.” So Sha’ul (Saul) ate with Shmuel (Samuel) that day,
[1 Shmuel] [9]:[25] and then they went back from the high place down into the city, and Shmuel spoke with Sha’ul on his house roof.
[1 Shmuel] [9]:[26] They rose early the next day. At dawn, Shmuel had called to Sha’ul on the roof, saying, “Get up and I will send you off.” So Sha’ul got up, and the two of them went outside.
[1 Shmuel] [9]:[27] When they reached the edge of the city, Shmuel said to Sha’ul, “Tell your servant to go on ahead,” and so he went on ahead. “But you stand here, and I’ll give you the message from God.”
[1 Shmuel] [10]:[1] Then Shmuel took a flask of oil, and poured it on Sha’ul’s head and kissed him, and told him, “It’s Yahweh who has anointed you to be ruler over his chosen people.
[1 Shmuel] [10]:[2] After you leave me today and get back to Benyamite territory, then you’ll see two men near Rahel’s (Rachel) tomb in Tseltsah, and they’ll say to you, ‘The donkeys that you went to look for have been found. But, wow, your father has stopped worrying about the donkeys and now he’s worried about you and trying to figure out what he should do.’
[1 Shmuel] [10]:[3] Then further on from there, as you approach the oak tree at Tavor, you’ll find three men going to Beyt-El (Bethel) to worship God. One will be taking three young goats, one will be carrying three rounds loaves of bread, and one will be carrying a wine in a container.
[1 Shmuel] [10]:[4] They’ll ask about how you’re doing and give you two loaves of bread which you should accept.
[1 Shmuel] [10]:[5] After that, you’ll come to the hill of God (where there’s a camp of Pelishti warriors). When you enter the town, you’ll meet a group of prophets descending from the altar area,
[1 Shmuel] [10]:[6] and Yahweh’s spirit will rush onto you. Then you’ll join them in prophesying, and you’ll be transformed into a different person.
[1 Shmuel] [10]:[7] When this all comes true, do whatever you think is correct because God will be helping you.
[1 Shmuel] [10]:[8] Then go ahead of me to Gilgal and wait there for seven days, until I get there and tell you what to do. I’ll join you to offer burnt offerings and to sacrifice peace offerings.
[1 Shmuel] [10]:[9] Then as Sha’ul (Saul) started to leave Shmuel (Samuel), God changed his thinking. Then all Shmuel’s predictions came true that day,
[1 Shmuel] [10]:[10] so when Sha’ul and his servant came to the hill, a group of prophets met them and God’s spirit rushed onto Sha’ul and he joined them in prophesying.
[1 Shmuel] [10]:[11] Then everyone who had known Sha’ul previously heard him prophesying with the prophets, they asked each other, “What’s happened to Kish’s son? Is Sha’ul really a prophet now?”
[1 Shmuel] [10]:[12] A man from there answered, “And who is their father?” So after that it became a common saying, “Has Sha’ul also become a prophet?”
[1 Shmuel] [10]:[13] When he had finished prophesying, he ascended to the altar area.
[1 Shmuel] [10]:[14] Later, Sha’ul’s uncle asked him and his servant, “Where did you two take off to?” “To look for the donkeys,” Sha’ul replied. “But we couldn’t find them, so we went to Shmuel.”
[1 Shmuel] [10]:[15] “And what did he tell you?” the uncle asked.
[1 Shmuel] [10]:[16] “He assured us that the donkeys had been found,” Sha’ul replied. But he didn’t tell him anything that Shmuel had said about becoming king.
[1 Shmuel] [10]:[17] Then Shmuel (Samuel) summoned the people to come before Yahweh at Mitspah,
[1 Shmuel] [10]:[18] and he told them, “Yahweh, the god of Yisrael (Israel), says, ‘I myself brought Yisrael out of Mitsrayim (Egypt). I rescued you from Mitsri (Egyptian) control, and from all the kingdoms that oppressed you.’
[1 Shmuel] [10]:[19] But since then, you all have rejected your god—the one who saves you from all your calamities and distresses. And you’ve all said to him, ‘We’d rather have a king over us.’ So station yourselves now in front of Yahweh by your tribes and clans.”
[1 Shmuel] [10]:[20] Then Shmuel had all the Israeli tribes approach, and the tribe of Benyamin was selected.
[1 Shmuel] [10]:[21] Then he had all the Benyamite clans approach, and the Matri clan was selected. Then Kish’s son, Sha’ul (Saul) was selected and they tried to find him, but they couldn’t find him anywhere
[1 Shmuel] [10]:[22] so they asked Yahweh again, “Is that man around here anywhere?” “Look, he’s hiding among the supplies,” Yahweh replied.
[1 Shmuel] [10]:[23] So they ran and got him from there, and when he took his place among the people, he was head and shoulders taller than anyone else.
[1 Shmuel] [10]:[24] Then Shmuel announced to everyone, “Can you see the one that Yahweh has chosen? Certainly there’s no one else like him among all the people.” All the people saw that and responded, “Long live the king.”
[1 Shmuel] [10]:[25] Then Shmuel explained how the kingship would work, and wrote it in a book and placed it in front of Yahweh. Then he sent everyone home.
[1 Shmuel] [10]:[26] Shmuel also went home to Giveah, accompanied by some of the powerful warriors whose hearts God had touched.
[1 Shmuel] [10]:[27] But some worthless men asked, “How can that one save us?” and they despised Sha’ul (Saul) and didn’t bring him any gifts, but he made no comment.
[1 Shmuel] [11]:[1] About a month later, Nahash the Amoni took his men and camped around Yavesh-Gilead, and the leaders of Yavesh told him, “Make a treaty with us, and we’ll serve you.”
[1 Shmuel] [11]:[2] “Yes, I’ll make an treaty with you,” Nahash replied, “by gouging out all of your right eyes in order to shame all Yisrael (Israel).”
[1 Shmuel] [11]:[3] “Oh! Then leave us alone for seven days,” the Yavesh elders responded, “so that we can send messengers through all the territory of Yisrael. If no one will come to rescue us, then we’ll surrender to you.”
[1 Shmuel] [11]:[4] When the messengers arrived where Sha’ul (Saul) lived at Giveah and passed the news onto the people, everyone started wailing loudly.
[1 Shmuel] [11]:[5] At that time, Sha’ul was walking home behind the cattle and he asked, “What’s with all the people wailing?” Then they told him what the messengers from Yavesh had said.
[1 Shmuel] [11]:[6] God’s spirit rushed on Sha’ul as he heard the message, and he became very angry.
[1 Shmuel] [11]:[7] Then he took a pair of cattle and chopped them into pieces, and sent messengers to take them throughout Yisrael and announce, “This is what will be done to the cattle of anyone who doesn’t join Sha’ul and Shmuel (Samuel) in battle.” Then Yahweh caused the people to be afraid of him, and they united together.
[1 Shmuel] [11]:[8] When Sha’ul assembled them at Bezek, there were three hundred thousand warriors from Yisrael and thirty thousand from Yehudah (Judah),
[1 Shmuel] [11]:[9] and they told the original messengers, “Go and tell the leaders of Yavesh-Gilead, ‘Tomorrow you’ll all be rescued by the time that the sun’s at its hottest.’ ”
[1 Shmuel] [11]:[10] So the Yavesh leaders told Nahash, “We’ll surrender to you all tomorrow, then you can do to us whatever seems good to you all.”
[1 Shmuel] [11]:[11] The next day, Sha’ul divided his warriors into three divisions, and they attacked the Amoni camp before the sun rose. Then they slaughtered the Amonim until the hottest part of the day. Their remaining warriors were scattered so completely that no two of them were able to stay together.
[1 Shmuel] [11]:[12] Then the people asked Shmuel (Samuel), “Who were the ones saying that Sha’ul (Saul) wasn’t fit to reign over us? Bring them here and we’ll execute them.”
[1 Shmuel] [11]:[13] “No one’s going to be executed today,” Sha’ul said, “because today Yahweh has rescued Yisrael (Israel).”
[1 Shmuel] [11]:[14] “Come on then,” said Shmuel. “Let’s go to Gilgal and renew the kingship there.”
[1 Shmuel] [11]:[15] So all the people when to Gilgal and in front of Yahweh they reaffirmed Sha’ul as king. Then they offered sacrifices as peace offerings to Yahweh, then Sha’ul and the people celebrated together.
[1 Shmuel] [12]:[1] Then Shmuel (Samuel) said to all Yisrael (Israel), “Listen to me now. I’ve listened to your voices and taken notice of everything that you all said to me. And I’ve appointed a king to reign over you all.
[1 Shmuel] [12]:[2] So look now and you can see your king walking here in front of you all. But as for me, I’m old and grey, and my sons are among you all. I’ve served you all openly from my youth right up to the present time,
[1 Shmuel] [12]:[3] and here I am now. Now with Yahweh listening, answer this truthfully: Have I ever taken anyone’s ox or donkey? Did I cheat anyone? Have I oppressed anyone or taken a bribe to not see something? I’ll pay back anything I owe anyone.”
[1 Shmuel] [12]:[4] “No, you haven’t cheated us,” they answered. “And you haven’t oppressed us or taken any payments.”
[1 Shmuel] [12]:[5] “Yahweh is a your witness,” he said. “And his anointed king is a witness today, that you have never found me taking anything that wasn’t mine.” “We witness that,” they agreed.
[1 Shmuel] [12]:[6] “It was Yahweh who appointed Mosheh (Moses) and Aharon (Aaron),” Shmuel continued, “and who brought your ancestors out of Mitsrayim (Egypt).
[1 Shmuel] [12]:[7] Now present yourselves to Yahweh as I confront you all in front of him by telling you about his righteousness that he displayed to you all as well as to your ancestors before you:
[1 Shmuel] [12]:[8] After Ya’akov (Jacob) went to Mitsrayim and your ancestors cried out to Yahweh, then Yahweh sent Mosheh and Aharon, and they brought your ancestors out of Mitsrayim and settled them into this place.
[1 Shmuel] [12]:[9] Then they forgot their god Yahweh, and he allowed them to be oppressed by Sisera (the commander of the army from Hatsor), and the Pelishtim, and the king of Moav (Moab). Then they fought against them
[1 Shmuel] [12]:[10] and cried out to Yahweh, ‘We have sinned, because we’ve abandoned Yahweh and have served the Baals and the Ashtarot. But if you rescue us now from our enemies, we will serve you.’
[1 Shmuel] [12]:[11] Then Yahweh sent Gid’on, Bedan, Yiftah (Jephthah), and Shimshon (Samson) to rescue you all from your enemies all around you, and so you all have had times of living securely.
[1 Shmuel] [12]:[12] But then you all saw Amoni King Nahash coming against you, and you demanded that you all wanted a king to reign over you rather than having your god Yahweh as your king.
[1 Shmuel] [12]:[13] So now, look, here’s the king that you all chose to have. Yes,, Yahweh has given you all a king.
[1 Shmuel] [12]:[14] If you all honour Yahweh and listen to his instructions and don’t rebel against his commands, then both you and your king will indeed be following your god Yahweh.
[1 Shmuel] [12]:[15] But if you all don’t listen to Yahweh, and you rebel against his commands, then he will work against you all just like he worked against your ancestors.
[1 Shmuel] [12]:[16] So now stay there and you’ll all see the incredible sign that Yahweh is about to do in front of you.
[1 Shmuel] [12]:[17] Now, isn’t it the time of the wheat harvest right now? I’ll call to Yahweh, and he’ll send unseasonal thunder and rain, and then you’ll all see and realise that in Yahweh’s view, asking for a king was very evil.”
[1 Shmuel] [12]:[18] So Shmuel (Samuel) called to Yahweh and he sent thunder and rain that day, and all the people became very afraid of Yahweh and Shmuel
[1 Shmuel] [12]:[19] and begged Shmuel, “Pray to your god Yahweh for your servants, so that we won’t die, because we’ve added more evil onto all our previous sins by requesting a king for ourselves.”
[1 Shmuel] [12]:[20] “Don’t be afraid,” Shmuel responded. “You yourselves have indeed done all this evil. However, don’t make it worse by turning away from Yahweh, but rather, serve him with all your being.
[1 Shmuel] [12]:[21] And don’t turn away from Yahweh and worship useless idols because they can’t benefit you or rescue you, because they’re empty of life.
[1 Shmuel] [12]:[22] Yahweh won’t abandon his people because he has an excellent reputation to uphold, especially since he’s declared you all to be his people.
[1 Shmuel] [12]:[23] Also, far be it from me to sin against Yahweh by not praying for you all, as well as instructing you all in the good and proper way.
[1 Shmuel] [12]:[24] Just honour Yahweh and serve him faithfully and sincerely—always remembering the incredible things he’s done for you all.
[1 Shmuel] [12]:[25] But if you all continue to do evil, both you and your king will get swept away.”
[1 Shmuel] [13]:[1] Sha’ul (Saul) was thirty years old when he began to reign over Yisrael (Israel), and when he’d reigned for two years,
[1 Shmuel] [13]:[2] he chose three thousand Israeli warriors for himself: two thousand were stationed with him in Mikmas, and one thousand were with his son Yonatan (Jonathan) in Benyamite Giveah. All the others, he sent back to their homes.
[1 Shmuel] [13]:[3] Then Yonatan attacked and defeated the Pelishti unit that was at Geva, and the Pelishtim heard about it. So Sha’ul had a trumpet blown throughout the country, with the message, “Listen all you Ivrim (Hebrews).”
[1 Shmuel] [13]:[4] All of Yisrael heard the news that Sha’ul had wiped out a Pelishti outpost, and realised that Yisrael had become repulsive to the Pelishtim. So the people were summoned to join Sha’ul at Gilgal.
[1 Shmuel] [13]:[5] The Pelishtim assembled themselves to fight Yisrael with thirty thousand chariots, six thousand mounted cavalry, and warriors as numerous as the sand on the beach. They went to Mikmas and camped there, east of Beyt-Aven.
[1 Shmuel] [13]:[6] But the Israeli warriors were very anxious because their troops were so outnumbered, so they hid in caves and thickets, among rocks, and in tombs and wells.
[1 Shmuel] [13]:[7] Some of them crossed the Yarden (Jordan) River to the Gad and Gilead regions. Sha’ul stayed at Gilgal, but the people with him were trembling.
[1 Shmuel] [13]:[8] He waited seven days until the time when Shmuel (Samuel) had said that he’d get there, but he didn’t appear so Sha’ul’s men began to desert him.
[1 Shmuel] [13]:[9] “Bring me the burnt offering and the peace offerings,” Sha’ul commanded, then he offered up the burnt offering.
[1 Shmuel] [13]:[10] Just as he’d finished, wow, Shmuel arrived at last, and Sha’ul went over to greet him.
[1 Shmuel] [13]:[11] “What have you done?” Shmuel asked. “When I saw the people leaving me,” Sha’ul replied “and you, you didn’t get here when you said you would, and the Pelishtim were gathering at Mikmas,
[1 Shmuel] [13]:[12] then I thought, ‘The Pelishtim are about to attack us at Gilgal, and I haven’t offered any gift to Yahweh.’ So I forced myself, and offered up the burnt up offering.”
[1 Shmuel] [13]:[13] “That was stupid of you,” Shmuel responded. “You haven’t obeyed what your god Yahweh instructed, because if you had, then Yahweh would have established your reign over Yisrael (Israel) forever.
[1 Shmuel] [13]:[14] But now your kingdom won’t survive. Yahweh has found a man who’s loyal to him and he’s commanded that man to lead his people, because you haven’t obeyed him.
[1 Shmuel] [13]:[15] Then Shmuel left Gilgal and went to Giveah in Benyamite territory. Meanwhile, Sha’ul counted up the warriors with him—around six hundred of them.
[1 Shmuel] [13]:[16] Sha’ul and his son Yonatan (Jonathan) and the people with them, were staying in Geva, whereas the Pelishtim were camped at Mikmas,
[1 Shmuel] [13]:[17] and they sent out three raiding parties—one went north to Ofrah in the Shual region,
[1 Shmuel] [13]:[18] one went west to Beyt-Horon, and one went towards the wilderness where the border overlooks the Tsevoeim valley.
[1 Shmuel] [13]:[19] At that time, there were no blacksmiths in Yisrael (Israel) because the Pelishtim didn’t want the Israelis to be able to make swords or spears,
[1 Shmuel] [13]:[20] so all the Israelis had to go to the Pelishtim to get their axes and plough blades, etc., sharpened.
[1 Shmuel] [13]:[21] (They were charged two-thirds of a shekel for larger things like plough blades, and one-third for picks and axes, and for straightening ox goads.)
[1 Shmuel] [13]:[22] So on the day of battle, Sha’ul and his son Yonatan had a sword and spear each, but none of their warriors had any.
[1 Shmuel] [13]:[23] Now one Pelishti unit had been sent out to guard the pass at Mikmas.
[1 Shmuel] [14]:[1] Then one day, Sha’ul’s (Saul) son Yonatan (Jonathan) said to the young man who carried his equipment, “Come on, let’s cross over to the Pelishti unit that’s over on the opposite side.” But he didn’t tell his father.
[1 Shmuel] [14]:[2] Meanwhile, Sha’ul was still waiting under the pomegranate tree in Migron on the outskirts of Geva with around six-hundred warriors.
[1 Shmuel] [14]:[3] Ahiyah the priest was also there wearing a sacred apron. (He was son of Ahituv the brother of I-Kavod, son of Pinhas, son of Eli, Yahweh’s priest at Shiloh.) But the people didn’t know that Yonatan had gone.
[1 Shmuel] [14]:[4] Meanwhile, for Yonatan to get to the Pelishti garrison, they had to go through a narrow pass between two cliffs. (The cliff on one side was named Botsets, and the other was named Seneh.
[1 Shmuel] [14]:[5] One cliff faced north toward Mikmas, and the other side faced south toward Geva.)
[1 Shmuel] [14]:[6] Yonatan said to his servant carrying his equipment, “Come on. Let’s pass over to that group of these uncircumcised ones. Perhaps Yahweh will help us, because it doesn’t matter to him whether he saves using many people or just a few.”
[1 Shmuel] [14]:[7] “Do everything that you feel is right,” he responded. “Go on ahead and be confident that I’ll be there supporting you.”
[1 Shmuel] [14]:[8] “Now listen,” Yonatan said. “We’ll cross over and then reveal ourselves to them.
[1 Shmuel] [14]:[9] Then if they tell us, ‘Stay there until we get down to you,’ then we’ll stay where we are and not go up to them.
[1 Shmuel] [14]:[10] But if they say, ‘Come on up to us,’ then we’ll go up, because that’ll be the sign to us that Yahweh will help us overpower them.”
[1 Shmuel] [14]:[11] So the two of them revealed themselves to the Pelishti unit, and the soldiers said, “Hey, look! The Ivrim (Hebrews) are coming out from the holes there where they’ve hidden themselves.”
[1 Shmuel] [14]:[12] Then some of the men called to Yonatan and his servant, “Come on up here to us and we’ll teach you a thing or two.” “Come on up behind me,” Yonatan told his servant, “because Yahweh has already declared Yisrael (Israel) to be the victor.”
[1 Shmuel] [14]:[13] So Yonatan climbed up on his hands and feet, with his servant following behind him. Then at the top, Yonatan struck them down with his sword while his servant followed behind and killed them.
[1 Shmuel] [14]:[14] In that first offensive, Yonatan and his servant killed about twenty men in an area of around 30m square.
[1 Shmuel] [14]:[15] At that time, Pelishtim in the camp started getting the jitters, then all the people, and even raiding parties. Then the ground shook, and it turned into a god-given panic.
[1 Shmuel] [14]:[16] Sha’ul’s (Saul) lookouts in Giveah (in Benyamite territory) saw to their surprise that their opponents were starting to scatter in every direction.
[1 Shmuel] [14]:[17] “Count our people and see who’s missing,” Sha’ul commanded, so they called the roll and wow, it was Yonatan (Jonathan) and his servant who weren’t accounted for.
[1 Shmuel] [14]:[18] “Bring the sacred chest here,” Sha’ul told Ahiyah the priest, because the Israelis had control of it again at that time.
[1 Shmuel] [14]:[19] But even as Sha’ul was speaking to him, the confusion in the Pelishti camp was continually increasing, and Sha’ul told him, “Oh, don’t worry about it.”
[1 Shmuel] [14]:[20] Then he called his warriors together and they went forward to battle. To their surprise, the Pelishtim were fighting each other in total confusion.
[1 Shmuel] [14]:[21] Now before that time, some Ivrim (Hebrews) had joined the Pelishti camp, but now they switched alliance back to Yisrael (Israel) with Sha’ul and Yonatan.
[1 Shmuel] [14]:[22] Also, there had been some Israeli deserters who’d hidden in the Efrati hill country heard that the Pelishtim were fleeing, and so they too also chased and attacked them.
[1 Shmuel] [14]:[23] So Yahweh saved Yisrael that day, and the fighting went as far as Beyt-Aven.
[1 Shmuel] [14]:[24] Now the Israeli warriors were getting exhausted that day, but Sha’ul (Saul) had made the them promise, “We need to avenge our enemies. Anyone who eats food before the evening is cursed.”
[1 Shmuel] [14]:[25] But when they reached the forest, there was honeycomb on the ground.
[1 Shmuel] [14]:[26] Although the warriors entered the forest and saw the honey, none of them tasted any because they were afraid of the curse.
[1 Shmuel] [14]:[27] But Yonatan (Jonathan) hadn’t heard his father’s oath, so he dipped his staff into the honeycomb and ate some honey and felt rejuvenated.
[1 Shmuel] [14]:[28] However, someone noticed it and mentioned, “Your father made the people promise, ‘Anyone who eats food today will be cursed.’ So the people are faint.”
[1 Shmuel] [14]:[29] “My father’s caused trouble for us,” Yonatan responded. “See how much better I feel now because I tasted a little bit of this honey.
[1 Shmuel] [14]:[30] Actually, if the troops had eaten what they’d found from the plunder of their enemies today, how much better it would have been because we might have had an even more decisive victory over the Pelishtim.”
[1 Shmuel] [14]:[31] That day they killed Pelishtim from Mikmas to Ayalon, but the fighters were totally exhausted.
[1 Shmuel] [14]:[32] They rushed greedily at the plunder, grabbing sheep, cattle, and calves which they slaughtered right there and ate with the blood still in them.
[1 Shmuel] [14]:[33] Then King Sha’ul (Saul) was told, “Look, the people are sinning against Yahweh by eating meat with the blood still in it.” “You’ve all acted treacherously,” he responded, “Now, roll a big stone over to me.”
[1 Shmuel] [14]:[34] Then he said, “Go out among the warriors and tell them to bring their animals over here to slaughter and to eat, so they don’t sin against Yahweh by eating meat with the blood still in it.” So the people brought their animals over and slaughtered them there.
[1 Shmuel] [14]:[35] Then Sha’ul built an altar to Yahweh—it was the first one he built.
[1 Shmuel] [14]:[36] Then Sha’ul said, “Let’s go after the Pelishtim tonight and plunder them until the light of morning. Let’s not leave any of them alive.” “Do what you feel is right,” they responded. But the priest said, “Let’s ask God here first.”
[1 Shmuel] [14]:[37] So Sha’ul asked God, “Should we go after the Pelishtim? Will you give Yisrael (Israel) victory over them?” But Yahweh didn’t answer him that day.
[1 Shmuel] [14]:[38] Then Sha’ul commanded, “All you leaders of the warriors. Gather here so we can find out what sin was committed today.
[1 Shmuel] [14]:[39] As Yahweh who saves Yisrael lives, even if it’s my own son Yonatan (Jonathan), whoever sinned today will certainly die.” But the people didn’t volunteer any information.
[1 Shmuel] [14]:[40] “You all can be on one side, and my son Yonatan and I will be on the other side,” Sha’ul said. “Do whatever feels right to you,” the people replied.
[1 Shmuel] [14]:[41] Then Sha’ul asked Yisrael’s god Yahweh, “Show us the truth.” And Sha’ul and Yonatan were selected—not the people.
[1 Shmuel] [14]:[42] Then Sha’ul asked again, “Choose between me and my son Yonatan.” And Yonatan was selected.
[1 Shmuel] [14]:[43] Sha’ul demanded from Yonatan, “Tell me what you’ve done.” “Actually,” Yonatan answered, “I did taste some honey from the end of my staff, so take me—I’m ready to die.”
[1 Shmuel] [14]:[44] “May God do to me whatever he wants,” Sha’ul said. “because you will certainly die, Yonatan.”
[1 Shmuel] [14]:[45] But the people stood up to Sha’ul, “Should Yonatan die? Wasn’t it him who saved Yisrael today? We won’t stand for it. As Yahweh lives, not even a hair on his head will be touched because he worked with God today.” And so the people rescued Yonatan and he wasn’t executed.
[1 Shmuel] [14]:[46] Then Sha’ul stopped chasing the Pelishtim and went home, and the Pelishtim also returned to their place.
[1 Shmuel] [14]:[47] After Sha’ul (Saul) had taken on the kingship of Yisrael (Israel), he fought against their enemies from all around: against the Moavim, the Amonim, the Edomim, the kings of Tsovah, and against the Pelishtim. Wherever he turned, he punished his enemies.
[1 Shmuel] [14]:[48] He acted bravely and defeated even the Amalekim, always rescuing Yisrael from those who came in to plunder it.
[1 Shmuel] [14]:[49] Sha’ul’s sons were Yonatan (Jonathan), Yishvi, and Malkishua. His oldest daughter was Merav, and the younger one was Mikal.
[1 Shmuel] [14]:[50] His wife’s name was Ahinoam (daughter of Ahima’ats). His army commander was Avner (son of Sha’ul’s uncle Ner—
[1 Shmuel] [14]:[51] Kish was Sha’ul’s father, and Avner’s father Ner was Aviel’s son).
[1 Shmuel] [14]:[52] The conflict with the Pelishtim was intensive for all of Sha’ul’s life, so whenever he saw a good warrior or any strong, young man, then he would conscript them.
[1 Shmuel] [15]:[1] One day Shmuel (Samuel) said to Sha’ul (Saul), “It was Yahweh who sent me to anoint you as king over his people Yisrael (Israel) back then, so now, listen to what he has to say.
[1 Shmuel] [15]:[2] Commander Yahweh says, ‘I’ve noticed what the Amalekim did to Yisrael when they came out of Mitsrayim (Egypt)—they attacked them as they passed by.
[1 Shmuel] [15]:[3] So go now and attack Amalek and destroy them completely without compassion, putting men and women, children and infants to death, along with their cattle and sheep, camels and donkeys.’ ”
[1 Shmuel] [15]:[4] So Sha’ul summoned the people to Telaim and counted them: two hundred thousand foot soldiers as well as ten thousand warriors from Yehudah (Judah).
[1 Shmuel] [15]:[5] Then Sha’ul took them to Amalek city, and they lay in wait in the valley.
[1 Shmuel] [15]:[6] Then he warned the Keynim, “You all need to move out from among the Amalekim, so that you all won’t be attacked along with them. That’s because you all were kind to our ancestors when they came out of Mitsrayim.” So the Keynim moved out from among the Amalekim.

[1 Shmuel] [15]:[8] and they captured King Agag alive but killed everyone else with swords.

[1 Shmuel] [15]:[12] Early the next morning, Shmuel got up to meet Sha’ul, but someone told him, “Sha’ul went to Karmel, and wow, he set up a monument to himself. Then he turned around and went to Gilgal.”

[1 Shmuel] [15]:[14] “Then what’s that bleating of sheep that I can hear?” asked Shmuel. “And I’m sure I can hear cattle sounds too?”
[1 Shmuel] [15]:[15] “Ah, the warriors took them from the Amalekim,” Sha’ul answered. “They wanted to save the best of the sheep and the cattle in order to sacrifice to your god Yahweh. But we completely destroyed the rest.”
[1 Shmuel] [15]:[16] “Stop,” said Shmuel, “and let me tell you what Yahweh told me last night.” “Go ahead,” Sha’ul responded.
[1 Shmuel] [15]:[17] So Shmuel told him, “Although you consider yourself insignificant, aren’t you the head of the tribes of Yisrael (Israel)? Yahweh anointed you as king over Yisrael,
[1 Shmuel] [15]:[18] then sent you off with the task of completely destroying the sinful Amalekim—fighting until they were all destroyed.
[1 Shmuel] [15]:[19] So why didn’t you obey Yahweh’s command? Instead, you headed straight for the plunder and disobeyed Yahweh.”
[1 Shmuel] [15]:[20] “I did listen to Yahweh’s instructions,” Sha’ul insisted. “and I did what he asked. So now I’ve brought Amaleki King Agag here and I’ve completely destroyed the Amalekim.
[1 Shmuel] [15]:[21] Yes, the people kept some of the best sheep and cattle to sacrifice to your god Yahweh here at Gilgal.”
[1 Shmuel] [15]:[22] But Shmuel asked, “Is Yahweh happier with burnt offerings and sacrifices than with those who follow his instructions? Listen, obedience is better than sacrifice— paying attention is worth more than the fat of rams.
[1 Shmuel] [15]:[23] Rebellion is as sinful as doing sorcery, and being stubborn is as sinful as worshipping idols. Because you have rejected Yahweh’s instructions, he has rejected you as king.”
[1 Shmuel] [15]:[24] “Yes, I’ve sinned,” Sha’ul (Saul) responded. “I can see that I’ve disobeyed Yahweh’s instruction, and yours too, because I feared the people and did what they were requesting.
[1 Shmuel] [15]:[25] But now, please forgive my sin and come back with me so I can worship Yahweh.”
[1 Shmuel] [15]:[26] “No, I won’t return with you.” Shmuel (Samuel) replied. “You’ve rejected Yahweh’s instructions, and Yahweh has already rejected you as Yisrael’s (Israel) king.”
[1 Shmuel] [15]:[27] As Shmuel turned around to go, Sha’ul grabbed the edge of his robe and it tore.
[1 Shmuel] [15]:[28] “Today, Yahweh has torn the kingdom of Yisrael away from you,” Shmuel told him. “And he’s given it to another man who’s better than you.
[1 Shmuel] [15]:[29] And by the way, Yisrael’s powerful God doesn’t go back on his word, and doesn’t change his mind like people tend to do.
[1 Shmuel] [15]:[30] “It’s true that I’ve sinned,” Sha’ul said, “but please honour me now in front of the Israeli people and their elders. And then return with me, so I can worship your god Yahweh.”
[1 Shmuel] [15]:[31] So Shmuel followed Sha’ul back, and Sha’ul worshipped Yahweh.
[1 Shmuel] [15]:[32] Then Shmuel commanded, “Bring the Amaleki King Agag over here to me.” So they brought him over, and trembling, he said, “I’ve faced up to death now.”
[1 Shmuel] [15]:[33] Then Shmuel told him, “Just as your sword has made women childless, so too will your mother be made childless among women.” And Shmuel hacked Agag to pieces in front of Yahweh there at Gilgal.
[1 Shmuel] [15]:[34] Then Shmuel went home to Ramah, and Sha’ul (Saul) returned to his house in Giveah.
[1 Shmuel] [15]:[35] After that, Shmuel never saw Sha’ul again, but he mourned for him, and Yahweh regretted that he’d made Sha’ul king over Yisrael (Israel).
[1 Shmuel] [16]:[1] Then Yahweh spoke to Shmuel (Samuel), “How long are you going to keep mourning for Sha’ul (Saul) for, when I myself have rejected him as king over Yisrael (Israel)? Fill your horn with oil and go. I’ll send you to Yishay (Jesse) from Beyt-Lehem (Bethlehem), because I’ve seen one of his sons who’d make a good king for me.”
[1 Shmuel] [16]:[2] “How can I do that?” asked Shmuel. “Sha’ul would kill me if he heard about it.” “Take a heifer with you,” Yahweh said, “and say, ‘I’ve come to sacrifice to Yahweh.’
[1 Shmuel] [16]:[3] Invite Yishay to the sacrifice, and I’ll show you what do to from there, and you should anoint the one I tell you to.”
[1 Shmuel] [16]:[4] So Shmuel did what Yahweh had told him, and went to Beyt-Lehem. The town elders trembled when they met him, and asked, “Do you come in peace?”
[1 Shmuel] [16]:[5] “Yes, in peace,” he answered “I’ve come to sacrifice to Yahweh. Purify yourselves and come with me to the sacrifice.” Then he purified Yishay and his sons and called them to the sacrifice.
[1 Shmuel] [16]:[6] When they arrived, Shmuel saw Eliav and thought, “Surely this man’s the one that Yahweh wants to anoint.”
[1 Shmuel] [16]:[7] But Yahweh told him, “Don’t look at his height or outward appearance, because I’ve rejected him. Because it isn’t what a person sees with their eyes, but Yahweh sees their motives and values.”
[1 Shmuel] [16]:[8] Then Yishay called for Avinadav to walk across in front of Shmuel, but he said again, “Yahweh hasn’t chosen that one.”
[1 Shmuel] [16]:[9] Then Yishay made Shamah walk across in front, but again he said, “Yahweh hasn’t chosen that one.”
[1 Shmuel] [16]:[10] So all up, Yishay made seven of his sons walk across in front of Shmuel, but Shmuel told him, “Yahweh hasn’t chosen any of them.”
[1 Shmuel] [16]:[11] Then Shmuel asked Yishay, “Is this all your sons?” “Well, there’s just the youngest,” he answered “but you see, he’s out looking after the flock.” “Send for him,” Shmuel instructed him, “because we won’t do anything else until he gets here.”
[1 Shmuel] [16]:[12] So he sent for him and brought him in. He was a good-looker with beautiful eyes and red colouring, and Yahweh said, “Stand up and anoint him, because he’s the one.”
[1 Shmuel] [16]:[13] So Shmuel took the horn full of olive oil and anointed him right there with his brothers, and Yahweh’s spirit rushed onto David from that day onwards. Then Shmuel left and went home to Ramah.
[1 Shmuel] [16]:[14] Meanwhile, Yahweh’s spirit left Sha’ul (Saul), and instead an evil spirit from Yahweh tormented him,
[1 Shmuel] [16]:[15] and his servants told him, “Look, an evil spirit from God is tormenting you.
[1 Shmuel] [16]:[16] Let our master please get your servants to find a man who knows how to play the harp. Then, whenever the evil spirit from God is on you, then he’ll play it and it’ll be good for you.”
[1 Shmuel] [16]:[17] “Okay,” Sha’ul responded, “Find a man for me who’s good at playing it, and bring him to me.”
[1 Shmuel] [16]:[18] Then one of his servants spoke up, “Listen, I’ve noticed one of the sons of Yishay (Jesse) in Beyt-Lehem (Bethlehem) who knows how to play. He’s also a very powerful warrior, as well as being good looking and wise in what he says. And Yahweh is with him.”
[1 Shmuel] [16]:[19] So Sha’ul sent messengers to Yishay to tell him, “Your son David who looks after your flock, send him to me.”
[1 Shmuel] [16]:[20] So Yishay loaded a donkey with bread, a skin of wine, and a young goat, and sent them to King Sha’ul with his son David.
[1 Shmuel] [16]:[21] When David got to the king, he became his servant, and he was liked so much that he was appointed as the one who carried the king’s equipment.
[1 Shmuel] [16]:[22] Sha’ul sent a message back to Yishay, saying, “Let David remain in my service, because I really like him.”
[1 Shmuel] [16]:[23] Then whenever the spirit from God tormented Sha’ul, David would take the harp and play it. That would bring relief to Sha’ul and make him feel better, and the evil spirit would leave him.
[1 Shmuel] [17]:[1] At that time, the Pelishtim gathered their army divisions together ready for battle. They assembled at Sokoh in Yehudah (Judah), and camped between Sokoh and Azekah in Efes-Damim.
[1 Shmuel] [17]:[2] Sha’ul (Saul) and the Israeli warriors gathered and camped in the Elah valley, then they arranged themselves for battle against the Pelishtim.
[1 Shmuel] [17]:[3] So the Pelishtim stood on one hill and the Israelis on the opposite hill, with the valley between them.
[1 Shmuel] [17]:[4] Then the Pelishtim sent a champion out from their camp to represent them. His name was Galyat (Goliath) and he came from Gat, and he was almost three metres tall.
