[1 Shmuel] [17]:[5] He wore a bronze helmet, and his body armour had overlapping plates weighing a total of some fifty-five kilograms.
[1 Shmuel] [17]:[6] He had bronze armour on his legs, and a bronze plate between his shoulders.
[1 Shmuel] [17]:[7] The wooden shaft of his spear was like a weaver’s beam and his spear time weighed around seven kilograms. His shield-bearer walked in front of him.
[1 Shmuel] [17]:[8] Galyat stood there and called out to the Israeli warriors, “Why have you all come out to line up for battle? Now, I’m down here as a Pelishti, and all of you are Sha’ul’s slaves, so choose a man for yourselves and let him come down here to fight me.
[1 Shmuel] [17]:[9] If he’s able to fight with me and kill me, then we’ll become your slaves. But if I’m the winner and kill him, then you’ll all become our slaves and work for us.”
[1 Shmuel] [17]:[10] Then he said, “I personally scoff at Yisrael’s (Israel) lines today. Give me a man so we can fight together.”
[1 Shmuel] [17]:[11] When Sha’ul and the Israelis heard all that, they were discouraged and very afraid.
[1 Shmuel] [17]:[12] Now David was the son of Yishay (Jesse) (from the Efrat clan, he lived in Beyt-Lehem (Bethlehem) in Yehudah (Judah)) who had eight sons, and by Sha’ul’s (Saul) time, was quite old compared to other men.
[1 Shmuel] [17]:[13] Yishay’s three oldest sons (Eliav, Avinadav, and Shamah) had gone to the battle with Sha’ul,
[1 Shmuel] [17]:[14] but David was the youngest. While the three oldest were with Sha’ul,
[1 Shmuel] [17]:[15] David went back and forth between Sha’ul’s camp and looking after his father’s flock at Beyt-Lehem.
[1 Shmuel] [17]:[16] For forty days, the Pelishti champion came out and presented himself in the early morning and again in the evening.
[1 Shmuel] [17]:[17] One day Yishay said to his son David, “Here’s a sack of roasted grain and ten loaves of bread. Take them straight away to your brothers at the camp.
[1 Shmuel] [17]:[18] And take these ten cuts of cheese to the commander of their unit. Find out how your brothers are doing and bring back anything they want to send to me.
[1 Shmuel] [17]:[19] Sha’ul and them and the other warriors are in the Elah valley, fighting against the Pelishtim.”
[1 Shmuel] [17]:[20] So David got up early in the morning and left the flock with a shepherd, and set out just like Yishay had told him to. When he got to the battleground and the camp, the warriors were just going out to the battle line and they were shouting the battle cry.
[1 Shmuel] [17]:[21] The Israelis and the Pelishtim arranged themselves—battle line to battle line.
[1 Shmuel] [17]:[22] David left what he’d brought with a guard, and ran into the battle line. Then he caught up with his brothers and asked them how they were doing.
[1 Shmuel] [17]:[23] While he was talking with them, look, the Pelishti champion from Gat was coming out with his challenge. Galyat (Goliath) spoke like he had before and David heard it all.
[1 Shmuel] [17]:[24] But when the Israelis saw the champion, they were terrified and fled away from him.
[1 Shmuel] [17]:[25] saying to each other, “Have you seen this man who’s coming out? He’s certainly coming to mock Yisrael (Israel)! Any man who can defeat him will be made very wealthy by the king, and he’ll give his daughter to him, plus his extended family will be exempt from paying taxes.”
[1 Shmuel] [17]:[26] “What was it that’ll be done for the man who kills this Pelishti and take’s Yisrael’s disgrace away?” David asked some of the men standing around him. “Because who does that uncircumcised Pelishti think he is that he would taunt the army of the living God?”
[1 Shmuel] [17]:[27] Then the men told him again what would be given to the man who defeats him.
[1 Shmuel] [17]:[28] But when David’s oldest brother Eliav heard him talking to the men, he got very angry and scolded him, “Why have you come down here? Who’s looking after those few sheep that you left in the desert? I know you have a big head and you’re just a troublemaker—you just want to watch the battle.”
[1 Shmuel] [17]:[29] “What have I done now?” David asked. “Wasn’t it just a question?”
[1 Shmuel] [17]:[30] Then he went over to another group and asked the same question and got the same answer.
[1 Shmuel] [17]:[31] So it got around what David was saying, and when Sha’ul (Saul) heard about it, he sent for him.
[1 Shmuel] [17]:[32] David told the king, “Don’t be discouraged. Your servant will go and fight against this Pelishti.”
[1 Shmuel] [17]:[33] “You can’t go against this Pelishti and fight him,” Sha’ul told David. “You’re still a lad, but he’s been a professional warrior since he was young.”
[1 Shmuel] [17]:[34] “Your servant has been working for his father tending the flock,” David replied. “Sometimes a lion or a bear has come and taken a sheep from the flock
[1 Shmuel] [17]:[35] and I would go after it and beat it and rescue the sheep from its mouth. If it went to attack me, then I’d grasp it by the jaw and beat it and kill it.
[1 Shmuel] [17]:[36] Your servant has killed both a lion and a bear, and that uncircumcised Pelishti will end up just like them, because he’s insulted the army of the living God.”
[1 Shmuel] [17]:[37] Then he added, “Yahweh who has saved me from the lion and from the bear, he will be the one to save me from that Pelishti.” “Go then, and Yahweh be with you.” Sha’ul assented.
[1 Shmuel] [17]:[38] Then Sha’ul had David dressed in his own battle attire, and then in body armour with a bronze helmet.
[1 Shmuel] [17]:[39] David strapped his sword over the top and then tried to walk because he hadn’t been trained in wearing it. But he told Sha’ul, “I couldn’t walk in all that without practice,” so he took it all off.
[1 Shmuel] [17]:[40] Then he picked up his staff, and selected five smooth stones from the riverbed. He placed them in the pouch of his shepherd’s bag, and picked up his sling and headed towards the Pelishti champion.
[1 Shmuel] [17]:[41] Then Galyat (Goliath) came closer and closer to David, with his shield-bearer walking in front of him.
[1 Shmuel] [17]:[42] When he looked and realised that David was a reddish, good-looking lad, he despised him
[1 Shmuel] [17]:[43] and asked him, “Are you coming to me with a stick because you think I’m a dog?” Then the Pelishti cursed David by his gods.
[1 Shmuel] [17]:[44] “Come over here,” he told David, “and let me give your flesh to the vultures and wild animals.”
[1 Shmuel] [17]:[45] “You’re coming to me with a sword and spear and dagger,” David shouted back. “But I’m coming to you in the name of commander Yahweh, the god of Yisrael’s (Israel) army that you’ve been taunting.
[1 Shmuel] [17]:[46] Today, Yahweh will help me defeat you and I’ll knock you down and cut off your head. What’s more, I’ll give the Pelishti army corpses to the vultures and wild animals today, then everyone will know that there’s a god in Yisrael.
[1 Shmuel] [17]:[47] Everyone here will learn that Yahweh doesn’t save with swords or spears, because he’s in charge of the battle and will help us defeat you all.”
[1 Shmuel] [17]:[48] Then as Galyat went closer to meet David, David ran quickly towards him at the battle line.
[1 Shmuel] [17]:[49] He slipped his hand into his bag and took out a single stone and slung it towards the Pelishti—striking him on the forehead. The stone sank into his forehead and he collapsed forwards onto the ground,
[1 Shmuel] [17]:[50] and so David defeated the Pelishti with a sling and a stone—knocking him down and killing him. Not having a sword with him,
[1 Shmuel] [17]:[51] David ran and stood over the Pelishti—drawing Galyat’s sword out of its sheath to kill him and cut off his head. When the Pelishtim saw that their powerful champion was dead, they fled
[1 Shmuel] [17]:[52] and the Israeli warriors started yelling and they chased the Pelishtim into the valley and as far as the gates of Ekron. The dead bodies of the Pelishtim could be seen on the road all the way from Sha’arayim to Gat and Ekron.
[1 Shmuel] [17]:[53] When the Israelis returned from chasing the Pelishtim, they raided the valuables from their camp.
[1 Shmuel] [17]:[54] David put Galyat’s equipment into his own tent, then he carried his head to Yerushalem (Jerusalem).
[1 Shmuel] [17]:[55] When Sha’ul (Saul) had seen David going out to meet Galyat (Goliath), he’d asked Avner, the army commander, “Whose son is this lad, Avner?” “As surely as you live, your majesty,” replied Avner, “I don’t know.”
[1 Shmuel] [17]:[56] “Find out whose son he is,” the king had commanded.
[1 Shmuel] [17]:[57] Then when David had returned from killing the Pelishti, Avner brought him to stand in front of Sha’ul, and he was holding Galyat’s head.
[1 Shmuel] [17]:[58] “Whose son are you, lad?” Sha’ul asked. “I’m the son of your servant Yishay (Jesse), who lives in Beyt-Lehem (Bethlehem),” replied David.
[1 Shmuel] [18]:[1] After David had finished speaking to the king, him and Yonatan (Jonathan) became close friends, in fact Yonatan really loved him.
[1 Shmuel] [18]:[2] From that day, Sha’ul (Saul) kept David with him, and wouldn’t allow him to return home.
[1 Shmuel] [18]:[3] Then Yonatan and David made an agreement together, because Yonatan loved him as much as he loved himself.
[1 Shmuel] [18]:[4] Yonatan took off the cloak that he was wearing and gave it to David, along with his armour, his sword and bow, and even his belt.
[1 Shmuel] [18]:[5] David went on missions wherever Sha’ul sent him and always succeeded. Sha’ul put him in charge of the warriors, and that pleased all the people, as well as Sha’ul’s servants.
[1 Shmuel] [18]:[6] When they’d all come back after killing the Pelishti, the women from the Israeli cities had come out to meet King Sha’ul (Saul) with singing and dancing—playing tambourines and other instruments with great happiness.
[1 Shmuel] [18]:[7] However, as they danced they sang, “Sha’ul has killed his thousands, and David his tens of thousands.”
[1 Shmuel] [18]:[8] Sha’ul found that offensive and it made him very angry. “They’ve attributed tens of thousands to David,” he complained, “but only thousands to me. Next thing he’ll end up as king.”
[1 Shmuel] [18]:[9] So from that day onwards, Sha’ul remained wary of David and kept an eye on him.
[1 Shmuel] [18]:[10] Then the next day, an evil spirit from God rushed on Sha’ul and even in the middle of the house he started prophesying. As David was playing near him (as he did every day), Sha’ul was holding a spear
[1 Shmuel] [18]:[11] and he suddenly hurled it, saying, “I’ll pin that David to the wall.” But twice when he did that, David managed to elude him.
[1 Shmuel] [18]:[12] So Sha’ul ended up afraid of David because Yahweh was with him, but was no longer with the king.
[1 Shmuel] [18]:[13] Then Sha’ul sent him out of the room and appointed him as the commander of a thousand warriors, so he came and went in front of the people.
[1 Shmuel] [18]:[14] Yahweh was with David and he was succeeding in everything he did.
[1 Shmuel] [18]:[15] Sha’ul knew about his successes and couldn’t stand looking at him,
[1 Shmuel] [18]:[16] but all the people of Yisrael (Israel) and Yehudah (Judah) loved David because they observed his comings and goings.
[1 Shmuel] [18]:[17] One day Sha’ul (Saul) told David, “Look, here’s my oldest daughter Merav—I’ll give her to you for a wife. The only condition is that you become a powerful warrior for me and fight Yahweh’s battles.” (Sha’ul had said to himself, “I don’t need to hurt him physically—I’ll let the Pelishtim do that for me.”)
[1 Shmuel] [18]:[18] “Who am I,” David asked, “and who are my relatives in my father’s clan in Yisrael (Israel), that I should become the king’s son-in-law?”
[1 Shmuel] [18]:[19] However, when it was the time for Sha’ul to give his daughter Merav to David, she was given to Adriel the Meholati to marry.
[1 Shmuel] [18]:[20] Now Sha’ul’s other daughter Mikal loved David, and when they told the king, he was pleased about it,
[1 Shmuel] [18]:[21] saying to himself, “I’ll give her to him so she can become a trap for him so the Pelishtim could be the ones to attack him.” So he said a second time, “You’ll become a son-in-law of mine today.”
[1 Shmuel] [18]:[22] Then Sha’ul commanded his servants, “Tell David privately, ‘Listen, the king is pleased with you, and all of us his servants love you. So now we think that you should become the king’s son-in-law.’ ”
[1 Shmuel] [18]:[23] So they told David privately, but he responded, “Something that significant isn’t likely to happen. I’m hard up and without much honour.”
[1 Shmuel] [18]:[24] When Sha’ul’s servants told him what David had said,
[1 Shmuel] [18]:[25] he replied, “Pass this onto David, ‘The king doesn’t want an expensive bride price—only a hundred Pelishti foreskins taken from the king’s enemies.’ ” But Sha’ul was still wanting the Pelishtim to be the ones to kill David.
[1 Shmuel] [18]:[26] Now when David heard this from the servants, he decided that he could indeed marry the king’s daughter within the time period that had been given,
[1 Shmuel] [18]:[27] so he and his men got ready and went and killed two hundred Pelishti men. He brought them to the king and had them counted to fulfill the pledge, and so Sha’ul had to give his daughter Mikal to become his wife.
[1 Shmuel] [18]:[28] But when Sha’ul realised that Yahweh was helping David, and that his daughter loved him,
[1 Shmuel] [18]:[29] he became more afraid of David, so he remained hostile to David from then on.
[1 Shmuel] [18]:[30] Whenever the Pelishti commanders decided to attack, David was more successful than any other of Sha’ul’s commanders, so he became very famous.
[1 Shmuel] [19]:[1] Then Sha’ul (Saul) urged his son Yonatan (Jonathan) and all his servants to kill David, but Yonatan really liked David
[1 Shmuel] [19]:[2] and told him, “My father Sha’ul wants to get rid of you, so please watch out in the morning. Find a hiding place and stay there.
[1 Shmuel] [19]:[3] And what I’ll do, I’ll go out and stand by my father in the countryside where you’re hiding, and I’ll bring you into the conversation to see what he’ll say about you.”
[1 Shmuel] [19]:[4] So the next morning, Yonatan spoke well of David to his father Sha’ul, saying, “Don’t let the king sin against his servant, against David, because he hasn’t sinned against you, and actually, he’s been a big help to you.
[1 Shmuel] [19]:[5] He took his life into his hands when he fought against Galyat (Goliath), and Yahweh used it to save all Yisrael (Israel). So why would you sin against innocent blood by putting David to death for no reason.”
[1 Shmuel] [19]:[6] Sha’ul listened to Yonatan, then he promised, “As surely as Yahweh lives, he won’t be put to death.”
[1 Shmuel] [19]:[7] Afterwards, Yonatan called David and told him what had been said. Then he brought David back to work for Sha’ul and things carried on as before.
[1 Shmuel] [19]:[8] Then war broke out again, and David went out and battled against the Pelishtim and defeated them so badly that they fled away from him.
[1 Shmuel] [19]:[9] One day as Sha’ul was sitting in his house, an evil spirit from Yahweh came on him. He had his spear in his hand, and David was playing the harp.
[1 Shmuel] [19]:[10] Sha’ul tried to hit David with the spear, but David eluded him and the spear went into the wall. Then David slipped away and fled that night.
[1 Shmuel] [19]:[11] Sha’ul sent messengers to watch David’s house to kill him in the morning, but his wife Mikal told him, “If you don’t do something to save your life tonight, you’ll be dead by tomorrow.”
[1 Shmuel] [19]:[12] So Mikal lowered David out through the window, and he was able to slip out and take off.
[1 Shmuel] [19]:[13] Then she took a household idol and put it in the bed, putting a goats’ hair quilt where the head should be and covering it with the bed-clothes.
[1 Shmuel] [19]:[14] When Sha’ul sent messengers to arrest David, she told them, “He’s sick.”
[1 Shmuel] [19]:[15] Sha’ul sent the messengers back, telling them, “Bring him up to me bed and all so I can kill him.”
[1 Shmuel] [19]:[16] But when the messengers returned, look, it was a household idol in the bed with a goats’ hair quilt as its head.
[1 Shmuel] [19]:[17] Sha’ul had Mikal brought in and questioned, “Why did you deceive me like that and sent my enemy off, so that he slipped away?” “He told me that he’d kill me,” Mikal answered Sha’ul, “if I didn’t help him escape.”
[1 Shmuel] [19]:[18] After David had slipped away, he went to Shmuel (Samuel) in Ramah and told him everything that Sha’ul had done to him, then the two of them went and stayed in Navit.
[1 Shmuel] [19]:[19] But Sha’ul was told that David was in Navit near Ramah,
[1 Shmuel] [19]:[20] so he sent messengers to capture David. When they saw a group of prophets prophesying and Shmuel standing as head over them, God’s spirit came onto Sha’ul’s messengers and they also prophesied.
[1 Shmuel] [19]:[21] They told Sha’ul and he sent more messengers and they also prophesied. He sent messengers a third time, and they started prophesying as well.
[1 Shmuel] [19]:[22] Finally Sha’ul himself headed towards Ramah and got as far as the large water cistern in Seku. He asked around about Shmuel and David, and was told that they were in Navit near Ramah.
[1 Shmuel] [19]:[23] So he went to Navit, and God’s spirit came on him as well. As he walked, he kept prophesying until he entered Navit.
[1 Shmuel] [19]:[24] He took off his outer clothes and prophesied in front of Shmuel. He lay undressed all that day and all night, so that’s why people ask, “Is Sha’ul a prophet as well?”
[1 Shmuel] [20]:[1] Then David fled from Navit near Ramah and went to Yonatan (Jonathan) and asked, “What have I done? What did I do wrong? What sin has made your father so angry that he wants to take my life?”
[1 Shmuel] [20]:[2] “Far from it,” Yonatan responded. “You won’t die. Listen, my father doesn’t do anything, big or small, without telling me. So why would my father hide this from me if it was his plan? No, you’re wrong.”
[1 Shmuel] [20]:[3] “For sure, your father knows that you’ve taken a liking to me,” said David, “and he would have decided not to tell you so you wouldn’t be upset.” Then David made an oath again, “Indeed, as Yahweh is alive, and as your soul is alive, death is definitely only a step away from me.”
[1 Shmuel] [20]:[4] “I’ll do anything for you—whatever you say,” Yonatan confirmed.
[1 Shmuel] [20]:[5] “Listen, the new moon celebration is tomorrow, and I’ll definitely be expected to sit with the king to eat,” David told him. “But you should let me go, and I’ll hide myself in the countryside until the third evening.
[1 Shmuel] [20]:[6] If your father misses me, then tell him, ‘David begged me to let him go to his home in Beyt-Lehem (Bethlehem), to join his clan for their yearly sacrifice.’
[1 Shmuel] [20]:[7] If your father says, ‘That’s fine,’ then your servant can relax. But if he gets really angry, you’ll know that he’s planning evil.
[1 Shmuel] [20]:[8] If that’s the case, it’ll be up to you to do what’s right with your servant in terms of our agreement before Yahweh. If I’ve been disloyal to the king, kill me yourself—no need to drag me to him.
[1 Shmuel] [20]:[9] “Don’t even think of it,” Yonatan responded. “If I find out that my father has decided to harm you, I’ll certainly tell you.”
[1 Shmuel] [20]:[10] “If your father does have a cruel plan, who’ll tell me?” David asked Yonatan.
[1 Shmuel] [20]:[11] “Come with me out to the countryside.” Yonatan replied. So they went out to the countryside together
[1 Shmuel] [20]:[12] and he promised David, “By Yahweh the god of Yisrael (Israel), I will definitely sound out my father around this time tomorrow, or soon after. If it looks good for you, then I’ll certainly send a message to let you know.
[1 Shmuel] [20]:[13] But if he’s planning evil for you, may Yahweh punish me similarly or even worse if I don’t inform you, and send you away so you can leave in peace. And may Yahweh be with you just like he used to be with my father.
[1 Shmuel] [20]:[14] But as long as I’m still alive, please keep our agreement of faithfulness before Yahweh so I won’t die.
[1 Shmuel] [20]:[15] Don’t ever terminate that agreement of faithfulness towards my family, even when Yahweh destroys your enemies wherever they are.
[1 Shmuel] [20]:[16] So Yonatan made a multi-generational agreement with David, adding, “And may Yahweh punish David’s enemies.”
[1 Shmuel] [20]:[17] Then Yonatan got David to promise again because he loved him as much as he loved his own life,
[1 Shmuel] [20]:[18] and he told him, “The new moon celebration is tomorrow, and you’ll be missed because your seat will be empty.
[1 Shmuel] [20]:[19] The following day, go to the place where you hid before and stay by the big rock.
[1 Shmuel] [20]:[20] I’ll shoot three arrows to the side of it, as if trying to hit a target.
[1 Shmuel] [20]:[21] Then I’ll send my boy to find the arrows. If I tell him that they’re on my side, then just as Yahweh lives it’ll be safe for you to come out.
[1 Shmuel] [20]:[22] But if I tell the boy that they’re on the far side, go because Yahweh is sending you away.
[1 Shmuel] [20]:[23] As for our pact, Yahweh will watch over us and our descendants.”
[1 Shmuel] [20]:[24] So David hid himself in the countryside, and at the new moon celebrations, the king sat down to eat—
[1 Shmuel] [20]:[25] sitting at his usual seat by the wall. Yonatan sat opposite, and Avner sat beside Sha’ul (Saul). No one was sitting in David’s seat
[1 Shmuel] [20]:[26] but Sha’ul didn’t say anything that day, thinking, “Something must have happened that made him ceremonially unclean.”
[1 Shmuel] [20]:[27] However, the next day of the celebration when David was still missing, Sha’ul asked his son Yonatan, “Why didn’t Yishay’s (Jesse) son come to the meal yesterday or today?”
[1 Shmuel] [20]:[28] “David begged me to let him go to Beyt-Lehem (Bethlehem),” Yonatan answered.
[1 Shmuel] [20]:[29] “He requested, ‘Please release me because our clan’s sacrifice will be in the city, and my brother has told me to be there. So now, if I’ve found favour in your eyes, please let me slip away and go to see my brothers.’ That’s why he hasn’t come to the king’s table.”
[1 Shmuel] [20]:[30] Sha’ul was furious at Yonatan and yelled at him, “You son of a perverse, rebellious woman! Do you think that I don’t know that you’re taking the side of Yishay’s son? It’s to your detriment and to the shame of your mother’s nakedness,
[1 Shmuel] [20]:[31] because as long as that son of Yishay stays alive on this earth, you and your kingdom will never be established. Now, send men and arrest him, because he’s on his way to the grave!”
[1 Shmuel] [20]:[32] “Why should he be put to death?” Yonatan retorted. “What wrong has he done?”
[1 Shmuel] [20]:[33] Then Sha’ul hurled his spear at him to kill him, and Yonatan knew then that his father had already determined to kill David.
[1 Shmuel] [20]:[34] Yonatan angrily got up from the table. He didn’t eat any food that second day of the celebration—he was upset about David because his father had dishonoured him.
[1 Shmuel] [20]:[35] So it was that the following morning, Yonatan went out to the countryside at the time agreed with David, taking a small boy with him.
[1 Shmuel] [20]:[36] “Run ahead—find the arrows that I’m about to shoot,” he told his boy. The boy ran and he shot the arrow to go over his head.
[1 Shmuel] [20]:[37] The boy went to where the arrow was, but Yonatan called out, “Isn’t the arrow further past you?”
[1 Shmuel] [20]:[38] Then he added, “Hurry up! Don’t mess around.” So the boy picked up the arrow and brought it back to his master,
[1 Shmuel] [20]:[39] but the boy didn’t realise what had just happened—only Yonatan and David knew.
[1 Shmuel] [20]:[40] Then Yonatan gave his equipment to the boy and sent him back to the city.
[1 Shmuel] [20]:[41] When the boy was gone, David came up from the side and dropped onto his knees, bowing three times with his face to the ground. Then they greeted each other with a kiss and cried together, although David cried the most.
[1 Shmuel] [20]:[42] Then Yonatan told David, “Go in peace, because us two have made a pact together in Yahweh’s name, agreeing, ‘Yahweh will watch between me and you, and between my descendants and your descendants forever.’ ” Then David set off and Yonatan went back to the city.
[1 Shmuel] [21]:[1] David went to the priest Ahimelek at Nov, but Ahimelek trembled when he saw David and asked him, “Why are you here by yourself? How come you don’t have a companion?”
[1 Shmuel] [21]:[2] “The king sent me on an errand,” David replied, “but he told me not to tell anyone about the matter that he sent me on. Plus I’ve told my young men where to meet me.
[1 Shmuel] [21]:[3] Now, what food do you have on hand? Give me five loaves of bread or whatever you can find.”
[1 Shmuel] [21]:[4] “There is no ordinary bread on hand,” the priest answered. “But there is the sacred bread, if only the young men have kept themselves from women.”
[1 Shmuel] [21]:[5] “There’s definitely been no women near us for three days,” David told the priest. “That’s how I always do missions. The men have been pure, even though it was a common journey, and today even more so.”
[1 Shmuel] [21]:[6] So the priest gave him the sacred bread, because there was no other bread there other than the previous day’s bread of the presence which had been removed from in front of Yahweh to be replaced by fresh bread.
[1 Shmuel] [21]:[7] Now it so happened that one of Sha’ul’s (Saul) servants was there that day presenting himself to Yahweh. He was Doeg the Edomi, a leader of Sha’ul’s herdsmen.
[1 Shmuel] [21]:[8] David asked Ahimelek, “Do you have any spear or sword here? I didn’t have time to grab my sword or my weapons when I left, because the king’s matter was urgent.”
[1 Shmuel] [21]:[9] “I’ve only got Galyat’s (Goliath) sword,” replied the priest. “From the Pelishti who you killed in the Elah valley. Look, it’s wrapped in the cloak behind the sacred apron. If you want to take it for yourself, take it, because there’s no other sword around here.” “Yes, there’s no other sword like it,” said David. “Get it for me.”
[1 Shmuel] [21]:[10] Then David left and continued moving to distance himself from Sha’ul (Saul), and he went to King Akish of Gat.
[1 Shmuel] [21]:[11] But Akish’s servants complained to him, “Isn’t that David who’ll become king of Yisrael (Israel)? Isn’t he the one they sing about when they dance, chanting, ‘Sha’ul has killed his thousands, and David his tens of thousands?’ ”
[1 Shmuel] [21]:[12] David listened to those words without any reaction because he was very afraid of what King Akish might do,
[1 Shmuel] [21]:[13] so he changed his behaviour when he was with them and pretended to be insane. He scratched on wooden doors and let his saliva dribble down his beard.
[1 Shmuel] [21]:[14] Then King Akish complained to his servants, “Look, that man’s insane. Why did you all bring him to me?
[1 Shmuel] [21]:[15] Don’t I already have enough madmen around here—why add another? Must that man come into my house?”
[1 Shmuel] [22]:[1] So David left there and slipped away to the cave at Adulam. When his brothers and other relatives found out, they went and joined him there.
[1 Shmuel] [22]:[2] Over time, any man who was in trouble, or in debt, or discontented gathered around him, and he became their leader—some four hundred men in all.
[1 Shmuel] [22]:[3] From there, David went to Mitspah in Moav (Moab), and he asked the king of Moav, “Please let my parents stay here in the palace with you until I find out what God will do for me.”
[1 Shmuel] [22]:[4] So he took them to the king where they stayed with him the entire time that David lived in the fortress.
[1 Shmuel] [22]:[5] Then the prophet Gad told David, “Don’t stay in the fortress. Leave it and come back to Yehudah’s (Judah) region.” So David left and went to the Heret forest in Yehudah.
[1 Shmuel] [22]:[6] One day, Sha’ul (Saul) was sitting holding his spear underneath the tamarisk tree on a hill near Giveah with all his servants stationed around him, when he heard where David and his men were,
[1 Shmuel] [22]:[7] and he accused his servants, “Listen now, you Benyamites. Will Yishay’s (Jesse) son also give fields and vineyards to all of you? Will he make all of you commanders of thousands and commanders of hundreds?
[1 Shmuel] [22]:[8] Yes, all of you have conspired against me. Not one of you informed me when my own son made a pact with that son of Yishay. And none of you took my side or even informed me that my son has encouraged my servant to lie in ambush against me as he is today!”
[1 Shmuel] [22]:[9] Now Doeg the Edomi was stationed there with Sha’ul’s servants, and he spoke up, “I saw Yishay’s son go to Nov and talk with Ahimelek the priest,
[1 Shmuel] [22]:[10] and the priest asked Yahweh for directions for him, and gave him food and Galyat’s (Goliath) sword.”
[1 Shmuel] [22]:[11] Then the king summoned Ahituv’s son Ahimelek and all his relatives who were priests to Nov, and they all came to the king.
[1 Shmuel] [22]:[12] “Listen now, son of Ahituv,” said Sha’ul. “Go ahead my master,” answered Ahimelek.
[1 Shmuel] [22]:[13] “Why have you all conspired against me?” asked Sha’ul. “You gave bread to Yishay’s son, and a sword, and you asked guidance from God for him, so now he’s risen up against me—lying in ambush this very day?”
[1 Shmuel] [22]:[14] “Isn’t David one of your most faithful servants?” Ahimelek answered the king. “He’s the king’s son-in-law and commander over your guards, and isn’t he honoured in your house?
[1 Shmuel] [22]:[15] Did I begin to inquire for him from God today? Far be it from me! Don’t let the king accuse his servant or any of my father’s household, because your servant doesn’t know about any of this—nothing at all.”
[1 Shmuel] [22]:[16] “For certain, Ahimelek,” the king declared. “you and all your father’s household will certainly die for that!”
[1 Shmuel] [22]:[17] Then the king commanded his messengers who were stationed beside him, “Turn around and put Yahweh’s priests to death because they’ve taken David’s side. And because they knew he was fleeing, but they didn’t inform me.” But the king’s servants weren’t willing to attack Yahweh’s priests.
[1 Shmuel] [22]:[18] So the king commanded Doeg the Edomi, “You turn around and attack the priests.” So Doeg turned and he himself attacked the priests. He killed eighty-five men that day who wore sacred linen aprons.
[1 Shmuel] [22]:[19] Also at Nov (the city of priests) he killed men and women with his sword, children and infants, cattle, donkeys, and sheep.
[1 Shmuel] [22]:[20] But one of Ahimelek’s sons was able to slip away. His name was Evyatar and he fled to join David,
[1 Shmuel] [22]:[21] and informed him that Sha’ul (Saul) had commanded Doeg to kill Yahweh’s priests.
[1 Shmuel] [22]:[22] “I knew on that day,” David responded, “when Doeg the Edomi was there, that he would probably tell Sha’ul. It’s my fault that your father and all his family were murdered.
[1 Shmuel] [22]:[23] Stick with me—don’t be afraid, because the one who wants to kill me would kill you as well. You’ll be safe with me.”
[1 Shmuel] [23]:[1] Some time later, David was told, “Listen, the Pelishtim are fighting against the city of Ke’ilah and they are stealing grain from the threshing floors,”
[1 Shmuel] [23]:[2] so he asked Yahweh, “Should I go and attack those Pelishtim?” “Go and attack the Pelishtim and save Ke’ilah,” Yahweh responded.
[1 Shmuel] [23]:[3] But David’s men warned him, “Listen, we’re afraid here in Yehudah (Judah), and we’d be even more afraid if we went to Ke’ilah against the Pelishtim’ battle lines.”
[1 Shmuel] [23]:[4] So David double-checked with Yahweh who answered, “Get ready and go to Ke’ilah, because I’m about to give you victory over the Pelishtim.”
[1 Shmuel] [23]:[5] Then David and his men went to Ke’ilah and battled against the Pelishtim—thoroughly defeating them and taking their livestock, thus saving the inhabitants of Ke’ilah.
[1 Shmuel] [23]:[6] Now when Ahimelek’s son Evyatar had fled to David at Ke’ilah, he’d brought a sacred apron with him.
[1 Shmuel] [23]:[7] Sha’ul (Saul) was told that David had gone to Ke’ilah, so he said, “Ah, God has deserted him and given him to me because he’s shut himself in by going into a walled city with doors that can be barred shut.”
[1 Shmuel] [23]:[8] So Sha’ul initiated preparations to go to Ke’ilah to entrap David and his men.
[1 Shmuel] [23]:[9] But David discovered that Sha’ul was planning to destroy him, so he summoned Evyatar the priest, “Bring the sacred apron here.”
[1 Shmuel] [23]:[10] Then David prayed, “Yahweh, God of Yisrael (Israel), your servant has heard that Sha’ul is intending to come to Ke’ilah—to destroy the city because of me.
[1 Shmuel] [23]:[11] Will Sha’ul come here, just as your servant has heard? Will the masters of Ke’ilah turn me over to him? Yahweh, God of Yisrael, please tell your servant.” “Yes, he will go there,” Yahweh answered.
[1 Shmuel] [23]:[12] “And will the masters of Ke’ilah hand me and my men over to Sha’ul?” David asked again. And Yahweh said, “They will deliver up.”
[1 Shmuel] [23]:[13] So David and his men (about 600 of them), left Ke’ilah and moved around from place to place. When Sha’ul was told that David had slipped away from Ke’ilah, he didn’t continue with his plans.
[1 Shmuel] [23]:[14] David stayed in various strongholds in the wilderness, and sometimes he stayed in the hill country in the Zif wilderness. Sha’ul (Saul) kept searching for them, but God didn’t allow him to capture them.
[1 Shmuel] [23]:[15] Once David was staying in the Zif wilderness and he saw that Sha’ul had arrived there to try to kill him.
[1 Shmuel] [23]:[16] Then Sha’ul’s son Yonatan (Jonathan) went to David at Horesh and encouraged him to keep trusting God,
[1 Shmuel] [23]:[17] saying, “Don’t be afraid, because my father Sha’ul won’t capture you. As for you, you’ll reign over Yisrael (Israel), and I’ll be your second in command. Even my father knows that.”
[1 Shmuel] [23]:[18] Again, the two of them made an agreement before Yahweh. Then David stayed at Horesh and Yonatan returned home.
[1 Shmuel] [23]:[19] Some men from Zif went to Sha’ul at Giveah, saying, “We’re pretty sure that David’s hiding himself among us in the strongholds in Horesh, on the Hakilah hill south of Yeshimon.
[1 Shmuel] [23]:[20] So now, your majesty, come over whenever you want, and we’ll make sure he’s handed over to you.”
[1 Shmuel] [23]:[21] “May you all be blessed by Yahweh,” Sha’ul responded, “because you’ve had compassion on me.
[1 Shmuel] [23]:[22] Please go back and double-check and find out who’s seen him there. Learn more and look at the place yourselves, because I’ve been told that he’s very crafty.
[1 Shmuel] [23]:[23] Find out all the other places where he hides himself. Return to me with definite information, then I’ll go with you all, and if he’s there in that region, then I’ll search for him among the population of Yehudah (Judah).”
[1 Shmuel] [23]:[24] So they left and returned to Zif ahead of Sha’ul. At that time, David and his men were in the Maeon wilderness south of Yeshimon
[1 Shmuel] [23]:[25] when Sha’ul and his men came to search for them. When David was told, he went further south to a rocky hill therein that wilderness, but Sha’ul also heard that and followed them.
[1 Shmuel] [23]:[26] At one point, Sha’ul was on one side of a hill, and David and his men were on the other side. David was hurrying to get away from Sha’ul, but Sha’ul and his men were trying to surround David and his men to capture them.
[1 Shmuel] [23]:[27] Just then, a messenger arrived for Sha’ul, saying, “Come quickly because the Pelishtim have raided our region.”
[1 Shmuel] [23]:[28] So Sha’ul had to give up chasing David and went to repel the Pelishtim.
[1 Shmuel] [23]:[29] David also left that area and stayed in the strongholds around Eyn-Gedi.
[1 Shmuel] [24]:[1] After Sha’ul (Saul) returned from repelling the Pelishtim, they told him that David was now in the Eyn-Gedi wilderness.
[1 Shmuel] [24]:[2] So Sha’ul chose three thousand Israeli warriors and went searching for David and his men at Wild Goats Rocks.
[1 Shmuel] [24]:[3] On the way, as they reached the sheep yards, Sha’ul went into a cave to relieve himself, but David and his men were hiding there further inside the cave.
[1 Shmuel] [24]:[4] David’s men whispered to him, “Wow, today what Yahweh told you is coming true when he said, ‘Listen, I’m about to give victory over your enemy, and you will do to him whatever you think is right.’ ” Then David sneaked up and quietly cut a piece off the edge of Sha’ul’s robe.
[1 Shmuel] [24]:[5] Afterwards however, David felt bad because he’d cut a piece off Sha’ul’s clothes
[1 Shmuel] [24]:[6] and he said to his men, “By Yahweh, I shouldn’t have done that to my master—to Yahweh’s anointed king—to do him harm because he’s the one Yahweh anointed.”
[1 Shmuel] [24]:[7] He restrained his men with a few quiet words and wouldn’t allow them to attack Sha’ul. Then Sha’ul left the cave and headed down the path.
[1 Shmuel] [24]:[8] After waiting a few moment, David went out of the cave and called out behind Sha’ul, “My master the king.” When Sha’ul turned and looked behind him, David bowed
[1 Shmuel] [24]:[9] and said, “Why do you listen to people when they say that I’m wanting to harm you?
[1 Shmuel] [24]:[10] Look, you can see for yourself that Yahweh gave me the opportunity to harm you today in the cave, and some of my men wanted me to kill you, but I showed you compassion and told them that I wouldn’t do harm to my master, because he’s Yahweh’s chosen king.
[1 Shmuel] [24]:[11] Your majesty, look of this piece of your robe that I’m holding, because when I cut it off, I didn’t kill you. So now you can see for yourself that I have no evil plans, and I haven’t do you any wrong, even though you’re ambushing me so you can kill me.
[1 Shmuel] [24]:[12] May Yahweh judge between you and me because I’ll let Yahweh repay you for any harm against me—it won’t be me who works against you.
[1 Shmuel] [24]:[13] As the ancient proverb says, ‘Evil things are done by evil people.’ But it won’t be me who harms you.
[1 Shmuel] [24]:[14] Who has Yisrael’s (Israel) king come to find? Who are you chasing after? A dead dog? A flea?
[1 Shmuel] [24]:[15] May Yahweh take his judgement seat and judge between me and you, and may he see my case and find me innocent and save me from you.”
[1 Shmuel] [24]:[16] When David finished saying that to Sha’ul, Sha’ul called back, “Is that your voice, my son David?” Then he cried loudly
[1 Shmuel] [24]:[17] and told David, “You’re more righteous than I am, because you were good to me even when I did evil things to you.
[1 Shmuel] [24]:[18] You’ve stated that you’ve treated me well—how Yahweh gave you the advantage over me, yet you didn’t kill me.
[1 Shmuel] [24]:[19] Now if a man finds his enemy unprepared, does he just send him off happily? Well, may Yahweh reward you for your mercy towards me today.
[1 Shmuel] [24]:[20] Now listen, I know for certain that you’re going to become king and that the kingdom of Yisrael will prosper under your leadership.
[1 Shmuel] [24]:[21] Now promise me by Yahweh that you won’t destroy my name from my family line by killing my descendants.”
[1 Shmuel] [24]:[22] David promised that to Sha’ul, then Sha’ul went back home and David and his men returned to their stronghold.
[1 Shmuel] [25]:[1] Later on, Shmuel (Samuel) died and all the Israelis gathered and mourned for him, then they buried him at his house in Ramah. Then David left and went to the Paran wilderness.
[1 Shmuel] [25]:[2] Now there was a man in Maeon whose business was in Karmel. He owned three thousand sheep and one thousand goats, and was busy shearing his sheep at Karmel.
[1 Shmuel] [25]:[3] The man’s name was Naval, and his wife was Avigayil. The wife was wise and very good-looking, whereas the man (who was a Kalevi) was harsh and cruel.
[1 Shmuel] [25]:[4] While David was in the wilderness, he heard that Naval was shearing his sheep,
[1 Shmuel] [25]:[5] so he told ten young men, “Go to Naval at Karmel and greet him in my name.
[1 Shmuel] [25]:[6] Then tell him, ‘Make you live long. Peace to you and your household and everything that belongs to you.
[1 Shmuel] [25]:[7] Now I’ve heard those shearers are working for you, and your shepherds have been living with us. We haven’t harmed them or taken anything of theirs while they’ve been in Karmel.
[1 Shmuel] [25]:[8] Ask your servants and they’ll confirm this. May these young men enjoy your favour because harvesting the wool is a prosperous time, so I request a gift for your servants and for your ‘son’, David.’ ”
[1 Shmuel] [25]:[9] So David’s men went and passed all that onto Naval, and then waited for his response.
[1 Shmuel] [25]:[10] But Naval answered them, “Why should I care about David? Yishay’s (Jesse) son isn’t anyone important. There’s lot of servants these days who are on the run from their masters.
[1 Shmuel] [25]:[11] This bread and water, and the meat that I’ve butchered, is for my shearers. Why should I give it to men when I don’t even know where they’re from?”
[1 Shmuel] [25]:[12] David’s men left and returned to inform him what Naval had been said.
[1 Shmuel] [25]:[13] Then David told his men, “Strap on your swords.” So David took around four hundred men, leaving around two hundred with their gear.
[1 Shmuel] [25]:[14] Meanwhile, Naval’s wife Avigayil had been informed by a servant, “Listen, David sent messengers from the wilderness to greet our master, but he yelled at them.
[1 Shmuel] [25]:[15] Their men had been very good to us—we were never harmed or had anything go missing when we were in the countryside.
[1 Shmuel] [25]:[16] They protected us both day and night for the whole time that we were tending the sheep.
[1 Shmuel] [25]:[17] So now you should think about it and decide what you can do, because no doubt disaster is about to hit our master and all his household. He’s a terrible man who listens to no one.”
[1 Shmuel] [25]:[18] So Avigayil quickly collected two hundred loaves of bread, two skins of wine, five butchered sheep, a large basket of roasted grain, a hundred bunches of raisins, and two hundred cakes of figs. She loaded it all on donkeys
[1 Shmuel] [25]:[19] and told her servants, “Go ahead with the donkeys. I’ll come along behind you all.” But she didn’t say a word to her husband Naval.
[1 Shmuel] [25]:[20] As she rode down a hill and into the ravine, suddenly she encountered David and his men coming down to meet her.
[1 Shmuel] [25]:[21] David had told them, “Well it was certainly a waste of time looking after that fellow in the wilderness, and taking such care not to take anything of his. Then all he did was to return insults for our good behaviour.
[1 Shmuel] [25]:[22] May God preserve my enemies, if I don’t eliminate all of the older and young men in his household before the morning.
[1 Shmuel] [25]:[23] When Avigayil saw David, she quickly dismounted from the donkey and fell to her knees in front of David and bowed her face to the ground.
[1 Shmuel] [25]:[24] She clutched his feet and said, “My master, let the guilt be on me myself. Please let your female servant explain to you—please listen to what your female servant has to say.
[1 Shmuel] [25]:[25] My master, please don’t remain angry at that worthless man, Naval. His name means ‘fool’ and so he is. He’s a senseless man, but my master, your female servant didn’t see the young men you sent.
[1 Shmuel] [25]:[26] And now, my master, as Yahweh lives and as your spirit lives, it’s Yahweh who’s prevented you from spilling blood and taking his punishment into your own hands. And now may your enemies and anyone who makes plans against my master be like Naval.
[1 Shmuel] [25]:[27] Now let this gift that your servant has brought to my master be given to the young men who serve my master.
[1 Shmuel] [25]:[28] Please forgive your female servant for being forward because Yahweh will certain advance my master’s reputation. My master is fighting Yahweh’s battles and all your life, you haven’t broken the law.
[1 Shmuel] [25]:[29] Even if someone decides to chase you and try to kill you my master, your god Yahweh will keep you wrapped in his bundle of the living, whereas your enemies will be slung away like stones from a sling.
[1 Shmuel] [25]:[30] If Yahweh does all the good things he’s promised for my master, then in time you’ll become Yisrael’s (Israel) ruler.
[1 Shmuel] [25]:[31] It would be good not to have someone’s unnecessary death as an obstacle for you or to be seen as my master just saving his own skin. Then Yahweh will bless my master, and you will appreciate your female servant.”
[1 Shmuel] [25]:[32] “May Yisrael’s god Yahweh be blessed,” David responded. “The one who sent you to meet me today.
[1 Shmuel] [25]:[33] And blessed be your discernment and blessed be you yourself, because you’ve prevented me from shedding blood today and from taking my own revenge.
[1 Shmuel] [25]:[34] Yes indeed, as Yahweh lives, Yisrael’s god prevented me from harming you. If you hadn’t hurried here to meet me, certainly neither Naval nor any of his older or young men would have survived to see the morning light.
[1 Shmuel] [25]:[35] Then David accepted the gifts that she had brought for him, and said, “Go back to your house in peace. See, I’ve listened to what you said and granted your request.”
[1 Shmuel] [25]:[36] When Avigayil got home to Naval, wow, he had put on a celebration at his house with a feast fit for a king. He was feeling very contented and was quite drunk, so she didn’t tell him anything at all until it was light in the morning.
[1 Shmuel] [25]:[37] And so it was in the morning, when Naval’s wine had worn off, his wife told him what she’d done. In his rage, he had a stroke and became totally paralysed
[1 Shmuel] [25]:[38] for about then days. Then Yahweh struck Naval and he died.
[1 Shmuel] [25]:[39] When David heard that Naval had died, he said, “Blessed be Yahweh, who has judged the case of Naval’s insult and has prevented his servant from doing the wrong thing. And Yahweh has repaid Naval for his own evil.” Then David sent messengers to Avigayil about taking her as a wife.
[1 Shmuel] [25]:[40] His servants went to her at Karmel and told her, “David sent us to take you back to become his wife.”
[1 Shmuel] [25]:[41] She knelt down with her face to the ground and replied, “See, your female servant is ready for washing the feet of my master’s servants like a slave woman.”
[1 Shmuel] [25]:[42] Then Avigayil and five of her servant girls quickly got ready, and she mounted the donkey. She followed the messengers to where David was and became a wife for him.
[1 Shmuel] [25]:[43] David had also married Ahinoam from Yizre’el (Jezreel), so both of them became his wives.
[1 Shmuel] [25]:[44] (Meanwhile Sha’ul (Saul) had given his daughter, David’ wife Mikal, to Palti, Layish’s son from Galim.)
[1 Shmuel] [26]:[1] One time some Zifim went to Sha’ul (Saul) at Giveah and told him, “Isn’t David hiding himself on the Hakilah hill opposite Yeshimon?”
[1 Shmuel] [26]:[2] So Sha’ul got ready with three thousand chosen Israeli warriors and went to the Zif wilderness to search for David.
[1 Shmuel] [26]:[3] They camped at Hakilah hill (opposite Yeshimon) by the path, but David stayed in the wilderness when he saw the Sha’ul was there trying to get him.
[1 Shmuel] [26]:[4] (He’d sent some spies and knew that Sha’ul had definitely arrived.)
[1 Shmuel] [26]:[5] That night, David moved out and got to the place where Sha’ul had camped. He could see where Sha’ul was sleeping, along with Ner’s son Avner, his army commander. Sha’ul was asleep in the secure centre with his warriors all around him.
[1 Shmuel] [26]:[6] David spoke to Ahimelek (the Hiti) and to Avishay (son of Yoav’s (Joab) brother Tseruyah) asking, “Who’ll go into the camp with me to Sha’ul?” Avishay answered, “I will. I’ll go with you.”
[1 Shmuel] [26]:[7] So that night David and Avishay crept into the camp. Sha’ul was asleep there in the centre with his spear stuck into the ground near his head, and Avner and others were lying in a circle around him.
[1 Shmuel] [26]:[8] Avishay whispered to David, “Today God has arranged for you to defeat your enemy. So please let me pierce him now with the spear through him and into the ground. Only one strike will do it—I won’t have to strike him a second time.
[1 Shmuel] [26]:[9] “Don’t kill him,” David responded, “because who can attack Yahweh’s anointed king and be considered innocent?”
[1 Shmuel] [26]:[10] As Yahweh lives, he will certainly strike him, or else his time will come and he’ll die, or maybe he’ll go into battle and be swept away.
[1 Shmuel] [26]:[11] May Yahweh prevent me from harming Yahweh’s anointed one. Just grab the spear that’s by his head, and the jug of water, then we can get out of here.”
[1 Shmuel] [26]:[12] So David took the spear and water jug that were near Sha’ul’s head and then got out of there. No one saw them, and no one woke up or realised, because Yahweh had caused them all to fall into a deep sleep.
[1 Shmuel] [26]:[13] Then David crossed the valley and stood on the top of the opposite hill—quite a distance away
[1 Shmuel] [26]:[14] and called out to Avner and the camp, “Won’t you answer, Avner?” “Who are you that’s shouting to the king?” Avner answered.
[1 Shmuel] [26]:[15] “Aren’t you a warrior?” David called out. “And who in Yisrael (Israel) is as good as you? But why didn’t you watch over your master the king? Because one of the people came to destroy the king your master.
[1 Shmuel] [26]:[16] Your performance wasn’t good. As Yahweh lives, all of you who were supposed to be watching over your master, over Yahweh’s anointed one, deserve to be executed. Look around, where’s the king’s spear and water jug that were by his head?”
[1 Shmuel] [26]:[17] Then Sha’ul recognised David’s voice and called back, “Is that your voice, my son David?” “Yes, it is my voice, my master the king.” David replied.
[1 Shmuel] [26]:[18] Then he asked, “Why is my master chasing his servant? What have I done? What wrong am I guilty of?
[1 Shmuel] [26]:[19] Now please listen, my master the king, to your servant’s words. If it’s Yahweh who’s incited you against me, may he accept an offering, but if it’s people, may they be cursed in front of Yahweh because they’ve driven me away from enjoying Yahweh’s inheritance for me, saying, ‘Go away and serve other gods.’
[1 Shmuel] [26]:[20] So now, don’t let me die far from Yahweh’s presence. It seems that Yisrael’s king has come all this way to chase a flea, just like someone chases a wild bird in the hills.”
[1 Shmuel] [26]:[21] Sha’ul responded, “Yes, I’ve sinned. Go home, my son David. I won’t wrong you again, because you spared my life today. Yes, I’ve acted foolishly and been following the wrong path.”
[1 Shmuel] [26]:[22] “Look, here’s your spear.” David called back. “Get one of your young men to come across and get it.
[1 Shmuel] [26]:[23] May Yahweh repay each person for their obedience and faithfulness. Yahweh put you in a vulnerable position today, but I wasn’t willing to hurt Yahweh’s anointed king.
[1 Shmuel] [26]:[24] Just as I honoured your life today, so to may Yahweh honour my life and rescue me from all my difficulties.
[1 Shmuel] [26]:[25] “May you be blessed, my son David,” Sha’ul told David. “You certainly have both ability and the skill to use it.” Then David went on his way and Sha’ul went back home.
[1 Shmuel] [27]:[1] But David thought to himself, “One of these days, I’m going to be caught off-guard by Sha’ul’s (Saul) actions. There’s no future for me here, so I definitely need to slip away to the Pelishtim region. Then hopefully Sha’ul will give up looking for me again across all Yisrael (Israel), and I’ll slip be able to stay under his radar.”
[1 Shmuel] [27]:[2] So he left Yisrael and crossed over with his six hundred men to Gat and King Akish (Maeok’s son).
[1 Shmuel] [27]:[3] Then David and his men settled with Akish in Gat. David had his two wives Ahinoam (from Yizre’el (Jezreel)) and Avigayil (widow of Naval from Karmel) with him.
[1 Shmuel] [27]:[4] When Sha’ul was told that David had fled to Gat, he stopped searching for him.
[1 Shmuel] [27]:[5] One day, David asked Akish, “If I’ve found favour in your eyes, ask them to give me a place in one of the cities in the countryside so I can live there. There’s no need for us to bludge on you here in the royal city.”
[1 Shmuel] [27]:[6] So Akish gave Tsiklag to David that day, and as a result, it still belongs to Yehudah’s (Judah) kings until today.
[1 Shmuel] [27]:[7] David ended up living in the Pelishti countryside for around sixteen months,
[1 Shmuel] [27]:[8] and during that time, he would take his men to raid the Geshurim, the Gizrim, and the Amalekim. They had lived in that region from long before—from Shur all the way to Mitsrayim (Egypt).
[1 Shmuel] [27]:[9] When David attacked a place, he would take the sheep and cattle, donkeys and camels, and clothes, but he didn’t leave anyone alive. Then he’d return home and visit Akish.
[1 Shmuel] [27]:[10] The king would ask him, “Which place did you raid today?” David would tell him, “In southern Yehudah,” or “South of the Yerahme’elim,” or “In the southern Keyni region”.
[1 Shmuel] [27]:[11] David never allowed any man or woman to live to be able to go back to Gat and report on what he’d really been doing. That was how he handled things for the entire time that he lived in the Pelishti countryside.
[1 Shmuel] [27]:[12] But King Akish was trusting David, thinking, “He’ll definitely be hated now by his people in Yisrael (Israel), so he’ll be forced to remain here as my servant.”
[1 Shmuel] [28]:[1] Some time later, the Pelishtim gathered their forces getting ready to battle against Yisrael (Israel), and King Akish complimented David, “We’ll definitely want you and your men to join with our forces.”
[1 Shmuel] [28]:[2] “Sounds good,” David replied, “because you’ll be able to see for yourself what your servant can do.” “I’ll appoint as my permanent bodyguard,” Akish told him.
[1 Shmuel] [28]:[3] By now, Shmuel (Samuel) was long dead and all Yisrael had mourned for him and had buried him in his town of Ramah, and Sha’ul (Saul) had had expelled all the mediums from the country, along with those who contacted the spirits.
[1 Shmuel] [28]:[4] Then the Pelishtim went to Shunem and camped there. Meanwhile Sha’ul gathered all Yisrael’s warriors and they camped at Gilboa,
[1 Shmuel] [28]:[5] but when he saw the Pelishti camp, he was afraid and trembled inside.
[1 Shmuel] [28]:[6] He asked Yahweh for direction, but Yahweh didn’t answer him either through a dream, nor by use of the sacred pouch, nor through any prophet.
[1 Shmuel] [28]:[7] Then Sha’ul instructed his servants, “Find a woman for me who talks to the spirits of dead people, so I can go to her and ask her something.” “Sure,” his servants told him, “there’s a woman in Eyn-Dor who can do that.”
[1 Shmuel] [28]:[8] So Sha’ul put on different clothes to disguise himself, and went off in the night with two of his men. They went to the woman and he asked, “Please divine for me with a spirit of the dead and bring up the person that I tell you.”
[1 Shmuel] [28]:[9] “Listen,” said the woman, “surely you’re aware of what Sha’ul has done—he’s expelled anyone out of the country brings back the dead or converses with the spirits. So why are you trying to trap me? Are you trying to get me killed?”
[1 Shmuel] [28]:[10] Sha’ul promised her in front of Yahweh, “As Yahweh lives, you won’t be punished for doing this.”
[1 Shmuel] [28]:[11] “Okay then, who do you want me to bring up for you?” “Bring Shmuel (Samuel) up for me.” he replied.
[1 Shmuel] [28]:[12] When the woman saw Shmuel, she yelled out and said to Sha’ul, “Oh no, you’ve tricked me! You’re Sha’ul!”
[1 Shmuel] [28]:[13] “Don’t be afraid,” said the king, “but what have you seen?” “I saw gods coming up out of the ground,” she replied.
[1 Shmuel] [28]:[14] “What does he look like?” he asked. “An old man’s appearing,” she said, “wearing a robe.” Sha’ul knew it was Shmuel, and he knelt down and bowed his face to the ground.
[1 Shmuel] [28]:[15] “Why’ve you disturbed me by bringing me up?” Shmuel asked. “I’m very distressed,” Sha’ul replied, “and the Pelishtim are about to go to war against me. And God has turned away from me and doesn’t answer me anymore—he hasn’t sent me any prophets or given me any dreams, So I’ve called to you so you can tell me what I should do.”
[1 Shmuel] [28]:[16] “If Yahweh’s turned away from you and become your enemy,” Shmuel responded, “what’s the point in asking me?”
[1 Shmuel] [28]:[17] He’s simply done what he told me to tell you that he’d do. He’s ripped the kingdom away from you and given it to your neighbour David.
[1 Shmuel] [28]:[18] You didn’t do what Yahweh instructed and you didn’t execute his anger against Amalek, so that’s why Yahweh is doing that to you today.
[1 Shmuel] [28]:[19] He will also allow Yisrael (Israel) to be defeated by the Pelishtim, and tomorrow you and your sons will be here with me. Yahweh will also allow Yisrael’s entire camp of warriors to be captured by the Pelishtim.”
[1 Shmuel] [28]:[20] Sha’ul, who’d been standing immediately toppled right over and crashed to the ground—he was very scared by Shmuel’s words, plus he didn’t have much strength because he hadn’t eaten for twenty-four hours.
[1 Shmuel] [28]:[21] The woman knelt over Sha’ul and saw that he was terrified, and told him, “Listen to me. Your female servant has risked my life to do what you said and follow your instructions.
[1 Shmuel] [28]:[22] So now, although you’re the king, please listen to your female servant. Let me get you some food, and then eat it to regain your strength for the journey home.
[1 Shmuel] [28]:[23] But he refused, saying, “No, I won’t eat anything.” However his servants and also the woman urged him, and he decided to take their advice so he got up from the ground and sat on the bed.
[1 Shmuel] [28]:[24] Now the woman had a calf in a stall at the house, and she quickly slaughtered it, She took flour and kneaded it and baked flat bread.
[1 Shmuel] [28]:[25] She placed the food in front of Sha’ul and his servants, and they ate before getting up and going out into the night.
[1 Shmuel] [29]:[1] Meanwhile, the Pelishtim had gathered in their camp at Afek, while the Israelis were camped near the Yizre’el (Jezreel) spring.
[1 Shmuel] [29]:[2] As the Pelishti leaders marched out groups of hundreds and thousands, David and his men were behind them with King Akish.
[1 Shmuel] [29]:[3] But the Pelishti commanders asked, “What are those Ivrim (Hebrews) doing here?” “That’s David,” Akish replied. “He was the servant of King Sha’ul (Saul) of Yisrael (Israel), but he’s been with me for over a year, and I haven’t found anything distrustful in him from when he lost favour until today?”
[1 Shmuel] [29]:[4] But the Pelishti commanders were furious at him and told him, “Send that man back to whatever place you’ve given him! There’s no way he’s joining us in the battle! What if he turned against us during the fight? What better way could he have to win back his master’s favour than by killing our men?
[1 Shmuel] [29]:[5] Isn’t this the David that when they dance they sing, ‘Sha’ul has struck down his thousands, and David his ten thousands’?”
[1 Shmuel] [29]:[6] So Akish called David and told him, “As Yahweh lives, you’ve definitely been honest, and everything I’ve seen of your activities has been good, because I haven’t seen you do anything wrong since the day you first arrived. However, these rulers don’t approve of you,
[1 Shmuel] [29]:[7] so turn back and go in peace so that you don’t do anything to displease them.”
[1 Shmuel] [29]:[8] “But what have I done?” David rebutted. “What wrong have you found in your servant from the day I arrived at your place until now? Why can’t I come and fight against the enemies of my master the king?”
[1 Shmuel] [29]:[9] “All I know, is that as far as I’m concerned you’re as reliable as a messenger from God.” Akish responded. “Nevertheless, the Pelishti commanders have said, ‘He can’t join our side in the battle.’
[1 Shmuel] [29]:[10] So you and your master’s servants who came with you should get up with the early morning light and leave.”
[1 Shmuel] [29]:[11] So David and his men packed up early in the morning to return to the Pelishtim region, but the Pelishti warriors headed towards Yizre’el (Jezreel).
[1 Shmuel] [30]:[1] David and his men got back to Tsiklag three days later and found that the Amalekim had raided Tsiklag and other parts of the wilderness in southern Yehudah (Judah). They had attacked Tsiklag then burnt it down,
[1 Shmuel] [30]:[2] capturing the women and children and everyone else. They hadn’t killed anyone, but had taken them away with them,
[1 Shmuel] [30]:[3] so when David and his men arrived at the town, wow, it had been burnt down and their wives, and sons and daughters had been taken captive.
[1 Shmuel] [30]:[4] David and his men cried loudly until they didn’t have the strength to cry any more.
[1 Shmuel] [30]:[5] David’s two wives, Ahinoam (from Yizre’el (Jezreel)) and Avigayil (Naval’s widow from Karmel), had been taken captive along with the others.
[1 Shmuel] [30]:[6] David was in a tight spot because the men were considering throwing rocks at him to kill him, because they were very upset about their children, but he found strength in his god Yahweh.
[1 Shmuel] [30]:[7] Then David asked the priest Evyatar (Ahimelek’s son), “Please get the sacred apron and come back to me.” So Evyatar got the sacred apron and went back to David.
[1 Shmuel] [30]:[8] Then David asked Yahweh, “If I chase after these raiders, will I catch up to them?” “Chase them because you’ll definitely catch up and you’ll certainly be able to rescue the captives,” Yahweh answered.
[1 Shmuel] [30]:[9] So David and the six hundred men who were with him took off and they reached the Besor riverbed, where some of the slower ones remained.
[1 Shmuel] [30]:[10] David and four hundred men continued, but two hundred more of the men who were exhausted stopped at the far end of the Besor riverbed.
[1 Shmuel] [30]:[11] They found an Mitsri (Egyptian) man in the countryside and took him to David. They gave him water to drink and bread to eat,
[1 Shmuel] [30]:[12] along with a slice of fig cake and two raisin clusters. He ate it and felt stronger again because he hadn’t eaten or drunk for three full days.
[1 Shmuel] [30]:[13] “Who do you belong to?” David asked. “And where are you from?” “I am an Mitsri,” he replied. “I’m an Amaleki man’s slave but my master left me three days ago because I got sick.
[1 Shmuel] [30]:[14] We’d raided the southern area of the Kereti as well as part of Yehudah (Judah) and the south of Kalev (Caleb). And we burnt down Tsiklag.”
[1 Shmuel] [30]:[15] David asked him, “Can you lead us to them?” “I’ll take you to them,” he answered, “if you promise by God that you won’t kill me and won’t hand me back over to my master.”
[1 Shmuel] [30]:[16] So he took David down to the plain, and sure enough, there were the Amalekim spread out, eating and drinking and celebrating because of all the plunder that they had taken from the Pelishti and Yehudah regions.
[1 Shmuel] [30]:[17] David attacked them from twilight until the evening of the next day, and none of the Amalekim were able to escape except for four hundred young men who jumped on camels and fled.
[1 Shmuel] [30]:[18] So David was able to rescue everyone that the Amalekim had taken, including his two wives.
[1 Shmuel] [30]:[19] None of their sons or daughters were missing, and they also recovered all the animals and all the plunder—nothing was missing—big or small.
[1 Shmuel] [30]:[20] David took all the flocks and herds and they drove them in front of the other livestock, saying, “This is David’s spoil.”
[1 Shmuel] [30]:[21] Then David got back to the two hundred men who’d been too exhausted to go all the way with them. They’d stayed at the Besor riverbed, and they went out to meet David and his men. As David approached to greet them,
[1 Shmuel] [30]:[22] all the evil and worthless men who’d gone with David complained, “Because they didn’t go with us, we won’t give them any of the plunder that we recovered, except that each man can get his wife and children then take them away and leave.”
[1 Shmuel] [30]:[23] “No, my brothers,” David said. “You won’t do that with what Yahweh has given to us. He’s protected us and helped us defeat the raiders who came against us.
[1 Shmuel] [30]:[24] Who’ll listen to you all when you talk like that? The portion for the ones who went and fought will be the same as for those who stayed with the equipment. They’ll all share alike.
[1 Shmuel] [30]:[25] So from that time onwards, it’s been a custom and law in Yisrael (Israel).
[1 Shmuel] [30]:[26] When David got back to Tsiklag, he sent a gift from some of the plunder to the elders in Yehudah (Judah), telling them, “Look, here’s a blessing for you—some of the spoil from Yahweh’s enemies.”
[1 Shmuel] [30]:[27] Gifts were sent to: those in Beyt-El (Bethel), Ramot-Negev, Yatir,
[1 Shmuel] [30]:[28] Aroer, Sifmot, Eshtemoa,
[1 Shmuel] [30]:[29] Rakal, the cities of the Yerahme’elim and the Keynim,
[1 Shmuel] [30]:[30] Hormah, Bor-Ashan, Atak,
[1 Shmuel] [30]:[31] Hevron, and all the places where David and his men had been to.
[1 Shmuel] [31]:[1] Meanwhile, the Pelishtim were battling against Yisrael (Israel), and the Israelis fled from the Pelishtim but many were killed on Mt. Gilboa.
[1 Shmuel] [31]:[2] The Pelishtim stayed hard on the tail of Sha’ul (Saul) and his sons, and they killed his sons Yonatan (Jonathan), Avinadav, and Malkishua.
[1 Shmuel] [31]:[3] Then the battle was fierce around Sha’ul, then the Pelishti archers sighted him and he writhed in terrible pain from the arrows.
[1 Shmuel] [31]:[4] He said to the man carrying his equipment, “Draw out your sword and pierce me through with it, lest these uncircumcised Pelishtim come and pierce me through then torture me as I’m dying.” But the man who carried his equipment was very scared and wouldn’t do it, so Sha’ul took his sword and fell on it.
[1 Shmuel] [31]:[5] When the man carrying his equipment saw that the king was dead, he too fell on his sword and died with him.
[1 Shmuel] [31]:[6] So Sha’ul, three of his sons, and the man carrying his equipment all died on that same day, along with all his warriors.
[1 Shmuel] [31]:[7] When the Israelis on the north side of the Yizre’el (Jezreel) valley and on the east side of the Yarden (Jordan) saw that the Israeli warriors had fled and that Sha’ul and his sons had been killed, they left their cities and fled, and the Pelishtim came and lived in them.
[1 Shmuel] [31]:[8] The next day when the Pelishtim came to strip anything valuable from the bodies, they found the bodies of Sha’ul and his three sons there on Mt. Gilboa.
[1 Shmuel] [31]:[9] They cut off the king’s head and took all his gear. Then they sent messengers all around the Pelishti region to spread their good news to the temples of their idols and to all their people.
[1 Shmuel] [31]:[10] They Sha’ul’s armour and weapons in the temple of the Ashtarot, and hung his body on the Beyt-Shean city wall.
[1 Shmuel] [31]:[11] When the residents of Yavesh-Gilead heard what the Pelishtim had done to Sha’ul’s body,
[1 Shmuel] [31]:[12] all their warriors walked all night to take Sha’ul’s body and those of his sons, off the wall at Beyt-Shean. They took them back to Yavesh and burnt them there.
[1 Shmuel] [31]:[13] Then they took their bones and buried them under the tamarisk tree in Yavesh, and fasted for seven days.
[2 Shmuel] [1]:[1] After David returned from slaughtering the Amalekim, he stayed in Tsiklag for two days. (King Sha’ul (Saul) was dead by this time.)
[2 Shmuel] [1]:[2] Then on the third day, wow, a man came from Sha’ul’s camp. He had torn clothes and dirt on his head, and when he got to David he fell onto his knees and bowed low.
[2 Shmuel] [1]:[3] “Where have you come from?” David asked him. “I was in Yisrael’s (Israel) camp, but managed to escape.” he replied.
[2 Shmuel] [1]:[4] “Why? What happened?” David demanded. “Tell me, please,” “Our people fled from the battle,” the man said. “Many fell and died. Even Sha’ul and his son Yonatan (Jonathan) died.”
[2 Shmuel] [1]:[5] “How do you know that Sha’ul and Yonatan died?” David asked the young man who’d brought the news.
[2 Shmuel] [1]:[6] “I happened to be on Mt. Gilboa,” the young man replied, “and listen, Sha’ul was leaning on his spear. Then wow, the chariots and the masters of the chariot horses overtook him,
[2 Shmuel] [1]:[7] and he turned around and saw me. He called me and I answered, ‘Here I am.’
[2 Shmuel] [1]:[8] ‘Who are you?’ he asked. ‘I’m an Amaleki,’ I told him.
[2 Shmuel] [1]:[9] Then he said to me, ‘Please, come over here and kill me, because although I’m still alive, the pain is unbearable.’
[2 Shmuel] [1]:[10] So I stood over him and killed him, because I knew that with those wounds, he wouldn’t live. Then I took the crown off his head and the bracelet on his arm, and I brought them here to you, my master.”
[2 Shmuel] [1]:[11] Then David pulled at his clothes with his hands and tore them, and all the men with him did the same,
[2 Shmuel] [1]:[12] and they mourned and wept and fasted until the evening for Sha’ul and for his son Yonatan, and for Yahweh’s people, because many Israelis had been killed.
[2 Shmuel] [1]:[13] Then David asked the young man who’d brought the news, “Where are you from?” “I’m a foreigner’s son,” he replied, “an Amaleki.”
[2 Shmuel] [1]:[14] “How come you weren’t afraid to kill Yahweh’s anointed king with your own hands?” David asked him.
[2 Shmuel] [1]:[15] Then David called to one of his young men, “Come over here and execute him.” So he struck him, and he died.
[2 Shmuel] [1]:[16] “Your blood’s on your own head,” David told the Amaleki, “because you admitted in your own words that you, yourself killed Yahweh’s anointed one.”
[2 Shmuel] [1]:[17] Then David sang this funeral song for Sha’ul (Saul) and his son Yonatan (Jonathan)
[2 Shmuel] [1]:[18] and said that it should be taught to the people of Yehudah (Judah). It’s called ‘The bow’ and indeed, it’s written down in the Book of Yashar:
[2 Shmuel] [1]:[19] “Yisrael’s (Israel) splendour was slain in the hills. How the powerful warriors have died.
[2 Shmuel] [1]:[20] Don’t tell them in Gat. Don’t let them take the news to Ashkelon’s streets, in case the Pelishti women celebrate, and the daughters of the uncircumcised are elated.
[2 Shmuel] [1]:[21] You mountains in Gilboa, may you have no dew or rain fall on you, nor fields producing grain for offerings. Because it was there that Sha’ul’s shield was splattered with his blood, and the leather won’t be preserved with oil again.
[2 Shmuel] [1]:[22] From the blood of those slain— from the fat of the warriors, Yonatan’s bow didn’t retreat and Sha’ul’s sword didn’t fail on its strikes.
[2 Shmuel] [1]:[23] Sha’ul (Saul) and Yonatan (Jonathan) were loved— they pleased the people. and even at their death they weren’t separated. They were swifter than eagles. they were stronger than lions.
[2 Shmuel] [1]:[24] Weep for Sha’ul you daughters of Yisrael (Israel), the one who dressed you in nice clothes with jewellery, and gave you all gold brooches to put on.
[2 Shmuel] [1]:[25] Those warriors have fallen in the middle of the battle. Yonatan has been killed there on the hills.
[2 Shmuel] [1]:[26] I grieve for you my dear friend Yonatan (Jonathan). You were so kind to me. Your friendship meant more to me than the women who say they love me.
[2 Shmuel] [1]:[27] Yes, those powerful warriors have fallen, and those weapons of war have been destroyed.”
[2 Shmuel] [2]:[1] After that was over, David inquired from Yahweh, “Should I go into one of Yehudah’s (Judah) cities?” “Yes,, go,” Yahweh answered. “Where should I go?” David asked again. “To Hevron,” he said.
[2 Shmuel] [2]:[2] So David took his two wives (Ahinoam the Yizre’eli and Avigayil the widow of Naval the Karmeli) and went there.
[2 Shmuel] [2]:[3] He took his men who were with him, along with their families, and went to live in Hevron and the surrounding towns.
[2 Shmuel] [2]:[4] Then the Yehudah leaders came and anointed David as king over Yehudah. They told him, “It was the men of Yavesh-Gilead who buried Sha’ul (Saul).”
[2 Shmuel] [2]:[5] So David sent messengers to Yavesh-Gilead to tell them, “May Yahweh bless you all because you showed that kindness to your master Sha’ul to bury him respectfully.
[2 Shmuel] [2]:[6] Now may Yahweh treat you all with kindness and faithfulness, and I myself will also be good to you because you did that.
[2 Shmuel] [2]:[7] Meanwhile now that Sha’ul your master is dead, continue to be courageous and become brave warriors as Yehudah has anointed me as king over their tribe.
[2 Shmuel] [2]:[8] However, Avner (Ner’s son) who’d been Sha’ul’s (Saul) army commander had taken Sha’ul’s son Ish-Boshet across to Mahanayim
[2 Shmuel] [2]:[9] and declared him to be king over Gilead, and over the Ashurim and Yizre’el (Jezreel), and over Efrayim (Ephraim) and Benyamin, and over all of Yisrael (Israel).
[2 Shmuel] [2]:[10] Ish-Boshet was forty years old when he started to rule over the Israelis, and he ruled them for two years. But the tribe of Yehudah (Judah) was loyal to David
[2 Shmuel] [2]:[11] and he ruled them for seven and a half years.
[2 Shmuel] [2]:[12] One day Avner left Mahanayim with some of Ish-Boshet’s servants and went to Giveon,
[2 Shmuel] [2]:[13] but Yoav (Joab) (Tseruyah’s son, traditionally called ‘Yoav’ in English) took some of David’s servants and went and confronted them at the Giveon pool—one group on each side of the pool.
[2 Shmuel] [2]:[14] Then Avner said to Yoav, “Let’s get some of these young warriors to fight it out in front of us.” “Sounds good to me,” said Yoav.
[2 Shmuel] [2]:[15] So they stood up and counted off twelve representing Benyamin and Sha’ul’s (Saul) son Ish-Boshet and twelve from David’s servants.
[2 Shmuel] [2]:[16] Each of them grabbed his opponent’s head and then thrust his sword into his side, so they both fell down dead together. So that place in Giveon was named ‘Helkat-Hatsurim’ (meaning ‘Field of Daggers’).
[2 Shmuel] [2]:[17] That led on to a very intense battle that day, but Avner and the Israeli men were defeated by David’s servants.
[2 Shmuel] [2]:[18] Tseruyah’s three sons were there: Yoav, Avishay, and Asahel, (Asahel was a fast runner—like a wild antelope.)
[2 Shmuel] [2]:[19] and Asahel chased after Avner and wouldn’t give up.
[2 Shmuel] [2]:[20] Avner turned and said, “Is that you, Asahel?” “Yes, it’s me,” he answered.
[2 Shmuel] [2]:[21] “I’m warning you: Stop chasing me and go after someone else instead,” Avner called back. But Asahel wouldn’t give up
[2 Shmuel] [2]:[22] so Avner tried again, “Stop chasing me! You’ll force me to kill you, then how could I face your brother Yoav?”
[2 Shmuel] [2]:[23] But Asahel wouldn’t give up so Avner thrust the butt end of his spear into his stomach and it went right through and came out his back. He fell to the ground and died there, and when the others caught up, they stopped there.
[2 Shmuel] [2]:[24] But Yoav and Avishay kept going after Avner. As the sun was setting, they came to the Amah hill (east of Giyah, along the road to the wilderness near Giveon)
[2 Shmuel] [2]:[25] and the Benyamites lined up behind Avner as an coordinated unit there on top of the hill.
[2 Shmuel] [2]:[26] Avner called out to Yoav, “Are we just going to keep killing each other? Don’t you know that the only result can be more bitterness? How long will you go on before you command your people to stop killing their cousins?”
[2 Shmuel] [2]:[27] “As God lives,” Yoav replied, “if you hadn’t said that, then surely it would have been morning before they would have pulled back from the chase.”
[2 Shmuel] [2]:[28] So Yoav had a trumpet blown and his men stopped fighting and pursing the Israelis.
[2 Shmuel] [2]:[29] Then Avner and his men walked all that night through the Yarden (Jordan) river plain, then crossed the river and walked all morning until they got back to Mahanayim.
[2 Shmuel] [2]:[30] When Yoav had assembled them all and counted them, only Asahel and nineteen others had been killed in the battle,
[2 Shmuel] [2]:[31] although they had killed 360 of Avner’s Benyamite warriors.
[2 Shmuel] [2]:[32] They retrieved Asahel’s body and buried it in his father’s tomb in Beyt-Lehem (Bethlehem). Then they walked all night and got back to Hevron at first light.
[2 Shmuel] [3]:[1] Nevertheless the war between Sha’ul’s (Saul) and David’s followers dragged on and on, but overall, David’s side had more wins than the followers of Ish-Boshet.
[2 Shmuel] [3]:[2] David’s wives gave birth to six sons while they were based there in Hevron: Ahinoam (the Yizre’eli) gave birth to Amnon,
[2 Shmuel] [3]:[3] then Avigayil (the widow of Naval the Karmeli) gave birth to Kilav, and Ma’akah (daughter of King Talmay of Geshur) gave birth to Avshalom (Absalom).
[2 Shmuel] [3]:[4] The fourth was Adoniyah (son of Hagit), the fifth was Shefatyah (son of Avital),
[2 Shmuel] [3]:[5] and the sixth was Yitream (son of David’s wife Eglah). All six of those sons were born to David in Hevron.
[2 Shmuel] [3]:[6] While the war between Sha’ul’s (Saul) son Ish-Boshet and David’s supporters continued, Avner was strengthening himself with Sha’ul’s supporters.
[2 Shmuel] [3]:[7] Now Sha’ul had had a slave-wife named Ritspah (daughter of Ayah) and Avner slept with her. So Ish-Boshet demanded, “Why have you slept with my father’s slave-wife?”
[2 Shmuel] [3]:[8] Avner became very angry at this challenge from Ish-Boshet and snapped back, “Do you think I’m Yehudah’s (Judah) dog hiding out over here? Today I’ve been helping Sha’ul’s family: your father, his brothers, and his friends, and I won’t let you fall into David’s hands. Yet today you bring some charge against me to do with a woman?
[2 Shmuel] [3]:[9] May God punish me if I don’t do for David exactly what Yahweh promised him
[2 Shmuel] [3]:[10] and help with the transfer of the kingdom away from your family and to establish David’s kingdom over both Yehudah and Yisrael (Israel), from Dan down to Be’er-Sheva (Beersheba).”
[2 Shmuel] [3]:[11] Ish-Boshet didn’t say a word back to Avner because he was very scared of him.
[2 Shmuel] [3]:[12] Then Avner sent messengers to David to tell him, “Who should be king of this country? Let’s come to an agreement and then I could join you and help make all of Yisrael turn to you.”
[2 Shmuel] [3]:[13] “Yes, good,” David replied. “I’m happy to come to an agreement with you on one condition: you must bring my wife—Sha’ul’s daughter, Mikal—if you want to be accepted here.”
[2 Shmuel] [3]:[14] Then David sent messengers to Sha’ul’s son Ish-Boshet saying, “Give Mikal back to me. I earnt her as my wife with the foreskins of one-hundred Pelishtim.”
[2 Shmuel] [3]:[15] So Ish-Boshet had her taken from her husband (Layish’s son Paltiel),
[2 Shmuel] [3]:[16] but he walked along behind her, weeping, as far as Bahurim where finally Avner told him to go back home and so he did.
[2 Shmuel] [3]:[17] Then Avner conferred with the Israeli elders saying, “Previously you were wanting David to be king over you,
[2 Shmuel] [3]:[18] but now it’s time for action. Yahweh has already said, ‘I’m going to use my servant David to rescue my people Yisrael from the Pelishtim and all their other enemies.’ ”
[2 Shmuel] [3]:[19] Avner also spoke privately with the Benyamites, then he went to Hevron to tell David privately what the Israelis and the Benyamites had agreed to.
