[2 Shmuel] [24]:[1] Then Yahweh was angry against Yisrael (Israel) again and he incited David to cause problems for them by saying, “Go and order a census of Yisrael and Yehudah (Judah).”
[2 Shmuel] [24]:[2] So the king told Yoav (Joab), the commander of his army, who was with him at the time, “Travel throughout all the regions of the Israeli tribes, from Dan (in the far north) down to Be’er-Sheva (Beersheba) (in the far south), and count the people so that I’ll know the number of fighting men.”
[2 Shmuel] [24]:[3] “May your god Yahweh multiply the people a hundred times over,” Yoav responded, “add may my master the king see that happen, but why would my master the king want to do that?”
[2 Shmuel] [24]:[4] However, the king insisted, so even though Yoav and the army commanders disagreed, at the king’s command they set off to count the Israeli people.
[2 Shmuel] [24]:[5] They crossed the Yarden (Jordan) river and camped in Aroer, south of the city in the middle of the Gad valley, then proceeded to Yazer.
[2 Shmuel] [24]:[6] Then they went north to Gilead and the land of Tahtim-Hodshi, before coming to Dan-Yaan and around to Tsidon (Sidon).
[2 Shmuel] [24]:[7] Then they came to the Tsor (Tyre) fortress and all the cities of the Hivim and the Kena’anim (Canaanites) before going east to Be’er-Sheva in the Negev wilderness (part of Yehudah).
[2 Shmuel] [24]:[8] So they travelled throughout the land for nine months and twenty days before returning to Yerushalem (Jerusalem).
[2 Shmuel] [24]:[9] Then Yoav reported the census results to the king: 800,000 fighting swordsmen in Yisrael (Israel), and 500,000 in Yehudah.
[2 Shmuel] [24]:[10] However, David had a guilty conscience after he’d had the people counted and he told Yahweh, “I’ve disobeyed you badly, but now, Yahweh, please take away the iniquity of your servant because I’ve been very foolish.”
[2 Shmuel] [24]:[11] When David got up in the morning, Yahweh gave the prophet Gad this message
[2 Shmuel] [24]:[12] to take to David, “I, Yahweh, am offering you three choices. You decide which one I should carry out against you.”
[2 Shmuel] [24]:[13] Then Gad asked him, “Do you want seven years of famine in your country, or three months of fleeing from your enemies, or three days of deadly disease in your country? Consider those and let me know which option to pass back to the one who sent me.”
[2 Shmuel] [24]:[14] David answered Gad, “This is very distressing, but please let Yahweh be the one to punish me because he’s very merciful—don’t let other men be the ones.”
[2 Shmuel] [24]:[15] So Yahweh sent a deadly disease to Yisrael (Israel) from the morning and until the time he’d decided. Seventy thousand people died from Dan in the north down to Be’er-Sheva (Beersheba) in the south.
[2 Shmuel] [24]:[16] When Yahweh’s messenger stretched out his hand to destroy Yerushalem (Jerusalem) with the deadly disease, Yahweh relented concerning the disaster and told the messenger who was destroying many people, “Now lower your hand.” When he said that, his messenger was near the threshing floor of Aravnah the Yevusi.
[2 Shmuel] [24]:[17] David had complained to Yahweh when he saw the messenger afflicting the people, saying, “Listen, it’s me alone who sinned, and I myself who disobeyed you. But these innocent people—what have they done? Please, just punish only me and my relatives.”
[2 Shmuel] [24]:[18] Gad came to David that day, and instructed him, “Go to the Yevusi Aravnah’s threshing floor and build an altar to Yahweh there.”
[2 Shmuel] [24]:[19] So David went there just as Yahweh had instructed him through Gad’s message.
[2 Shmuel] [24]:[20] When Aravnah looked out and saw the king and his servants approaching, he went out and fell to his knees in front of the king and bowed his face to the ground.
[2 Shmuel] [24]:[21] “Why would my master the king come to his servant?” Aravnah asked. “I want to buy your threshing floor to build an altar for Yahweh,” David answered. “So that the deadly disease afflicting the people can be stopped.”
[2 Shmuel] [24]:[22] “May my master the king take it,” Aravnah responded. “Use it in whatever way you think best. See, you can use the oxen for the burnt offering, and the threshing instruments and the oxen’s equipment for firewood.
[2 Shmuel] [24]:[23] I give it all to you, the king. May your god Yahweh accept your offering.”
[2 Shmuel] [24]:[24] “No,” the king answered. “I’ll definitely buy it from you. I couldn’t offer something to my god Yahweh that cost me nothing.”
[2 Shmuel] [24]:[25] So David built an altar there to Yahweh, and he instructed for burnt offerings and peace offerings to be made. Then Yahweh accepted prayers for the country and the deadly disease afflicting Yisrael (Israel) was stopped.

[1 Kings] [3]:[13] So I’ve also given you what you didn’t request: both riches and honour—there’ll be no other king like you for as long as you live,

[1 Kings] [3]:[18] Three days later, this woman also gave birth to her baby. Only the two of us were there in the house—no one else was around.
[1 Kings] [3]:[19] But then in the night, her son died because she rolled over onto him.
[1 Kings] [3]:[20] So she got up in the middle of the night and took my son from beside me, as your female servant was asleep. She left her dead son with me, and took my son to her bed.
[1 Kings] [3]:[21] When I woke up in the morning ready to breastfeed my son, to my horror he was dead. However when I examined him closely in the light, more shock, it wasn’t actually my son!”
[1 Kings] [3]:[22] “No, my son is the living one,” the other woman said, “and your son is the dead one.” “No, your son is the dead one,” the first woman countered, “and my son is the living one!” Then they continued to argue in front of the king.
[1 Kings] [3]:[23] The king spoke, “So both of you are claiming that your baby is the one that’s alive and that the dead one belongs to the other.”
[1 Kings] [3]:[24] Then he ordered, “Get me a sword.” So they brought a sword to the king.
[1 Kings] [3]:[25] Then the king commanded, “Cut the living child into two pieces and give them half each.”
[1 Kings] [3]:[26] But the mother of the surviving baby felt compassion for her son and yelled, “Please, my master, give the baby to her—you certainly mustn’t kill him!” Meanwhile the other woman was saying, “Well then, neither of us will have him. Cut him in half!”
[1 Kings] [3]:[27] The king spoke up, “Don’t harm the baby. Give the living child to the first woman—she’s his mother.”
[1 Kings] [3]:[28] All Yisrael (Israel) eventually heard about this case that the king had judged, and they felt an awesome respect for him because they saw that he had God’s wisdom to do justice within him.
[1 Kings] [4]:[1] So Shelomoh (Solomon) was king over all Yisrael (Israel),
[1 Kings] [4]:[2] and these were his officials: Tsadok’s son Azaryah was the priest.
[1 Kings] [4]:[3] Shisha’s sons Elihoref and Ahiyah were secretaries. Ahilud’s son Yehoshafat (Jehoshaphat) was the recorder.
[1 Kings] [4]:[4] Yehoyada’s son Benayah was the army commander. Tsadok and Evyatar were priests.
[1 Kings] [4]:[5] Natan’s (Nathan) son Azaryah was supervisor of the governors, and his son Zavud was a priest and adviser to the king.
[1 Kings] [4]:[6] Ahishar was in charge of the palace, and Avda’s son Adoniram supervised the forced labourers.
[1 Kings] [4]:[7] Shelomoh (Solomon) appointed twelve governors over all Yisrael (Israel), and they sent in food for the palace—each governor was responsible for one month of the year.
[1 Kings] [4]:[8] Their names were: Ben-Hur in the hill country of Efrayim (Ephraim),
[1 Kings] [4]:[9] Ben-Deker in Makats, Sha’alvim, Beyt-Shemesh (Heliopolis), and Elon-Beyt-Hanan,
[1 Kings] [4]:[10] Ben-Hesed in Arubot, Sokoh, and all the land of Hefer,
[1 Kings] [4]:[11] Ben-Avinadav (who was married to Shelomoh’s daughter Tafat) in Nafat-Dor,
[1 Kings] [4]:[12] Ahilud’s son Ba’ana in Ta’anak and Megidon and all Beyt-Shean next to Tseretan below Yizre’el (Jezreel), from Beyt-Shean to Avel-Meholah, as far as the other side of Yakemeam,
[1 Kings] [4]:[13] Ben-Gever in Ramot-Gilead, including the villages of Menasheh’s (Manasseh) son Yair that were in Gilead, as well as the Argov area in the Bashan region, and including sixty large cities with walls and bronze gate bars.
[1 Kings] [4]:[14] Ido’s son Ahinadav in Mahanayim.
[1 Kings] [4]:[15] Ahima’ats (who had married Shelomoh’s daughter Basemat) in Naftali (Naphtali),
[1 Kings] [4]:[16] Hushay’s son Ba’ana in Asher and Be’alot,
[1 Kings] [4]:[17] Paruah’s son Yehoshafat (Jehoshaphat) in Yisakar (Issachar),
[1 Kings] [4]:[18] Elah’s son Shimei in Benyamin,
[1 Kings] [4]:[19] Uri’s son Gever in the Gilead region, including the lands of the Amori King Sihon and King Og of the Bashan. There was also one district governor over Yehudah (Judah).
[1 Kings] [4]:[20] Now Yehudah (Judah) and Yisrael (Israel) had become as numerous as the sand on the seashore. They had plenty to eat and drink and they were contented.
[1 Kings] [4]:[21] Shelomoh (Solomon) controlled all the kingdoms from the Perat (Euphrates) River to the land of the Pelishtim and as far as the Mitsri (Egyptian) border, so they brought tribute to him and followed his orders during his lifetime.
[1 Kings] [4]:[22] The daily requirements for the palace included five tonnes of fine flour and eleven tonnes of coarse flour,
[1 Kings] [4]:[23] ten fattened cattle, twenty pasture cattle, one hundred sheep, wild game including deer, gazelle, and roebuck, and fattened fowls.
[1 Kings] [4]:[24] He controlled all the kingdoms west of the Perat from Tifsah in the north-east to Azah (Gaza) in the south-west, and there was peace with all his neighbours.
[1 Kings] [4]:[25] So all Yehudah and Yisrael lived peacefully, from Dan in the north to Be’er-Sheva (Beersheba) in the south—everyone focusing on their own property.
[1 Kings] [4]:[26] Shelomoh had forty thousand stalls for his chariot horses, and twelve thousand horsemen.
[1 Kings] [4]:[27] The district governors provided supplies for the palace—one governor for each month. They ensured that nothing was lacking for the king and his visitors.
[1 Kings] [4]:[28] They also provided the barley and straw for the chariot horses and the other horses, delivered to the designated locations.
[1 Kings] [4]:[29] God gave Shelomoh (Solomon) wisdom and incredible understanding, and the breadth of his interests seemed without limit.
[1 Kings] [4]:[30] He was wiser than anyone in the countries east of Yisrael (Israel) or in Mitsrayim (Egypt).
[1 Kings] [4]:[31] He was wiser than anyone else, including Eytan the Ezrahi and Mahol’s son Heyman and Kalkol and Darda, and his reputation spread to all the surrounding countries.
[1 Kings] [4]:[32] He could tell three thousand proverbs and he composed over a thousand songs.
[1 Kings] [4]:[33] He could lecture on plant life from the cedars in Levanon to the hyssop that grows on walls. He taught about animals, birds, reptiles, and fish.
[1 Kings] [4]:[34] People from all around came to listen to Shelomoh’s wisdom—many having been sent by other kings who’d heard about him.
[1 Kings] [5]:[1] Then King Hiram of Tsor (Tyre) sent his servants to Shelomoh (Solomon) when he heard that he’d been anointed as king to replace his father, because Hiram had always been a friend of David.
[1 Kings] [5]:[2] Shelomoh replied to Hiram,
[1 Kings] [5]:[3] “You yourself knew David my father, and you knew that he wasn’t able to build a temple for his god Yahweh his god because of the constant state of warfare until Yahweh would allow us to defeat all our enemies.
[1 Kings] [5]:[4] But now, my god Yahweh has enabled us to have peace from all around. We have no enemy, and there’s no threat of danger.
[1 Kings] [5]:[5] So listen, I’m planning to build a residence for my god Yahweh, just as Yahweh spoke to my father David, ‘Your son who I’ll put in your place on your throne, he’ll be the one to build the house to honour me.’
[1 Kings] [5]:[6] So now, please give the command to fell cedars for me from the Levanon forest. Let my servants accompany your servants and I’ll pay your servants’ wages whatever amount you set, because you yourself know that there are no other workers who know how to fell trees like the Tsidonim (Sidonians).”
[1 Kings] [5]:[7] When Hiram got Shelomoh’s message, he was very happy and said, “Blessed be Yahweh today, who has given David a wise son to rule over that great nation.”
[1 Kings] [5]:[8] He sent this message back to Shelomoh, “I’ve received the message that you sent me and I myself will supervise everything you want including cedar and cypress logs.
[1 Kings] [5]:[9] My servants will transport them down from the forest to the ocean, and I’ll get them tied into rafts and float them to the place you specify and disassemble the rafts. Then it’ll be up to you to get them where you need them. All I ask for, is food for my family and workers.”
[1 Kings] [5]:[10] So Hiram supplied all the cedar and cypress logs that Shelomoh ordered
[1 Kings] [5]:[11] and each year Shelomoh supplied Hiram with three thousand tonnes of wheat and four hundred thousand litres of pure olive oil.
[1 Kings] [5]:[12] Yahweh gave Shelomoh wisdom just like he’d said he would, and there was peace between Hiram and Shelomoh and the two of them made a treaty with each other.
[1 Kings] [5]:[13] King Shelomoh forced thirty thousand men from all over Yisrael (Israel) to become his workers,
[1 Kings] [5]:[14] and each month he sent a group of ten thousand of them to work in Levanon. Each group would spend a month in Levanon and then two months at home again. Adoniram was put in charge of all that.
[1 Kings] [5]:[15] Shelomoh also forced eighty thousand men to cut stones in the hill country and seventy thousand men to haul loads.
[1 Kings] [5]:[16] Then besides Shelomoh’s chief officers who were in charge of the work, there were another three thousand three hundred supervisors of the workers.
[1 Kings] [5]:[17] The king commanded them to quarry large, valuable blocks of dressed stone for the temple foundations.
[1 Kings] [5]:[18] Shelomoh’s and Hiram’s workers and the Givlim shaped the stones and prepared the timber for building the temple.
[1 Kings] [6]:[1] So it was that four hundred and eighty years after the Israelis left Mitsrayim (Egypt), in the second month of the fourth year of Shelomoh’s (Solomon) reign over Yisrael (Israel), he began the construction of Yahweh’s residence.
[1 Kings] [6]:[2] It would be twenty-seven metres long, nine metres wide, and fourteen metres high.
[1 Kings] [6]:[3] The five-metre wide porch on the front was the same length as the temple width, so nine metres long.
[1 Kings] [6]:[4] The window openings narrowed towards the outer edge of the wall.
[1 Kings] [6]:[5] Against the outside of the back wall and the two sides, he built three-storey (but lower than the wall) side rooms.
[1 Kings] [6]:[6] The lowest level was just over two metres wide, the middle level was half a metre wider, and the top level the same again (because the temple wall got thinner as it went up). The temple walls had ledges built into them for the beams to sit on, so they wouldn’t have to go through the walls.
[1 Kings] [6]:[7] While the temple was being built, all of the huge stones were dressed at the quarry site, so there was no noise from any hammer or axe or iron tool at the construction site.
[1 Kings] [6]:[8] The entrance to the bottom level of siderooms was on the south side of the temple, then from there, stairs went up to the middle level, and more stairs to the top level.
[1 Kings] [6]:[9] So he built the temple walls, then it was roofed with cedar beams and planks,
[1 Kings] [6]:[10] and he built the siderooms—each level just over two metres high and attached to the temple with cedar beams.
[1 Kings] [6]:[11] Then Yahweh had this message sent to Shelomoh (Solomon),
[1 Kings] [6]:[12] “This residence that you’re building, if you comply with my regulations and follow my judgements and obey all my commands, then I’ll ensure that everything I promised your father David will come to pass.
[1 Kings] [6]:[13] I will live among you Israelis and I’ll never abandon my people Yisrael (Israel).”
[1 Kings] [6]:[14] So Shelomoh (Solomon) finished the construction of the temple,
[1 Kings] [6]:[15] and on the inside he made walls of cedar boards. The floor was made with cypress boards, and the walls were panelled from the floor to the ceiling.
[1 Kings] [6]:[16] Inside the temple, nine metres at the rear were closed off to make an inner room called ‘the very holy place’. That too had walls made of cedar boards.
[1 Kings] [6]:[17] That left the main temple room as eighteen metres long,
[1 Kings] [6]:[18] and it had cedar boards on the walls decorated with carvings of buds and flowers in blossom. All the internal walls were covered with cedar so none of the large stones were visible.
[1 Kings] [6]:[19] The inner room at the back was to house the box containing Yahweh’s agreement,
[1 Kings] [6]:[20] and the room (nine metres long and wide and high) was overlaid with pure gold and equipped with an incense altar overlaid with cedar.
[1 Kings] [6]:[21] Then Shelomoh overlaid the main room with pure gold, and he hung gold chains crossing across the entrance to the inner room that was overlaid with gold.
[1 Kings] [6]:[22] He overlaid the interior of the entire temple with gold until it was all finished, including overlaying the altar belonging to the inner room with gold.
[1 Kings] [6]:[23] In the inner room, he made two winged creatures that were five metres high and made of olive wood.
[1 Kings] [6]:[24] Each wing was over two metres long, giving each one a total wingspan of four and a half metres.
[1 Kings] [6]:[25] Both creatures were the same size and shape,
[1 Kings] [6]:[26] and they were both five metres high.
[1 Kings] [6]:[27] The two winged creatures were placed across the inner room where their wingtips touched each other in the centre and their outer wings touched the walls.
[1 Kings] [6]:[28] Both of the wooden carvings were overlaid with gold.
[1 Kings] [6]:[29] He had all the interior walls of the temple engraved with winged creatures and palm trees and flowers in bloom,
[1 Kings] [6]:[30] and he overlaid the floor of both rooms with gold.
[1 Kings] [6]:[31] He made doors and doorposts for the inner room with olive wood,
[1 Kings] [6]:[32] and both doors were decorated with carvings of winged creatures and palm trees and flowers in bloom, then they were overlaid with gold that was hammered over the carvings.
[1 Kings] [6]:[33] He made the doorposts for the main temple entrance with olive wood,
[1 Kings] [6]:[34] and the two folding doors themselves each had two folding sections made of cypress.
[1 Kings] [6]:[35] These doors were also decorated with carvings of winged creatures and palm trees and flowers in bloom, and then overlaid with gold smoothed down over the carvings.
[1 Kings] [6]:[36] He built the inner courtyard with three rows of dressed stones and a row of cedar beams.
[1 Kings] [6]:[37] The foundation for Yahweh’s residence was laid in the second month of the fourth year of Shelomoh’s (Solomon) reign,
[1 Kings] [6]:[38] and it was completed in the eighth month of his eleventh year—meeting all his specifications and requirements. So it took over seven years to build it.
[1 Kings] [7]:[1] Shelomoh (Solomon) also spent thirteen years getting his own palace finished.
[1 Kings] [7]:[2] He built the ‘Levanon Forest Hall’ that was forty-six metres long, twenty-three metres wide, and fourteen metres high, with four rows of cedar pillars and cedar beams sitting across the pillars.
[1 Kings] [7]:[3] It was roofed with cedar boards on forty-five supports set out into three rows of fifteen.
[1 Kings] [7]:[4] There were three rows of window gaps arranged in sets of three.
[1 Kings] [7]:[5] All the entrances and doorposts were made with wood planed with square sides, and they were arranged in sets of three.
[1 Kings] [7]:[6] He made his covered porch with pillars. It was twenty-three metres long and fourteen metres wide.
[1 Kings] [7]:[7] He made a hall for his throne where he would judge cases—called ‘The Judgement Hall’. It was covered with cedar from floor to ceiling.
[1 Kings] [7]:[8] His actual residence behind the hall was constructed in a similar way. Shelomoh (Solomon) also built a house for his wife who was Par’oh’s (Pharaoh) daughter.
[1 Kings] [7]:[9] All these buildings were constructed with expensive stones that had been cut to size and trimmed with saws inside and out. They went from the foundation up to the eaves, and from the outside across to the great courtyard.
[1 Kings] [7]:[10] These large, costly stones in the foundations were cut in two sizes, with the largest almost five metres long.
[1 Kings] [7]:[11] On top of those were other costly stones of various sizes, and then cedar beams.
[1 Kings] [7]:[12] The largest courtyard had three rows of dressed stones and one row of cedar beams, as did the inner temple courtyard and the palace hall.
[1 Kings] [7]:[13] King Shelomoh (Solomon) sent for a craftsman in Tsor (Tyre) called Huram.
[1 Kings] [7]:[14] His mother was a widow with Naftali (Naphtali) ancestry, and his father had been a bronze engraver in Tsor. He was very knowledgeable and skilled in everything to do with bronze, and so he came to work for King Shelomoh.
[1 Kings] [7]:[15] He cast two hollow bronze pillars—each being just over eight metres tall and measuring over five metres around.
[1 Kings] [7]:[16] Then he made two decorative bronze caps for those pillars—each over two metres high.
[1 Kings] [7]:[17] To hang over them, he made ornamental chains and wreaths—seven sets over the cap on each pillar.
[1 Kings] [7]:[18] Then he made two rows of decorative bronze pomegranates to go around each of the two caps.
[1 Kings] [7]:[19] The two caps were each shaped like lilies that were nearly two metres high
[1 Kings] [7]:[20] and there were two hundred bronze pomegranates in rows around each cap. NEED A DIAGRAM
[1 Kings] [7]:[21] Huram stood the two pillars at the temple entrance porch. (The left pillar got nicknamed ‘Yakin’ and the one on the right, ‘Boaz’.)
[1 Kings] [7]:[22] The two bronze caps shaped like lilies were placed on top of the pillars and so the pillar construction was completed.
[1 Kings] [7]:[23] Huram also cast a very large round basin nicknamed ‘The sea’ that was five metres across (so a circumference of fourteen metres) and over two metres high.
[1 Kings] [7]:[24] Part of the same casting was two rows of decorative buds that went around it under the lip of the basin. There were about eighteen buds for each metre of circumference.
[1 Kings] [7]:[25] Twelve bronze cattle had also been cast and the large basin was sitting on their backs. The cattle were facing outwards with three facing towards each of the four compass points.
[1 Kings] [7]:[26] The basin was about 8cm thick and it had a lip around the outside like a lily blossom. It could contain around forty-four thousand litres of water.
[1 Kings] [7]:[27] Then Huram cast ten bronze carts for individual water basins. Each one was nearly two metres long and two metres wide and just over a metre tall,
[1 Kings] [7]:[28] and they had frames on the sides with panels between them.
[1 Kings] [7]:[29] There were bronze lions, oxen, and winged creatures in relief on the panels, and above and below those, wreaths were inset into the bronze.
[1 Kings] [7]:[30] Each cart had two bronze axles with four bronze wheels attached to them. At each of the top four corners, there were bronze supports to hold a wash basin, and these were also cast with decorative wreaths.
[1 Kings] [7]:[31] Inside those supports there was a round frame that protruded half a metre upwards and was inset by a quarter of a metre. It also had engravings on it inside square frames.
[1 Kings] [7]:[32] The axles were part of the main casting, and the four 70cm bronze wheels were below the panels.
[1 Kings] [7]:[33] The design of the wheels was similar to chariot wheels, but with their axles, rims, spokes, and hubs all cast from bronze.
[1 Kings] [7]:[34] Each cart had four handles as part of the casting—one projecting from each corner.
[1 Kings] [7]:[35] There was a 25cm bronze band around the top of each cart as well as supports and frames—all part of the main casting.
[1 Kings] [7]:[36] He engraved winged creatures, lions, and palm trees on the flat areas of the carts wherever there was space, and engraved wreaths around them.
[1 Kings] [7]:[37] So that’s how he made the ten carts—all the same shape and size using the same mold.
[1 Kings] [7]:[38] Huram also cast ten bronze wash basins for the ten carts—each one was almost two metres across and could hold 900 litres of water.
[1 Kings] [7]:[39] He put five basins on carts on each side of the temple (north and south of the east-facing temple), and he put the huge basin on its bronze cattle near the south-east corner.
[1 Kings] [7]:[40] Huram also made the basins and the ash shovels and the bowls. So Huram finished everything that King Shelomoh (Solomon) had requested him to make for Yahweh’s residence:
[1 Kings] [7]:[41] two massive pillars with large decorated caps and then networks of chain over the caps,
[1 Kings] [7]:[42] the four hundred pomegranates with each pillar having two strings of one hundred of them placed over them,
[1 Kings] [7]:[43] the ten carts and the ten basins on them,
[1 Kings] [7]:[44] the huge water tank and the twelve cattle supporting it,
[1 Kings] [7]:[45] and the pots and shovels and bowls and all the other containers. All the above was made from polished bronze by Huram for King Shelomoh for Yahweh’s residence.
[1 Kings] [7]:[46] The king had them cast in the clay in the Yarden (Jordan) valley between Sukot and Tseretan.
[1 Kings] [7]:[47] None of the above was weighed, because bronze was so plentiful that it didn’t matter.
[1 Kings] [7]:[48] Shelomoh also had the gold items made for Yahweh’s residence, including the gold incense altar and the gold table for the sacred bread,
[1 Kings] [7]:[49] the ten pure gold lampstands that were placed five on each side of the entrance to the inner room, along with the gold flowers, lamps, and tongs,
[1 Kings] [7]:[50] the pure gold cups, trimmers, bowls, dishes, and firepans, and also the gold door sockets for the inner holiest room and the main room of the temple.
[1 Kings] [7]:[51] Finally all the work that King Shelomoh did for Yahweh’s residence was completed, and he had all the holy things from his father David, including the silver and the gold and the containers, taken into the storerooms of the temple.
[1 Kings] [8]:[1] So Shelomoh (Solomon) assembled the Israeli leaders, and the tribal and clan heads, in Yerushalem (Jerusalem) to celebrate the arrival of the box containing Yahweh’s agreement coming from David’s city, i.e., Tsiyon (Zion).
[1 Kings] [8]:[2] This all happened during the Celebration in Shelters in the seventh month of Etanim.
[1 Kings] [8]:[3] The Israeli elders and the priests lifted the sacred box
[1 Kings] [8]:[4] and carried it to the temple. Other priests and Levites brought all the sacred objects from the sacred tent.
[1 Kings] [8]:[5] King Shelomoh and all the Israelis who were there, walked ahead of the box, sacrificing more sheep and cattle than could be counted, because there were so many.
[1 Kings] [8]:[6] Then the priests brought the box containing the agreement into the inner room in the temple (the very holy place), and placed it beneath the wings of the two wooden winged creatures,
[1 Kings] [8]:[7] The two creatures had their wings stretched out and touching in the middle of the room where the sacred box was placed, so their wings covered over the top of the box and its carrying poles.
[1 Kings] [8]:[8] The poles were very long and the ends of them could be seen from the entrance to that inner room, but otherwise they couldn’t be seen from the outside, and they’re still there to this day.
[1 Kings] [8]:[9] There was nothing in the box except for the two stone slabs that Mosheh (Moses) had put inside at Mt. Sinay (also called Horev) where Yahweh made the agreement with the Israelis after he’d brought them out of Mitsrayim (Egypt).
[1 Kings] [8]:[10] When the priests came back out of the holy place, a cloud filled Yahweh’s residence
[1 Kings] [8]:[11] and the priests were unable to stand to minister because of the cloud, because Yahweh’s presence had filled his temple.
[1 Kings] [8]:[12] Then Shelomoh (Solomon) said, “Yahweh stated that he would dwell in the cloudy darkness.
[1 Kings] [8]:[13] Actually, I’ve built a raised house for you—where you can live forever.”
[1 Kings] [8]:[14] Then while all the people stood there, the king turned around and pronounced a blessing on all Yisrael (Israel),
[1 Kings] [8]:[15] saying, “Blessed is Yahweh, the god of Yisrael, who spoke audibly to my father David, and then put into action the promise he’d given,
[1 Kings] [8]:[16] ‘From the day when I brought my people Yisrael out of Mitsrayim (Egypt), I didn’t choose a city from among all the tribes of Yisrael to build a house in so that my name would be established there. Instead I chose David to lead my people Yisrael.’ ”
[1 Kings] [8]:[17] Shelomoh (Solomon) continued, “My father David wanted to build a temple to confirm Yahweh’s power and authority here.
[1 Kings] [8]:[18] However, Yahweh told him that it was good that he wanted to build a temple for him,
[1 Kings] [8]:[19] however he wouldn’t be the one to build it, because it would be his biological son who would do it.
[1 Kings] [8]:[20] Now Yahweh has put his promise into action, and I’m here now having succeeded my father David—sitting on Yisrael’s throne just as Yahweh said, and I’ve been the one to build the residence for Yisrael’s god Yahweh.
[1 Kings] [8]:[21] I’ve included a place for the box containing the two stone tablets with the agreement that Yahweh made with our ancestors when he brought them out of Mitsrayim.”
[1 Kings] [8]:[22] Then Shelomoh (Solomon) stood between Yahweh’s altar and all the gathered Israelis, and held his arms up towards the sky
[1 Kings] [8]:[23] and prayed, “Yahweh, the god of Yisrael (Israel), there’s no god like you in the heavens above or here on the earth below, keeping the agreement and showing loyal affection to your servants, the ones who serve you with honest devotion.
[1 Kings] [8]:[24] You have done what you told your servant David, my father, that you said you’d do—you said it with your mouth and then put it into action with your hands as we can see today.
[1 Kings] [8]:[25] Now, Yahweh, the god of Yisrael, do the other things for your servant David my father, when you told him that there’ll always be one of his descendants on Yisrael’s throne, provided they follow you like he did.
[1 Kings] [8]:[26] So now, God of Yisrael, show that you’re faithful to do what you say, by doing what you told your servant David, my father.
[1 Kings] [8]:[27] “But would God really reside on the earth? The sky and the heavens aren’t big enough for you so how could this building I’ve constructed contain you?
[1 Kings] [8]:[28] But still, please give attention to your servant’s prayer and my request for favour, Yahweh my god. Please listen to my humble prayer that your servant is praying to you today
[1 Kings] [8]:[29] that your eyes be on this house night and day—the place that you’ve said will be associated with your name. May you answer the prayers that your servant will pray towards this place.
[1 Kings] [8]:[30] Listen to your servant’s plea for favour, and the prayers that your people Yisrael will pray toward this place. Keep listening from where you live in the heavens, and hear and forgive.
[1 Kings] [8]:[31] “When someone is accused of sinning against his neighbour and says on oath that the accusation is false, and makes that oath in front of your altar here in this temple,
[1 Kings] [8]:[32] then you should listen from the heavens and judge your people Yisrael, so that wicked people will be condemned and bear the appropriate punishment, and innocent people should be declared not guilty and dealt with appropriately.
[1 Kings] [8]:[33] When your people Yisrael are defeated by an enemy because they’ve sinned against you, and they turn back to you and confess your name and pray, and plead for favour toward you in this temple,
[1 Kings] [8]:[34] then you should listen from the heavens and forgive the sin of your people Yisrael, and bring them back to this land that you gave to our ancestors.
[1 Kings] [8]:[35] “Or when the rain is held back in the sky because your people have sinned against you, and then they pray towards this place and acknowledge you and turn away from the disobedience that caused the problem,
[1 Kings] [8]:[36] then listen to them from the heavens and forgive the sin of your servants and your people Yisrael, because you’ll direct them towards the right way to conduct themselves. Then you’ll send rain onto your land that you gave to your people as an inheritance.
[1 Kings] [8]:[37] “Suppose that there was a drought in the land, or diseases like blight or mildew, or swarms of locusts or grasshoppers, or if an enemy besieges them in a gated city, or some other trouble or calamity,
[1 Kings] [8]:[38] then if anyone from your people Yisrael who knows about their own disobedience would spread out their palms toward this temple,
[1 Kings] [8]:[39] then listen to them from your heavenly abode and forgive their sin, and give them what they need. You and you alone are the only one who knows what’s inside a human heart.
[1 Kings] [8]:[40] Then the people will want to obey you as long as they’re alive here in the land that you gave to our ancestors.
[1 Kings] [8]:[41] “Also the foreigners who are not descendants of Yisrael and who came from distant countries because of your reputation
[1 Kings] [8]:[42] (when they heard about your nature and saw your power in action), and they come and pray toward this temple,
[1 Kings] [8]:[43] then listen to them from your abode in the heavens and do what that foreigner begged of you, so that all the countries will know your reputation and respect you like your people Yisrael do. Then they’ll know that your authority is connected with this residence that I’ve built.
[1 Kings] [8]:[44] “When your people go out to battle against the enemy, and on the road where you sent them they pray to you Yahweh, in this city that you’ve chosen, with this house that I’ve built for your honour,
[1 Kings] [8]:[45] Then listen from the heavens to their prayer and their request, and help their situation.
[1 Kings] [8]:[46] “If they disobey you (because everyone sins) and you’re angry with them and cause them to be defeated by their enemies, and then they get taken prisoner and led away to the enemy’s country (even a far away country),
[1 Kings] [8]:[47] and then they have a change of mind in the land where they were taken to as captives, and while they’re still living in that land, they turn back and beg for your favour and confess, ‘We’ve disobeyed and done wrong—we’ve behaved wickedly,’
[1 Kings] [8]:[48] and they return to you with all their hearts and all their souls in the land of their enemies where they were taken captive, and they pray to you toward the direction of their country which you gave to their fathers, the city that you chose, and the residence that I’ve built for your honour,
[1 Kings] [8]:[49] then listen to their prayers and requests from your abode in the heavens, and help their situation.
[1 Kings] [8]:[50] Forgive your people who’ve disobeyed you and forgive the wicked things that they’ve done. Help their captors to be compassionate to them,
[1 Kings] [8]:[51] because they’re your people and your special possession who you brought out from Mitsrayim (Egypt)—from the middle of the iron-smelting furnace.
[1 Kings] [8]:[52] “May you notice the plea for favour from your servant and from your people Yisrael (Israel)—to listen to them in all their crying out to you.
[1 Kings] [8]:[53] Because you yourself separated them for yourself as a special possession out of all the people groups in the world, just as you said through your servant Mosheh (Moses) when you brought our ancestors out from Mitsrayim, my master Yahweh.”
[1 Kings] [8]:[54] Once Shelomoh (Solomon) was finished praying this prayer and request for favour to Yahweh, he stood up from bowing on his knees with his palms spread out toward the heavens in front of Yahweh’s altar,
[1 Kings] [8]:[55] then stood there and blessed all the Israeli people, saying,
[1 Kings] [8]:[56] “Blessed be Yahweh, who has given peace to his people Yisrael (Israel) like he said he would. He didn’t fail to do even one part out of all the good things that he told his servant Mosheh (Moses) that he’d do.
[1 Kings] [8]:[57] May our god Yahweh be with us, just as he was with our ancestors. May he not leave us or abandon us,
[1 Kings] [8]:[58] help us to want to follow him and walk on all his paths and obey his commands and statutes and judgements that he gave our ancestors.
[1 Kings] [8]:[59] May this prayer of mine pleading for Yahweh’s favour, be remembered by our god Yahweh day and night—to protect both his servant and his people Yisrael as each day requires,
[1 Kings] [8]:[60] so that all the people groups in the worlds would know that Yahweh is the god—there’s no other besides him.
[1 Kings] [8]:[61] And you people, may your purpose be to completely follow our god Yahweh, by obeying his statutes, and by keeping his commands like you’re doing today.”
[1 Kings] [8]:[62] Then the king and all the Israelis offered sacrifices to Yahweh,
[1 Kings] [8]:[63] and King Shelomoh (Solomon) sacrificed peace offerings to Yahweh (twenty-two thousand cattle and one hundred and twenty thousand sheep) and the king and the Israelis dedicated Yahweh’s residence.
[1 Kings] [8]:[64] On that day the king reserved the middle of the courtyard that was in front of the temple, because that was where he made the burnt up offerings and the grain offerings and the fat pieces of the peace offerings. This was because the bronze altar was too small to handle all those offerings.
[1 Kings] [8]:[65] Then Shelomoh and Israelis from all over the country celebrated in front of Yahweh at that time—people from Levo-Hamat in the far north down to the Mitsri (Egyptian) border in the far south—one week, then a second week—a total of fourteen days.
[1 Kings] [8]:[66] The next day, he instructed the people to go home, and they blessed the king, then went home feeling happy and encouraged because of all the good things that Yahweh had done for his servant David’s family and for his people Yisrael (Israel).
[1 Kings] [9]:[1] Once Shelomoh (Solomon) had finished the construction of the temple and his palace, and various other projects of his,
[1 Kings] [9]:[2] Yahweh appeared a second time to him, similar to his appearance at Giveon
[1 Kings] [9]:[3] and said, “I’ve heard your prayer and your plea for favour requested from me. I’ve declared that this residence that you built is holy by associating my name with it forever, and my eyes and my heart will constantly be there.
[1 Kings] [9]:[4] And as for you, if you’ll behave with godliness just like your father David lived with total dedication and honesty, by following everything that I’ve commanded you including keeping my statutes and my judgements,
[1 Kings] [9]:[5] then I’ll continue your dynasty over Yisrael (Israel) forever, just like I told your father David when I said, ‘your descendants will never be removed from Yisrael’s throne.’
[1 Kings] [9]:[6] If you or your descendants ever turn back from following me and don’t keep my commands and statutes, and you go and serve other gods and bow down to them,
[1 Kings] [9]:[7] then I’ll cut Yisrael off from the land that I’ve given them and from the temple that’s dedicated to my name—I’ll send them far away, and Yisrael will become an example and a laughing stock among all the other countries.
[1 Kings] [9]:[8] As this temple is on a hill and very visible, everyone who passes anywhere nearby will see it and will be appalled and will hiss and they’ll say, ‘What did the people do that was so bad that Yahweh did that to this country and to this temple?’
[1 Kings] [9]:[9] Then they’ll answer, ‘It’s because they abandoned their god Yahweh who brought their ancestors out of Mitsrayim (Egypt), but they held on to other gods and bowed down to them and served them. Therefore Yahweh brought all this calamity onto them.’ ”
[1 Kings] [9]:[10] It took twenty years for Shelomoh (Solomon) to construct the temple for Yahweh and the palace for himself.
[1 Kings] [9]:[11] King Hiram from Tsor (Tyre), had supported Shelomoh with cedar and cypress logs, and with gold—as much as he’d needed. So King Shelomoh gave him twenty cities in the Galil region,
[1 Kings] [9]:[12] but when Hiram came down from Tsor to see the cities that Shelomoh had given him, he wasn’t very happy about them
[1 Kings] [9]:[13] and asked, “My friend, what sort of cities are these that you’ve given me?” and he called the area ‘Kavul’ (meaning ‘Worthless’), which it’s still called to this day.
[1 Kings] [9]:[14] Hiram had sent four tonnes of gold to Shelomoh.
[1 Kings] [9]:[15] Now this is the matter of the forced labour that King Shelomoh (Solomon) brought up to build Yahweh’s residence and his palace, the raised terraces and the Yerushalem (Jerusalem) city wall, and the cities of Hatsor, Megidon and Gezer.
[1 Kings] [9]:[16] (Mitsrayim’s (Egypt) King Par’oh (Pharaoh) had seized Gezer and set fire to it and killed the Kena’anim (Canaanites) who had lived in the city. Then he’d given it as a wedding present to his daughter when Shelomoh had married her.)
[1 Kings] [9]:[17] Shelomoh rebuilt Gezer and lower Beyt-Horon,
[1 Kings] [9]:[18] Ba’alat, Tadmor in the Yehudah (Judah) wilderness,
[1 Kings] [9]:[19] all of Shelomoh’s storehouse cities, and the cities for his chariots and horses. They also built whatever else Shelomoh wanted—in Yerushalem, in Levanon, and in the entire area of his dominion.
[1 Kings] [9]:[20] All the remaining Amori, Hiti, Perizi, Hivi, and Yevusi people (they weren’t descendants of Yisrael (Israel)),
[1 Kings] [9]:[21] had descendants who continued living in Yisrael. These were people groups that the Israelis hadn’t been able to annihilate so Shelomoh used them for forced labour (where they remain to this day).
[1 Kings] [9]:[22] But he didn’t consign any Israelis to slavehood, because they were his warriors and servants, and his officers and captains, and the commanders of his chariots and horsemen.
[1 Kings] [9]:[23] Some were commanders of the five hundred and fifty work supervisors.
[1 Kings] [9]:[24] Once Par’oh’s daughter moved out of the City of David to the palace that he’d built for her, then he built the raised terraces.
[1 Kings] [9]:[25] Shelomoh offered burnt offerings and peace offerings three times that year on the altar that he’d built for Yahweh, and he burnt incense to Yahweh with it, and he completed the temple.
[1 Kings] [9]:[26] King Shelomoh constructed a fleet of ships in Etsyon-Gever, which is near Eylot on the shore of the Red Sea in the Edom region.
[1 Kings] [9]:[27] King Hiram sent some of his servants who were experienced sailors to serve with Shelomoh’s men.
[1 Kings] [9]:[28] They sailed to Ofir and brought back fourteen tonnes of gold that they took to Shelomoh.
[1 Kings] [10]:[1] Now the queen from Sheva had heard a report about how Yahweh had blessed Shelomoh (Solomon), and she came to test him with difficult questions.
[1 Kings] [10]:[2] She came to Yerushalem (Jerusalem) with lots of her top people, camels carrying spices and gemstones and a lot of gold. Then she went to Shelomoh and started asking him everything that had been on her mind.
[1 Kings] [10]:[3] He answered all her questions—there wasn’t any topic that he wasn’t able to shed light on.
[1 Kings] [10]:[4] When the queen from Sheva saw the extent of Shelomoh’s wisdom, the palace that he’d built,
[1 Kings] [10]:[5] the food on his table, the seating of his servants, the uniforms and the service of his waiters, and the burnt offerings that he sacrificed at Yahweh’s temple, she was totally lost for words.
[1 Kings] [10]:[6] She told the king, “Wow, everything that I heard about you back in my own country, and about how wise you are, is true.
[1 Kings] [10]:[7] I hadn’t believed it until I got here and saw it with my own eyes, but then I find that what I heard is only half of how incredible it is. Your wisdom and your goodness is way more than what I’d heard described.
[1 Kings] [10]:[8] Your men are so fortunate and especially your servants who are always standing in front of you and able to hear the wise things that you say.
[1 Kings] [10]:[9] May your god Yahweh be blessed, who was pleased with you and placed you on Yisrael’s (Israel) throne. He appointed you as king to rule them fairly and honestly because Yahweh loves Yisrael forever.”
[1 Kings] [10]:[10] Then the queen gave to king four tonnes of gold and very many spices and precious gemstones. Never again did King Shelomoh receive more spices than what the queen gave him that day.
[1 Kings] [10]:[11] King Hiram’s fleet also brought gold from Ofir as well as a lot of almug wood and precious gemstones.
[1 Kings] [10]:[12] The king used the almug timber to make railings for the temple and the palace, and lyres and harps for the musicians. Such a quantity and quality of almug wood has never again been brought in or seen in Yisrael to this day.
[1 Kings] [10]:[13] Then King Shelomoh gave the queen from Sheva everything she wanted—whatever she requested on top of what he had already given to her. Then she departed with her servants and returned to her country.
[1 Kings] [10]:[14] The amount of gold that came to Shelomoh (Solomon) in one year was around twenty-two tonnes,
[1 Kings] [10]:[15] not counting what came from explorers and traders, and all the Aravi kings, and the governors of the land.
[1 Kings] [10]:[16] King Shelomoh had two hundred body shields made from beaten gold overlaid over wood—each shield took six kilograms of gold.
[1 Kings] [10]:[17] He also had three hundred smaller shields made—each of them covered with two kilograms of gold—and placed in his ‘Levanon Forest Hall’.
[1 Kings] [10]:[18] The king had a large ivory throne made and overlaid with pure gold.
[1 Kings] [10]:[19] It had six steps going up to it and the seat-back was rounded at the top. It had armrests on both sides, then a lion on each side next to the armrests,
[1 Kings] [10]:[20] plus twelve lions standing one on each side of the six steps. There was nothing like it in any other kingdom.
[1 Kings] [10]:[21] All of Shelomoh’s cups were gold, and the various dishes in the ‘Levanon Forest Hall’ were also pure gold. Nothing was made out of silver because it was considered to be of little value during Shelomoh’s time
[1 Kings] [10]:[22] because the king had a fleet of ships that joined King Hiram’s fleet. Every three years the fleet would return bringing gold and silver, ivory, monkeys and baboons.
[1 Kings] [10]:[23] King Shelomoh became richer and wiser than any other king in the world,
[1 Kings] [10]:[24] and even people from distant countries would come to see Shelomoh to listen to the wisdom that God had given him.
[1 Kings] [10]:[25] Every visitor would bring a gift: gold containers, clothes, weapons, spices, horses and mules. This continued year after year.
[1 Kings] [10]:[26] Shelomoh acquired 1,400 chariots and twelve thousand horsemen. He stationed most of them in his chariot cities and some with him there in Yerushalem (Jerusalem).
[1 Kings] [10]:[27] While he was king, silver in Yerushalem was given a value similar to stones, and cedar timber was given a value like that of the sycamores that grow in plenty in the lowlands.
[1 Kings] [10]:[28] Shelomoh acquired horses from Mitsrayim (Egypt) and from Kue—his traders would acquire them from Kue for the king for a price.
[1 Kings] [10]:[29] An Mitsri (Egyptian) chariot went for six hundred silver coins and a horse for one hundred and fifty. Then they’d export them again to the Hiti and Aramean kings.
[1 Kings] [11]:[1] Now King Shelomoh (Solomon) loved many foreign women—besides Par’oh’s (Pharaoh) daughter there were Moavi women, Amoni women, Edomi women, Tsidoni women, and Hiti women.
[1 Kings] [11]:[2] They were from the nations that Yahweh had told Yisrael (Israel) about, “You must not mix with people from those nations, and they must not join together with you. They will certainly entice you to worship their gods.” However, Shelomoh clung to them for love.
[1 Kings] [11]:[3] He had seven hundred wives who were kings’ daughters, as well as three hundred slave-wives, and his wives were instrumental in his turning away from Yahweh.
[1 Kings] [11]:[4] By the time of his old age, Shelomoh’s wives had persuaded him to worship the gods from their countries—his heart wasn’t totally dedicated to Yahweh like his father David had been.
[1 Kings] [11]:[5] So Shelomoh started to worship the Tsidonim’ (Sidonians) God Ashtoret and the Amonim’ detestable God Malkam,
[1 Kings] [11]:[6] so he did many things that Yahweh had said were evil—he didn’t remain fully committed to Yahweh like his father David had been.
[1 Kings] [11]:[7] Then Shelomoh built a place to worship Kemosh, the Moavim detestable God, on a hill facing Yerushalem (Jerusalem), and also for Molek, the Amonim’ detestable God.
[1 Kings] [11]:[8] He did those things for his foreign wives who were burning incense and sacrificing to their gods.
[1 Kings] [11]:[9] Although Yisrael’s god Yahweh had appeared twice to Shelomoh, he now turned his devotion away from Yahweh, who then became angry with him.
[1 Kings] [11]:[10] Yahweh had warned Shelomoh not to follow after other gods, but he didn’t obey Yahweh’s instructions,
[1 Kings] [11]:[11] and Yahweh told him, “You have this against you: you haven’t kept my agreement and you’ve disobeyed my statutes that I gave you. So I’ll definitely tear the kingdom away from you and give it to your servant,
[1 Kings] [11]:[12] except that for the sake of your father David I won’t do it in your lifetime, rather, I’ll tear the kingdom away from your son.
[1 Kings] [11]:[13] What’s more, I won’t tear the whole kingdom away—I’ll leave one tribe for your son to rule for my servant David’s sake, and for the sake of my chosen city Yerushalem.”
[1 Kings] [11]:[14] Then Yahweh caused Hadad the Edomi (and a descendant of the Edomi king) to stand against Shelomoh (Solomon).
[1 Kings] [11]:[15] In the past when David had been in Edom with his army commander Yoav (Joab) to bury their dead, they had killed every male in Edom.
[1 Kings] [11]:[16] (Yoav and the Israeli warriors had had to stay there for six months to kill the Edomi males.)
[1 Kings] [11]:[17] However, Hadad had been a small child at that time, and he’d fled to Mitsrayim (Egypt) with some of his father’s Edomi servants.
[1 Kings] [11]:[18] They’d passed through Midyan and then Paran where they’d gained some more men before entering Mitsrayim where King Par’oh (Pharaoh) gave him a house and land, and provided him with food.
[1 Kings] [11]:[19] Par’oh took a liking to Hadad and gave him his wife Queen Tahpeneys’ sister to marry.
[1 Kings] [11]:[20] Tahpeneys’ sister gave birth to his son Genuvat, his son, and Tahpeneys weaned him in the midst of the house of Par’oh. And Genuvat was in the house of Par’oh in the midst of the sons of Par’oh.
[1 Kings] [11]:[21] When Hadad in Mitsrayim heard that both David and his army commander Yoav had died, Hadad said to Par’oh, “Give me permission to leave, and I’ll go back to my land.”
[1 Kings] [11]:[22] But Par’oh asked him, “But what’s wrong with staying here? You’ve stunned me by asking to go to your land.” “Nothing’s lacking here,” he replied, “but I have to go—please give me permission to leave.”
[1 Kings] [11]:[23] God also caused Elyada’s son Rezon to stand against Shelomoh (Solomon). He’d run away from his master, King Hadadezer in Tsovah,
[1 Kings] [11]:[24] then he’d gathered men for himself and had become a commander of a raiding band. When David attacked them, they went to Damesek (Damascus). They lived there and gained control of the city.
[1 Kings] [11]:[25] Then during all of Shelomoh’s reign, he’d been outspoken against Yisrael (Israel)—encouraged by the evil that Hadad did. He reigned over Aram (Syria) (Aram) and he loathed Yisrael.
[1 Kings] [11]:[26] Nevat’s son Yarov’am (Jeroboam), an Efrati from Tseredah also rebelled against the king. (His widowed mother Tseruah was one of Shelomoh’s (Solomon) servants.)
[1 Kings] [11]:[27] This is the background about how it started: Shelomoh had built the raised terrace and had repaired a gap in the wall of the city of David his father.
[1 Kings] [11]:[28] Shelomoh had noticed Yarov’am as a strong and hard-working young man, so he’d appointed him as supervisor over all the forced labour from Menasheh (Manasseh) and Efrayim’s (Ephraim) regions.
[1 Kings] [11]:[29] One time when Yarov’am was away from Yerushalem (Jerusalem), the prophet Ahiyah the Shiloni met him on the road. He was wearing a brand-new a new cloak, and there was just the two by themselves in the countryside.
[1 Kings] [11]:[30] Ahiyah then pulled the new cloak off his shoulders and tore it into twelve pieces,
[1 Kings] [11]:[31] and told Yarov’am, “Take ten pieces for yourself, because this is what Yisrael’s (Israel) god Yahweh says, ‘Listen, I’m about to tear the kingdom away from Shelomoh’s control, and I’ll give the ten tribes to you.
[1 Kings] [11]:[32] The one tribe will be for him, for the sake of my servant David and for the sake of Yerushalem city which I’ve chosen from all the tribes of Yisrael.
[1 Kings] [11]:[33] This is because they’ve abandoned me. Instead they’ve bowed down to the Tsidonim’ (Sidonians) God Ashtoret, to the Moavi god Kemosh, and to the Amoni God Malkam. They’re no longer following my instructions or doing what they know I’ve said is right—not obeying my statutes or my judgements like the king’s father David did.
[1 Kings] [11]:[34] But I won’t take the entire kingdom off him, but rather I’ll leave him as a leader while he’s still alive for the sake of my chosen servant David, who obeyed my commands and my statutes.
[1 Kings] [11]:[35] However, I’ll take the kingship away from his son and I’ll give the ten tribes to you to rule.
[1 Kings] [11]:[36] I’ll give Shelomoh’s son one tribe to rule so that one of David’s descendants will always rule in my chosen city Yerushalem because it’s associated with my name.
[1 Kings] [11]:[37] But I’ll use you, and you’ll be able to reign over the area where you want to rule—you’ll become king over Yisrael.
[1 Kings] [11]:[38] Then if you’ll listen to everything that I command you, and walk on the right path and do what pleases me and keep my statutes and my commands, just like my servant David did, then I’ll be with you. I’ll establish a dynasty for you just like I did for David, and I’ll give Yisrael to you.
[1 Kings] [11]:[39] I’ll make David’s descendants suffer because of Shelomoh’s behaviour, but not forever.’ ”
[1 Kings] [11]:[40] Shelomoh tried to kill Yarov’am (Jeroboam), but he left the area and fled to Mitsrayim (Egypt). He remained in Mitsrayim under the protection of King Shishak until Shelomoh’s death.
[1 Kings] [11]:[41] A record of all the other things that Shelomoh (Solomon) did, and all the wise things that he said, was written in the ‘Record of Shelomoh’s Achievements’.
[1 Kings] [11]:[42] Shelomoh reigned over all Yisrael (Israel) from Yerushalem (Jerusalem) for forty years,
[1 Kings] [11]:[43] then he died and was buried in the City of David, and his son Rehav’am (Rehoboam) became king.
[1 Kings] [12]:[1] Shelomoh’s (Solomon) son Rehav’am (Rehoboam) went to Shekem, because all Yisrael (Israel) had assembled there to make him king.
[1 Kings] [12]:[2] Meanwhile, Nevat’s son Yarov’am (Jeroboam) in Mitsrayim (Egypt) (where he’d fled from King Shelomoh) heard the news and returned to Yisrael.
[1 Kings] [12]:[3] The leaders of the northern tribes summoned him, and they all went to petition King Rehav’am,
[1 Kings] [12]:[4] “Your father Shelomoh required us to contribute too much labour. If you’ll lighten the burden on us, then we’ll serve you.”
[1 Kings] [12]:[5] “Come back in three days,” he replied, “and I’ll give my response.” So the people left.
[1 Kings] [12]:[6] Then King Rehav’am consulted with the elders (who’d served his father Shelomoh while he was alive), asking them for advice on how to respond.
[1 Kings] [12]:[7] “If you want to serve these people well,” they replied, “answer them with kindness now then they’ll serve you well in the future.”
[1 Kings] [12]:[8] However he decided to ignore that advice from the elders, and he consulted with the young men who were standing in front of him and that he’d grown up with,
[1 Kings] [12]:[9] so he asked them, “What would you all recommend that we tell the people who wanted me to lighten the burden that my father placed on them?”
[1 Kings] [12]:[10] “You should tell them this,” his young companions replied. “They’ve asked that you should lighten the load on them from what your father demanded, but on the contrary, you should tell them that your little finger is thicker than your father’s thigh bone was.
[1 Kings] [12]:[11] Tell them that your father placed a heavy burden on them, but that you’ll add to that. He punished them with whips, but you’ll punish them with scorpions.”
[1 Kings] [12]:[12] So when Yarov’am (Jeroboam) and all the leaders came back to King Rehav’am (Rehoboam) on the third day as he’d instructed them,
[1 Kings] [12]:[13] he answered them harshly—ignoring the advice of the elders at the beginning.
[1 Kings] [12]:[14] Instead he spoke to them according to the advice of the young men, saying, “My father placed a heavy burden on you all, but as for me, I’ll add to those demands. My father punished you all with whips, but as for me, I’ll punish you all with scorpions.”
[1 Kings] [12]:[15] So the king didn’t listen to the people. This change came from Yahweh so that what he’d had Ahiyah the Shiloni tell Nevat’s son Yarov’am would all indeed happen.
[1 Kings] [12]:[16] When all Yisrael (Israel) saw that the king hadn’t listened to them, the people responded, “What share in David do we have? We won’t get any inheritance from Yishay’s (Jesse) son. Go back to your tents, Yisrael. Look at your dynasty now, David.” So the northern Israeli leaders went home again.
[1 Kings] [12]:[17] However, Rehav’am continued to rule over the cities in Yehudah (Judah).
[1 Kings] [12]:[18] Then King Rehav’am (Rehoboam) took Adoniram who was over the forced labour, to go north but the people killed him by throwing rocks at him and the king had to hurriedly jump into his chariot to flee to Yerushalem (Jerusalem).
[1 Kings] [12]:[19] Ever since then, the northern tribes of Yisrael have rebelled against David’s dynasty.
[1 Kings] [12]:[20] So as soon as all Yisrael heard that Yarov’am (Jeroboam) had returned from Mitsrayim (Egypt), they summoned him to their assembly and appointed him as king over all northern Yisrael. Only the Yehudah region was left under the rule of David’s grandson Rehav’am.
[1 Kings] [12]:[21] So when Shelomoh’s (Solomon) son Rehav’am (Rehoboam) returned to Yerushalem (Jerusalem), he assembled all the tribes of Yehudah (Judah) and Benyamin, and 180,000 warriors were chosen to fight against the northern tribes to return the kingship to him.
[1 Kings] [12]:[22] But God told the prophet Shemayah,
[1 Kings] [12]:[23] “Go and tell Shelomoh’s son Rehav’am, the king of Yehudah, and tell all the descendants of Yehudah and Benyamin, and the remainder of the people, saying,
[1 Kings] [12]:[24] ‘Yahweh says this: Don’t go and fight against your Israeli relatives. Everyone should just return home because everything that happened there was initiated by me.’ ” When they heard Yahweh’s message, they took note of it and everyone went back home.
[1 Kings] [12]:[25] Then Yarov’am (Jeroboam) built Shekem in the hill country of Efrayim (Ephraim) and he lived there for a while. Then he left there and built Penuel.
[1 Kings] [12]:[26] After that, he worried that the entire country might want to go back under David’s dynasty.
[1 Kings] [12]:[27] He worried that if the people went down to Yerushalem (Jerusalem) to offer sacrifices in Yahweh’s temple, they might shift their allegiance to King Rehav’am (Rehoboam) in Yehudah (Judah) and then his life might be in danger.
[1 Kings] [12]:[28] So after getting advice, the king made two gold calves, and he told his people, “Going all the way down to Yerushalem is too far for you. Look, these can be your gods, Yisrael (Israel), who brought you out from Mitsrayim (Egypt).”
[1 Kings] [12]:[29] He set one up at Beyt-El (Bethel) (in the south) and the other one at Dan (in the north).
[1 Kings] [12]:[30] This caused the people to sin, and some people went up as far as the one in Dan.
[1 Kings] [12]:[31] He built temples on hills and appointed priests from various tribes—not just from the tribe of Levi.
[1 Kings] [12]:[32] In the eighth month on the 15th, Yarov’am (Jeroboam) put on a celebration like the one in Yehudah (Judah). He’d made an altar at Beyt-El (Bethel) and he got the priests from the hill temples he’d made to come and stand there, then he offered a sacrifice on that altar to the calves that he’d made.
[1 Kings] [12]:[33] That date of the 15th day of the eighth month was one that he’d just decided for himself, and he instituted a new celebration for the Israelis and he burnt incense on the altar as a sacrifice.
[1 Kings] [13]:[1] Then a prophet from of God came from Yehudah, taking Yahweh’s message to Beyt-El. as Yarov’am was standing by the altar to burn incense.
[1 Kings] [13]:[2] The prophet called out against the altar with Yahweh’s message: “Altar! Altar! Yahweh says this: Listen, one of David’s descendants will have a son who’ll be named Yoshiyah (Josiah), and he’ll sacrifice the priests from the hill temples on you—the ones who are burning incense on you. Yes, human bones will be burnt on you.”
[1 Kings] [13]:[3] Then he offered them evidence that what he said came from Yahweh, “Listen, that altar will be broken into pieces, and the ashes in it will spill all over the ground.”
[1 Kings] [13]:[4] The moment the King Yarov’am heard the message that the man of God had called out against the altar at Beyt-El, he called for the man to be arrested. However, the arm that he used to point to him over the altar suddenly became paralysed and he wasn’t able to pull it back.
[1 Kings] [13]:[5] Then the altar itself broke open and ashes poured out onto the ground, exactly as Yahweh had promised through that man of God.
[1 Kings] [13]:[6] Then the king begged the prophet, “Please, pray to your god Yahweh for me, so my hand will return to normal.” So the man of God interceded with Yahweh, and the king was able to use his hand again.
[1 Kings] [13]:[7] “Come home with me,” the king told the prophet, “and have something to eat. Then I’ve got a gift to give you.”
[1 Kings] [13]:[8] But the man of God replied, “Even if you offered me half of your house, I wouldn’t go with you, and I wouldn’t eat or drink in this place.
[1 Kings] [13]:[9] Yahweh already told me not to eat or drink here, and not to return home by the same road I came on.”
[1 Kings] [13]:[10] Then he left for home taking a different route from the one he’d used to come to Beyt-El.
[1 Kings] [13]:[11] Now at that time there was an old prophet who lived in Beyt-El (Bethel), and his sons had been and told him all the news about what that man of God had done that day in Beyt-El and they told him the message that had been passed on to the king.
[1 Kings] [13]:[12] “Oh, what road did he take when he left?” their father asked, and indeed his sons had noticed which road the man of God from Yehudah (Judah) had taken.
[1 Kings] [13]:[13] So he told his sons to saddle his donkey, and he rode off
[1 Kings] [13]:[14] after the man of God, and found him sitting under an oak tree. “Are you the man of God,” he asked him, “who came from Yehudah?” “I am,” he said.
[1 Kings] [13]:[15] “Come home with me and have something to eat.” he invited him.
[1 Kings] [13]:[16] “Sorry,” he replied. “I can’t go with you or visit your home, and I can’t eat or drink with you in this place,
[1 Kings] [13]:[17] because Yahweh instructed me not to eat or drink here, or to go home by the same road that I came on.”
[1 Kings] [13]:[18] Then the old prophet told him, “I’m also a prophet like you, and Yahweh sent a messenger to tell me that I should take you home with me so you can have something to eat and drink.” (But that was a lie.)
[1 Kings] [13]:[19] So the prophet accompanied him to his house and had a meal there.
[1 Kings] [13]:[20] Then while they were still seated at the table, Yahweh spoke through the old prophet,
[1 Kings] [13]:[21] and he called out to the man of God who’d come from Yehudah (Judah), “Yahweh says this: Because you have been rebellious against Yahweh and because you didn’t obey what Yahweh instructed you
[1 Kings] [13]:[22] and you’ve returned and you’ve had food and drink in the place where he told you not to eat or drink, your body won’t be buried in your home town.”
[1 Kings] [13]:[23] After the meal was finished, the old prophet saddled the donkey for the prophet that he’d brought back,
[1 Kings] [13]:[24] and he left. But on the road, a lion came across him and killed him. His corpse ended up lying on the road with the donkey standing beside it, and the lion also standing beside it.
[1 Kings] [13]:[25] Some passers-by saw the corpse on the road and the unusual sight of the lion standing beside it, and when they got to the city where the old prophet lived, they told everyone the news.
[1 Kings] [13]:[26] When the prophet who had brought him back from the road heard he said, “That will be the man of God who was rebellious against Yahweh. Yahweh must have given him to the lion, and it tore him into pieces and put him to death according what Yahweh had said would happen.”
[1 Kings] [13]:[27] Then he told his sons, “Saddle the donkey for me.” They put the saddle on,
[1 Kings] [13]:[28] and he went and found the body lying on the road, and the donkey and the lion standing by it. The lion hadn’t eaten any of the man of God’s body, nor had it attacked the donkey.
[1 Kings] [13]:[29] The prophet lifted the body and laid it across the donkey and brought it back to his city to be buried in his own tomb.
[1 Kings] [13]:[30] They wailed over him, saying, “Oh dear, my brother,” and they laid his body in the old prophet’s grave.
[1 Kings] [13]:[31] When the period of mourning was over, he told his sons, “When I die, bury me in the grave where the man of God is buried. My bones will end up beside his bones.
[1 Kings] [13]:[32] The message from Yahweh that he shouted out against the altar in Beyt-El (Bethel) will certainly happen, and against all the hilltop worship places in Shomron (Samaria).
[1 Kings] [13]:[33] Despite the man of God’s warning, King Yarov’am (Jeroboam) didn’t stop his evil ways—in fact he chose more people from across the country to become priests. Anyone who wanted to be a priest would be appointed and he would become one of the priests of the hilltop worship places.
[1 Kings] [13]:[34] Those were the sins of Yarov’am that would eventually lead to the rejection and destruction of his entire family.
[1 Kings] [14]:[1] At that time, one of Yarov’am’s (Jeroboam) sons, Aviyah, became very sick
[1 Kings] [14]:[2] and Yarov’am told his wife, “Go and get changed so that no one will recognise you as my wife. Then go to Shiloh where the prophet Ahiyah is—he’s the one who prophesied that I’d become king.
[1 Kings] [14]:[3] Take ten loaves of bread and some cakes and a jar of honey to give to him. He’ll tell you what will happen to the boy.”
[1 Kings] [14]:[4] So his wife got ready and went to Ahiyah’s house at Shiloh. Ahiyah was now very elderly and not able to see,
[1 Kings] [14]:[5] but Yahweh had told him, “Listen, Yarov’am’s wife will be coming to ask for your guidance about her son, because he’s sick. I want you to tell her so-and-so. And when she comes, she won’t be dressed like a queen.”
[1 Kings] [14]:[6] So as soon as Ahiyah heard her walk through the doorway, he said, “Come in, wife of Yarov’am. Why did you get changed like that? Now I’ve been instructed to pass bad news onto you—
[1 Kings] [14]:[7] go back and give Yarov’am this message from Yisrael’s (Israel) god Yahweh, ‘I chose you out from the people and placed you as a leader over my people Yisrael,
[1 Kings] [14]:[8] and I tore the kingdom away from David’s descendants and gave it to you. But you haven’t been like my servant David who obeyed my instructions and followed me with integrity—only doing what he knew that I approved of.
[1 Kings] [14]:[9] However, you’ve done more evil things than any of those who ruled before you. You’ve rejected me and made cast images of other gods, and have provoked me into anger.
[1 Kings] [14]:[10] Because of that, I’m about to bring calamity to your family: I’ll cause all your male descendants to die, either before or after they’ve left home. I’ll eliminate your family just like dried dung burns until it’s all gone.
[1 Kings] [14]:[11] The family members who die in the city will be eaten by dogs, and those who die in the countryside will be eaten by birds. All this comes from Yahweh.’
[1 Kings] [14]:[12] So go back home, but as soon as you set foot in the city, your son will die.
[1 Kings] [14]:[13] All Yisrael will mourn for him and they’ll bury him. He’ll be the only one of your children to be buried, because out of all of Yarov’am’s descendants, he’s the only one that Yisrael’s god Yahweh found good in.
[1 Kings] [14]:[14] In the future, Yahweh will appoint for himself, a king over Yisrael who will get rid of Yarov’am’s descendants—in fact it’s beginning to come about even now.
[1 Kings] [14]:[15] And Yahweh will strike Yisrael just like the reeds bend over in the swamps, and he’ll uproot Yisrael from this good soil that he gave to their ancestors and he’ll scatter them beyond the Perat (Euphrates), because they made their Asherah statues which provoked Yahweh to anger.
[1 Kings] [14]:[16] He will hand Yisrael over to their enemies because of Yarov’am’s sins and how he encouraged Yisrael to sin.”
[1 Kings] [14]:[17] So Yarov’am’s wife left and went home to Tirtsah. As she entered the doorway of their home, their son died.
[1 Kings] [14]:[18] Just as Yahweh had told them, all Yisrael mourned for the boy and he was buried.
[1 Kings] [14]:[19] Everything else that Yarov’am (Jeroboam) did, including the record of wars that his army fought and how he ruled, is written in the book of the events of the kings of Yisrael (Israel).
[1 Kings] [14]:[20] Yarov’am reigned for twenty-two years, then he died and was buried with his ancestors, and his son Nadav replaced him as king.
[1 Kings] [14]:[21] Meanwhile, Shelomoh’s (Solomon) son Rehav’am (Rehoboam) reigned in Yehudah (Judah). He was forty-one when he started reigning, and he reigned for seventeen years from Yerushalem (Jerusalem)—the city that Yahweh had chosen to associate his name with out of all the tribes of Yisrael (Israel). Rehav’am’s mother was Na’amah the Amoni.
[1 Kings] [14]:[22] The people of Yehudah did what Yahweh had decided was evil—in fact they made him more jealous (by worshipping other gods) than their ancestors ever had.
[1 Kings] [14]:[23] They even built hilltop temples and sacred pillars and poles on every high hill and under every large evergreen tree.
[1 Kings] [14]:[24] There were also male prostitutes associated with them, and the Israelis did the same abhorrent things as the nations that Yahweh had removed ahead of their entering the land.
[1 Kings] [14]:[25] In the fifth year of King Rehav’am’s reign, Mitsrayim’s (Egypt) King Shishak attacked Yerushalem
[1 Kings] [14]:[26] and took away the valuables from Yahweh’s temple, and the king’s palace. He took everything of value, including all the gold shields that Shelomoh had made.
[1 Kings] [14]:[27] To replace them, King Rehav’am made some bronze shields and assigned them to the officers who protect the entrance to the palace.
[1 Kings] [14]:[28] Whenever the king would enter the temple, the guards would quickly take the shields there, and when he left, they’d run them back to the palace.
[1 Kings] [14]:[29] Everything else that Rehav’am did is written in the book of the events of the kings of Yehudah.
[1 Kings] [14]:[30] Rehav’am and Yarov’am (Jeroboam) were in a continual state of war during their reigns.
[1 Kings] [14]:[31] Then Rehav’am (his mother was Na’amah the Amoni) died and was buried with his ancestors in the City of David, and his son Aviyam replaced him as king.
[1 Kings] [15]:[1] In the eighteenth year of (Nevat’s son) King Yarov’am’s (Jeroboam) reign over Yisrael (Israel), Aviyam became king of Yehudah (Judah).
[1 Kings] [15]:[2] (His mother’s name was Ma’akah, one of Avshalom’s (Absalom) daughters.) He reigned from Yerushalem (Jerusalem) for three years
[1 Kings] [15]:[3] but he disobeyed God in ways similar to his father—he wasn’t interested in following his god Yahweh completely like his ancestor David had done.
[1 Kings] [15]:[4] However for David’s sake, his god Yahweh gave Aviyam a son to rule after him—to allow Yerushalem to continue on with a flicker of light
[1 Kings] [15]:[5] because David had done what Yahweh had said was correct, and throughout his life he hadn’t deviated from what Yahweh had instructed him, except in the matter concerning Uriyah the Hiti.
[1 Kings] [15]:[6] Rehav’am’s (Rehoboam) and Yarov’am’s factions were in a continual state of war during Aviyam’s reign.
[1 Kings] [15]:[7] Everything else that Aviyam did is written in the book of the events of the kings of Yehudah, as the war between Aviyam and Yarov’am continued.
[1 Kings] [15]:[8] Then Aviyam died and was buried with his ancestors in the City of David, and his son Asa replaced him as king.
[1 Kings] [15]:[9] In the twentieth year of King Yarov’am’s (Jeroboam) reign over Yisrael (Israel), Asa became king of Yehudah (Judah)
[1 Kings] [15]:[10] and reigned from Yerushalem (Jerusalem) for forty-one years. (His grandmother was Avshalom’s (Absalom) daughter Ma’akah.)
[1 Kings] [15]:[11] Asa did what was pleasing to Yahweh, like his ancestor David had done,
[1 Kings] [15]:[12] and he expelled the male prostitutes from the country and removed all the idols made by the previous generations.
[1 Kings] [15]:[13] He also removed his grandmother Ma’akah from being queen-mother because she had made a horrid Asherah goddess, then he cut down her horrid idol and burnt it in the Kidron valley.
[1 Kings] [15]:[14] He didn’t remove the hilltop temples, but despite that he was fully devoted to Yahweh all his life.
[1 Kings] [15]:[15] He brought everything that father had dedicated, plus more of his own, into Yahweh’s temple, including gold, silver, and containers.
[1 Kings] [15]:[16] Asa and King Baesha of Yisrael were in a continual state of war during their reigns.
[1 Kings] [15]:[17] King Baesha invaded Yehudah (Judah) and fortified Ramah so that no one could pass in or out to help King Asa of Yehudah.
[1 Kings] [15]:[18] So Asa took all the remaining gold and silver from the temple and palace storerooms, and sent it with his servants to take to Ben-Hadad, son of Tavrimon, son of King Hezyon of Aram (Syria) who lived in Damesek (Damascus), to tell him,
[1 Kings] [15]:[19] “You and me have an agreement between us that was made by our two fathers, so look, I’ve sent a present of gold and silver to you. So then, break your agreement with King Baesha of Yisrael so he’ll give up on attacking me.”
[1 Kings] [15]:[20] Ben-Hadad did what king Asa requested, and he sent the commanders of his best warriors to attack Israeli cities including Iyon, Dan, Avel-Beyt-Ma’akah, and all Kineret along with all Naftali (Naphtali) region.
[1 Kings] [15]:[21] When King Baesha heard about that, he stopped fortifying Ramah and withdrew to Tirtsah.
[1 Kings] [15]:[22] Then King Asa informed all Yehudah that they were needed at Ramah. They removed the stones and timber from Baesha’s fortifications, and king Asa used the materials to build Geva (in Benyamin) and Mitspah.
[1 Kings] [15]:[23] Everything else that Asa did, and all his great works and all the cities he built, are described in the book of the events of the kings of Yehudah. However in his old age, he developed problems with his feet.
[1 Kings] [15]:[24] Then he died and was buried with his ancestors in the City of David (also his ancestor) and his son Yehoshafat (Jehoshaphat) replaced him as king.
[1 Kings] [15]:[25] In the second year of Asa’s reign over Yehudah (Judah), Yarov’am’s (Jeroboam) son Nadav became king of Yisrael (Israel) where he reigned for two years.
[1 Kings] [15]:[26] He did what Yahweh had said was evil, following his father’s behaviour and his sin that in turn, caused Yisrael to sin.
[1 Kings] [15]:[27] A man named Baesha (from the Yisakar (Issachar) tribe) plotted against King Nadav and killed him at the Pelishti city of Gibton when Nadav and all Yisrael were besieging the city.
[1 Kings] [15]:[28] It was the third year of King Asa’s reign in Yehudah when Baesha killed King Nadav, then Baesha took over as king of Yisrael.
[1 Kings] [15]:[29] As soon as he took over, he had Yarov’am’s entire family executed—not leaving a single one of them alive. This fulfilled what Yahweh had said through his servant Ahiyah the Shiloni,
[1 Kings] [15]:[30] because Yarov’am’s own sins, as well as his causing Yisrael to sin, had provoked Yahweh into getting angry.
[1 Kings] [15]:[31] Everything else that Nadav did is written in the book of the events of the kings of Yisrael.
[1 Kings] [15]:[32] King Asa and King Baesha of Yisrael were in a continual state of war during their reigns.
[1 Kings] [15]:[33] Ahiyah’s son Baesha began to reign over Yisrael (Israel) in the third year of King Asa’s reign over Yehudah (Judah), and he ruled from Tirtsah for twenty-four years.
[1 Kings] [15]:[34] He did what Yahweh had said was evil, similar to Nevat’s son Yarov’am’s (Jeroboam) behaviour and his sin that in turn, caused Yisrael to sin.
[1 Kings] [16]:[1] Then Yahweh told Hanani’s son Yehu (Jehu) to tell Baesha,
[1 Kings] [16]:[2] “I took a nobody and promoted you to leader over my people Yisrael, yet you followed Yarov’am’s behaviour and provoked me to anger by causing my people Yisrael to sin,
[1 Kings] [16]:[3] so now I’ll get rid of you and your family—I’ll do the same to you that I did to Yarov’am and his family.
[1 Kings] [16]:[4] The bodies of those in your family who die in the city will be eaten by dogs, and those who die in the countryside will be eaten by vultures.
[1 Kings] [16]:[5] Everything else that Baesha did is written in the book of the events of the kings of Yisrael.
[1 Kings] [16]:[6] When Baesha died he was buried in Tirtsah, and his son Elah replaced him as king.
[1 Kings] [16]:[7] Yahweh sent that message via Hanani the prophet’s son Yehu. It was for Baesha and his family—speaking against the evil that they’d done that had provoked Yahweh to get angry with their behaviour which was as bad as Yarov’am’s family had been. Yahweh was also angry with Baesha because he had killed all of Yarov’am’s family.
[1 Kings] [16]:[8] Baesha’s son Elah began to reign in the twenty-sixth year of King Asa’s reign over Yehudah (Judah), and he ruled from Tirtsah for two years.
