[1 Kings] [16]:[9] However, his servant Zimri who was the commander of half of the chariots conspired against him. Once when Elah was in Tirtsah getting himself drunk at the house of Artsah (who was in charge of the palace),
[1 Kings] [16]:[10] Zimri went in and attacked and killed him, and took over his place as king. (That was in the twenty-seventh year of King Asa’s reign over Yehudah.)
[1 Kings] [16]:[11] As soon as Zimri took over and sat on his throne, he had all of Baesha’s family executed—he didn’t leave a single male or relative or friend.
[1 Kings] [16]:[12] In that way, Zimri eliminated all of Baesha’s descendants just as Yahweh had said via the prophet Yehu (Jehu)
[1 Kings] [16]:[13] concerning all of Baesha’s sins and the sins of his son Elah, and because they caused Yisrael (Israel) to sin by provoking Yisrael’s god Yahweh to get angry with their idols.
[1 Kings] [16]:[14] Everything else that Elah did is written in the book of the events of the kings of Yisrael.
[1 Kings] [16]:[15] Zimri reigned from Tirtsah for seven days in the twenty-seventh year of King Asa’s reign over Yehudah (Judah). At the time, the Israeli army were besieging the Pelishti city of Gibton,
[1 Kings] [16]:[16] and when the army camped around the city heard that Zimri had rebelled and assassinated the king, that day all the people in the camp installed the army commander Omri as king to reign over Yisrael (Israel).
[1 Kings] [16]:[17] So Omri took all his warriors from Gibton and besieged Tirtsah.
[1 Kings] [16]:[18] As soon as Zimri realised that the city was surrounded, he went into the saferoom in the palace and set fire to the building and died in the flames
[1 Kings] [16]:[19] because he’d done what Yahweh had said was evil—following Yarov’am’s (Jeroboam) behaviour including causing Yisrael to sin.
[1 Kings] [16]:[20] Everything else that Zimri did, including his rebellion, is written in the book of the events of the kings of Yisrael.
[1 Kings] [16]:[21] At that time, the people of Yisrael (Israel) were divided concerning their leadership—half of them supported Ginat’s son Tivni as king, and the other half supported Omri,
[1 Kings] [16]:[22] but those supporting Omri prevailed, so Tivni was executed and Omri remained in power.
[1 Kings] [16]:[23] Omri became king in the thirty-first years of King Asa’s reign over Yehudah (Judah), and reigned over Yisrael for twelve years—six of them from Tirtsah.
[1 Kings] [16]:[24] He bought a hill from a man named Shemer for seventy kilograms of silver, then built his capital city on it. He named it Shomron (Samaria) in honour of Shemer who’d owned the hill.
[1 Kings] [16]:[25] Omri did what Yahweh had said was evil—in fact he did more evil things than all those kings who preceded him.
[1 Kings] [16]:[26] He followed (Nevat’s son) Yarov’am’s (Jeroboam) behaviour including causing Yisrael to sin by provoking Yisrael’s god Yahweh to get angry with their idols.
[1 Kings] [16]:[27] Everything else that Omri did, including his military victories, is written in the book of the events of the kings of Yisrael.
[1 Kings] [16]:[28] Then Omri died and was buried in Shomron, and his son Ahav replaced him as king.
[1 Kings] [16]:[29] Omri’s son Ahav became king of Yisrael (Israel) in the thirty-eighth year of King Ahav’s reign over Yehudah (Judah), and he reigned Yisrael from Shomron (Samaria) for twenty-two years.
[1 Kings] [16]:[30] Ahav did what Yahweh had said was evil—in fact he did more evil things than all those kings who preceded him.
[1 Kings] [16]:[31] As if following Yarov’am’s (Jeroboam) behaviour wasn’t bad enough, he married Izevel (Jezebel), the daughter of the Tsidoni King Etba’al, then went and served Ba’al and bowed down to him.
[1 Kings] [16]:[32] He built a temple for Ba’al in Shomron and placed an altar in it.
[1 Kings] [16]:[33] Ahav also made an Asherah pole and went on to provoke Yisrael’s god Yahweh to get angry, more than any of the previous kings of Yisrael had done.
[1 Kings] [16]:[34] During his reign, Hiel from Beyt-El (Bethel) rebuilt Yeriho (Jericho) city. As they laid the foundations, his eldest son Aviram died, and when they hung the city gates, his youngest son Seguv died, just as Yahweh had told (Nun’s son) Yehoshua (Joshua).
[1 Kings] [17]:[1] One day the prophet Eliyah (Elijah) from the Tishbim in the Gilead region said to Ahav, “As Yisrael’s (Israel) god Yahweh lives, the one who I serve, there won’t be any rain or even dew these next years unless I give the command.”
[1 Kings] [17]:[2] Then Yahweh told Eliyah,
[1 Kings] [17]:[3] “Get away from here and travel eastward towards the Kerit stream that enters the Yarden (Jordan) river to hide.
[1 Kings] [17]:[4] You’ll be able to drink from the stream, and I’ve commanded the ravens to bring food to you there.”
[1 Kings] [17]:[5] So he did what Yahweh told him, and went and lived by the Kerit stream near the Yarden.
[1 Kings] [17]:[6] Ravens brought bread and meat to him every morning and again in the evening, and he was able to drink from the stream.
[1 Kings] [17]:[7] However, the stream dried up after a while because there was no rain anywhere in the country.
[1 Kings] [17]:[8] Then Yahweh told Eliyah (Elijah),
[1 Kings] [17]:[9] “Leave here and go to Tserefat in the Tsidon (Sidon) region and stay there. Listen, I’ve commanded a widow lady there to keep you fed.”
[1 Kings] [17]:[10] So he got ready and went to Tserefat. As he entered the town, he saw a woman picking up bits of firewood, and he asked her, “Can you please get me a drink of water.”
[1 Kings] [17]:[11] As she went to get it, he called out, “Would you have a piece of bread to go with it?.”
[1 Kings] [17]:[12] But she replied, “As your god Yahweh lives, I don’t have any bread at all—only a handful of flour in the jar, and a little bit of oil in the jug. See, I’m gathering a few bits of firewood so I can make a little bread for me and my son. After we’ve eaten that, then we’ll die.”
[1 Kings] [17]:[13] But Eliyah told her, “Don’t be worried. Go and do what you said, except make some bread for me first and bring it out to me. Then after that, you can make some for you and for your son,
[1 Kings] [17]:[14] because Yisrael’s (Israel) god Yahweh has told me that your flour won’t run out and your oil won’t come to an end until the day when Yahweh gives us rain again.”
[1 Kings] [17]:[15] So the woman went and did what Eliyah said, then sure enough Eliyah and the widow and her household had enough food every day.
[1 Kings] [17]:[16] The jar of flour never got empty and the jug of oil never ran out, just as Yahweh had promised via Eliyah.
[1 Kings] [17]:[17] Some time afterwards, the woman’s son got sick and then it got so bad that he died,
[1 Kings] [17]:[18] so she hassled Eliyah, “You man of God, why did you come here! Now my sins have been brought to God’s mind, and he’s caused my son to die!”
[1 Kings] [17]:[19] But he told her to bring her son to him, and taking the boy from her arms, he took the body upstairs to the room he was staying in, and laid him down on his bed.
[1 Kings] [17]:[20] Then he called out to Yahweh, “Yahweh, my god, would you really bring tragedy to this widow that I’m staying with by causing her son to die?”
[1 Kings] [17]:[21] Then three times he stretched himself over the boy’s body and begged Yahweh, “Yahweh, my god, please let this child’s life return into his organs.”
[1 Kings] [17]:[22] Yahweh took notice of Eliyah and the boy’s life returned and he revived.
[1 Kings] [17]:[23] Then Eliyah carried the boy back downstairs and gave him to his mother and told her, “Look, your son’s alive.”

[1 Kings] [18]:[1] In the third year of drought, Yahweh told Eliyah (Elijah) to go and show himself to King Ahav and tell him that it would soon rain,
[1 Kings] [18]:[2] so he went to present himself to Ahav. Meanwhile in Shomron (Samaria), the food shortage was terrible
[1 Kings] [18]:[3] and King Ahav had summoned his palace manager Ovadyah (Obadiah). (Ovadyah was a sincere follower of Yahweh.
[1 Kings] [18]:[4] When Queen Izevel (Jezebel) had tried to kill Yahweh’s prophets, Ovadyah had hidden a hundred prophets—fifty in each of two caves and kept them supplied with food and water.)
[1 Kings] [18]:[5] King Ahav told Ovadyah, “We’ll go across the country to all the springs and all the valleys that water sometimes flows in. Perhaps we’ll find some grass so we can keep a horse or a mule or two alive and not lose our breeding stock.”
[1 Kings] [18]:[6] So they divided the country into two, and they each went off in a different direction.
[1 Kings] [18]:[7] While Ovadyah was on a path, Eliyah came to meet him. Ovadyah recognised him and fell to his knees with his face to the ground, and asked, “Is it really you, my master Eliyah?”
[1 Kings] [18]:[8] “Yes, it’s me,” he replied. “Now go and tell your master that I’m here.”
[1 Kings] [18]:[9] “How have I sinned,” Ovadyah responded, “that you’re giving your servant a death sentence?
[1 Kings] [18]:[10] As your god Yahweh lives, my master sent people to every kingdom to try to find you, and if they said you weren’t there, then he made them promise under oath that it was true.
[1 Kings] [18]:[11] So now you tell me to tell my master that you’re here,
[1 Kings] [18]:[12] but as soon as I leave you, Yahweh’s spirit will take you to goodness knows where. Meanwhile I’ll go and tell Ahav, and he’ll come here and not find you, so then he’ll kill me, even though I’ve been trying to obey Yahweh since I was young.
[1 Kings] [18]:[13] Haven’t you heard, my master, what I did when Izevel (Jezebel) was killing Yahweh’s prophets and I hid a hundred of them in two caves and kept them supplied with food and water?
[1 Kings] [18]:[14] Yet now you’re trying to get me killed by telling my master that he’ll find you here.”
[1 Kings] [18]:[15] “As Commander-in-chief Yahweh lives—the one I serve,” Eliyah (Elijah) replied, “I’ll definitely be here to see him today.”
[1 Kings] [18]:[16] So Ovadyah (Obadiah) went and informed Ahav who then came to meet Eliyah.
[1 Kings] [18]:[17] When he saw Eliyah, Ahav asked him, “Is that you—the one who causes trouble for Yisrael (Israel)?”
[1 Kings] [18]:[18] “It’s not me who brings trouble onto Yisrael,” Eliyah replied. “But rather it’s you and your father’s families who decided to ignore Yahweh’s commands and serve the Baals instead.
[1 Kings] [18]:[19] So now, get all Yisrael to go to Mt. Karmel, along with the 450 prophets of Ba’al and the 400 prophets of Asherah who Queen Izevel (Jezebel) feeds at her table.”
[1 Kings] [18]:[20] So Ahav summoned all the Israelis and the prophets to go to Mt. Karmel,
[1 Kings] [18]:[21] and Eliyah addressed the people, “How much longer are you all going to remain unsure who to follow? If Yahweh is God, follow him, but if it’s Ba’al, follow him.” But the people just stayed silent.
[1 Kings] [18]:[22] Then he said, “I’m Yahweh’s only remaining prophet, but Ba’al has 450 prophets.
[1 Kings] [18]:[23] Let them get us two bulls and they can choose one for themselves. Then they can cut it into pieces and lay them a pile of wood that they’ve set for a fire, but they can’t light the fire. I’ll do the same with the other bull, but also won’t light the fire.
[1 Kings] [18]:[24] Then they must call to their god and I’ll call to Yahweh, and the god who answers by setting the wood on fire must be the true God.” “It sounds good to us,” the people answered.
[1 Kings] [18]:[25] So Eliyah told Ba’al’s prophets, “Okay, there’s a lot more of you guys, so you choose your bull and go first and call out to your god, but don’t set fire to the pile.”
[1 Kings] [18]:[26] So they took the bull he gave them and prepared it all, and then they called out to Ba’al from morning until midday, shouting, “Ba’al, answer us!” But they didn’t hear any voice and got no answer. Then they hopped around the altar they’d made.
[1 Kings] [18]:[27] Finally at noon, Eliyah began mocking them, saying, “Call out louder because he’s a god. Maybe he’s thinking about something else, or busy with something, or travelling somewhere. Pehaps he’s asleep and needs waking up.”
[1 Kings] [18]:[28] So they shouted even louder and did their usual cutting of their bodies with knives and swords until a lot of blood flowed.
[1 Kings] [18]:[29] Midday passed and they continued raving all afternoon, but they didn’t hear any voice, and they got no answer or even any suggestion that their god was listening.
[1 Kings] [18]:[30] Then Eliyah told the people, “Okay, now come over here by me.” So all the people came over by him, and he repaired the altar of Yahweh that had been torn down.
[1 Kings] [18]:[31] He took twelve stones (the number of the sons of Ya’akov (Jacob) who Yahweh told would be called Yisrael)
[1 Kings] [18]:[32] and used them to rebuild Yahweh’s altar. Then around the altar he made a trench large enough to hold the water to water in two drums of seed.
[1 Kings] [18]:[33] He arranged the firewood, and cut the bull into pieces and placed them on top,
[1 Kings] [18]:[34] and then ordered, “Fill four jars with water and pour it on the burnt offering and the firewood.” Then he said “Now do it a second time,” and they did it a second time, and again he said, “Do it a third time,” and they did it a third time.
[1 Kings] [18]:[35] The water ran around the altar and even filled the trench.
[1 Kings] [18]:[36] When it was time to offer the evening sacrifices, the prophet Eliyah approached the altar and prayed, “Yahweh, God of Avraham, Yitshak (Isaac), and Yisrael (Israel), let it be known today that you are God in Yisrael and I’m your servant, and I’ve done all these things following your instructions.
[1 Kings] [18]:[37] Answer me, Yahweh! Answer me, so that this country will understand that you, Yahweh, are God, and that you can turn their hearts back again.”
[1 Kings] [18]:[38] Then Yahweh sent fire down from the sky that consumed the pieces of meat, the firewood, the stones, and the dirt around the altar, including all the water that had been in the trench.
[1 Kings] [18]:[39] When all the people saw what had happened, they fell onto their knees and bowed their faces to the ground, saying, “Yahweh is God! Yahweh is God!”
[1 Kings] [18]:[40] Then Eliyah ordered them, “Grab hold of Ba’al’s prophets. Don’t let any of them sneak away.” So they seized them, and Eliyah brought them down to the Kishon valley and he slaughtered them there.
[1 Kings] [18]:[41] Then Eliyah (Elijah) told King Ahav, “Get ready and have something to eat and drink, because I can hear the noise of heavy rain coming.”
[1 Kings] [18]:[42] So Ahav got ready and had something to eat and drink, but Eliyah went further up Mt. Karmel and squatted with his face down between his knees
[1 Kings] [18]:[43] and told his servant, “Go up now, and look towards the ocean.” He went up and looked and said, “There’s nothing there.” This happened seven times,
[1 Kings] [18]:[44] but on the seventh time he came back and said, “Wow, there’s a small cloud out above the ocean about the size of a man’s palm.” Then Eliyah ordered him, “Rush and tell Ahav to get his chariot ready and head down so he won’t be caught in the rain.”
[1 Kings] [18]:[45] Very soon the sky was full of dark clouds, then wind and heavy rain. Ahav kept riding and made it to the city of Yizre’el (Jezreel).
[1 Kings] [18]:[46] Yahweh gave Eliyah extra strength and he tucked his robe into his belt, and ran ahead of Ahav going into Yizre’el.

[1 Kings] [19]:[4] Then he went an extra day’s travel further south into the wilderness where he sat down under a broom bush and prayed that he might be allowed to die, saying, “This is now too much, Yahweh. Take my life, because I’m no better than my ancestors.”

[1 Kings] [19]:[10] “I’ve been very zealous for you, Commander-in-chief Yahweh,” he replied. “But the Israeli people have abandoned your agreement, and they’ve torn down your altars and killed your prophets with the sword. So here I am, left by myself while meanwhile they’re trying to kill me.”
[1 Kings] [19]:[11] Then Yahweh said, “Go out and stand on the mountain in front of me, Yahweh. Then look, I’m about to go past you.” Then there was an incredibly strong wind that hit the mountain and broke off bits of rock that then shattered. But Yahweh wasn’t in the wind, and after the wind there was an earthquake but Yahweh wasn’t in the earthquake either.
[1 Kings] [19]:[12] After the earthquake there was a fire, but Yahweh wasn’t in the fire. Then after the fire, there was the sound of a soft whisper.

[1 Kings] [20]:[1] At that time, King Ben-Hadad of Aram (Syria) joined with thirty-two smaller kingdoms and they brought their combined armies and horses and chariots and besieged Yisrael’s (Israel) capital Shomron (Samaria) ready to attack it.

[1 Kings] [22]:[11] Kena’anah’s son Tsidkiyah (Zedekiah) made some horns for himself out of iron and said, “Yahweh says that you’ll gore Aram (Syria) with these until they’re destroyed.”
[1 Kings] [22]:[12] All the other prophets were prophesying similarly, saying things like, “Yes, attack Ramot-Gilead and be successful, and Yahweh will restore it back to you.”
[1 Kings] [22]:[13] Meanwhile the messenger who had gone to call Mikayah told him, “Listen, please, all the other prophets agree together as they prophesy victory for the king. Please let your message be similar to theirs and be positive.”
[1 Kings] [22]:[14] “As surely as Yahweh lives,” Mikayah responded, “I’ll only tell Ahav what Yahweh tells me to say.”
[1 Kings] [22]:[15] When he got to King Ahav, the king asked him, “Mikayah, should we attack Ramot-Gilead, or not?” “Go ahead and be successful,” he replied, “and Yahweh will give it back to the king.”
[1 Kings] [22]:[16] But looking at him, the king said to him, “How many times do I have to make you promise that you’ll only tell the truth about me when you pass on Yahweh’s messages?
[1 Kings] [22]:[17] “Well,” he said, “I saw all Yisrael (Israel) scattered into the hills like sheep without a shepherd, and Yahweh said that they have no leaders so they should all return peacefully to their homes.”
[1 Kings] [22]:[18] “Ah,” King Ahav told King Yehoshafat (Jehoshaphat), “Didn’t I tell you that he wouldn’t prophesy anything good about me—only bad news?”
[1 Kings] [22]:[19] But Mikayah continued, “Listen to Yahweh’s message then: I saw Yahweh sitting on his throne, and all the heavenly army were standing at both sides of him.
[1 Kings] [22]:[20] Then Yahweh asked who could deceive Ahav to attack Ramot-Gilead so that he’d get killed there. Some suggested one thing and others suggested something else.
[1 Kings] [22]:[21] Then a spirit came out and stood in front of Yahweh and offered to deceive the king, and Yahweh asked him how he intended to do it.
[1 Kings] [22]:[22] He replied that he’d go and be a false spirit so the kings prophets would tell lies, and Yahweh said that that would work and told him to go ahead and do it.
[1 Kings] [22]:[23] So now, listen, Yahweh has put a lying a spirit into all these prophets of yours, and Yahweh has declared disaster on you.”
[1 Kings] [22]:[24] Then Tsidkiyah (Zedekiah) (Kena’anah’s son) went over and slapped Mikayah on the face, and said, “Since when did Yahweh’s spirit leave me and start speaking through you?”
[1 Kings] [22]:[25] “Listen here,” Mikayah replied, “you’ll find that out soon enough when you sneak into an inner room to try and hide.”
[1 Kings] [22]:[26] King Ahav commanded, “Take Mikayah to Amon, the city commander, and to my son Yoash.
[1 Kings] [22]:[27] Tell them that the king orders them to imprison this man and limit his bread and water until I return safely.”
[1 Kings] [22]:[28] “If you do return safely,” Mikayah remarked, “then Yahweh hasn’t spoken through me.” And he added, “Take note all you people.”
[1 Kings] [22]:[29] So Yisrael’s (Israel) King Ahav and Yehudah’s (Judah) King Yehoshafat (Jehoshaphat) left to go and attack Ramot-Gilead,
[1 Kings] [22]:[30] and Ahav told Yehoshafat, “I’ll go into the battle incognito, but you can wear your royal robes.” So Yisrael’s king changed into ordinary clothes before heading into the battle.
[1 Kings] [22]:[31] Meanwhile, Aram’s (Syria) king had ordered his thirty-two chariot commanders, “Don’t fight with the rank and file—only attack Yisrael’s king.”
[1 Kings] [22]:[32] As soon as the chariot commanders saw Yehudah’s King Yehoshafat, they thought to themselves, “Surely that’s Yisrael’s king.” So then they came over to attack him, but Yehoshafat yelled out,
[1 Kings] [22]:[33] and as soon as they realised that he wasn’t the king of Yisrael, they stopped chasing him.
[1 Kings] [22]:[34] But one man casually shot an arrow with his and it struck Yisrael’s king between the plates of his body armour, and he called to his chariot driver, “Turn around and get me out of the battle because I’ve been wounded.”
[1 Kings] [22]:[35] The battle carried on all that day and King Ahav was propped up in his chariot opposite Aram, however he died that evening and the blood from his wound pooled into the bottom of his the chariot.
[1 Kings] [22]:[36] Then the call went through the battle lines just as the sun was going down, “Every man should abandon the battlefield and return to his home”
[1 Kings] [22]:[37] So King Ahav died and was taken back to Shomron (Samaria) where he was buried.
[1 Kings] [22]:[38] They washed out the chariot beside the pool in Shomron (where the prostitutes bathed themselves), and dogs licked up the blood, just as Yahweh had said would happen.
[1 Kings] [22]:[39] Everything else about Ahav and everything that he did, including the ivory palace and all the cities that he had built, is written in the book of the events of the kings of Yisrael.
[1 Kings] [22]:[40] Now that Ahav was dead, his son Ahazyah replaced him as king.
[1 Kings] [22]:[41] Asa’s son Yehoshafat (Jehoshaphat) started his reign over Yehudah (Judah) when King Ahav had ruled Yisrael (Israel) for four years.
[1 Kings] [22]:[42] Yehoshafat was thirty-five when he became king and he reigned from Yerushalem (Jerusalem) for twenty-five years. (His mother was Shilhi’s daughter Azuvah.)
[1 Kings] [22]:[43] He followed his father Asa in every way in doing what Yahweh wanted—he didn’t veer away from it, except that they didn’t demolish the hilltop temples so the people were still sacrificing and burning incense at those places.
[1 Kings] [22]:[44] Yehoshafat did make a peace treaty with Yisrael’s king.
[1 Kings] [22]:[45] Everything else about Yehoshafat, including his great achievements and his battle record, is written in the book of the events of the kings of Yehudah,
[1 Kings] [22]:[46] and including how he banished the male prostitutes from the land who had remained from the time of his father Asa.
[1 Kings] [22]:[47] At that time, there was no king in Edom—a governor appointed by Yehoshafat ruled there.
[1 Kings] [22]:[48] Yehoshafat had trading ships made to go to Ofir for gold, but they didn’t go because the ships got wrecked at Etsyon-Gever.
[1 Kings] [22]:[49] Ahav’s son Ahazyah had said to Yehoshafat, “Let my servants go with your servants in the ships.” But Yehoshafat hadn’t accepted the offer.
[1 Kings] [22]:[50] Then Yehoshafat died and was buried with his ancestors in the City of his ancestor David, and his son Yehoram (Jehoram) replaced him as king.
[1 Kings] [22]:[51] Ahav’s son Ahazyah began to reign over Yisrael (Israel) from Shomron (Samaria) in the seventeenth year of King Yehoshafat’s (Jehoshaphat) reign over Yehudah (Judah), and he reigned over Yisrael for two years.
[1 Kings] [22]:[52] He followed the behaviour of his father and mother and Nevat’s son Yarov’am (Jeroboam), and did what Yahweh had said was evil—causing Yisrael to sin like they had.
[1 Kings] [22]:[53] He served Ba’al and bowed down to him, and he provoked Yisrael’s god Yahweh to get angry, similarly to everything that his father had done.
[2 Kings] [1]:[1] After the death of Yisrael’s (Israel) King Ahav, Moav (Moab) rebelled against Yisrael.
[2 Kings] [1]:[2] One day, King Ahazyah fell through a lattice in his upper room in Shomron (Samaria) and was injured, so he sent messengers to go and ask Ekron’s god Ba’al-Zevuv if he would recover.
[2 Kings] [1]:[3] But Yahweh’s messenger told Eliyah (Elijah) (from Tishbeh), “Leave here and go and meet the Shomron king’s messengers and ask them, ‘Is it because there’s no god in Yisrael that you’re all going to inquire from Ekron’s god Ba’al-Zevuv?
[2 Kings] [1]:[4] Because of that, Yahweh says that the king won’t get out of the bed that he’s lying in—he’s definitely going to die.” So Eliyah told them and continued on his way.
[2 Kings] [1]:[5] When the messengers returned to the king, he asked them, “What’s this? Why are you back here so soon?”
[2 Kings] [1]:[6] “A man came to meet us,” they told him, “and he said to us, ‘Go and return to the king who sent you, and tell him that Yahweh says this: Is it because there’s no god in Yisrael that you are sending messengers to inquire from Ekron’s god Ba’al-Zevuv? Therefore you’ll never leave that bed that you’re lying in but you’ll certainly die in it.’ ”
[2 Kings] [1]:[7] “What was the man like,” the king asked them, “who met you and gave you all that message?”
[2 Kings] [1]:[8] “He had a cloak made of animal hair,” they answered, “and was wearing a leather belt.” “Ah,” said the king. “That’s Eliyah from Tishbeh.”
[2 Kings] [1]:[9] So he sent a captain with his fifty soldiers to look for Eliyah and they found him sitting on the top of a hill. The captain called out, “Man of God, the king wants to see you.”
[2 Kings] [1]:[10] But Eliyah replied, “Well, if I am a man of God, let fire come down from the sky and consume you and your men,” and fire came down from the sky, and it burnt up the captain and his men.
[2 Kings] [1]:[11] So the king sent another captain with his fifty men and they went to where Eliyah was and called out to him, “Prophet, the king commands that you come with us right now.”
[2 Kings] [1]:[12] Again Eliyah replied, “If I am a man of God, let fire come down from the sky and consume you and your men,” and God’s fire came down from the sky, and it burnt up the captain and his men.
[2 Kings] [1]:[13] So the king sent a third captain with his fifty men. They went to where Eliyah was and the officer knelt down in front of him and pleaded, “Prophet, I beg you, be kind to me and my fifty soldiers, and don’t kill us.
[2 Kings] [1]:[14] Listen, fire came down from the sky and burnt up the first two captains and their men, but please treat my life as valuable in your sight.”
[2 Kings] [1]:[15] Then Yahweh’s messenger told Eliyah, “Go with them. Don’t be afraid of him.” So Eliyah went with them to the king
[2 Kings] [1]:[16] and told him, “Yahweh says that you sent messengers to inquire from Ekron’s god Ba’al-Zevuv, as if there’s no god in Yisrael (Israel) to ask. Therefore, he says, you certainly won’t get off that bed that you’re on because you’ll die in it.”
[2 Kings] [1]:[17] So King Ahazyah died just as Yahweh had said via Eliyah. Then Ahazyah’s younger brother Yehoram (Jehoram) became king in his place, because Ahazyah didn’t have any sons. This happened in the second year of the reign of Yehoshafat’s (Jehoshaphat) son King Yehoram over Yehudah (Judah).

[2 Kings] [2]:[2] Eliyah had told Elisha, “Now, you stay here because Yahweh has told me to go to Beyt-El (Bethel).” “By the life of Yahweh,” Elisha had responded, “and by the life of your spirit, I won’t leave you.” So they’d headed to Beyt-El.
[2 Kings] [2]:[3] Also the prophets-in-training who were in Beyt-El had gone out to Elisha and told him, “Do you know that today Yahweh is going to take your master away from you?” “I already know that,” he’d replied. “Don’t say anything.”

[2 Kings] [2]:[5] The prophets-in-training who were in Yeriho had approached Elisha and briefed him, “Do you know that today Yahweh is taking your master away from you?” “Yes, I realise that,” he’d responded. “Say no more.”

[2 Kings] [2]:[14] and he took Eliyah’s cloak and hit the river with it, saying, “Where is Eliyah’s god Yahweh?” Then as he hit the water, the river divided into two parts and Elisha crossed through the middle.
[2 Kings] [2]:[15] The prophets-in-training who were on the Yeriho (Jericho) side, affirmed, “Elisha now has the spirit that Eliyah had.” Then they came forward to meet him and knelt down in front of him as a sign of respect,

[2 Kings] [2]:[17] But they kept insisting so much that Elisha was embarrassed and he said, “Ok then.” So they sent fifty men, and they searched for three days, but they didn’t find Eliyah.
[2 Kings] [2]:[18] When they returned to Elisha (he was staying in Yeriho), he said to them, “Didn’t I tell you not to bother?”

[2 Kings] [2]:[23] From there Elisha went to Beyt-El (Bethel), and as he was going up on the road, some young men came out from the city, and started mocking him, saying, “Keep moving, baldy. Keep moving, baldy.”
[2 Kings] [2]:[24] Then Elisha turned back around and looked at them, and he cursed them in Yahweh’s name. Just then, two female bears came out from the forest and mauled forty-two of them.

[2 Kings] [3]:[1] Ahav’s son Yehoram (Jehoram) became king over Yisrael (Israel) in the eighteenth year of King Yehoshafat’s (Jehoshaphat) reign over Yehudah (Judah), and he reigned from Shomron (Samaria) for twelve years.

[2 Kings] [3]:[8] What’s our strategy? Which way should we go in?” he asked. “Through the Edom wilderness,” he replied.

[2 Kings] [3]:[10] and Yisrael’s king complained, “Oh dear, it seems that Yahweh has sent in us three kings to allow Moav to defeat us.”

[2 Kings] [3]:[12] “Yes, he receives Yahweh’s messages,” said Yehoshafat. So the kings of Yisrael, Yehudah, and Edom, went to see him.
[2 Kings] [3]:[13] But Elisha asked Yisrael’s king, “What do you and me have in common? Go and inquire from your father’s prophets and your mother’s prophets.” “No,” the king of Yisrael said. “We came because Yahweh has called for us three kings to allow us to be defeated by Moav.”
[2 Kings] [3]:[14] “As Commander-in-chief Yahweh lives,” Elisha responded, “the one who I serve, I wouldn’t be talking to you or even face you, if I hadn’t recognised King Yehoshafat of Yehudah.

[2 Kings] [3]:[18] That’s a piece of cake for Yahweh. What’s more, he’ll give you victory over Moav.
[2 Kings] [3]:[19] You’ll all attack every important city, including their fortified ones. You can chop down their fruit trees, block up their springs, and ruin their good land with stones.”
[2 Kings] [3]:[20] The next day at the time of the morning sacrifice, to their amazement there was water flowing from Edom and covering the ground.
[2 Kings] [3]:[21] By then, the people of Moav had heard that the kings had come to battle them, so they summoned everyone who could wear a sword and stationed them beside the border.
[2 Kings] [3]:[22] But when they got up early the next morning and the sun rose, from the direction where they were, the water appeared to be red like blood.

[2 Kings] [4]:[38] and Elisha returned to Gilgal. At that time, there was a drought and the prophets-in-training were sitting facing him, and Elisha told his servant, “Get the large pot and boil a stew for these prophets-in-training.”
[2 Kings] [4]:[39] One person went out to the countryside to gather herbs, and he found a wild vine, and he collected wild fruit from it—as many as he could hold in the fold of his robe. Then not realising that they were poisonous, he came and he sliced them into the pot of stew.
[2 Kings] [4]:[40] Then they served it up for the men to eat, but when they ate it, they called out, “Man of God, there’s poison in that pot!”
[2 Kings] [4]:[41] “Bring me some flour,” Elisha said. Then he threw it into the pot, and said, “Serve it up for the people to eat,” and no one was harmed.
[2 Kings] [4]:[42] One day a man came from Ba’al-Shalishah, and he brought to the man of God an offering from the beginning of his harvest: twenty loaves of barley bread, and newly-harvested corn in his sack, and Elisha said to his servant, “Give it to our people so they can eat.”
[2 Kings] [4]:[43] “How can I divide that out to one hundred men?” asked his servant. “Give them to the people so they can eat,” he replied, “because Yahweh says that they can eat and have left-overs.”
[2 Kings] [4]:[44] So he laid it out in front of them and they ate and had left-overs, just like Yahweh had said would happen.
[2 Kings] [5]:[1] Now Na’aman was the captain in Aram’s (Syria) army. He was highly respected by Aram’s king, and was promoted to a high position because Yahweh had helped Aram win many battles because of him. However, despite his military prowess, he suffered from a serious skin disease called leprosy.
[2 Kings] [5]:[2] Previously troops that had been sent out from Aram, had taken a young Israeli girl captive and she had become Na’aman’s wife’s servant.
[2 Kings] [5]:[3] One day she said to her mistress, “I wish that my master would go and see the prophet who lives in Shomron (Samaria), and then he would cure him of his leprosy.”
[2 Kings] [5]:[4] In due course, Na’aman heard and went and told his master what the young Israeli girl had said.
[2 Kings] [5]:[5] The king of Aram responded, “Ok, I’ll write a letter to the king of Yisrael (Israel) for you to take.” So Na’aman set off, taking along 70kg of gold, 300kg of silver, and ten sets of fine clothes,
[2 Kings] [5]:[6] and he took the letter to the king of Yisrael. The letter said, “Greetings. When this letter gets to you, see, I’ve sent my servant Na’aman to you so that you can heal his skin disease.”
[2 Kings] [5]:[7] However when Yisrael’s king read the letter, he tore his clothes in despair, and he said, “Do they think that I’m God who ends people’s lives and gives life to others? Why’s this person sending a man here for me to take away his skin disease? Surely he must be creating a situation so he has an excuse to attack me!”
[2 Kings] [5]:[8] Later when Elisha the man of God heard that Yisrael’s king had torn his clothes, he sent a message to the king, “Why did you tear your clothes? Please, let that man come to me so he can know that there is a prophet in Yisrael.”
[2 Kings] [5]:[9] So Na’aman came on his chariots and horses, and he stood at the entrance to Elisha’s house.
[2 Kings] [5]:[10] Elisha sent a messenger out to him to tell him, “Go and wash seven times in the Yarden (Jordan) river, and then you’ll be better and your skin will go back to normal.”
[2 Kings] [5]:[11] But Na’aman was furious, and he left, saying, “Listen, I said to myself that he’d surely come out and stand there and call on the name of his god Yahweh, then he’d wave his hand over my body and take away the skin disease.
[2 Kings] [5]:[12] Aren’t the Damesek (Damascus) rivers Avanah and Parpar better than any river in Yisrael? Can’t I bathe in them instead and get healed?” So he turned and he went off angrily.
[2 Kings] [5]:[13] Then some of his servants approached him and suggested, “My master, if the prophet had told you to do something more significant, wouldn’t you have done it? So maybe you could do the simple thing that he told you: wash and get better.”
[2 Kings] [5]:[14] So Na’aman went down to the Yarden river and dipped in it seven times like the man of God had told him to. Then his skin became clear again, like the skin of a young boy, and he was healed.
[2 Kings] [5]:[15] Then he returned to the man of God along with his entire retinue. Standing in front of him, he said, “Look, please. I know that there is no god in all the earth except in Yisrael. Now, please, accept a blessing from your servant.”
[2 Kings] [5]:[16] “By the life of Yahweh who I serve,” he responded, “I won’t take anything.” Na’aman urged him to take something, but he kept refusing.
[2 Kings] [5]:[17] Then Na’aman said, “Well if not, please, at least may we load a pair of mules with some soil to take back with us, because from now on, your servant will no longer make a burnt offering or a sacrifice to other gods—only to Yahweh.
[2 Kings] [5]:[18] However, I’ll ask in advance: May Yahweh forgive your servant when my master goes to the house of the god Rimon to prostrate himself there, and he’s leaning on my hand, and I prostrate myself in the house of Rimon. When I prostrate myself in the house of Rimon, please may Yahweh forgive your servant for this one activity.”
[2 Kings] [5]:[19] “Go in peace,” Elisha replied. After they’d gone a short distance,
[2 Kings] [5]:[20] Elisha’s servant said to himself, “Hmmh, my master wouldn’t take anything from that Na’aman the Aramean. By the life of Yahweh, I think I should run after him and take something that he brought.”
[2 Kings] [5]:[21] So Geyhazi hurried after Na’aman. When Na’aman saw a person running after him, he got down from his chariot to meet him, and he said, “Is there a problem?”
[2 Kings] [5]:[22] “Peace,” he said, “My master sent me to tell you that two young prophets-in-training arrived from the hill country of Efrayim (Ephraim). Can we please have 30kg of silver and two sets of clothing for them?”
[2 Kings] [5]:[23] “Sure,” said Na’aman. “Take 60kg,” he urged him. Then he separated 60kg of silver into two bags along with two sets of clothes, then he gave them to two of his young men to carry back for him.
[2 Kings] [5]:[24] When Geyhazi reached the hill, he sent the men back and they returned to Na’aman. Then he took the sacks that they’d brought and hid them in the house.
[2 Kings] [5]:[25] When he went back in to his master, Elisha asked him, “Where did you go, Geyhazi?” “Your servant hasn’t been anywhere,” he replied.
[2 Kings] [5]:[26] “Wasn’t I there in spirit when a man turned from on his chariot to meet you?” Elisha said to him, “Is this a time to take silver or clothing, or to take olive trees or vineyards, or sheep or cattle, or male or female servants?
[2 Kings] [5]:[27] Because of that, Na’aman’s leprosy will transfer to you and to your offspring forever.” When Geyhazi left the room, his skin had gone white as snow and he was now a leper.
[2 Kings] [6]:[1] One day, the prophets-in-training said to Elisha, “Please look, The place where we’re sitting to learn from you is too narrow to fit us all in.
[2 Kings] [6]:[2] Please, let us go down by the Yarden (Jordan) river, and let each of us cut down and bring back a log from there to make a new classroom for us to sit in.” “Go ahead,” he answered.
[2 Kings] [6]:[3] One of them insisted, “Please, say that you’ll come with your servants.” “Okay then, I’ll come,” he said.
[2 Kings] [6]:[4] So he went with them to the Yarden valley to cut down some trees,
[2 Kings] [6]:[5] but while one of them was chopping down a tree, suddenly the axe head separated from the handle and went flying into the water. The man called out to Elisha, “Oh, Master, what should I do? It’s not my axe—I borrowed it!”
[2 Kings] [6]:[6] “Where did it fall in?” the man of God asked. After the man had shown him the place, Elisha cut off a stick and threw it there, and the iron axe head rose to the surface.
[2 Kings] [6]:[7] “Now get it out,” he said, and the man stretched out and grabbed it.
[2 Kings] [6]:[8] In those days, the king of Aram (Syria) was fighting against Yisrael (Israel), and he’d instruct his servants, “Set up our camp in such and such a place.”
[2 Kings] [6]:[9] However, the man of God sent to Yisrael’s king to warn him, “Beware of passing by such and such a place, because the Aramean army will be attacking there.”
[2 Kings] [6]:[10] So the king would send messengers to the people at that place to warn them to watch and be prepared. That happened several times
[2 Kings] [6]:[11] and the Aramean king got very upset about it. He called in his servants and demanded, “Which one of you is a traitor—passing military intelligence to the king of Yisrael?”
[2 Kings] [6]:[12] “No, my master the king,” a servant answered. “It’s the prophet Elisha in Yisrael who tells their king the things that you say even in your bedroom.”
[2 Kings] [6]:[13] “Go and find out where he is,” he instructed, “and I’ll send some men there to capture him.” “He’s in Dotan,” he was told later.
[2 Kings] [6]:[14] So he sent chariots and horses and a large contingent, and they arrived there at night and surrounded the town.
[2 Kings] [6]:[15] Early the next morning, the servant of the man of God got up, and going outside he was shocked to see chariots and horses and an army surrounding the town, so he called Elisha, “Oh, my master! What will we do?”
[2 Kings] [6]:[16] “Don’t be afraid,” he said, “because we have many more than that on our side.”
[2 Kings] [6]:[17] Then Elisha prayed, “Yahweh, please enable his sight so he can see.” Then Yahweh enabled the eyes of the young man, and he was stunned to see that the hill was covered with chariots of fire and horses all around Elisha.
[2 Kings] [6]:[18] When the Arameans approached to swoop in, Elisha prayed to Yahweh, “Please, strike those warriors with blinding light.” So Yahweh struck them with blinding light just as Elisha had requested,
[2 Kings] [6]:[19] and Elisha told them, “This isn’t the right way, and this isn’t the town. Follow me, and let me lead you to the man you’re looking for.” Then he led them to Shomron (Samaria),
[2 Kings] [6]:[20] and when they’d entered the city, Elisha said, “Yahweh, open the eyes of these people so they can see.” So Yahweh opened their eyes, and then they were stunned to see that they were in the middle of Shomron.
[2 Kings] [6]:[21] When he saw them, the king of Yisrael (Israel) asked Elisha, “Should I kill them? Should I kill them, my father?”
[2 Kings] [6]:[22] “No, don’t kill them,” he replied. “Would you cold-bloodedly kill your prisoners of war? No, give them bread and water and let them eat and drink, and then they can return to their master.”
[2 Kings] [6]:[23] So the king prepared a large meal for them, and they ate and drank, and he sent them off to return to their master. After that, the Aramean troops didn’t continue their ventures into Yisrael.
[2 Kings] [6]:[24] Sometime after that, King Ben-Hadad of Aram (Syria) assembled all of his warriors and attacked Shomron (Samaria), and besieged it.
[2 Kings] [6]:[25] Being surrounded like that caused a terrible famine inside the city, until a donkey’s head would be sold for eighty silver coins, and a cup of doves’ droppings was sold for five silver coins.
[2 Kings] [6]:[26] One day as the king of Yisrael (Israel) was walking past on the top of the city wall, a woman cried out to him, “Save me, my master, the king!”
[2 Kings] [6]:[27] “If Yahweh won’t save you, how could I possibly save you?” he snapped. “Some grain from the threshing floor or some wine from the wine-pressing pit?”
[2 Kings] [6]:[28] Then he asked her, “Okay, what’s your problem?” “This woman said to me, ‘Let’s have your son and we’ll eat him today, then we’ll eat my son tomorrow,’ ” she answered.
[2 Kings] [6]:[29] “So we boiled my son and ate him, and then the next day I said, ‘Hand over your son and we’ll eat him,’ but she’d hidden him.”
[2 Kings] [6]:[30] When he heard that, the king (standing up on the wall) tore his clothes, and the people could see to their astonishment that he was wearing sackcloth underneath,
[2 Kings] [6]:[31] and he said, “May God do that to me and more, if Shafat’s son Elisha still has his head on him by the end of the day.”
[2 Kings] [6]:[32] Meanwhile, Elisha was sitting at home, joined by the city elders. The king had sent a warrior ahead of him, and before he’d arrived at the house, Elisha had told the elders, “Well now, that son of a murderer has sent an assassin to separate me from my head. Listen, when that hit-man arrives, shut the door and lean against it. His master won’t be far behind him.”
[2 Kings] [6]:[33] He was still talking with them, when, wow, the warrior was coming towards the house soon followed by the king who said, “Listen, Yahweh caused this disaster so why should I trust him any longer?”
[2 Kings] [7]:[1] “Listen to what Yahweh says,” Elisha responded, “Yahweh says that at this time tomorrow, a drum of flour will be sold for a shekel, and two drums of barley will be sold for a shekel at the city gate.”
[2 Kings] [7]:[2] “That’s impossible,” interjected the captain at the king’s side. “Yahweh would have to make windows in the sky.” “Oh, it’ll happen,” the man of God answered, “and you’ll see it with your own eyes, but you won’t get to eat any of it.”
[2 Kings] [7]:[3] That day, four men who were isolated due to a skin disease were at the city gate, and they asked each other, “Why are we just sitting here until we starve?
[2 Kings] [7]:[4] If we go into the city, we’ll starve to death in there, but if we sit here, we’ll die anyway. Why don’t we go into the Aramean army camp—if they kill us then we’ll die, but if they let us live, then we’ll live.”
[2 Kings] [7]:[5] So as it was getting dark, they went to go into the camp, but as they came to the edge of it, to their surprise there wasn’t a person in sight.
[2 Kings] [7]:[6] It turned out that the master had caused the Aramean army to hear the sounds of chariots and horses and a large army, so they’d said to each other that the king of Yisrael (Israel) must have hired the Hiti and Mitsri (Egyptian) kings to join together to fight them.
[2 Kings] [7]:[7] As a result, they’d taken off and fled in the twilight. They’d abandoned their tents and horses and donkeys—leaving the camp just as it was, and fled for their lives.
[2 Kings] [7]:[8] So those four men with leprosy approached the edge of the camp and went into the first tent, and ate and drank. Then they took some gold and silver and clothes out, and they went and hid it. Then they returned and went into another tent, and stole some stuff from that one, and went and hid that.
[2 Kings] [7]:[9] Then they said to each other, “We shouldn’t really be doing this today. It’s a day of good news, but we’ve been keeping it to ourselves. If we wait until the light of the morning, we’ll get punished for it, so let’s go now and inform the king’s household.”
[2 Kings] [7]:[10] So they went and called out to one of the city gatekeepers, and they informed them, “We went to the Aramean camp, but listen, there wasn’t anyone there, or any voices. The horses and donkeys were still tethered, and the tents were left just as they were.”
[2 Kings] [7]:[11] The gatekeepers called out, and the news was reported to the palace.
[2 Kings] [7]:[12] Although it was already night-time, the king got up and warned his servants, “I’ll tell you what’s going on here: The Arameans know that we’re hungry, so they left their camp to go and hide in the countryside, thinking that we’d go out from the city, and then they could capture us and take over the city.”
[2 Kings] [7]:[13] But one of his servants answered, “Sir, please, let us take five of the remaining horses. They’re pretty much finished anyway, like the remaining population of Yisrael (Israel), so there’s not much to lose. Let us go and investigate.”
[2 Kings] [7]:[14] So with the king’s permission, they took two chariot horses and went to check out the Aramean camp.
[2 Kings] [7]:[15] They went as far as the Yarden (Jordan) river, and were amazed that the whole road was full of clothing and equipment that the Arameans had thrown off in their rush, and the messengers returned and informed the king.
[2 Kings] [7]:[16] So the people went out and plundered the camp. Then it happened: a drum of fine flour was sold for a shekel, and two drums of barley for the same amount, just as Yahweh had said would happen.
[2 Kings] [7]:[17] The king had appointed the captain who had argued with Elisha to be in charge at the city gate, but the people trampled him there and he died, just as the man of God had said when the king had gone to his place.

[2 Kings] [7]:[20] That’s exactly what happened, because he got trampled by the rush of people at the gate and died.
[2 Kings] [8]:[1] One day Elisha spoke to the Shunamit woman whose son he’d brought back to life, “Pack up and leave here, you and your household, and go and stay somewhere else, because Yahweh’s going to send a seven-year drought.”

[2 Kings] [8]:[3] Then eventually after seven years, the woman returned from the Pelishtim’ region and she went to petition the king about her house and land.

[2 Kings] [8]:[6] So the king questioned the woman and she told him her story. Then the king appointed a court official to attend to her case, saying, “Return everything that belongs to her plus the profit from her field from the day she left until now.”

[2 Kings] [8]:[9] So Hazael went to meet Elisha and took presents with him loaded on forty camels—some of every good thing that he could find in Damesek. He went and stood in front of him and asked, “Your servant, King Ben-Hadad sent me to ask you if he’ll recover from his sickness?”
[2 Kings] [8]:[10] “Go and tell him that he’ll surely live,” Elisha answered. “But Yahweh has shown me that he’ll definitely die.”

[2 Kings] [8]:[12] “Why are you crying, my master?” Hazael asked. “Because I know what evil things you’ll do to the Israelis,” he said. “You’ll burn down their fortresses and kill their young men with the sword. You’ll smash their children’s heads on rocks, and rip open the bellies of their pregnant women.”
[2 Kings] [8]:[13] Hazael asked, “But how could your servant be in a position to do such a major thing when he’s only minor, like a dog in the palace?” “Yahweh has let me see you as king over Aram (Syria).” Elisha replied.

[2 Kings] [9]:[19] So the king sent out a second horse and chariot, and he approached and asked, “The king wants to know if you’re all coming in peace?” Again Yehu replied, “What’s that got to do with you? Turn around and follow us.”

[2 Kings] [9]:[21] “Quick, get my chariot ready!” Yoram (Joram) ordered. They harnessed his chariot and King Yoram of Yisrael (Israel) and Yehudah’s (Judah) King Ahazyah both went out—each man in his chariot. They went out to meet Yehu and they found him at Navot’s field (the Yizre’eli).
[2 Kings] [9]:[22] When Yoram saw Yehu, he asked, “Have you come in peace, Yehu?” “How could there be peace,” he answered, “when your mother Izevel (Jezebel) is serving idols and embracing witchcraft?”
[2 Kings] [9]:[23] Then Yoram swung the chariot reigns around and fled, shouting to Ahazyah, “It’s treason, Ahazyah!”
[2 Kings] [9]:[24] Yehu grabbed his bow, and the arrow struck Yoram between his shoulder blades and came out from his heart, and he slumped down dead in his chariot.
[2 Kings] [9]:[25] Then Yehu said to his third officer Bidkar, “Pick up his body and throw it out into the field of Navot, the Yizre’eli. I’m sure you remember how you and I were riding as pairs after his father Ahav, when Yahweh said this against him:
[2 Kings] [9]:[26] ‘Yesterday I saw Navot and his sons killed here, declared Yahweh, and I will repay you in this very place, declares Yahweh.’ So now, throw his body down here because Yahweh declared that it would happen.”
[2 Kings] [9]:[27] Yehudah’s (Judah) King Ahazyah saw that happen, and he sped away through the garden by a house with Yehu chasing after him shouting, “Get him too in his chariot when he starts climbing upwards to Gur near Yivleam.” So as he fled towards Megidon, he was killed there,
[2 Kings] [9]:[28] and his servants took his body to Yerushalem (Jerusalem), where they buried him in his ancestral tomb in the City of David.
[2 Kings] [9]:[29] (Ahazyah had become king over Yehudah in the eleventh year of the reign of Ahav’s son Yoram over Yisrael (Israel).)
[2 Kings] [9]:[30] Then Yehu (Jehu) came to Yizre’el (Jezreel) and Queen Izevel (Jezebel) heard about it. She painted her eyelids and did her hair nicely, then she looked down through the window,
[2 Kings] [9]:[31] and when Yehu came in the gate, she said, “Greetings, Zimri the second, murderer of his master.”
[2 Kings] [9]:[32] Yehu looked up at the window and called out, “Who is with me? Who?” And two or three servants poked their heads out windows and looked down to him.
[2 Kings] [9]:[33] “Okay,” he called up, “toss her out!” So they tossed her out the window, and some of her blood splashed onto the wall and onto the horses as she was trampled by them.
[2 Kings] [9]:[34] Then Yehu and his men went in and ate and drank, and then he said, “Now, you all better attend to that evil woman and bury her, because she’s a king’s daughter.”
[2 Kings] [9]:[35] But when they went to bury her, they could only find her skull and her hands and feet.
[2 Kings] [9]:[36] They came back inside and told him, “It’s just like what Yahweh said via his servant the Tishbi Eliyah (Elijah), when he said that the dogs would eat Izevel’s flesh just outside Yizre’el,
[2 Kings] [9]:[37] and then her body would become like dung on the ground and no one would be able to recognise her specific bones.”
[2 Kings] [10]:[1] King Ahav had seventy sons who lived in Shomron (Samaria), so Yehu (Jehu) sent letters to the leaders and elders of Yizre’el (Jezreel), and to the guardians of Ahav’s children, saying,
[2 Kings] [10]:[2] “When you all receive this letter, you’ll have the sons of your masters with you, as well as chariots and horses, and weapons within your fortified city.
[2 Kings] [10]:[3] So select the best and the most honest one out of your masters’ sons or nephews, and establish him on his father’s throne, and then be prepared to defend your masters’ family.”
[2 Kings] [10]:[4] But they were extremely frightened and said, “Listen—those two kings couldn’t stand against Yehu, so how could we?”
[2 Kings] [10]:[5] Then the man who was now in charge of the household and leading the city elders sent a message to Yehu, “We are your servants and we’ll do whatever you tell us to. We don’t plan to select a king. Do whatever you think best.”
[2 Kings] [10]:[6] So Yehu sent a second letter saying, “If you’re all on my side and ready to follow me, come and meet me at Yizre’el tomorrow with the heads of your masters’ sons.” The late King Ahav had seventy sons who were being brought up by the city leaders,
[2 Kings] [10]:[7] and when that letter arrived, they killed and beheaded all of them, put the heads in baskets, and sent them to him at Yizre’el.
[2 Kings] [10]:[8] A messenger went and informed Yehu that the heads had been brought, and he instructed them to pile them up in two piles at the city gate until the next morning.
[2 Kings] [10]:[9] In the morning he went out and stood there, and he told all the people, “You are innocent. Listen—it was me myself who conspired against my master and killed him. But who killed all these?
[2 Kings] [10]:[10] You all should know that when Yahweh says something will happen, then it will happen. He said via his servant Eliyah (Elijah) that this is what would happen to Ahav’s family, and so it has.”
[2 Kings] [10]:[11] Then Yehu killed all Ahav’s remaining family members in Yizre’el, and all his chosen leaders, and his associates and priests, leaving no survivors.
[2 Kings] [10]:[12] Then Yehu (Jehu) left Yizre’el (Jezreel) and headed towards Shomron (Samaria). When he reached the shepherds’ shearing house,
[2 Kings] [10]:[13] he met the late King Ahazyah’s brothers there, and he asked them, “Who are you?” “We’re King Ahazyah’s brothers,” they said, “and we’re coming to look after the sons of the king and of the queen mother.”
[2 Kings] [10]:[14] “Arrest them,” he ordered, so they grabbed and slaughtered them near the pit at the shearing house. There were forty-two men and none were spared.
[2 Kings] [10]:[15] Then continuing on from there, Yehu (Jehu) found Rekav’s son Yonadav coming to meet him. Yehu greeted him and asked, “Are you wanting to do what is right just like I am?” IS THAT WHAT HE WAS REALLY ASKING??? “Yes, I am.” Yonadav replied. “Great,” Yehu said. “Give me your hand,” and he gave him his hand, and Yehu pulled him up to join him in the chariot,
[2 Kings] [10]:[16] telling him, “Come with me and see my zeal for Yahweh.” So they rode together in the chariot.
[2 Kings] [10]:[17] When they got to Shomron (Samaria), Yehu killed the remainder of Ahav’s family who were there, until they were finally exterminated, just as Yahweh had said via Eliyah (Elijah).
[2 Kings] [10]:[18] Then Yehu assembled all the people and told them, “Ahav served Ba’al a little, but Yehu will serve him a lot.
[2 Kings] [10]:[19] So now, call all the prophets of Ba’al to come here—all his servants and all his priests. Don’t let anyone stay away because I’m going to make a large sacrifice to Ba’al. Anyone who’s absent will be executed.” However Yehu was being cunning in order to destroy Ba’al’s followers.
[2 Kings] [10]:[20] Yehu ordered, “Announce a special holiday to assemble and worship Ba’al,” and so they did.
[2 Kings] [10]:[21] On that day, Yehu brought in all the people, and all the servants of the Ba’al came, leaving no one out. They entered the temple of the Ba’al and it was packed full.
[2 Kings] [10]:[22] He told the wardrobe supervisor, “Bring out uniforms for all the servants of the Ba’al,” so he brought robes out for them.
[2 Kings] [10]:[23] Then Yehu and Rekav’s son Yonadav entered the temple of the Ba’al and instructed the servants of the Ba’al, “Make sure that it’s only the servants of Ba’al in here—we don’t want any servants of Yahweh.”
[2 Kings] [10]:[24] So they entered to make sacrifices and burnt offerings. Meanwhile, Yehu had stationed eighty men outside, and had told them, “Don’t let any of the ones I send you escape, or it will be your life in place of theirs.”
[2 Kings] [10]:[25] Then when he finished making the burnt offering in the outer area, Yehu told the guards and officers, “Come in now and strike them down. Don’t let any of them get out.” So they attacked them with swords, and the guards and officers threw the bodies over the fence. Then they went inside the temple,
[2 Kings] [10]:[26] and pulled the sacred posts outside and burnt them.
[2 Kings] [10]:[27] They broke down the pillar of the Ba’al, and they broke down the temple. Since then it’s been used as an out-house.
[2 Kings] [10]:[28] That’s how Yehu put an end to Ba’al worship in Yisrael (Israel).
[2 Kings] [10]:[29] There was only one of the things with which Nevat’s son Yarov’am (Jeroboam) had caused Yisrael to sin that Yehu didn’t destroy: the golden calves at Beyt-El (Bethel) and Dan.
[2 Kings] [10]:[30] Then Yahweh told Yehu, “Because you did good by following my principles and doing what I’ve said is right, including what you did to Ahav’s family, you’ll have four generations sitting on Yisrael’s throne.”
[2 Kings] [10]:[31] But Yehu didn’t take care to follow the instructions of Yisrael’s god Yahweh whole-heartedly—he didn’t reject all of Yarov’am’s evil customs which had caused Yisrael to sin.
[2 Kings] [10]:[32] During that period, Yahweh began to reduce the size of Yisrael’s (Israel) territory and Aram’s (Syria) King Hazael attacked along their border
[2 Kings] [10]:[33] from the Yarden (Jordan) river in the east as far south as Aroer city on the Arnon river—capturing the Gilead and Bashan regions where the tribes of Gad, Re’uven, and Menasheh (Manasseh) lived.
[2 Kings] [10]:[34] Everything else that Yehu (Jehu) said and did is written in the book of the events of the kings of Yisrael.
[2 Kings] [10]:[35] Then Yehu died and was buried in their ancestral tomb in Shomron (Samaria), and his son Yehoahaz replaced him as king.
[2 Kings] [10]:[36] Yehu had ruled from Shomron as the king of Yisrael for twenty-eight years.
[2 Kings] [11]:[1] When Ahazyah’s mother Atalyah (Athaliah) saw that her son had been killed, she went and had all of his descendants executed so that none of them could claim the throne.
[2 Kings] [11]:[2] However, King Yoram’s (Joram) daughter Yehosheva took Yoash, the son of her sister Ahazyah, and hid him in the bedroom along with his wet-nurse. Although he was on the list of the king’s sons to be executed, they hid him from Atalyah, and so he wasn’t killed.
[2 Kings] [11]:[3] Then he was able to stay hidden with her in the temple for the six years while Atalyah ruled Yehudah (Judah).
[2 Kings] [11]:[4] In the seventh year, Yehoyada the priest sent for the officers over the royal bodyguards and the palace bodyguards to come to him inside Yahweh’s temple. He made them agree to take an oath of secrecy and loyalty in the temple, then he let them see the king’s son.
[2 Kings] [11]:[5] Then he commanded them, “This is what you all need to do: On the Rest Day, one third of you must go and guard the king’s palace.
[2 Kings] [11]:[6] The second third must guard the Sur gate, and the remainder must stay behind the others roaming back and forth,
[2 Kings] [11]:[7] and the two off-duty groups must guard the temple and protect the young king.
[2 Kings] [11]:[8] You’ll surround the king—each man holding his weapons at the ready right around him—killing any person who approaches your ranks, and accompanying the king when he goes out or comes in.
[2 Kings] [11]:[9] So the officers over the royal bodyguards did everything that the priest Yehoyada had commanded. Both the on-duty and the off-duty men fulfilled their roles under Yehoyada’s direction that Rest Day.
[2 Kings] [11]:[10] The priest had taken the spears and the shields out of the temple that had belonged to King David and given them to the officers over the royal bodyguards,
[2 Kings] [11]:[11] and they all stood in position, each man holding his weapons ready in his hand, right around the palace and the temple and the altar, and the king.
[2 Kings] [11]:[12] Then the priest brought young Yoash out and put the crown on his head. He handed him the official scroll, and they anointed him and made him king. Then they clapped their hands and shouted, “Long live the king!”
[2 Kings] [11]:[13] When Atalyah (Athaliah) heard the sound of the people and the guards, she came to the people gathered at Yahweh’s temple
[2 Kings] [11]:[14] and was stunned to see the young, new king standing near the pillar as was the custom, with the captains and the trumpeters near the king, and all the people of the land rejoicing and sounding trumpets. Then Atalyah tore her clothes and shouted out, “Treachery! Treason!”
[2 Kings] [11]:[15] Then Yehoyada the priest commanded the officials over the bodyguards and the army officers, “Bring her out away from these public buildings. Don’t kill her in the temple, but kill anyone who tries to rescue her.

[2 Kings] [11]:[17] Then Yehoyada led the making of an agreement between Yahweh and the king and the people, for the people to serve Yahweh, and also between the king and between the people.
[2 Kings] [11]:[18] Then people from all over the country went to the temple of Ba’al and broke down the altars. They smashed his images to pieces and killed Matan the priest of the Ba’al in front of the altars. Meanwhile, Yehoyada the priest placed guards over Yahweh’s temple.
[2 Kings] [11]:[19] Then he organised the officers over the royal guard and the palace guards to bring the king down from the temple of Yahweh, and along with all the people, they entered the palace via the gate usually used by the king’s bodyguards, and he sat on the throne.
[2 Kings] [11]:[20] All the people celebrated and the city was quiet because Atalyah (Athaliah) had been put to death with the sword at the palace.

[2 Kings] [12]:[1] Yoash became king in Yerushalem (Jerusalem) in the seventh year of Yehu’s (Jehu) reign over Yisrael (Israel). (His mother was Tsivyah from Be’er-Sheva (Beersheba).) He reigned for forty years
[2 Kings] [12]:[2] and all his life, he did what Yahweh had said was correct because he was instructed by Yehoyada the priest.
[2 Kings] [12]:[3] However, they didn’t remove the hilltop shrines where the people continued sacrificing and burning incense.
[2 Kings] [12]:[4] Then Yoash told the priests, “You all must collect all the money that’s donated to Yahweh’s temple, whether it’s the money they’re required to pay or the money that they themselves decide to give as sacred offerings to buy things for the temple.
[2 Kings] [12]:[5] Each priest must bring what they’ve collected from their acquaintances, and use it to make repairs wherever they find that there’s been damage to the temple.”
[2 Kings] [12]:[6] However, when the priests still hadn’t repaired the damaged portions by the twenty-third year of Yoash’s reign,
[2 Kings] [12]:[7] he sent for Yehoyada the priest and the other priests, and questioned them, “Why aren’t you all strengthening the temple where it was damaged? From now on, you all won’t take any money from acquaintances, but you’ll give it directly for repairing the damage.”
[2 Kings] [12]:[8] So the priests agreed to not accept money from the people, and that they themselves wouldn’t be the ones to repair the temple.
[2 Kings] [12]:[9] Then Yehoyada the priest took a wooden chest and he made a hole in the top, and he placed it at the right of the altar. When a person came into the temple, the priests guarding the entrance would place any donated money into the chest.
[2 Kings] [12]:[10] Whenever they noticed the chest getting full, the king’s secretary and the high priest would go and count the money as they bagged it up.
[2 Kings] [12]:[11] They used the funds to pay the supervisors and inspectors and the tradesmen doing the repair work: carpenters and builders,
[2 Kings] [12]:[12] and the masons and stone-cutters. They also paid for the timber and stones, and everything else that was needed for the temple repairs.
[2 Kings] [12]:[13] However, they didn’t use the donated silver coins that were brought to the temple to make silver bowls, snuffers, basins, or trumpets, or for any other gold or silver instruments within the temple,
[2 Kings] [12]:[14] because they passed on the donations to the people doing the work, and in this way Yahweh’s residence got repaired.
[2 Kings] [12]:[15] They didn’t audit the men who took the silver coins to the workers because the whole system was based on trust.
[2 Kings] [12]:[16] The silver coins that came as part of the guilt offering and the sin offerings were not used for temple repairs—they belonged to the priests.
