[2 Kings] [14]:[23] In the fifteenth year of Yoash’s son King Amatsyah’s reign over Yehudah (Judah), Yehoash’s son Yarov’am (Jeroboam) became king of Yisrael (Israel) and reigned from Shomron (Samaria) for forty-one years.
[2 Kings] [14]:[24] He did what Yahweh had said was evil—he imitated the customs of Nevat’s son Yarov’am who’d caused Yisrael to sin.
[2 Kings] [14]:[25] Yarov’am restored Yisrael’s border from Levo-Hamat through to the Sea of the Desert, as Yisrael’s god Yahweh had foretold via his servant Yonah (Jonah)—the son of the prophet Amitay from Gat-Hahefer.
[2 Kings] [14]:[26] That was because Yahweh had seen how Yisrael had suffered badly and had been unable to control their own destinies, and that no other country would help them.
[2 Kings] [14]:[27] But Yahweh had said that he wouldn’t allow Yisrael to be destroyed, so he’d used Yehoash’s son Yarov’am to save them.
[2 Kings] [14]:[28] Everything else that Yarov’am said and did, including how he fought and restored Damesek (Damascus) and Hamat to Yisrael, is written in the book of the events of the kings of Yisrael.
[2 Kings] [14]:[29] Then Yarov’am died and was buried with the former kings of Yisrael, and his son Zekaryah (Zechariah) replaced him as king.
[2 Kings] [15]:[1] In the twenty-seventh year of King Yarov’am’s (Jeroboam) reign over Yisrael (Israel), Amatsyah’s son Azaryah became king of Yehudah (Judah).
[2 Kings] [15]:[2] He was sixteen when he became king, and he reigned from Yerushalem (Jerusalem) for fifty-two years. (His mother’s name was Yekaleyah from Yerushalem.)
[2 Kings] [15]:[3] He did what Yahweh had said was correct behaviour like his father Amatsyah had done,
[2 Kings] [15]:[4] although the hilltop shrines weren’t removed—the people continued to sacrifice at them and burn incense.
[2 Kings] [15]:[5] Yahweh caused Azaryah to become a leper and he had to live separately from others for the rest of his life, so his son Yotam (Jotham) ran the palace and dealt with the people’s problems.
[2 Kings] [15]:[6] Everything else that Azaryah said and did is written in the book of the events of the kings of Yehudah.
[2 Kings] [15]:[7] Azaryah died and was buried in the ancestral tomb in the city of David, and his son Yotam replaced him as king.
[2 Kings] [15]:[8] In the thirty-eighth year of King Azaryah’s reign over Yehudah (Judah), Yarov’am’s (Jeroboam) son Zekaryah (Zechariah) became king over Yisrael (Israel) and ruled for six months from Shomron (Samaria).
[2 Kings] [15]:[9] He did what Yahweh had said was evil, just as his ancestors had done—he didn’t avoid the kinds of behaviour that had been done by Nevat’s son Yarov’am who had caused Yisrael to sin.
[2 Kings] [15]:[10] Then Yavesh’s son Shalum plotted to assassinate him, and he attacked him in front of the people and killed him, and he replaced him as king.
[2 Kings] [15]:[11] Everything else that Zekaryah said and did is written in the book of the events of the kings of Yisrael.
[2 Kings] [15]:[12] Previously Yahweh had told King Yehu (Jehu) that his descendants would sit on the throne for four generations, and that had come true.
[2 Kings] [15]:[13] Yavesh’s son Shalum became king in the thirty-ninth year of King Azaryah’s reign over Yehudah (Judah), but he only reigned from Shomron (Samaria) for one month.
[2 Kings] [15]:[14] Then Gadi’s son Menahem came to Shomron from Tirtsah, and he attacked Yavesh’s son Shalum there in Shomron and killed him, replacing him as king.
[2 Kings] [15]:[15] Everything else that Shalum said, including his assassination plot, is written in the book of the events of the kings of Yisrael (Israel).
[2 Kings] [15]:[16] At that time, Menahem attacked Tifsah and everyone in the city, and its borders from Tirtsah, because they wouldn’t open their gates. Then he ripped open the bellies of all the pregnant women there.
[2 Kings] [15]:[17] In the thirty-ninth year of King Azaryah’s reign over Yehudah (Judah), Gadi’s son Menahem became king over Yisrael (Israel) and he reigned from Shomron (Samaria) for ten years.
[2 Kings] [15]:[18] He did what Yahweh had said was evil—he didn’t avoid the kinds of behaviour that had been done by Nevat’s son Yarov’am (Jeroboam) who had caused Yisrael to sin. During his reign,
[2 Kings] [15]:[19] King Pul of Ashur (Assyria) attacked Yisrael, and Menahem gave Pul over thirty tonnes of silver, so he would support Menahem’s reign.
[2 Kings] [15]:[20] (Menahem had taxed all the wealthy families across Yisrael—fifty silver coins per adult male.) As a result, the Assyrian king cancelled his plans to attack and returned home.
[2 Kings] [15]:[21] Everything else that Menahem said and did is written in the book of the events of the kings of Yisrael.
[2 Kings] [15]:[22] Then Menahem died and was buried, and his son Pekahyah replaced him as king.
[2 Kings] [15]:[23] In the fiftieth year of King Azaryah’s reign over Yehudah (Judah), Menahem’s son Pekahyah became king over Yisrael (Israel) and reigned from Shomron (Samaria) for two years.
[2 Kings] [15]:[24] He did what Yahweh had said was evil—he didn’t avoid the kinds of behaviour that had been done by Nevat’s son Yarov’am (Jeroboam) who had caused Yisrael to sin.
[2 Kings] [15]:[25] But Pekah the son of Remalyah, Pekahyah’s third officer, plotted to assassinate him, and he attacked him in the palace in Shomron with the assistance of Argov and Aryeh and fifty Giladim. So Pekah killed King Pekahyah and replaced him as king.
[2 Kings] [15]:[26] Everything else that Pekahyah said and did is written in the book of the events of the kings of Yisrael—look at it.
[2 Kings] [15]:[27] In the fifty-second year of King Azaryah’s reign over Yehudah (Judah), Remalyah’s son Pekah became king over Yisrael (Israel) and reigned from Shomron (Samaria) for twenty years.
[2 Kings] [15]:[28] He did what Yahweh had said was evil—he didn’t avoid the kinds of behaviour that had been done by Nevat’s son Yarov’am (Jeroboam) who had caused Yisrael to sin.
[2 Kings] [15]:[29] During the reign of King Pekah over Yisrael, Ashur’s (Assyria) King Tiglat-Pileser came, and he captured the cities of Iyon, Avel-Beyt-Ma’akah, Yanoah, Kedesh, and Hatsor, and the regions of Gilead, Galil, and Naftali (Naphtali), and he exiled their people to Ashur.
[2 Kings] [15]:[30] Then Elah’s son Hoshea plotted to assassinate Remalyah’s son Pekah, and he attacked him, killing him and replacing him as king in the twentieth year of King Yotam’s (Jotham) reign over Yehudah.
[2 Kings] [15]:[31] Everything else that Pekah said and did is written in the book of the events of the kings of Yisrael.
[2 Kings] [15]:[32] In the second year of Remalyah’s son Pekah’s reign over Yisrael (Israel), Azaryah’s son Yotam (Jotham) began to reign over Yehudah (Judah).
[2 Kings] [15]:[33] He was twenty-five when he became king, and he reigned from Yerushalem (Jerusalem) for sixteen years. (His mother’s name was Yerusha, the daughter of Tsadok.)
[2 Kings] [15]:[34] He did what Yahweh had said was correct behaviour like his father Azaryah/Uziyah had done,
[2 Kings] [15]:[35] although the hilltop shrines weren’t removed—the people continued to sacrifice at them and burn incense. Yotam built the upper gate to Yahweh’s temple.
[2 Kings] [15]:[36] Everything else that Yotam said and did is written in the book of the events of the kings of Yehudah.
[2 Kings] [15]:[37] In those days, Yahweh began to send Aram’s (Syria) King Retsin and Remalyah’s son Pekah against Yehudah.
[2 Kings] [15]:[38] Then Yotam died and was buried in their ancestral tomb in the city of his ancestor David, and his son Ahaz replaced him as king.
[2 Kings] [16]:[1] In the seventeenth year of Remalyah’s son Pekah’s reign over Yisrael (Israel), Yotam’s (Jotham) son Ahaz began to reign over Yehudah (Judah).
[2 Kings] [16]:[2] Ahaz was twenty when he became king and he reigned from Yerushalem (Jerusalem) for sixteen years, but he didn’t follow what his god Yahweh had said was correct behaviour like his ancestor David had done.
[2 Kings] [16]:[3] Actually he followed the behaviour of the kings of Yisrael, and he even sacrificed his son as a burnt offering like they do in the nations that Yahweh hated and which Yahweh had driven out of the land as the Israelis had entered.
[2 Kings] [16]:[4] Also he sacrificed on the hilltop shrines and burnt incense on them, and on the hills and under every large tree.
[2 Kings] [16]:[5] Then Aram’s (Syria) King Retsin and Yisrael’s King Pekah (Remalyah’s son) came uphill to attack Yerushalem, and they laid siege against King Ahaz but they weren’t able to conquer the city.
[2 Kings] [16]:[6] At that time, Aram’s King Retsin recaptured Eylot City for Aram, then he drove the Yehudim (Judeans) out of Eylot and Arameans moved in instead and they have lived there to this day.
[2 Kings] [16]:[7] So Ahaz sent messengers to Ashur’s (Assyria) King Tiglat-Pileser, “I’m your servant and your son. Come up and rescue me from the kings of Aram and Yisrael who are here attacking me.”
[2 Kings] [16]:[8] Ahaz took the gold and silver from Yahweh’s temple and from the palace treasuries, and sent it as a gift to the Assyrian king.
[2 Kings] [16]:[9] The king of Ashur listened to him and went in and attacked Damesek (Damascus), and he captured it and exiled its people to Kir, and he executed King Retsin.
[2 Kings] [16]:[10] King Ahaz went to meet the Assyrian King Tiglat-Pileser in Damesek, and he saw the altar that was there. So he sent a drawing and the detailed measurements of the altar to the priest Uriyah.
[2 Kings] [16]:[11] So Uriyah built the altar according to the plans that King Ahaz had sent from Damesek and had it finished before King Ahaz returned from Damesek.
[2 Kings] [16]:[12] When the king got back to Yerushalem and saw the altar, he went up onto it
[2 Kings] [16]:[13] and made his burnt offering and his grain offering, and he poured out his drink offering, and he sprinkled the blood of his peace offerings onto the altar.
[2 Kings] [16]:[14] He got the bronze altar that had been dedicated to Yahweh moved back away from the temple and placed beside the newer, bigger altar.
[2 Kings] [16]:[15] Then King Ahaz ordered Uriyah, “Use the large altar for the morning burnt offerings and the evening grain offerings, and for the king’s burnt offerings and grain offerings, and for the people’s burnt offerings and grain offerings and drink offerings. Use it for sprinkling all the blood of the burnt offerings and of the sacrifices on. But I will use the bronze altar for seeking guidance.”
[2 Kings] [16]:[16] So Uriyah the priest put everything into effect that King Ahaz had commanded.
[2 Kings] [16]:[17] Then King Ahaz cut the frames off the stands outside the temple, and he removed the basins off them. He took down ‘The Sea’ that had been sitting on top of bronze bulls and put it on the stone floor.
[2 Kings] [16]:[18] He also removed the canopy that had been built at the temple for use on the Rest Days, and blocked up the king’s outer entrance to the temple so that the Assyrian king couldn’t use it.
[2 Kings] [16]:[19] Everything else that Ahaz said and did is written in the book of the events of the kings of Yehudah (Judah).
[2 Kings] [16]:[20] Then Ahaz died and was buried in their ancestral tomb in the city of David, and his son Hizkiyah (Hezekiah) replaced him as king.
[2 Kings] [17]:[1] In the twelfth year of King Ahaz’s reign over Yehudah (Judah), Elah’s son Hoshea became king over Yisrael (Israel) and he reigned from Shomron (Samaria) for nine years.
[2 Kings] [17]:[2] He did what Yahweh had said was evil, although nothing like the Israeli kings who’d preceded him.
[2 Kings] [17]:[3] Ashur’s (Assyria) King Shalmaneser attacked and defeated him, and Hoshea became his servant and paid tribute to him.
[2 Kings] [17]:[4] But the Assyrian king discovered that Hoshea was planning a revolt and had sent messengers to the Mitsri (Egyptian) King So and hadn’t kept up the annual tribute payment. So the Assyrian king arrested Hoshea and imprisoned him.
[2 Kings] [17]:[5] Then the Assyrian king attacked the whole country, including besieging Shomron (Samaria) for three years.
[2 Kings] [17]:[6] In the ninth year of Hoshea’s reign, the Assyrian king captured Shomron. He exiled the Israelis to Ashur (Assyria) and settled them in Halah, and in Havor along the Gozan River, and in the cities of the Madim (Medes).
[2 Kings] [17]:[7] That happened because the Israelis had sinned against their god Yahweh who had rescued them from King Par’oh (Pharaoh) in Mitsrayim (Egypt). They had sinned by worshipping other gods
[2 Kings] [17]:[8] and imitating the customs of the people groups who Yahweh had driven out of the country ahead of them. They had also followed their kings in doing evil things.
[2 Kings] [17]:[9] The Israelis had done things secretly that their god Yahweh had said weren’t right, and they’d built hilltop shrines everywhere from the largest fortified cities to the smallest towns.
[2 Kings] [17]:[10] They’d also erected stone pillars to honour gods and Asherah poles on every high hill and under every large tree,
[2 Kings] [17]:[11] and they’d burnt incense there on all those hilltops just like the people groups that Yahweh had driven off the land ahead of them—doing those evil things had made Yahweh angry.
[2 Kings] [17]:[12] They’d served idols even when Yahweh had forbidden them from doing that.
[2 Kings] [17]:[13] So Yahweh had warned Yisrael (Israel) and Yehudah (Judah) by the declarations by all of his prophets who said, “Turn from your evil ways and obey my commands and statutes, following all of the instructions that I gave your ancestors and which I delivered to you through my servants, the prophets.”
[2 Kings] [17]:[14] However, they hadn’t listened and had hardened their attitudes just like their ancestors who wouldn’t put their trust in their god Yahweh.
[2 Kings] [17]:[15] They rejected his statutes and the agreement that he made with their ancestors, and the warning that he gave them. They chose to worship lifeless objects, and they became hollow and empty themselves, just like the people of the surrounding countries which Yahweh had commanded them not to imitate.
[2 Kings] [17]:[16] They disobeyed the instructions given to them by their god Yahweh by molding two metal calves for themselves and making an Asherah pole. Then they bowed down and worshipped the sun, moon, and stars, and they served Ba’al.
[2 Kings] [17]:[17] They sacrificed their sons and daughters, and used fortune-tellers and witchcraft—making themselves slaves to evil by doing what Yahweh had forbidden, and so making him angry.
[2 Kings] [17]:[18] So that’s why Yahweh had become very angry at the northern kingdom of Yisrael and caused them to be removed from the land. Only the Southern kingdom of Yehudah remained,
[2 Kings] [17]:[19] but even they didn’t obey the commands of their god Yahweh, but copied much of the bad behaviour of the northern kingdom.
[2 Kings] [17]:[20] So Yahweh rejected all the Israelis and he caused them to suffer, including being plundered by enemy armies, until he banished them from his presence.
[2 Kings] [17]:[21] Firstly he’d torn the northern kingdom out from the leadership of David’s descendants and they’d made Nevat’s son Yarov’am (Jeroboam) king. Then Yarov’am had driven them away from following Yahweh, and had induced them into serious sin.
[2 Kings] [17]:[22] So the Israelis had followed Yarov’am into sin and then didn’t turn away from it,
[2 Kings] [17]:[23] and finally Yahweh had removed the people of the northern kingdom of Yisrael from his presence just like he’d warned he would through the messages of his servants, the prophets. So the people were deported to Ashur (Assyria) where they remain to this day.
[2 Kings] [17]:[24] Then the Assyrian king sent people from Bavel (Babylon) and from Kut and from Ivah and from Hamat and Sefarvayim, and he settled them in the cities of the northern kingdom in place of the Israelis. And they possessed Shomron (Samaria) and lived in its towns.
[2 Kings] [17]:[25] At first the new inhabitants living there didn’t respect Yahweh, however he sent lions among them and they started killing them.
[2 Kings] [17]:[26] They told the Assyrian king, “The people groups that you exiled from their own countries and settled in the towns around Shomron, don’t know the customs of the god of the land. So he’s sent lions against them, and look at them—killing them because they don’t know the customs of the god of the land.”
[2 Kings] [17]:[27] “Send one of the priests back that was brought from there,” the Assyrian king commanded. “He can go back there and settle there again, then he can teach them the customs of the god of that place.”
[2 Kings] [17]:[28] So they found one of the priests who had been exiled from Shomron and sent him back to Yisrael (Israel). He settled in Beyt-El (Bethel) and taught the people how Yahweh wanted to be served.
[2 Kings] [17]:[29] But each people group had made their own gods and put them in the hilltop shrines that the Israelis had made before being exiled. Each people group did that in the area where they’d been resettled.
[2 Kings] [17]:[30] Those from Bavel made their god Sukot-Benot, those from Kut made Nergal, those from Hamat made their god Ashima,
[2 Kings] [17]:[31] and the Avim made Nivhaz and Tartak. The Sefarvim sacrificed their own sons in the fire to their gods Adramelek and Anamelek.
[2 Kings] [17]:[32] At the same time, they tried placating Yahweh, but they also made their own priests to make sacrifices for them in their hilltop shrines.
[2 Kings] [17]:[33] So they were worshipping Yahweh along with their own gods—they’d brought those customs with them from the countries they’d been exiled from
[2 Kings] [17]:[34] and which they still follow to this day. They’re not actually obeying Yahweh because they’re not obeying the statutes or laws, or instructions or behaviour that Yahweh commanded the descendants of Ya’akov (Jacob) (who he’d renamed to ‘Yisrael’).
[2 Kings] [17]:[35] Yahweh had made an agreement with them and had commanded them, “You all must not honour other gods or bow to them. You all must not serve them or sacrifice to them.
[2 Kings] [17]:[36] Only serve Yahweh who used his incredible power to rescue you all out of Mitsrayim (Egypt). Honour him, and only bow to him and sacrifice to him.
[2 Kings] [17]:[37] Always take care to obey the statutes and customs, and the law and the instructions that he wrote for you, and you all must not honour other gods.
[2 Kings] [17]:[38] Don’t forget the agreement that I made with you all, and don’t honour other gods—
[2 Kings] [17]:[39] only your god Yahweh, and then he himself will rescue you from all your enemies.”
[2 Kings] [17]:[40] However, they didn’t listen, preferring to follow the customs from their former places of residence.
[2 Kings] [17]:[41] So those people groups honoured Yahweh, but also served their idols. This continued through the generations with their descendants continuing the same behaviour.
[2 Kings] [18]:[1] In the third year of Elah’s son King Hoshea’s reign over Yisrael (Israel), Ahaz’s son Hizkiyah (Hezekiah) became king of Yehudah (Judah).
[2 Kings] [18]:[2] He was twenty-five when he became king and he reigned from Yerushalem (Jerusalem) for twenty-nine years. (His mother was Zekaryah’s (Zechariah) daughter Avi.)
[2 Kings] [18]:[3] He did what Yahweh had said was correct behaviour like his ancestor King David had done.
[2 Kings] [18]:[4] He demolished the hilltop shrines and shattered their pillars, and he cut down the Asherah poles. He crushed the bronze serpent that Mosheh (Moses) had made, because the Israelis had named it ‘Nehushtan’ and had been offering incense to it until then.
[2 Kings] [18]:[5] Hizkiyah fully trusted in Yisrael’s god Yahweh, and no other king was like him among all the kings of Yehudah that either preceded or followed him.
[2 Kings] [18]:[6] He relied completely on Yahweh—not turning away from following him, and he obeyed the instructions that Yahweh had commanded Mosheh.
[2 Kings] [18]:[7] So Yahweh helped him and he was successful in everything he did. He rebelled against the Assyrian king and refused to submit to his demands.
[2 Kings] [18]:[8] He attacked and defeated the Pelishtim as far as Azah (Gaza) and its borders—both the smaller towns and the fortified city.
[2 Kings] [18]:[9] Then in the fourth year of King Hizkiyah’s reign (it was the seventh year of Elah’s son Hoshea’s reign over Yisrael), the Assyrian King Shalmaneser had attacked Shomron (Samaria) and besieged it.
[2 Kings] [18]:[10] They had finally captured the city after three years. That was the sixth year of Hizkiyah’s reign over Yehudah and the ninth year of Hoshea’s reign over Yisrael.
[2 Kings] [18]:[11] So that was when the Assyrian king had exiled the people of the northern kingdom of Yisrael to Halah and to Havor along the Gozan River, and to the cities of the Madim (Medes).
[2 Kings] [18]:[12] That happened because they didn’t obey their god Yahweh, but instead they broke the agreement with him—everything that Yahweh’s servant Mosheh had commanded. They didn’t take notice of it and they didn’t obey it.
[2 Kings] [18]:[13] In the fourteenth year of King Hizkiyah’s (Hezekiah) reign, Assyrian King Sanheriv (Sennacherib) attacked all the fortified cities in Yehudah (Judah) and captured them.
[2 Kings] [18]:[14] So King Hizkiyah of Yehudah sent messengers to the Assyrian king at Lakish, saying, “I apologise for my mistake. Stop attacking me and I’ll give you whatever you demand of us.” Then the Assyrian king demanded a tribute of ten tonnes of gold and ten tonnes of silver.
[2 Kings] [18]:[15] So Hizkiyah gave him all the silver out of the temple and from the palace treasuries.
[2 Kings] [18]:[16] He cut the doors off Yahweh’s temple and the pillars that he’d overlaid gold onto, and gave them to the Assyrian king.
[2 Kings] [18]:[17] However, the Assyrian king still sent his general and some of his top officials from Lakish to King Hizkiyah in Yerushalem (Jerusalem). They arrived at Yerushalem with a large army and camped by the aquifer supplying the upper pool that was near the field where the people washed their clothes.
[2 Kings] [18]:[18] They called out to the king, and Hilkiyah’s son Elyakim who was the palace manager, and the scribe Shevna, and Asaf’s son Yoah the secretary, went out to them.
[2 Kings] [18]:[19] Then the top Assyrian commander said to them, “Now, tell Hizkiyah that the great Assyrian king asks him who he thinks he’s trusting in.
[2 Kings] [18]:[20] He claims to be powerful enough to fight us. Who is he trusting to help you all that gives you confidence to rebel against us?
[2 Kings] [18]:[21] Listen, your king’s trusting in a broken stick to lean on which will just splinter and pierce his hand. That’s what King Par’oh (Pharaoh) of Mitsrayim (Egypt) is like to everyone who puts their trust in him.
[2 Kings] [18]:[22] Ah, but he might tell me that he’s trusting in your god Yahweh to help you all. If so, I’d ask him if he isn’t the one whose hilltop shrines King Hizkiyah demolished when he told you people in Yerushalem and all Yehudah (Judah) that you have to worship at the altar there?
[2 Kings] [18]:[23] “So now ask your king if he’ll make a deal with my master, the king of Ashur (Assyria): He’ll give you two thousand horses, on the condition that you can supply two thousand horsemen who can ride them.
[2 Kings] [18]:[24] If you can’t do that, how could you all possibly repel even one of our army units? Haha, but of course you trust in Mitsrayim to supply chariots and horsemen.
[2 Kings] [18]:[25] Do you think that we’ve come here to destroy this place without Yahweh’s permission? No, no, it was Yahweh himself who told us to attack and destroy you.”
[2 Kings] [18]:[26] But Elyakim and Shevna and Yoah asked the Assyrian commander, “Please speak Aramit to your servants because we understand it. Don’t speak our language because our people on the nearby city wall will be able to understand it.”
[2 Kings] [18]:[27] “Ha ha, do you think my master sent this message just to you three and your king?” he replied. “No, don’t you think that this message is also for the hungry people sitting on the wall who’ll soon have to eat their own dung and drink their own urine along with you?”
[2 Kings] [18]:[28] Then he stood up and called out loudly in Hebrew, “Everyone listen to what the great king from Ashur says:
[2 Kings] [18]:[29] He’s warning you all not to let Hizkiyah (Hezekiah) deceive you, because he’s unable to save you all from our army.
[2 Kings] [18]:[30] And don’t let him force you all to trust in Yahweh thinking that we won’t capture your city and that Yahweh will somehow rescue you all.
[2 Kings] [18]:[31] Don’t listen to Hizkiyah because the Assyrian king is offering you all a chance to come out of the city and surrender. In exchange for saving me some trouble, you’ll be able to drink fresh water again and enjoy the fruit off your own trees out here
[2 Kings] [18]:[32] until he comes here. Then he’ll take you to another country like your own—with grain and wine, and bread and vineyards, olive oil and honey. That way you’ll live and not die of starvation. So don’t listen to Hizkiyah when he misleads you saying that Yahweh will rescue you all.”
[2 Kings] [18]:[33] Did the gods of any of the other countries rescue their people from the power of the Assyrian king?
[2 Kings] [18]:[34] Where were the gods of Hamat and Arpad? Where were the gods of Sefarvayim, Hena, and Ivah? Were they able to save Shomron (Samaria) from the king’s power?
[2 Kings] [18]:[35] From all the other countries, which of their gods was able to save their people, that might give confidence that Yahweh might be able to rescue Yerushalem (Jerusalem) from the king’s power?”
[2 Kings] [18]:[36] But the people on the wall listening remained silent—they didn’t say a word because the king had already ordered them not to answer the Assyrians.
[2 Kings] [18]:[37] Then Hilkiyah’s son Elyakim the palace manager, Shevna the scribe and Asaf’s son Yoah the secretary went back in the city to Hizkiyah, tearing their clothes as they went, and they relayed the words of the chief commander to him.
[2 Kings] [19]:[1] When King Hizkiyah (Hezekiah) heard the threats from the Assyrian king, he tore his clothes and dressed in sackcloth, and went into Yahweh’s temple.
[2 Kings] [19]:[2] He sent his palace manager Elyakim and the scribe Shevna, along with the elders of the priests, all dressed in sackcloth, to Amots’s son Yeshayah (Isaiah) the prophet
[2 Kings] [19]:[3] to tell him, “Hizkiyah says: ‘Today is a day of distress and rebuke and disgrace, as if the baby is right there ready to be delivered, but the mother has lost all her strength.
[2 Kings] [19]:[4] Perhaps your god Yahweh has heard everything that the chief commander said when his master the Assyrian king sent him: he defied the living God, and so maybe your god Yahweh will punish him for his words. Lift up a prayer on behalf of the people that are still left here.’ ”

[2 Kings] [19]:[19] But now Yahweh our god, please save us from his army, then all the kingdoms in the world will know that you, Yahweh, are God—you alone.”

[2 Kings] [19]:[24] You said that you’ve dug wells far away and drunk their water, yet with your own feet you dried up all of Mitsrayim’s (Egypt) rivers.

[2 Kings] [20]:[1] By that time, King Hizkiyah (Hezekiah) was terminally ill and Amots’s son the prophet Yeshayah (Isaiah) came to him and told him, “Yahweh says to get your affairs in order because you’re dying and won’t recover.”
[2 Kings] [20]:[2] But Hizkiyah rolled over to face the wall and prayed to Yahweh,
[2 Kings] [20]:[3] “Oh Yahweh, please remember that I’ve served you faithfully, and done what you asked with total sincerity.” Then Hizkiyah cried loudly.
[2 Kings] [20]:[4] As Yeshayah was leaving, Yahweh gave him this message before he’d even reached the middle courtyard,
[2 Kings] [20]:[5] “Go back and tell Hizkiyah, the leader of my people, ‘Your ancestor David’s god Yahweh says that he’s heard your prayer and seen your tears. He’s decided to heal you and you’ll be well enough to go to the temple within three days.
[2 Kings] [20]:[6] He’s added fifteen years to your life, plus he’ll rescue you and this city from the Assyrian king. Yahweh will defend Yerushalem (Jerusalem) for his own sake and for the sake of his servant David.”
[2 Kings] [20]:[7] Then Yeshayah told them to bring some pressed figs, and they brought them and placed them on the sore, and Hizkiyah started getting better.
[2 Kings] [20]:[8] Hizkiyah asked Yeshayah, “What’s the sign that Yahweh will heal me and that I’ll be able to go to the temple on the third day?”
[2 Kings] [20]:[9] “Yes, Yahweh will give you a sign that he’ll do what he said,” Yeshayah replied. “Do you want the shadows to advance suddenly or go back?”
[2 Kings] [20]:[10] “It’s easy for the shadows to go forward,” said Hizkiyah. “So make them go backwards ten steps.”
[2 Kings] [20]:[11] So the prophet Yeshayah called to Yahweh, and he made the shadow go back on the steps made by King Ahaz—the shadow went ten steps backward.
[2 Kings] [20]:[12] At that time, Baladan’s son former King Merodak-Bal’adan of Bavel (Babylon) heard that Hizkiyah (Hezekiah) was sick and sent him letters and a gift.
[2 Kings] [20]:[13] When the messengers arrived, Hizkiyah listened to them, then he showed them his entire treasure house: the gold and silver, the spices and the best oil, the house of his armour, and everything that was in his treasuries. He didn’t keep anything in his palace or in his kingdom secret from them.
[2 Kings] [20]:[14] Later the prophet Yeshayah (Isaiah) came to King Hizkiyah and he asked him, “Where were those men from and what did they say?” “They came from a distant land—from Bavel,” he replied.
[2 Kings] [20]:[15] “What did they see in your house?” Yeshayah asked. “They saw everything that’s in my house,” he replied. “There wasn’t anything in my treasuries that I didn’t show them.”

[2 Kings] [20]:[18] What’s more, some of your own biological descendants will be taken and they’ll be castrated to become servants of the Babylonian king.”
[2 Kings] [20]:[19] “What you said from Yahweh is fine,” Hizkiyah replied to Yeshayah. “At least I might have peace and stability in my time.”

[2 Kings] [20]:[21] In due course, Hizkiyah died and his son Menasheh (Manasseh) replaced him as king.
[2 Kings] [21]:[1] Menasheh (Manasseh) was twelve when he became king, and he reigned over Yehudah (Judah) from Yerushalem (Jerusalem) for fifty-five years. (His mother was Heftsi-Bah.)
[2 Kings] [21]:[2] He did what Yahweh had said was evil like the evil behaviour of the people groups that Yahweh had driven out of the region ahead of the Israelis.
[2 Kings] [21]:[3] In fact he went backwards from his father and rebuilt the hilltop shrines that Hizkiyah (Hezekiah) had destroyed, and he made altars for Ba’al, and he made an Asherah pole, just like Yisrael’s (Israel) King Ahav had, and he worshipped the constellations and followed astrology.
[2 Kings] [21]:[4] Also he built altars in Yahweh’s residence, where Yahweh had said, “I will establish my reputation in Yerushalem.”
[2 Kings] [21]:[5] Menasheh built altars to all the constellations in the two temple courtyards .
[2 Kings] [21]:[6] He even sacrificed his own son as a burnt offering. He practised divination and read omens, and consulted mediums and fortune-tellers. He did so much that Yahweh had said was evil, provoking Yahweh to get angry.
[2 Kings] [21]:[7] He placed the Asherah idol that he’d made in the temple about which Yahweh had said to David and to his son Shelomoh (Solomon), “I will establish my reputation forever in this house and in Yerushalem in Yehudah, which I’ve chosen out of all the tribes of Yisrael.
[2 Kings] [21]:[8] If only the Israelis will take care to obey everything that I’ve commanded them, and all the instructions that my servant Mosheh (Moses) gave them, then I won’t continue to cause them to leave the area that I gave to their ancestors.”
[2 Kings] [21]:[9] But they didn’t listen and Menasheh led them astray to do more evil things even than the people groups that Yahweh had destroyed as the people had entered the region.
[2 Kings] [21]:[10] So Yahweh announced via his servants the prophets,
[2 Kings] [21]:[11] “Because Yehudah’s King Menasheh has done such terribly evil things, worse even than the Amorim who were there before him, and because he’s even made Yehudah sin with his idols,
[2 Kings] [21]:[12] then Yisrael’s god Yahweh says: Listen, I’ll bring such terrible disaster to Yehudah including Yerushalem that people won’t even be able to handle hearing the news about it.
[2 Kings] [21]:[13] I’ll use the same tape measure for Yerushalem that I used for Shomron (Samaria), and I’ll use the same plumb line that I used for Ahav’s extended family. I’ll wipe Yerushalem away, just like someone dries a bowl—they wipe it dry and then turn it upside down.
[2 Kings] [21]:[14] I’ll abandon the small remainder of my people here, and I’ll hand them over to their enemies—they’ll become the spoil and plunder of all their enemies,
[2 Kings] [21]:[15] because they’ve done what I told them was evil, and they’ve been making me angry from the time that their ancestors were brought out of Mitsrayim (Egypt) right up to this day.”
[2 Kings] [21]:[16] Menasheh even poured out so much innocent blood that he filled Yerushalem with it from one side to the other, and that was on top of his other sin of leading Yehudah into doing what Yahweh had said was evil.
[2 Kings] [21]:[17] Everything else that Menasheh said and did, including the sins that he committed, is written in the book of the events of the kings of Yehudah.
[2 Kings] [21]:[18] Then Menasheh died and was buried in the palace garden (made by Uza), and his son Amon replaced him as king.
[2 Kings] [21]:[19] Amon was twenty-two when he became king, and he reigned from Yerushalem (Jerusalem) for two years. (His mother was Haruts’s daughter Meshulemet from Yotvah.)
[2 Kings] [21]:[20] He did what Yahweh had said was evil, just like his father Menasheh (Manasseh) had done.
[2 Kings] [21]:[21] In fact, he followed everything that his father had done, including serving the same idols and bowing to them.
[2 Kings] [21]:[22] He abandoned Yahweh, the god of his ancestors, and didn’t obey his instructions.
[2 Kings] [21]:[23] But Amon’s servants plotted to assassinate him, and they killed him in the palace.
[2 Kings] [21]:[24] However, the people executed everyone who’d been involved in the conspiracy against King Amon, and they installed his son Yoshiyah (Josiah) as king in his place.
[2 Kings] [21]:[25] Everything else that Amon said and did is written in the book of the events of the kings of Yehudah (Judah).
[2 Kings] [21]:[26] He was buried in his tomb in the garden made by Uza, and his son Yoshiyah replaced him as king.
[2 Kings] [22]:[1] Yoshiyah (Josiah) was eight when he became king, and he reigned from Yerushalem (Jerusalem) for thirty-one years. (His mother was Adayah’s daughter Yedidah from Batsekat.)
[2 Kings] [22]:[2] He did what Yahweh had said was correct behaviour, following all the customs of his ancestor King David, and obeying Yahweh’s instructions.
[2 Kings] [22]:[3] In the eighth month of the eighteenth year of King Yoshiyah’s (Josiah) reign, he sent the scribe Shafan (the son of Atsalyah the son of Meshulam) to the temple, saying

[2 Kings] [22]:[6] the craftsmen, builders, and masons, as well as buying wood and quarried stones for the repairs.”
[2 Kings] [22]:[7] They won’t need to submit detailed accounts for it because they’re trustworthy people.
[2 Kings] [22]:[8] During the repairs, the high priest Hilkiyah told the scribe Shafan, “I found a scroll in the temple with Yahweh’s instructions written on it.” So Hilkiyah gave the scroll to Shafan to read.
[2 Kings] [22]:[9] Then Shafan the scribe went to the king with this report, “Your servants handed over the money that had been collected in the temple, and they gave it to the supervisors of the workers doing the repairs.”
[2 Kings] [22]:[10] Then he added, “And the priest Hilkiyah gave me a scroll.” Then he read it out loud to King Yoshiyah.
[2 Kings] [22]:[11] When the king heard the contents of the scroll, he tore his clothes

[2 Kings] [22]:[14] So Hilkiyah the priest and Ahikam, Akbor, Shafan, and Asayah went to the prophetess Huldah (the wife of Shalum, the son of Tikvah, the son of Harhas, the one in charge of looking after the priests’ uniforms who lived in the newer part of Yerushalem (Jerusalem)), and they spoke to her.
[2 Kings] [22]:[15] She told them that Yisrael’s (Israel) god Yahweh had said, “Tell the man who sent you all to me

[2 Kings] [22]:[17] because they abandoned me. They offered sacrifices to other gods in order to make me angry at everything they do, so now my anger will be directed against this place and it’s not stoppable.
[2 Kings] [22]:[18] But to the king of Yehudah who sent you all to seek Yahweh, tell him that Yisrael’s god Yahweh says: The words that you heard from the scroll,
[2 Kings] [22]:[19] because you’re open to learn and because you humbled yourself in front of Yahweh when you heard my promise that this place and its inhabitants would become a horror and a curse, and because you’ve torn your clothes and wept in front of me, then Yahweh said that he’s taken notice of you.
[2 Kings] [22]:[20] Because of that, he’ll allow you to die and be buried peacefully, and you yourself won’t witness the destruction that will come to this place.” So they relayed those messages back to King Yoshiyah (Josiah).
[2 Kings] [23]:[1] Then King Yoshiyah (Josiah) summoned all the elders of Yerushalem (Jerusalem) and across Yehudah (Judah),
[2 Kings] [23]:[2] and he went to the temple, and all the inhabitants of Yerushalem and from all across Yehudah went with him, along with the priests and prophets, and all the people from the most to the least important. Then he read to them every word on the scroll of the agreement that had been found in Yahweh’s residence.
[2 Kings] [23]:[3] Then the king stood by the pillar and he made a commitment in front of Yahweh to follow Yahweh and to obey his commands and testimonies and statutes with all sincerity, and with every desire to respect the words of that agreement that had been written on that scroll. All the people were also included in that commitment.
[2 Kings] [23]:[4] Then the king commanded the high priest Hilkiyah and the other priests, and the temple guards to bring out all the utensils that were made for Ba’al and Asherah and for all the constellations, and he burnt them outside Yerushalem in the Kidron countryside, and carried their ashes to Beyt-El (Bethel).
[2 Kings] [23]:[5] He got rid of the pagan priests that the kings of Yehudah had appointed to burn incense in the hilltop shrines around Yerushalem and across the rest of Yehudah, and the ones who burnt incense to Ba’al, and to the sun and moon and to the planets and constellations.
[2 Kings] [23]:[6] He got the Asherah pole out from Yahweh’s temple and burnt it in the Kidron valley outside Yerushalem, then he pounded the ashes to dust and threw it over people’s graves.
[2 Kings] [23]:[7] He demolished the cubicles of the male temple prostitutes that were inside Yahweh’s temple where the women were weaving Asherah coverings.
[2 Kings] [23]:[8] He brought all the priests to Yerushalem from the cities of Yehudah, and he desecrated the hilltop shrines where the priests had burnt incense, from Geva to Be’er-Sheva (Beersheba). He demolished the hilltop shrines that Yehoshua (Joshua) (a city official) had built near the city gate (on the left of the gate as you entered the city).
[2 Kings] [23]:[9] However those priests from those hilltop shrines weren’t allowed to serve at the altar in Yerushalem, but they were allowed to eat unleavened bread like the other priests.

[2 Kings] [23]:[11] The horses that the kings of Yehudah had offered to the sun, he prevented from approaching the hall of the official Netan-Melek that was in the courtyards of Yahweh’s temple, and he set fire to the chariots of the sun.
[2 Kings] [23]:[12] Then the king tore down the altars that were on the roof in Ahaz’s upper chamber that the kings of Yehudah made, and the altars that Menasheh (Manasseh) made in the two courtyards of Yahweh’s temple and he threw the rubble into the Kidron valley.
[2 Kings] [23]:[13] The king desecrated the hilltop shrines that faced Yerushalem—they were south of the Mt. of Destruction’ (the Mt. of Olives). King Shelomoh (Solomon) had built shrines for Ashtarot (the disgusting god of the Tsidonim (Sidonians)) and for Kemosh (the disgusting god of Moav (Moab)) and for Molek (the disgusting god of the Amonim).
[2 Kings] [23]:[14] He also smashed the sacred pillars and cut down the Asherah poles, then he desecrated those places by filling them with human bones.
[2 Kings] [23]:[15] He also demolished the altar that was in Beyt-El (Bethel)—the hilltop shrine that Nevat’s son Yarov’am (Jeroboam) had made when he’d caused Yisrael (Israel) to sin. He demolished both that altar and the hilltop shrine, then he burnt the shrine. He crushed everything to dust, and he burnt the Asherah pole.
[2 Kings] [23]:[16] As Yoshiyah turned around, he noticed some graves that were there on the hillside, so he had some bones removed from the graves, and he burnt them on the altar to desecrate it. This fulfilled what Yahweh had said through the man of God who’d proclaimed these things.
[2 Kings] [23]:[17] Yoshiyah turned again and asked, “Whose tomb is that?” “It’s the prophet’s tomb,” the people of Beyt-El replied, “The one who came from Yehudah and predicted that what you just did to that altar would happen.”
[2 Kings] [23]:[18] “Don’t disturb it then,” the king ordered. “Don’t let anyone remove his bones.” So they left his bones alone, along with the bones of the other prophet who came from Shomron (Samaria).
[2 Kings] [23]:[19] So King Yoshiyah removed all the hilltop shrines that the Israeli kings had made in the cities of Shomron, provoking Yahweh’s anger. The king destroyed them just like he’d done to the ones in Beyt-El.
[2 Kings] [23]:[20] He executed all the priests from those hilltop shrines on the altars there, and then he burnt human bones on them to desecrate them. Then he returned to Yerushalem (Jerusalem).
[2 Kings] [23]:[21] Then the king commanded all the people, “Celebrate ‘pass-over’ for your god Yahweh according to what’s written on this scroll with the agreement.”
[2 Kings] [23]:[22] Since the days of the leaders who judged Yisrael (Israel), or in all the days of the kings of Yisrael and Yehudah (Judah), a ‘pass-over’ had never been celebrated like that one
[2 Kings] [23]:[23] in the eighteenth year of King Yoshiyah’s (Josiah) reign. That ‘pass-over’ celebration in Yerushalem (Jerusalem) was to honour Yahweh.
[2 Kings] [23]:[24] King Yoshiyah (Josiah) also removed the ritual pits and the soothsayers, and the images and idols, and all the abhorrences that were seen in Yerushalem (Jerusalem) and in the Yehudah (Judah) region, in his diligence to obey everything that was written on the scroll that the priest Hilkiyah found in the temple.
[2 Kings] [23]:[25] No other king had been like Yoshiyah who’d led the people back to obeying Yahweh—following Mosheh’s (Moses) written instructions with all his heart and all his spirit and all his energy. What’s more, there’s never been a king like him since then either.
[2 Kings] [23]:[26] However, Yahweh’s anger against Yehudah hadn’t cooled down after everything that King Menasheh (Manasseh) had done to make him angry,
[2 Kings] [23]:[27] and Yahweh said, “I will also remove Yehudah out of my sight, just like I removed Yisrael (Israel). I’ll also reject this city of Yerushalem that I chose, as well as the house where I’d said that my name would be established.”
[2 Kings] [23]:[28] Everything else that Yoshiyah said and did is written in the book of the events of the kings of Yehudah.
[2 Kings] [23]:[29] While he was still king, the Mitsri (Egyptian) king Par’oh (Pharaoh) Nekoh attacked the Assyrian king near the Perat (Euphrates) River. King Yoshiyah went to meet him, but Nekoh killed him at Megidon when he saw him.
[2 Kings] [23]:[30] His servants brought his body back to Yerushalem from Megidon, and they buried him in his own tomb. Then the people got his son Yehoahaz, and they anointed him and made him king in place of his father.
[2 Kings] [23]:[31] Yehoahaz was twenty-three when he became king, and he reigned from Yerushalem (Jerusalem) for only three months. (His mother was Yirmiyah’s (Jeremiah) daughter Hamutal from Livnah.)

[2 Kings] [23]:[33] Par’oh (Pharaoh) Nekoh took him from Yerushalem and imprisoned him at Rivlah in the Hamat region, and he forced the residents of Yehudah (Judah) to pay him thirty kilograms of gold and three tonnes of silver.
[2 Kings] [23]:[34] Then Nekoh appointed Yoshiyah’s (Josiah) son Elyakim as the new king but changed his name to Yehoyakim. Then he took Yehoahaz to Mitsrayim (Egypt) where he eventually died.

[2 Kings] [23]:[36] Yehoyakim was twenty-five when he became king, and he reigned from Yerushalem (Jerusalem) for eleven years. (His mother was Pedayah’s daughter Zevidah from Rumah.)
[2 Kings] [23]:[37] He did what Yahweh had said was evil like many of his ancestors had done.
[2 Kings] [24]:[1] During his reign, the Babylonian King Nevukadnetsar (Nebuchadnezzar) attacked, and Yehoyakim ruled under him for three years before rebelling against him.
[2 Kings] [24]:[2] Then Yahweh sent troops of Kasdim (Chaldeans), troops from Aram (Syria), troops from Moav (Moab), and Amoni troops against Yehudah (Judah) at different times to destroy them, just as Yahweh had said through his servants the prophets.
[2 Kings] [24]:[3] Those things troubled Yehudah at Yahweh’s command to remove them out of his sight because of all of King Menasheh’s (Manasseh) sins
[2 Kings] [24]:[4] and because he’d killed innocent people—Yahweh wouldn’t forgive him because he’d filled Yerushalem with innocent blood.
[2 Kings] [24]:[5] Everything else that Yehoyakim said and did is written in the book of the events of the kings of Yehudah.
[2 Kings] [24]:[6] Then Yehoyakim died and his son Yehoyakin replaced him as king.
[2 Kings] [24]:[7] The Mitsri (Egyptian) king didn’t continue his attacks on other countries, because the Babylonian king captured land all the way from the Mitsri river as far as the Perat (Euphrates) River—everything that had been controlled by Mitsrayim (Egypt).
[2 Kings] [24]:[8] Yehoyakin was eighteen when he became king, but he reigned from Yerushalem (Jerusalem) for only three months.
[2 Kings] [24]:[9] He did what Yahweh had said was evil just like his father had done.
[2 Kings] [24]:[10] At that time, the Babylonian king Nevukadnetsar (Nebuchadnezzar) sent his army to besiege Yerushalem,
[2 Kings] [24]:[11] and Nevukadnetsar himself travelled there to observe the operation.
[2 Kings] [24]:[12] Yehudah’s (Judah) King Yehoyakin went out to surrender to the Babylonian king, along with his mother, his servants, his captains, and his officials. So the Babylonian king took him captive in the eighth year of his reign.
[2 Kings] [24]:[13] Then all the valuables were brought out of Yahweh’s temple and the palace. All the gold furnishings that had been made for the temple by King Shelomoh (Solomon) were cut into pieces.
[2 Kings] [24]:[14] Then all the army leaders and officials, and all the craftsmen and blacksmiths from Yerushalem (some ten thousand people) were taken into exile, leaving only the poorer people behind.
[2 Kings] [24]:[15] King Yehoyakin was exiled from Yerushalem to Bavel (Babylon), along with his mother and wives, his officials,
[2 Kings] [24]:[16] seven thousand top soldiers, and a thousand skilled craftsmen and blacksmiths—leaving no one behind to fight or make weapons.
[2 Kings] [24]:[17] Then the Babylonian king appointed Yehoyakin’s uncle Matanyah as king in his place and he changed his name to Tsidkiyah (Zedekiah).
[2 Kings] [24]:[18] Tsidkiyah (Zedekiah) was twenty-one when he became king and he reigned from Yerushalem (Jerusalem) for eleven years. (His mother was Yirmiyah’s (Jeremiah) daughter Hamutal from Livnah.)
[2 Kings] [24]:[19] He did what Yahweh had said was evil, just like Yehoyakin had done.
[2 Kings] [24]:[20] Because Yahweh was still very angry, he had the people of Yerushalem and all Yehudah (Judah) driven away out of his sight. Then Tsidkiyah rebelled against the Babylonian king.
[2 Kings] [25]:[1] In the ninth year of Tsidkiyah’s (Zedekiah) reign, on the tenth day of the tenth month, the Babylonian King Nevukadnetsar (Nebuchadnezzar) brought all his army to Yerushalem (Jerusalem). They made their camp outside the city, and then built attack structures all around it
[2 Kings] [25]:[2] and besieged the city for two years.
[2 Kings] [25]:[3] The people didn’t have enough to eat and the famine became severe.
[2 Kings] [25]:[4] Then the Babylonians began breaking into the city, but the local fighters sneaked out at night through a gate between two walls near the king’s garden and escaped down to the desert plain.
[2 Kings] [25]:[5] However, the Babylonian soldiers chased after the king and they overtook him on the Yeriho (Jericho) plains, and his army scattered.
[2 Kings] [25]:[6] King Tsidkiyah was captured and taken to the Babylonian king at Rivlah, where he was sentenced—
[2 Kings] [25]:[7] He was forced to watch as his sons were slaughtered, then his eyes were gouged out and he was taken to Bavel (Babylon) restrained with two bronze chains.
[2 Kings] [25]:[8] On the seventh day of the fifth month of Babylonian King Nevukadnetsar’s (Nebuchadnezzar) nineteenth year as king, his servant Nevuzar-Adan, who was his chief bodyguard, went to Yerushalem (Jerusalem).
[2 Kings] [25]:[9] He set fire to Yahweh’s temple and the palace, and all of Yerushalem’s houses, so no important building remained.
[2 Kings] [25]:[10] Then the army under the command of Nevuzar-Adan tore down the walls surrounding Yerushalem.
[2 Kings] [25]:[11] He exiled all the rest of the people from the city, all the surrendered soldiers, and the rest of the population,
[2 Kings] [25]:[12] but he let some of the poorest people remain on the land to look after the vineyards and as farmers.
[2 Kings] [25]:[13] The Babylonians smashed the bronze pillars and the bases and the bronze ‘sea’ from the temple, and took all the bronze to Bavel (Babylon).
[2 Kings] [25]:[14] They also took the pots and shovels, the snuffers and spoons, and all the bronze utensils used in the temple activities.
[2 Kings] [25]:[15] They took the fire-pans and the gold and silver bowls.
[2 Kings] [25]:[16] The bronze from the two pillars, the ‘sea’, and the bases that had been made for the temple by Shelomoh (Solomon) was too heavy to be weighed.
[2 Kings] [25]:[17] Each pillar was over eight metres high, plus a bronze capital on top that was over a metre high. They were decorated with latticework with bronze pomegranates all around.
[2 Kings] [25]:[18] Nevuzar-Adan exiled to Bavel (Babylon) the high priest Serayah, the second priest Tsefanyah (Zephaniah), and the three temple entrance guards.
[2 Kings] [25]:[19] From the city, he took one official who was a military inspector, five of the king’s advisors, and the army commander’s secretary in charge of recruitment, plus sixty other important men.
[2 Kings] [25]:[20] Nevuzar-Adan took them all to the Babylonian king at Rivlah
[2 Kings] [25]:[21] in the Hamat region, but the king had them all executed there. So the large majority of the people of Yehudah (Judah) were exiled out of their country.
[2 Kings] [25]:[22] From those who the Babylonian King Nevukadnetsar (Nebuchadnezzar) allowed to remain, he appointed Gedalyah (son of Shafan’s son Ahikam) over them.
[2 Kings] [25]:[23] When all the army captains and their men heard that the Babylonian king had appointed Gedalyah, they came to Gedalyah at Mitspah. This was Netanyah’s son Yishmael (Ishmael), Kareah’s son Yohanan, Tanhumet’s son Serayah the Netofati, and the Ma’akati’s son Ya’azanyah, along with their men.
[2 Kings] [25]:[24] Gedalyah made an agreement with them and their men, telling them, “Don’t be afraid of the Babylonian officials. Stay in the land and serve the Babylonian king, and he’ll be good to you.”
[2 Kings] [25]:[25] But in the seventh month, Yishmael (the son of Netanyah, the son of Elishama who was a descendant of King David) brought ten men with him and attacked Gedalyah, and killed him, along with the Yehudim (Judeans) and the Kasdim (Chaldeans) who were with him at Mitspah.
[2 Kings] [25]:[26] After that, all the people, with or without any official status, along with the army commanders fled to Mitsrayim (Egypt) because they were afraid of what the Babylonians might do to them.
[2 Kings] [25]:[27] Thirty-seven years after Yehudah’s (Judah) King Yehoyakin had been exiled to Bavel (Babylon), Evil-Merodak had just become the new king of Bavel and he released Yehoyakin from prison on the 27th of the twelfth month.
[2 Kings] [25]:[28] He spoke kindly to Yehoyakin and honoured him more than the other kings who’d been taken to Bavel.
[2 Kings] [25]:[29] He was allowed to change out of his prison clothes, and was permitted to eat at the king’s table for the rest of his life,
[2 Kings] [25]:[30] as well as being given a daily monetary allowance.

[1 Chronicles] [1]:[43] These are the kings who ruled the region of Edom (where Se’ir’s descendants lived) before any kings ruled over Yisrael (Israel): Bela son of Be’or, and his city’s name was Dinhavah.

[1 Chronicles] [2]:[4] His daughter-in-law Tamar had twin boys named Perets and Zerah, so altogether Yehudah had five sons.
[1 Chronicles] [2]:[5] Perets’s sons were Hetsron and Hamul.

[1 Chronicles] [2]:[17] Avigayil had Amasa. Amasa’s father was Yeter, a descendant of Yishmael (Ishmael).
[1 Chronicles] [2]:[18] Hetsron’s third son Kalev (Caleb) had sons with Azuvah, one of his wives. The sons were Yesher, Shovav, and Ardon. (The other wife’s name was Yerieot.)
[1 Chronicles] [2]:[19] When Azuvah died, Kalev married Efrat, and they had a son named Hur.
[1 Chronicles] [2]:[20] Hur was the father of Uri, and Uri was the father of Betsalel.
[1 Chronicles] [2]:[21] Later, when Hetsron was sixty years old, he had sexual intercourse with a daughter of Makir from the region of Gilead and married her. Hetsron’s new wife gave birth to their son Seguv.
[1 Chronicles] [2]:[22] Seguv was the father of Yair, and Yair controlled twenty-three cities in the Gilead region.
[1 Chronicles] [2]:[23] But Geshur and Aram captured Havot-Ya’ir and Kenat from them, plus their surrounding towns—sixty towns in all, populated by descendants of Makir (the father of Gilead).
[1 Chronicles] [2]:[24] After Hetsron’s death in Kalev-Efratah, his wife Aviyah gave birth to his son Ashur (Assyria), the father of Tekoa.
[1 Chronicles] [2]:[25] Hetsron’s oldest son was Yerahme’el and his sons were Ram (the oldest), Bunah, Oren, Otsem, and Ahiyah.
[1 Chronicles] [2]:[26] Yerahme’el had another wife named Atarah. She was the mother of Onam.

[1 Chronicles] [4]:[2] Shoval had a son Reayah, Reayah had a son Yahat, and Yahat had Ahumay and Lahad. Those were the ancestors of the Tsor’atim.

[1 Chronicles] [4]:[4] Hur was the first son born to his mother Efratah, and he founded Beyt-Lehem (Bethlehem) city. Hur had these descendants: Penuel and Ezer. Penuel started the clans that lived in Gedor city, and Ezer started the clans that lived in Hushah city.
[1 Chronicles] [4]:[5] Hetsron’s son Ashur (Assyria), the father of Tekoa, had two wives, Helah and Na’arah,
[1 Chronicles] [4]:[6] and Na’arah bore him Ahuzam, Hefer, Teymeni, and Ha’ahashtari.
[1 Chronicles] [4]:[7] Ashur and his wife Helah’s sons were Tseret, Yitshar, Etnan,
[1 Chronicles] [4]:[8] and Kots. Kots was the father of Anuv and Tsovevah, and the ancestor of the clans descended from Harum’s son Aharhel.
[1 Chronicles] [4]:[9] Yaebets was more respected than his brothers. His mother had named him Yaebets (which sounds like the word meaning ‘pain’), saying, “It’s because I bore him in pain.”
[1 Chronicles] [4]:[10] Yaebets called out to Yisrael’s (Israel) god, saying, “Oh, please give me a real blessing, and help me and enlarge my territory, and don’t do anything to harm me, so that I won’t be in pain.” And God did what Yaebets requested.
[1 Chronicles] [4]:[11] Another of Yehudah’s (Judah) descendants was Shuhah. His brother Keluv was the father of Mehir. Mehir was the father of Eshton.
[1 Chronicles] [4]:[12] Eshton was the father of Beyt-Rafa, Paseah, and Tehinah. Tehinah founded Nahash city, but lived in Rekah.
[1 Chronicles] [4]:[13] Kenaz’s sons were Otniel and Serayah. And Otniel’s sons were Hatat and Me’onotay.
[1 Chronicles] [4]:[14] Me’onotay had a son Ofrah, and Serayah fathered Yoav (Joab), the founder of Craftsmen’s Valley, because they were craftsmen.
[1 Chronicles] [4]:[15] The sons of Kalev (Caleb) (Yefuneh’s son) were Iru, Elah, and Na’am, and Elah’s son was Kenaz.
[1 Chronicles] [4]:[16] Yehalel’el’s sons were Zif, Zifah, Tirya, and Asarel.
[1 Chronicles] [4]:[17] Ezra’s sons were Yeter, Mered, Efer, and Yalon. And Mered’s wife Bityah conceived Miryam (Miriam), Shamay, and Yishbah, the father of Eshtemoa.
[1 Chronicles] [4]:[18] She was one of Par’oh’s (Pharaoh) daughters. Mered’s wife, who was a descendant of Yehudah (Judah), gave birth to Yered (Jared) the father of Gedor, Hever the father of Sokoh, and Yekutiel the father of Zanoah.
[1 Chronicles] [4]:[19] The sons of Hodiyah’s wife (Naham’s sister) were the father of Ke’ilah the Garmi and the father of Eshtemoa the Ma’akati.
[1 Chronicles] [4]:[20] Shim’on’s sons were Amnon, Rinah, Ben-Hanan, and Tulon. Yishei’s sons were Zohet and Ben-Zohet.
[1 Chronicles] [4]:[21] The sons of Shela (one of Yehudah’s (Judah) sons) were Er (father of Lekah), Laedah (father of Mareshah and the clans who worked with linen at Beyt-Eshbea),
[1 Chronicles] [4]:[22] Yokim and the men of Kozava, and Yoash and Saraf, who ruled in Moav (Moab) and Yashuvi-Lehem. (All this is from ancient records.)
[1 Chronicles] [4]:[23] They were the potters who lived in Netaeim and Gederah—they lived there and worked for the king.
[1 Chronicles] [4]:[24] Shim’on’s (Simeon) sons were Nemuel, Yamin, Yariv, Zerah, and Shaul.
[1 Chronicles] [4]:[25] Shaul’s son was Shalum. Shalum’s son was Mivsam. Mivsam’s son was Mishma.
[1 Chronicles] [4]:[26] The following were Mishma’s descendants: Mishma’s son was Hamuel. Hamuel’s son was Zakur. Zakur’s son was Shimei.
[1 Chronicles] [4]:[27] Shimei had sixteen sons and six daughters, but none of his brothers had many children, so Shim’on’s descendants were never as numerous as those of his younger brother Yehudah (Judah).
[1 Chronicles] [4]:[28] Shim’on’s descendants lived in these cities and towns: Be’er-Sheva (Beersheba), Moladah, Hatsar-Shual,
[1 Chronicles] [4]:[29] Bilhah, Etsem, Tolad,
[1 Chronicles] [4]:[30] Betuel, Hormah, Tsiklag,
[1 Chronicles] [4]:[31] Beyt-Hamarkavot, Hatsar-Susim, Beyt-Biri, and Sha’arayim. They lived in those places until David became king.
[1 Chronicles] [4]:[32] They also lived in five villages: Eytam, Ayin, Rimon, Token, and Ashan,
[1 Chronicles] [4]:[33] and all the villages around these towns as far as Ba’al. Those were their settlements, and they kept their genealogical records.
[1 Chronicles] [4]:[34] Their clan leaders were Meshovav, Yamlek, Yoshah the son of Amatsyah,
[1 Chronicles] [4]:[35] Yoel (Joel), Yehu (Jehu) the son of Yoshivyah, the son of Serayah, the son of Asiyel,
[1 Chronicles] [4]:[36] as well as Elyehoeynay, Ya’akovah, Yeshohayah, Asayah, Adiel, Yeshimael, Benayah,
[1 Chronicles] [4]:[37] and Ziza the son of Shifei, the son of Alon, the son of Yedayah, the son of Shimri, the son of Shemayah.
[1 Chronicles] [4]:[38] Those who are named above were the leaders of their clans, and their extended families increased greatly in number,
[1 Chronicles] [4]:[39] and they went to the entrance of Gedor (to the east of the valley) in search of pasture for their flocks.
[1 Chronicles] [4]:[40] They found good, fertile pasture, and the land was wide, and quiet and peaceful, because Ham’s descendants had lived there previously.
[1 Chronicles] [4]:[41] Those listed by name went there in the days of Yehudah’s (Judah) King Hizkiyah (Hezekiah) and struck down the tents of the Meunim who were found there. They completely annihilated them (to this day), and they lived there in their place because there was pasture for their flocks there.
[1 Chronicles] [4]:[42] Then five hundred of their men who were descendants of Shim’on (Simeon) went to Mt. Se’ir, led by Yishei’s sons Pelatyah, Nearyah, Refayah, and Uziel.
[1 Chronicles] [4]:[43] They also struck down the rest of the Amalekim who escaped, and they’ve lived there to this day.
[1 Chronicles] [5]:[1] Re’uven was the first child born to Yisrael (Israel) (also known as Ya’akov (Jacob) ), but when he had sex with one of his father’s slave-wives, his birthright was given to the sons of Yosef (Joseph), another one of Yisrael’s sons. So Re’uven wasn’t recorded as inheriting the birthright,
[1 Chronicles] [5]:[2] and although Yehudah (Judah) was stronger than his other brothers and would be the son to produce a ruler, the birthright went to Yosef.
[1 Chronicles] [5]:[3] The sons of Yisrael’s eldest son Re’uven were Hanok, Palu, Hetsron, and Karmi.
[1 Chronicles] [5]:[4] Another of Re’uven’s descendants was Yoel (Joel), and his son was Shemayah. Shemayah’s son was Gog. Gog’s son was Shimei.
[1 Chronicles] [5]:[5] Shimei’s son was Mikah. Mikah’s son was Reayah. Reayah’s son was Ba’al.
[1 Chronicles] [5]:[6] Ba’al’s son was Be’erah, who became a leader of the Re’uvenim, but the Assyrian King Tiglat-Pileser captured him and took him back to Ashur (Assyria).
[1 Chronicles] [5]:[7] His brothers by their clans, as listed in their genealogical records: Yeiel the leader, Zekaryah (Zechariah),
[1 Chronicles] [5]:[8] Bela son of Azaz, son of Shema, son of Yoel. Re’uven’s clan lived near the city of Aroer as far north as the cities of Nevo and Ba’al-Me’on.
[1 Chronicles] [5]:[9] Some of them lived further east, as far as the edge of the desert that extends to the Perat (Euphrates) River, because their livestock had multiplied back in the Gilead region.
[1 Chronicles] [5]:[10] (In the days of King Sha’ul (Saul), they’d battled with the Hagrim and defeated them, so then they’d lived in their tents all over eastern Gilead.)
[1 Chronicles] [5]:[11] Gad’s descendants lived opposite them in the Bashan region as far as Salkah:
[1 Chronicles] [5]:[12] Yoel (Joel) was their leader, Shafam was second-in-command, others were Ya’anay and Shafat in Bashan.
[1 Chronicles] [5]:[13] Their cousins who were leaders of seven clans were Mika’el (Michael), Meshulam, Sheva, Yoray, Ya’akan, Ziea, and Ever.
[1 Chronicles] [5]:[14] Those were descendants of Avihayil, the son of Huri, the son of Yaroah, the son of Gilead, the son of Mika’el, the son of Yeshishay, the son of Yahdo, the son of Buz.
[1 Chronicles] [5]:[15] Ahi was the son of Avdiel, the son of Guni, head of their clans.
[1 Chronicles] [5]:[16] Those descendants of Gad lived in towns in the Gilead and Bashan regions, and on all the pastureland throughout the Sharon Plain.
[1 Chronicles] [5]:[17] All of them were listed in the genealogies in the days of Yehudah’s (Judah) King Yotam (Jotham) and Yisrael’s (Israel) King Yarov’am (Jeroboam).
[1 Chronicles] [5]:[18] There were 44,760 warriors descended from strong men in the tribes of Re’uven and Gad and the eastern half of the tribe of Menasheh (Manasseh). They all carried shields and swords, and bows and arrows, and were all trained to fight in battles.
[1 Chronicles] [5]:[19] They went to war against the Hagrim, Yetur, Nafish, and Nodav,
[1 Chronicles] [5]:[20] and were helped because they called out to God in the battle. So with God answering their prayers because of their trust in him, they were able to defeat the Hagrim and their allies.
[1 Chronicles] [5]:[21] They captured their livestock, including 50,000 camels, 250,000 sheep, and 2,000 donkeys, as well as 100,000 people,
[1 Chronicles] [5]:[22] because many were killed as a result of God’s assistance. Then they lived in that area until the exile.
[1 Chronicles] [5]:[23] The descendants of the half tribe of Menasheh (Manasseh) lived in the Bashan region as far as Ba’al-Hermon and Senir, and Mt. Hermon, and they increased in number.
[1 Chronicles] [5]:[24] Their clan leaders were Efer, Yishei, Eliel, Azriel, Yirmiyah (Jeremiah), Hodavyah, and Yahdiyel. They were all powerful and famous warriors, and leaders of their clans.
[1 Chronicles] [5]:[25] But they disobeyed their ancestors’ god, and they prostituted themselves to the gods of the peoples that God had destroyed ahead of them in that region.
[1 Chronicles] [5]:[26] So Yisrael’s (Israel) god stirred up the spirit of the Assyrian King Pul (also known as Tiglat-Pileser). He took them into exile—that is, the Re’uvenim, the Gadim, and the half tribe of Menasheh (Manasseh). Then he took them to Halah, Havor, Hara, and the river of Gozan (where they still are to this day).

[1 Chronicles] [6]:[49] It was Aharon (Aaron) and his sons who were responsible for offering the sacrifices on the altar for burnt offerings and on the altar for incense, for all the work of the holiest place, and for making atonement for Yisrael (Israel), according to everything that God’s servant Mosheh (Moses) had instructed.
[1 Chronicles] [6]:[50] These were Aharon’s descendants: Aharon’s son was Eleazar. Eleazar’s son was Pinhas. Pinhas’s son was Avishua.

[1 Chronicles] [7]:[1] Yisakar’s (Issachar) four sons were Tola, Puah, Yashuv, and Shimron.
[1 Chronicles] [7]:[2] Tola’s sons were Uzi, Refayah, Yeriel, Yahmay, Yivsam, and Shmuel (Samuel), who all became leaders of their clans. There were strong warriors in the record of Tola’s descendants in each generation. (During the time when David was Yisrael’s (Israel) king, there were 22,600 such men.)
[1 Chronicles] [7]:[3] Uzi’s son was Yizrahyah. Yizrahyah’s five sons were Mika’el (Michael), Ovadyah (Obadiah), Yoel (Joel), and Yishiyah. They were all leaders of their clans.
[1 Chronicles] [7]:[4] Along with them, according to their family records, were 36,000 troops in the army, because they had numerous wives and sons.
[1 Chronicles] [7]:[5] Altogether, Yisakar’s clans had 87,000 strong warriors listed in their genealogy.
[1 Chronicles] [7]:[6] Benyamin’s three sons were Bela, Beker, and Yedieael.
[1 Chronicles] [7]:[7] Bela’s five sons were Etsbon, Uzi, Uziel, Yerimot, and Iri, who were leaders of their clans. According to their family records, they had 22,034 strong warriors.
[1 Chronicles] [7]:[8] Beker’s sons were Zemirah, Yoash, Eliezer, Elyehoeynay, Omri, Yerimot, Aviyah, Anatot, and Alemet.
[1 Chronicles] [7]:[9] Altogether, their clans had 20,200 strong warriors listed in their genealogy.
[1 Chronicles] [7]:[10] Yedieael’s son was Bilhan. Bilhan’s sons were Ye’ush, Benyamin, Ehud, Kena’anah, Zeytan, Tarshish, and Ahishahar.
[1 Chronicles] [7]:[11] All those descendants of Yedieael were clan leaders and strong warriors, having 17,200 men ready to go to war.
[1 Chronicles] [7]:[12] The Shupim and Hupim were descendants of Ir, and the Hushim were descendants of Aher.
[1 Chronicles] [7]:[13] Naftali’s (Naphtali) sons were Yahtsiel, Guni, Yetser, and Shalum. (They were descendants of Ya’akov’s (Jacob) slave-wife Bilhah.)
[1 Chronicles] [7]:[14] Menasheh (Manasseh) had sons by his Arami (Syrian) (Heb. Aramean) slave-wife. She gave birth to Asriel and Makir (who fathered Gilead).
[1 Chronicles] [7]:[15] Makir married a wife from the Hupim and Shupim. (His sister’s name was Ma’akah.) Another descendant was Tselofehad, and he had daughters.
[1 Chronicles] [7]:[16] Makir’s wife (also called Ma’akah) bore a son and named him Peresh (and named his brother Sheresh) and his sons were Ulam and Rekem.
[1 Chronicles] [7]:[17] Ulam’s son was Bedan. Those were the descendants of Gilead (Makir’s son and Menasheh’s grandson).
[1 Chronicles] [7]:[18] Gilead’s sister was Hamoleket. She was the mother of Ishehod, Aviezer, and Mahlah.
[1 Chronicles] [7]:[19] Another of Gilead’s sons was Shemida, whose sons were Ahyan, Shekem, Likhi, and Anieam.
[1 Chronicles] [7]:[20] These are Efrayim’s (Ephraim) descendants: One of Efrayim’s sons was Shutelah. Shutelah’s son was Bered. Bered’s son was Tahat. Tahat’s son was Eleadah. Eleadah’s son was also named Tahat.
[1 Chronicles] [7]:[21] Tahat’s son was Zavad. Zavad’s son was Shutelah. Efrayim’s other sons, Ezer and Elead, went to Gat city to steal some cattle but were killed by some of the natives of that area.
[1 Chronicles] [7]:[22] Their father Efrayim mourned for quite some time, and his relatives came to comfort him.
[1 Chronicles] [7]:[23] Then he slept with his wife and she got pregnant and gave birth to a son. Efrayim named him Beriah (which sounds like the Hebrew word for ‘trouble’), because of the recent tragedy in their family.
[1 Chronicles] [7]:[24] Efrayim’s daughter was She’erah and she founded three towns: Lower Beyt-Horon, Upper Beyt-Horon, and Uzen-She’erah.
[1 Chronicles] [7]:[25] Another of Efrayim’s sons was Refah. Refah’s son was Reshef. Reshef’s son was Telah. Telah’s son was Tahan.
[1 Chronicles] [7]:[26] Tahan’s son was Laedan. Laedan’s son was Amihud. Amihud’s son was Elishama.
[1 Chronicles] [7]:[27] Elishama’s son was Nun. Nun’s son was Yehoshua (Joshua) (or Yehoshua, who led Yisrael’s (Israel) descendants after Mosheh (Moses) died).
[1 Chronicles] [7]:[28] This is a list of the cities and areas where Efrayim’s descendants lived: Beyt-El (Bethel) and the nearby villages, Na’aran to the east, Gezer to the west and the nearby villages, and Shekem and the nearby villages extending north as far as Ayah and its villages.
[1 Chronicles] [7]:[29] Along the border of the area where Menasheh’s (Manasseh) descendants lived were these towns: Beyt-Shean, Ta’anak, Megidon, Dor, and all the nearby villages. The people who lived in all those places were descendants of Ya’akov’s (Jacob) son Yosef (Joseph).

[1 Chronicles] [9]:[1] So the genealogy of all Israelis was listed—yes, written on the scroll of Yisrael’s (Israel) kings. Then Yehudah (Judah) was taken into exile to Bavel (Babylon) because of their unfaithfulness.

[1 Chronicles] [9]:[4] Utay son of Amihud (Amihud was Omri’s son, Omri was Imri’s son, Imri was Bani’s son, Bani was a descendant of Perets, Perets was Yehudah’s son),

[1 Chronicles] [9]:[9] In all, there were 956 of Benyamin’s descendants living in Yerushalem. All those above were leaders of their clans.

[1 Chronicles] [9]:[13] Altogether there were 1,760 priests who returned to Yehudah. They were leaders of their clans, and they were all capable and responsible to work in God’s residence.
[1 Chronicles] [9]:[14] From Levi’s descendants who returned to Yehudah (Judah) there were: Shemayah (who was Hashuv’s son, Hashuv was Azrikam’s son, Azrikam was Hashavyah’s son, Hashavyah was a descendant of Levi’s youngest son Merari),

[1 Chronicles] [9]:[17] From Levi’s descendants who returned to Yehudah and who guarded the temple gates there were Shalum, Akuv, Talmon, Ahiman, and some of their relatives. Shalum was their leader.
[1 Chronicles] [9]:[18] Those descendents of Levi were gatekeepers at the King’s Gate on the east, and their descendants still are, even to this day.
[1 Chronicles] [9]:[19] Shalum was Kore’s son, Kore was Evyasaf’s son, and Evyasaf was Korah’s son. Shalum and his relatives from his clan (Korah’s descendants) had the duty of being gatekeepers, responsible for guarding the entrances to Yahweh’s temple, as their ancestors had done.
[1 Chronicles] [9]:[20] Previously Pinhas (Eleazar’s son) had supervised the gatekeepers. Yahweh was with Pinhas.
[1 Chronicles] [9]:[21] Zekaryah (Zechariah) (Meshelemyah’s son) was gatekeeper of the entrance to the assembly tent.
[1 Chronicles] [9]:[22] Altogether, there were 212 men chosen to guard the gates. The records of the clans in their villages listed their names. King David and the prophet Shmuel (Samuel) appointed them because they were dependable.
[1 Chronicles] [9]:[23] They and their sons watched over the gates of Yahweh’s house, that is, the sacred tent, as guards.
[1 Chronicles] [9]:[24] There were gatekeepers on each of the temple’s four sides: east, west, north, and south.
[1 Chronicles] [9]:[25] Their relatives in their villages would come in from time to time to relieve them for seven days,
[1 Chronicles] [9]:[26] because the four leaders of the gatekeepers were Levites, and they were also trusted to supervise the rooms and the treasuries in God’s residence.
[1 Chronicles] [9]:[27] They would spend the night around the temple while they were in charge, and would open it with the key each morning.
[1 Chronicles] [9]:[28] Some of them monitored the utensils used in the activities—counting them as they brought them out and when they put them away again.
[1 Chronicles] [9]:[29] Others took care of the containers and utensils used in the sanctuary, along with the fine flour, the wine and oil, and the frankincense and spices.
[1 Chronicles] [9]:[30] Some of the priests mixed the fragrances and spices.
[1 Chronicles] [9]:[31] There was a Levite named Matityah (Shalum’s oldest son, who was a descendant of Korah) whose official duty was supervising the baking of the flat breads.
[1 Chronicles] [9]:[32] Some of Kohat’s descendants prepared the rows of bread to be laid out on the sacred table every rest day.
[1 Chronicles] [9]:[33] Some of Levi’s descendants were temple musicians and singers. The leaders of those families stayed in the temple accommodations. They didn’t have other duties, because they were expected to serve day and night.
[1 Chronicles] [9]:[34] Those were the heads of the Levite families according to their generations, and they lived in Yerushalem (Jerusalem).
