[Nehemyah] [11]:[34] in Hadid, Tsevoim, and Nevalat,
[Nehemyah] [11]:[35] in Lod, Ono, and in the Craftsmen’s valley.
[Nehemyah] [11]:[36] Also some Levites previously connected with Yehudah (Judah) settled in Benyamin.
[Nehemyah] [12]:[1] These are the priests and the Levites who came back with Shealtiyel’s son Zerubavel and with Yeshua: Serayah, Yirmiyah (Jeremiah), and Ezra,
[Nehemyah] [12]:[2] Amaryah, Maluk, and Hatush,
[Nehemyah] [12]:[3] Shekanyah, Rehum, and Meremot,
[Nehemyah] [12]:[4] Ido, Gineton, and Aviyah,
[Nehemyah] [12]:[5] Miyamin, Moeadyah, and Bilgah,
[Nehemyah] [12]:[6] Shemayah, Yoyariv, and Yedayah,
[Nehemyah] [12]:[7] Salu, Amok, Hilkiyah, and another Yedayah. Those were the leaders of the priests and their brothers in Yeshua’s time.
[Nehemyah] [12]:[8] The Levites were: Yeshua, Binuy, Kadmiel, Shereveyah, Yehudah (Judah), and Matanyah who led the thanksgiving songs along with his brothers,
[Nehemyah] [12]:[9] Bakbukyah and Uni—their brothers who stood opposite them in the services.
[Nehemyah] [12]:[10] Yeshua fathered Yoyakim who then fathered Elyashiv, and Elyashiv fathered Yoyada.
[Nehemyah] [12]:[11] Then Yoyada fathered Yonatan (Jonathan) who then fathered Yadua.
[Nehemyah] [12]:[12] In Yoyakim’s time, these were the heads of the priestly families: Merayah was the head of Serayah’s family, Hananyah for Yirmiyah’s (Jeremiah),
[Nehemyah] [12]:[13] Meshulam for Ezra’s family, Yehohanan for Amaryah’s,
[Nehemyah] [12]:[14] Yonatan (Jonathan) for Maluk’s family, Yosef (Joseph) for Shevanyah’s,
[Nehemyah] [12]:[15] Adna for Harim’s family, Helkay for Merayot’s,
[Nehemyah] [12]:[16] Zekaryah (Zechariah) for Ido’s family, Meshulam for Gineton’s,
[Nehemyah] [12]:[17] Zikri for Aviyah’s family, Piltay for Moeadyah’s,
[Nehemyah] [12]:[18] Shamua for Bilgah’s family, Yonatan (Jonathan) for Shemayah’s,
[Nehemyah] [12]:[19] Matenay for Yoyariv’s family, Uzi for Yedayah’s,
[Nehemyah] [12]:[20] Kalay for Salu’s family, Ever for Amok’s,
[Nehemyah] [12]:[21] Hashavyah for Hilkiyah’s family, and Netanel for Yedayah’s.
[Nehemyah] [12]:[22] In the days of Elyashiv, Yoyada, Yohanan, and Yadua, during the reign of Persian King Dareyavesh (Darius), the heads of the families of the Levites and priests were recorded.
[Nehemyah] [12]:[23] The names of the descendants of Levi who were heads of families were written in the official history records up till the time of Elyashiv’s son Yohanan.
[Nehemyah] [12]:[24] The Levites’ leaders were Hashavyah, Shereveyah, and Kadmiel’s son Yeshua with their brothers serving opposite them in each service to praise and give thanks as had been commanded by David, the man of God.
[Nehemyah] [12]:[25] Matanyah, Bakbukyah, Ovadyah (Obadiah), Meshulam, Talmon, and Akuv were gatekeepers who stood guard at the storerooms near the temple gates.
[Nehemyah] [12]:[26] That was at the time of Yoyakim (son of Yeshua, son of Yotsadak), and at the time of Nehemyah (Nehemiah) the governor and Ezra the priest and scribe.
[Nehemyah] [12]:[27] At the dedication of the wall around Yerushalem (Jerusalem), they summoned Levites from all over the region to come to Yerushalem to perform the dedication with rejoicing and thanksgiving, and with musical instruments and singing,
[Nehemyah] [12]:[28] plus the next generation of singers came both from Yerushalem and its surrounds, and from the Netofati villages.
[Nehemyah] [12]:[29] They also came from Beyt-Hagilgal, and from the fields of Geva and Azmavet, because the singers had built villages near Yerushalem to live in.
[Nehemyah] [12]:[30] The priests and Levites held a purification ceremony for themselves, then they purified the people and the gates and the wall.
[Nehemyah] [12]:[31] Then I assembled Yehudah’s (Judah) leaders together up on top of the wall, and I assigned them into two large groups who would give thanks as they walked around it. The first group headed towards the Dung Gate on the right.
[Nehemyah] [12]:[32] Hoshayah and half of Yehudah’s officials were in that group
[Nehemyah] [12]:[33] along with Azaryah, Ezra, and Meshulam,
[Nehemyah] [12]:[34] Yehudah, Benyamin, Shemayah, and Yirmiyah (Jeremiah),
[Nehemyah] [12]:[35] plus some of the next generation of priests with trumpets: Zekaryah (Zechariah) (son of Yonatan (Jonathan), son of Shemayah, son of Matanyah, son of Mikayah, son of Zakur, son of Asaf)
[Nehemyah] [12]:[36] and his brothers Shemayah, Azarel, Milalay, Gilalay, Ma’ay, Netanel, Yehudah, and Hanani. They used the instruments as per the instructions of the late King David, the man of God. Ezra the scribe went in front of them.
[Nehemyah] [12]:[37] When they got to the Fountain Gate, they went up the stairs at the City of David, and along the higher portion of the wall by David’s palace as far as the Water Gate (on the east side of the city).
[Nehemyah] [12]:[38] The other group giving thanks with the other half of the people went in the opposite direction around the top of the wall—going past the Ovens Tower to the wider part of the wall.
[Nehemyah] [12]:[39] We passed Efrayim Gate, the Old Gate, Fish Gate, and Hananel Tower, the Hundred Tower, and all the way to the Sheep Gate, and we stopped at the Guard Gate.
[Nehemyah] [12]:[40] Then both groups ended up at the temple and stood there. I was there with the half of the city officials who’d accompanied me,
[Nehemyah] [12]:[41] as well as the priests with their trumpets: Elyakim, Ma’aseyah, Minyamin, Mikayah, Elyehoeynay, Zekaryah, Hananyah,
[Nehemyah] [12]:[42] another Ma’aseyah, Shemayah, Eleazar, Uzi, Yehohanan, Malkiyah, Eylam, and Ezer. The singers sang loudly with their leader Yizrahyah.
[Nehemyah] [12]:[43] Then that same day they offered many sacrifices, and they celebrated because God had made them very pleased. The women and children also celebrated, in fact the sound of the celebrations in Yerushalem (Jerusalem) was so loud that it can be heard far away.
[Nehemyah] [12]:[44] Then still on that same day, men were appointed to be in charge of the storerooms for the tithes and offerings. The percentages for the priests and the Levites were gathered from the fields around the cities as per the written law, because the people of Yehudah (Judah) were happy to have the priests and the Levites serving.
[Nehemyah] [12]:[45] They served God with their daily duties and the purification ceremonies, as well as the duties of the singers and gatekeepers—all done according to the instructions left by King David and his son Shelomoh (Solomon),
[Nehemyah] [12]:[46] because it was handed down from the original singers who sang songs of praise and thanksgiving to God in the time of David and Asaf.
[Nehemyah] [12]:[47] In Zerubavel and Nehemyah’s (Nehemiah) times, all Yisrael (Israel) contributed the daily food allowance for the singers and gatekeepers. They also gave a percentage to the Levites who then gave a percentage of that to the priests (Aharon’s (Aaron) descendants).
[Nehemyah] [13]:[1] That day, the Mosheh (Moses) scroll was read out aloud to the people, and it was discovered that it had been written that no Amoni or Moavi is ever allowed to join the congregation
[Nehemyah] [13]:[2] because instead of helping the travelling Israelis with food and water, they had hired Bil’am (Balaam) to curse them (even though God had turned that curse into blessing).
[Nehemyah] [13]:[3] After hearing that, they separated out all of the foreigners.
[Nehemyah] [13]:[4] Prior to that time, the high priest Elyashiv (closely related to Toviyah) had been in charge of the temple storerooms
[Nehemyah] [13]:[5] and he’d allowed Toviyah to have a large room that had previously been used to store offerings: the frankincense, the utensils, and donated grain, wine, and oil, (the percentage commanded to be given to the Levites, the singers, and the gatekeepers), and the offerings for the priests.
[Nehemyah] [13]:[6] During all that period, I hadn’t been in Yerushalem (Jerusalem) because I’d returned to the Babylonian king in the 32nd year of Artahshashta’s (Artaxerxes) reign (Artaxerxes). However, after a while I requested leave again from the king
[Nehemyah] [13]:[7] and I came back to Yerushalem. It was then that I discovered how evil Elyashiv had been by making a storeroom for Toviyah in the courtyards of God’s residence.
[Nehemyah] [13]:[8] It made me very upset and I threw everything of Toviyah’s out of the room.
[Nehemyah] [13]:[9] Then I ordered the storerooms to be purified by the priests before I returned the temple utensils to the room, along with the grain offerings and the incense.
[Nehemyah] [13]:[10] I found out that the Levites and the singers weren’t being given their percentage, so they’d left their duties and returned to cultivate their own fields.
[Nehemyah] [13]:[11] I made a complaint to the officials asking why the operation of the temple had been neglected, and then I rounded up the Levites and the singers and sent them back to their duties.
[Nehemyah] [13]:[12] After that, the people of Yehudah (Judah) started bringing a tenth of their grain and wine and oil to the storerooms.
[Nehemyah] [13]:[13] I appointed book-keepers over the storerooms: the priest Shelemyah, the scribe Tsadok, and the Levite Pedayah with Hanan (the son of Zakur, the son of Matanyah) helping. They were all considered trustworthy, and their job included distributing the produce among their colleagues. i
[Nehemyah] [13]:[14] My god, remember me handling all these issues and don’t wipe out my loyal kindness for your temple and its operation that I’ve shown.
[Nehemyah] [13]:[15] In those days I saw people in Yehudah (Judah) working on the rest day—treading wine, bringing in grain, and loading donkeys, yes, even bringing wine, grapes, figs, and all kinds of loads into Yerushalem (Jerusalem) on the rest day. I complained to them when they were selling the goods.
[Nehemyah] [13]:[16] Also, people from Tsor (Tyre) were bringing in fish and all kinds of merchandise and were selling it on the rest day to the Israelis, even in Yerushalem.
[Nehemyah] [13]:[17] I rebuked the Yehudah business leaders, asking them, “What’s this evil thing that you’re all doing—profaning the rest day by treating it like a regular day?
[Nehemyah] [13]:[18] Wasn’t that what your ancestors did—the very reason our god brought all this evil on us and on this city? Now you’re all making God angry with Yisrael (Israel) again by profaning the rest day.”
[Nehemyah] [13]:[19] So after that, when it started to get dark on Friday evenings, I ordered that the city gates be closed, and not to be opened until after the rest day. I also stationed some of my young men to stand at the gates to ensure that no load could enter on the rest day.
[Nehemyah] [13]:[20] Some traders and merchants selling various goods camped outside the city walls once or twice,
[Nehemyah] [13]:[21] but I warned them, “Why are you camping there outside the wall? If you do it again, I’ll have you all removed.” After that, they no longer came on the rest days.
[Nehemyah] [13]:[22] Then I told the Levites that they should purify themselves and then come to the gates to monitor them on the rest day. i My god, remember me having to deal with this, and show your amazing loyal faithfulness towards me.
[Nehemyah] [13]:[23] During that time, I also saw Yehudim (Jews) who’d married women from Ashdod, Amon, and Moav (Moab),
[Nehemyah] [13]:[24] and half of their children spoke a foreign language from those other people groups and couldn’t speak Hebrew.
[Nehemyah] [13]:[25] So I scolded those men and cursed them and hit some of them and pulled out their hair. Then I forced them to promise in front on God that they wouldn’t allow their daughters to marry foreign men, or their sons to take foreign wives.
[Nehemyah] [13]:[26] I explained, “Didn’t Yisrael’s (Israel) own King Shelomoh (Solomon) sin concerning that same matter? Among all the countries in the world, there wasn’t any other king like, and he was loved by his god who’d placed him there as king over all Yisrael. But even then, the foreign women caused him to sin.
[Nehemyah] [13]:[27] So do we need to hear about all of you doing this terrible evil of being unfaithful to God by marrying foreign wives?”
[Nehemyah] [13]:[28] Also one of Yoyada’s sons (grandson of the high priest Elyashiv) was a son-in-law of Sanvalat the Horoni, so I banished him from my sight. i
[Nehemyah] [13]:[29] My god, remember them for bringing shame to the priesthood and dishonouring the vows made by the priests and the Levites.
[Nehemyah] [13]:[30] Then I purified them from everything foreign, established regulations for each part of the work done by the priests and the Levites,
[Nehemyah] [13]:[31] and organised the firewood supply at certain times, including for the first-fruits celebrations. i My god, remember me for good.
[Ester] [1]:[1] The following events happened during the reign of Emperor Ahashverosh (Ahasuerus/Xerxes). (Also known as King Ahashverosh, he ruled the 127 provinces of Paras (Persia) extending from Hodu to Kush (Ethiopia).)
[Ester] [1]:[2] In those days, he ruled his empire from Shushan (Susa), city.
[Ester] [1]:[3] In the third year of his reign, he hosted a celebration for all of his officials and for every important person who worked for him, the wealthy landowners, the officials of the provinces, as well as the officers who served in the army of the combined empire of Paras and Maday (Media). He was present in person
[Ester] [1]:[4] to host the six-month celebration which, displayed the incredible wealth and prestige of his empire and his personal wealth and power.
[Ester] [1]:[5] At the end of that time, the emperor hosted another celebration, but this time for all the people in the royal fort in Shushan, from the nobles to the least prestigious. He held this celebration over an entire week in the enclosed garden of the royal palace.
[Ester] [1]:[6] There were white and blue curtains hanging from white and purple cords attached to silver rings on marble pillars. The guests reclined on gold and silver couches set on a mosaic floor made of red and white marble, mother-of-pearl and other expensive stones.
[Ester] [1]:[7] Drinks were served in golden goblets, and each one was a unique design. The king’s wine seemed limitless as he displayed his generosity,
[Ester] [1]:[8] and it was served according to his rule: there was no compulsion to drink, but his servants were to give each guest however much they wanted.
[Ester] [1]:[9] Meanwhile, Queen Vashti was hosting a celebration for the women in a different part of the royal palace.
[Ester] [1]:[10] On the last day of the celebrations, when the emperor was pleasantly tipsy, he ordered seven of his chief servants (Mehuman, Bizta, Harvona, Bigta, Avagta, Zetar, and Karkas)
[Ester] [1]:[11] to bring Queen Vashti to him, wearing her royal crown, in order to show the officials and other people how good-looking she was, because she was very beautiful.
[Ester] [1]:[12] The servants told her Ahashverosh’s (Ahasuerus/Xerxes) command, but Queen Vashti refused to come. When they reported back to Ahashverosh, he was furious and sat there raging for a while.
[Ester] [1]:[13] Eventually he discussed it with his close advisors who knew the law and could make good decisions. (These seven officials; Karshena, Shetar, Admata, Tarshish, Meres, Marsena and Memukan; were from various places. They advised the emperor personally, so were the most powerful officials in the empire.)
[Ester] [1]:[15] ‘According to our law,’ he asked, ‘what should be done with Empress Vashti, since she refused to obey my command when the servants passed it on to her?’
[Ester] [1]:[16] Memukan replied, addressing the whole group, ‘Empress Vashti has done wrong, and not only against the emperor. She has also done wrong against all the officials and people groups of the empire.
[Ester] [1]:[17] Soon women all over the empire will hear about what the empress did and they’ll say, “Emperor Ahashverosh commanded his servants to bring Empress Vashti to him, but she didn’t go!” Then women will stop respecting their husbands.
[Ester] [1]:[18] Even today, the important wives in the empire will hear what the empress did and start doing the same to their husbands; it will result in contempt on her part and anger on his.
[Ester] [1]:[19] If it pleases you to do so, your majesty, you should personally issue a royal decree and have it added to the laws of Paras (Persia) and Maday (Media) which cannot be repealed. This decree should say that Vashti can never again come into your presence. Then you should choose a different woman for the royal position – someone who’s better than her.
[Ester] [1]:[20] Have your decree proclaimed throughout your empire, even though it’s so huge, and then all women, whatever their status or position, will respect their husbands.’
[Ester] [1]:[21] Memukan’s advice seemed like a good idea to the emperor and his officials, so that’s what they did.
[Ester] [1]:[22] They wrote letters to every province using its own alphabet and to each people group in its own language. The letters said that men should be the masters over their wives and children, and that a husband should be able to give orders to his wife in his own language and that she should understand and obey him.
[Ester] [2]:[1] Some time later when King Ahashverosh (Ahasuerus/Xerxes) no longer felt so angry, he started to miss Vashti. But when she’d disobeyed his command, he had made a decree that she could never come into his presence again.
[Ester] [2]:[2] So some of the young men who served the king suggested to him, “Your majesty, you should get a new wife for yourself. You could tell your servants to look for young virgins who are very beautiful.
[Ester] [2]:[3] You could assign officers in each province of your empire to bring every virgin who is very beautiful here to your capital city of Shushan (Susa). They could stay in the harem for virgins under the custody of Hegay, the castrated royal guardian who takes care of the young women who live there and he could arrange for them to receive beauty treatments.
[Ester] [2]:[4] Then you could decide which young woman you like best and then make her queen instead of Vashti.” The king liked what they suggested, so he did it.
[Ester] [2]:[5] At that time, there was a Jewish man named Mordekai living in the capital city of Shushan. (He was from the tribe of Benyamin: his father was Yair, his grandfather was Shimei, and his great-grandfather was Kish
[Ester] [2]:[6] who’d been taken away from Yerushalem (Jerusalem) and led to Bavel (Babylon) when King Nevukadnetsar (Nebuchadnezzar) of Bavel had exiled Yekaneyah, the king of Yehudah (Judah), along with many of his people.)
[Ester] [2]:[7] Now Mordekai was taking care of his cousin, who was an orphan. When her father and mother had died, Mordekai had adopted her as his own daughter. Her Hebrew name was Hadasah, and her Persian name was Ester. Ester was now a young woman and she was exceptionally attractive.
[Ester] [2]:[8] So when the king’s command and decree became known, many young women were being brought into the capital city of Shushan and placed under Hegay’s charge, and this is what happened to Ester. (Hegay was the overseer of the women.)
[Ester] [2]:[9] Hegay was very impressed with Ester, and he treated her favourably. He quickly arranged for Ester to receive her beauty treatments and her allotment of food, as well as choosing seven female servants from the king’s palace and assigning them to be her personal attendants. He also moved Ester and her attendants to the best rooms in the harem for virgins.
[Ester] [2]:[10] (Ester hadn’t revealed her family ties or her Jewishness to anyone, because Mordekai had instructed her not to.)
[Ester] [2]:[11] Every day Mordekai would walk around in front of the courtyard of the women’s harem to find out from others how Ester was doing and how she was being treated.
[Ester] [2]:[12] Each young woman would get twelve months of beauty treatment according to the Persian law for women—there would be six months of applying oil of myrrh, then six months of perfumes and other lotions designed for women. Then their turn would come, one at a time, to be taken to King Ahashverosh (Ahasuerus/Xerxes).
[Ester] [2]:[13] The young woman was allowed to take whatever she wanted from the harem when she went to the king’s house.
[Ester] [2]:[14] She’d be taken across in the evening, and in the morning she’d be led out to the other harem which was for the concubines. (That harem was overseen by Sha’ashgaz, another castrated royal guardian.) The women taken there wouldn’t go again to the king’s house unless he had especially liked them and summoned her back by name.
[Ester] [2]:[15] Now Ester was the daughter of Mordekai’s uncle, Avihayil, from whom Mordekai had adopted her as his own daughter. When it was her turn to go to the king, she didn’t ask for anything other than what Hegay, the king’s trusted official in charge of the harem, had advised, and everyone who saw Ester liked her.
[Ester] [2]:[16] So Ester was taken to King Ahashverosh (Ahasuerus/Xerxes) at his royal palace in January, in the seventh year of his reign,
[Ester] [2]:[17] and the king loved Ester more than any of the other women. He treated her more kindly and more favourably than any of the other young women who had become his concubines. He put a royal crown on her head and made her the new queen to replace Vashti.
[Ester] [2]:[18] Then the king hosted a large celebration and invited all his officials and servants to a feast to celebrate Ester becoming queen. He proclaimed that this would be a time to celebrate for people in all of the provinces of his empire when they wouldn’t have to pay taxes, and he gave many generous gifts.
[Ester] [2]:[19] Later on, King Ahashverosh (Ahasuerus/Xerxes) had his officers bring more virgins to Shushan (Susa). During this time, Mordekai had been given a position by the king so he sat there at the king’s gate.
[Ester] [2]:[20] Ester had still not told anyone that she was Jewish because Mordekai had warned her not to tell anyone. What’s more, she continued to follow all of Mordekai’s instructions, just as she had done when she was still under his guardianship.
[Ester] [2]:[21] One day when Mordekai was on duty at the king’s gate, two of the king’s guards who protected the doorway to the king’s private rooms became angry with the king and so they planned to assassinate King Ahashverosh. (Their names were Bigtan and Teresh.)
[Ester] [2]:[22] But when Mordekai heard what they were planning, he told Queen Ester about it and she told the king, explaining that Mordekai had given her the information.
[Ester] [2]:[23] When the matter was investigated and the facts discovered, both conspirators were impaled on sharpened wooden poles, and in the presence of the king, the incident was recorded in the royal record of events.
[Ester] [3]:[1] Some time later, King Ahashverosh (Ahasuerus/Xerxes) promoted Haman, one of his officials (and the son of Hamedata who was a descendant of Agag). The king gave Haman a very important position—more important than any of his other officials.
[Ester] [3]:[2] Then the king commanded that all his other officials had to bow down in front of Haman to honour him, and they were doing this at the king’s gate, except for Mordekai who refused to bow down to reverence Haman.
[Ester] [3]:[3] “Why are you disobeying the king’s command?” asked the other royal servants at the king’s gate.
[Ester] [3]:[4] Mordekai told them that it was because he was a Yehudi (Jew) (and Yehudim (Jews) only worship Yahweh). He didn’t listen to their warnings so they told Haman about it to see if he would tolerate Mordekai in keeping refusing to bow down.
[Ester] [3]:[5] When Haman saw that Mordekai would not bow down to him or show him reverence, he was furious.
[Ester] [3]:[6] But Haman despised the idea of just punishing Mordekai because he’d been told that Mordekai didn’t bow to him because Mordekai was a Yehudi. So Haman decided to annihilate all of Mordekai’s people, i.e., all the Yehudim throughout the kingdom of Ahashverosh.
[Ester] [3]:[7] In early April of the twelfth year of King Ahashverosh’ reign, Haman got his servants to throw dice to select the best month and the best day to kill the Yehudim, and the 13th of March was chosen.
[Ester] [3]:[8] Then Haman went to King Ahashverosh and said, “Your Majesty, there is a certain group of people who live among the other peoples in every province of your empire. They have their own set of laws, so they don’t obey your laws. It’s not good for you to allow them to continue to live in your empire.
[Ester] [3]:[9] Your majesty, if you approve of this plan, then write a decree saying that all of the Yehudim must be destroyed. When they’re dead, we can take all of their possessions, and from that I will give 300 tons of silver to your administrators for them to put into your royal treasuries.”
[Ester] [3]:[10] This seemed sensible to the king so he removed his signet ring from his finger and he gave it to Haman (the son of Hamedata, the Agagi, the adversary of the Yehudim).
[Ester] [3]:[11] The king told Haman, “You can keep the money for yourself, and you can do whatever you want to do with those people.”
[Ester] [3]:[12] On the thirteenth day of that same month, Haman called in the royal scribes, and he dictated a letter to them. He told them to send copies to the royal officials, the governors of each province, and the leaders of each people group within the empire. The scribes translated the letter so it could be sent to each province using its own alphabet and to each people group in its own language. To show that he was sending the letter under the king’s own authority, Haman sealed each copy of the letter with the ring that had the king’s official seal on it.
[Ester] [3]:[13] Couriers delivered the letters to the officials in every province in the empire. The letters said to completely destroy all the Yehudim, including the children and women, on a single day. That was to be the thirteenth day of March early in the following year. The letters also stated that those who killed the Yehudim could take everything that belonged to them.
[Ester] [3]:[14] The letter told the officials to display copies where everyone could see them—that way all the people in every single province would know that the king had commanded this, and they could get ready for when the day came.
[Ester] [3]:[15] So couriers hurried off with the letters as the king had commanded. A herald in the capital city of Shushan (Susa) also proclaimed what the letters said. Then the king and Haman relaxed and drank together, but there was total confusion in Shushan about how all of this would work out.
[Ester] [4]:[1] When Mordekai found out about what had been done, he tore his clothes and dressed in sackcloth and threw ashes over himself (as a sign of mourning or distress) and went out into the city centre, wailing loudly and bitterly.
[Ester] [4]:[2] But no one was wearing mourning garb was allowed inside the king’s gate, so when Mordekai reached the gate, he had to stay just outside it.
[Ester] [4]:[3] In every province of the empire, the letter that said to destroy the Yehudim (Jews) was publicly displayed and when the Yehudim heard about it, they were incredibly upset. They skipped meals and wailed loudly, and many of them also wore sackcloth and threw ashes on themselves and lay on the ground.
[Ester] [4]:[4] When Queen Ester’s young female attendants came with her guardians and told her what was going on outside, even the queen became very scared. She sent Mordekai some good clothes to wear instead of the sackcloth, but he wouldn’t accept them.
[Ester] [4]:[5] The king had assigned some of the royal guardians to Ester personally, so Ester called for one of them—a man named Hatak. She told him to go out and speak with Mordekai and find out what he was so distressed about.
[Ester] [4]:[6] So Hatak went out to talk to Mordekai who was out in the plaza in front of the king’s gate.
[Ester] [4]:[7] Mordekai told him everything that Haman was planning to do and even told him how much money Haman had said the king would get for his treasuries if the king commanded people to kill all the Yehudim.
[Ester] [4]:[8] Mordekai also gave Hatak a copy of the letter that the announcers had read out loud in Shushan (Susa), that said that people must kill all the Yehudim. He told Hatak to show the letter to Ester so that she would know exactly what it said and also told him to urge her to go to the king personally and to beg him desperately to save her people from destruction.
[Ester] [4]:[9] So Hatak returned to the queen and told her what Mordekai had said,
[Ester] [4]:[10] and Ester told him to go back to Mordekai with this message:
[Ester] [4]:[11] “There’s a law about going to the king that applies to everyone in the kingdom, both men and women. If anyone goes into the inner courtyard of the palace, where the king can see them, and the king has not summoned them, that person will be executed. Only if the king holds out his golden scepter to them, then they will live. (Everyone in the whole empire knows this law.) The king hasn’t called for me in over a month, and if I go in without being summoned, I could be put to death.”
[Ester] [4]:[12] So Hatak went back to Mordekai and told him what the queen had said.
[Ester] [4]:[13] Mordekai told Hatak to tell this to Ester: “Don’t imagine that just because you live there in the king’s palace that you’ll be safe when they kill all the other Yehudim.
[Ester] [4]:[14] If you say nothing at all now, someone from some other place will rescue the Yehudim, but you and your relatives will not survive. Who knows, perhaps it was for a time just like this that God allowed you to become queen?”
[Ester] [4]:[15] Then Ester sent this reply to Mordekai:
[Ester] [4]:[16] “Go and assemble all the Yehudim who live here in Shushan (Susa), and tell them to fast and pray for my sake—tell them to not eat or drink anything for three days and three nights. My female attendants and I will also fast in the same way. At the end of the three days, I will go in to talk to the king even though it’s against the law. I will do that even if it costs me my life.”
[Ester] [4]:[17] So Mordekai went and did everything that Ester had told him to do.
[Ester] [5]:[1] Three days later, Queen Ester put on her royal robes and went and stood in the inner courtyard of the palace, across from the king’s house. He was in the royal palace, sitting on the royal throne and facing the room’s entrance.
[Ester] [5]:[2] As soon as the king noticed Ester standing there in the courtyard, he was very pleased to see her. So he held out his golden scepter to her and Ester came up to the throne and touched the top of the scepter.
[Ester] [5]:[3] “Why have you come here, Queen Ester?” the king asked. “What do you want? Tell me, and I’ll give you anything you ask for—even half of the empire.”
[Ester] [5]:[4] “If it pleases your majesty,” Ester replied, “please come with Haman today to the banquet that I’ve prepared for you.”
[Ester] [5]:[5] The king said to his servants, “Go and get Haman” the king told his servants, “and bring him quickly so that we can do what the queen has asked us.” So the king and Haman went to the banquet that Ester had had prepared for them.
[Ester] [5]:[6] While they were drinking wine, the king said to Ester, “Now please tell me what you really want. I’ll give you anything you ask for, no matter how much it is. I truly mean what I am saying.”
[Ester] [5]:[7] “This is what I really want.” Ester replied.
[Ester] [5]:[8] “Your majesty, if you’re pleased with me and if you’re happy to give me what I want, please come with Haman to another banquet that I’ll prepare for you tomorrow and I’ll answer your question then.”
[Ester] [5]:[9] Haman was feeling very happy as he left the banquet that day. But then he saw Mordekai sitting at the king’s gate and noticed that Mordekai didn’t stand up or show fearful reverence to him. This made Haman furious with Mordekai
[Ester] [5]:[10] but he restrained himself and went home. Then he sent for his friends and brought in his wife, Zeresh,
[Ester] [5]:[11] boasting to them about how rich he was and about how many sons he had, and how the king had promoted him many times and given him a position above all of the other officials and administrators.
[Ester] [5]:[12] “And that is not all,” Haman added. “I was the only one that Queen Ester invited to go with the king to a banquet that she prepared for us today. And she’s also invited only me to go with the king again tomorrow.
[Ester] [5]:[13] However, I still can’t be happy as long as I keep seeing that Yehudi (Jew), Mordekai, sitting there at the king’s gate.”
[Ester] [5]:[14] Then Zeresh his wife and all his friends said to him, “Get them to install 25-metre high pole, and in the morning get permission from the king, and get them to impale Mordekai on it. Then you can go with the king to the banquet and enjoy yourself.” That idea sounded good to Haman, so he got the pole erected.
[Ester] [6]:[1] That night the king was unable to sleep so he ordered the royal records to be fetched and to be read to him.
[Ester] [6]:[2] The records mentioned that Bigtan and Teresh, two of the royal guardians who protected the doorway to the king’s private quarters, had planned to assassinate the king, but that Mordekai had reported it.
[Ester] [6]:[3] “What honour or recognition did I give Mordekai for saving my life?” the king asked. “Nothing was done for him,” replied the young men who were attending him.
[Ester] [6]:[4] At that moment, Haman had entered the outer courtyard of the king’s house. He had come to tell the king that he wanted to execute Mordekai on the pole that he’d had set up for him. “Who’s out in the courtyard?” the king asked.
[Ester] [6]:[5] “Haman’s out there standing in the courtyard,” replied the young men. “Bring him in then,” the king instructed.
[Ester] [6]:[6] When Haman came in, the king asked him, “What should I do for a man that I would really like to honour?” Haman thought to himself, “Surely it must be me that the king would like to honour more than anyone else?”
[Ester] [6]:[7] so he replied to the king, “If you really want to honour someone,
[Ester] [6]:[8] tell your servants to bring one of your own royal robes that you have already worn yourself and also bring a horse that you have already ridden yourself and put a royal crown on its head.
[Ester] [6]:[9] Then have one of your most noble officials present the man with the robe and the horse. Have your servants put the robe on the man whom you really want to honour and have them seat that man on the horse and then lead the horse through the public square of the city while they shout out to everyone in front of them, ‘The king is doing this because he really wants to honour this man!’ ”
[Ester] [6]:[10] The king agreed so he replied to Haman, “Go quickly and take the robe and the horse and do what you’ve just described for Mordekai the Yehudi (Jew) who sits by the gate to the palace. Make sure that you do absolutely everything that you’ve said.”
[Ester] [6]:[11] So Haman got the robe and the horse and put the robe on Mordekai, seated him on the horse, and then led the horse through the public square of the city. As he did, he shouted out to everyone in front of him, “The king is doing this because he really wants to honour this man!”
[Ester] [6]:[12] Afterwards, Mordekai returned to the king’s gate but Haman hurried to his house, covering his head like a mourner.
[Ester] [6]:[13] At home he explained to Zeresh his wife and to all his friends everything that had happened to him. Then his advisors and his wife said to him, “Mordekai has begun to defeat you and since he is one of the Jewish people, you won’t win against him—instead, he’ll certainly defeat you.”
[Ester] [6]:[14] While they were still talking together, some of the royal guardians arrived to bring Haman quickly to the banquet that Ester had had prepared.
[Ester] [7]:[1] So the king and Haman went to Queen Ester’s banquet.
[Ester] [7]:[2] While they were drinking wine at that second banquet, the king asked Ester again, “Now please tell me what you really want, Queen Ester. Tell me, and I’ll do it for you—I’ll give you anything you ask for, no matter what it is.”
[Ester] [7]:[3] “Your majesty,” Queen Ester replied, “if you are pleased with me, I hope you’ll be willing to do what I ask. Please allow me to live, and please save my people. That is what I am asking for
[Ester] [7]:[4] because someone has turned me and my people over to our enemies and they’re going to completely destroy us. If someone had just sold the men and even the women to be slaves, I wouldn’t have said anything, because that wouldn’t have been important enough to bother your majesty with.”
[Ester] [7]:[5] “Who has done this?” King Ahashverosh (Ahasuerus/Xerxes) asked her. “Where is the man who has dared to do such a thing?”
[Ester] [7]:[6] “The man who is our bitter enemy is this evil man Haman!” answered Ester. By this time, Haman was terrified standing there in front of the king and the queen.
[Ester] [7]:[7] Now the king became so angry that he got up and abandoned his wine-drinking at the banquet and went outside into the palace garden. But Haman stayed inside to beg his life from Queen Ester because he recognized that the king wanted to execute him.
[Ester] [7]:[8] As he was pleading for his life, Haman knelt down very close to Ester as she was reclining on a couch. When the king returned from the palace garden to the room where they had been drinking wine, he saw this and exclaimed, “Now he’s even trying to rape the queen in my presence and in my own house!” As soon as the king said this, some of his servants covered Haman’s face (as a sign that he would be executed).
[Ester] [7]:[9] Then Harvona, who was one of the guardians who served the king personally, said, “Your majesty, Haman has also set up a pole twenty-five metres high at his house because he wants to hang Mordekai on it. But Mordekai saved your life.” “Execute Haman on it!” the king commanded.
[Ester] [7]:[10] So they impaled Haman on the pole that he had set up for Mordekai, and then the king’s anger dissipated.
[Ester] [8]:[1] That same day, King Ahashverosh (Ahasuerus/Xerxes) gave Queen Ester all the property that had belonged to Haman, the enemy of the Yehudim (Jews). Ester told the king that Mordekai was her cousin and that he had been like a father to her, and so the king summoned Mordekai to come to him.
[Ester] [8]:[2] Then the king removed his signet ring which he had retrieved from Haman, and gave it to Mordekai. The queen also put Mordekai in charge of all the property that had belonged to Haman.
[Ester] [8]:[3] Then Ester came to speak to the king again, and she knelt down and put her face right on top of his feet. She cried as she begged him to stop Haman’s terrible plan to destroy the Yehudim.
[Ester] [8]:[4] The king held out his golden scepter toward Ester, so she stood up and waited facing the king.
[Ester] [8]:[5] “Your majesty,” she said, “if you think that it’s the right thing to do, and if you’re pleased with me, please write a new letter revoking the letters that Haman (the son of Hamedata, the Agagi) sent out instructing the people to destroy all the Yehudim throughout your empire.
[Ester] [8]:[6] I couldn’t bear to see the terrible thing that is about to happen to my people. I certainly couldn’t bear to see all my relatives destroyed!”
[Ester] [8]:[7] Then king Ahashverosh said to Queen Ester and to Mordekai the Yehudi (Jew), “Listen, I’ve given the house of Haman to Ester, and they’ve executed him on the pole because he attempted to destroy the Yehudim.
[Ester] [8]:[8] But as you both know, no one can revoke a letter that has my name and my official seal on it. So this is what you should do: write a new letter to help the Yehudim, as you think best and put my name on it and seal the letter with my signet ring.”
[Ester] [8]:[9] It was now June, and the king sent for his scribes and they wrote a letter to the Yehudim containing everything that Mordekai dictated. It was also addressed to royal officials, and to the governors and leaders in each province. The empire had 127 provinces, extending all the way from Hodu in the east to Kush (Ethiopia) in the west. The scribes wrote to every province using its own alphabet and to each people group in its own language, and to the Yehudim in their language and using their alphabet.
[Ester] [8]:[10] The letters were written in King Ahashverosh’ name, and each one was sealed with the king’s signet ring. Then the letters were distributed by mounted couriers riding on swift horses bred from the royal mares.
[Ester] [8]:[11] The letters stated that the king permitted the Yehudim in each and every city to get together and defend themselves, and what’s more to destroy, kill, and annihilate all the forces of any people or province hostile to them, including women and children, and then to plunder their possessions.
[Ester] [8]:[12] This was to take place on a certain day in every province throughout the empire: the 13th of March (the same day on which Haman’s law was to take effect).
[Ester] [8]:[13] A copy of the decree was to be included as law in every province and to be displayed to all the people so that the Yehudim could be prepared to fight back against their enemies on that day.
[Ester] [8]:[14] So the couriers on the royal horses rode out quickly under the king’s orders to deliver the letters. The new law was also proclaimed throughout the capital city of Shushan (Susa).
[Ester] [8]:[15] The king gave Mordekai royal clothing that was blue and white, with a large gold crown, and a purple robe made from fine linen. The people of Shushan cheered happily when Mordekai exited the palace.
[Ester] [8]:[16] For the Yehudim, it was a time of light and happiness, and they were honoured by those around them.
[Ester] [8]:[17] In every single province and in every single city, wherever the letter announcing the king’s decree was brought, the Yehudim were very cheerful and had big celebrations. Many people from other groups in the empire became afraid of the Yehudim, so they converted to Youdaismos themselves.
[Ester] [9]:[1] Finally when the 13th of March arrived, it was time for everyone to do what the letters from the king said that he had decreed for them to do. The enemies of the Yehudim (Jews) had expected to destroy the Yehudim on that day but just the opposite happened—instead, it was the Yehudim who destroyed their enemies.
[Ester] [9]:[2] Throughout the empire, the Yehudim joined together in their cities to defend themselves against those who wanted to harm them. No one was able to fight back against them because everyone else in the empire had become afraid of them.
[Ester] [9]:[3] All the leaders in each province, the royal officials, the governors, and everyone who worked for the king helped the Yehudim because they had become afraid of Mordekai
[Ester] [9]:[4] because he was now a very important royal official, and his fame spread throughout the provinces as he became more and more powerful.
[Ester] [9]:[5] So the Yehudim took their weapons and fought against all of their enemies and completely destroyed them. They were able to do everything that they wanted to do against their enemies.
[Ester] [9]:[6] In the capital city of Shushan (Susa), the Yehudim killed 500 men
[Ester] [9]:[7] including Haman’s ten sons Parshandata, Dalfon, Aspata,
[Ester] [9]:[8] Porata, Adalya, Aridata,
[Ester] [9]:[9] Parmashta, Arisay, Ariday, and Vayzata.
[Ester] [9]:[10] Those were the ten sons of Haman (son of Hamedata), the enemy of the Yehudim, but the Yehudim didn’t take their possessions.
[Ester] [9]:[11] At the end of the day, the king received a report about how many people the Yehudim had killed in the capital city of Shushan
[Ester] [9]:[12] and he told Queen Ester, “Here in the capital city of Shushan the Yehudim have killed 500 men, including Haman’s ten sons. In the rest of my empire, they must have killed many more than that! So tell me what else you want and I’ll do it for you. I’ll do whatever you ask, so do tell me.”
[Ester] [9]:[13] “If it seems like a good plan to you, your majesty,” Ester replied, “then please allow the Yehudim who live here in Shushan to do again tomorrow what you allowed them to do today. Also, command that the bodies of Haman’s ten sons be impaled on the wooden pole.”
[Ester] [9]:[14] Then the king ordered for this to be done and a decree was made throughout in Shushan, and they publicly impaled the bodies ofHaman’s ten sons.
[Ester] [9]:[15] So the next day on the 14th, the Yehudim in Shushan gathered together again and killed 300 more men in Shushan. But once again they did not take the things that belonged to those men.
[Ester] [9]:[16] The Yehudim in the other parts of the empire, who had gathered together to fight for their lives had defeated their enemies and killed 75,000 of them. But they too did not take the things that had belonged to their enemies.
[Ester] [9]:[17] That all happened on the 13th (as the law had said), and then they stopped on the 14th and made it a day of feasting and celebration.
[Ester] [9]:[18] But the Yehudim in Shushan had gathered together and fought their enemies on both the 13th and the 14th, so they stopped on the 15th and made it a day of feasting and celebration.
[Ester] [9]:[19] So that’s why the Yehudim who live in the rural villages observe this holiday on the 14th rather than the 15th. They celebrate with feasting and by giving gifts to each other.
[Ester] [9]:[20] Now Mordekai recorded everything that had happened and sent letters to all the Yehudim (Jews) throughout the empire, in both the near provinces and the far away ones.
[Ester] [9]:[21] That decree established an annual holiday on the 14th and 15th of March every year,
[Ester] [9]:[22] because those were the days when the Yehudim no longer had to oppose their enemies and that was the month when their sorrow and mourning had changed into a good day. Now they were instructed to make them days of feasting and happiness, and sending of gifts—to each other but also to the needy.
[Ester] [9]:[23] The Yehudim had already celebrated those days that way, so they readily agreed to do what Mordekai had written.
[Ester] [9]:[24] Yes, Haman (the son of Hamedata, the Agagi), the enemy of all the Yehudim, had plotted to annihilate them, and he had thrown a ‘Pur’ (which is ‘lot’ or perhaps ‘dice’) choose the date to crush them and to destroy them.
[Ester] [9]:[25] But instead they would remember how Queen Ester stood in front of the king, and how he had said in the letter, “Let his evil plot that he plotted concerning the Yehudim return on his head, and let them execute him and his sons on the pole.”
[Ester] [9]:[26] Therefore they called this celebration ‘Purim’ because of what they had experienced and because of the contents of Mordekai’s letter.
[Ester] [9]:[27] The Yehudim agreed to establish those two days as holidays and to observe them on those specific days as they’d been instructed. They agreed that they and their descendants and everyone who became part of the Jewish people would celebrate it every year.
[Ester] [9]:[28] So that’s why every Jewish family in every generation since has celebrated these days as holidays, wherever they live. The Jewish community and its descendants will always faithfully observe this festival of ‘Purim’.
[Ester] [9]:[29] Then Queen Ester (the daughter of Avihayil), with help from Mordekai the Yehudi (Jew), wrote a second letter about ‘Purim’.
[Ester] [9]:[30] He sent this second letter to all the Yehudim throughout the empire of King Ahashverosh (Ahasuerus/Xerxes), with words of peace and truth
[Ester] [9]:[31] to set up the ‘Purim’ celebration on the given dates according to what Mordekai the Yehudi and Queen Ester had determined for them. They also confirmed that the Yehudim should continue the times of fasting and mourning that they had established for themselves and their future descendants.
[Ester] [9]:[32] So Ester’s decree confirmed these regulations about ‘Purim’ and they were written into the official record.
[Ester] [10]:[1] Then King Ahashverosh (Ahasuerus/Xerxes) imposed a tax on everyone throughout his empire, including those on the islands of the Mediterranean Sea.
[Ester] [10]:[2] Everything he accomplished through his power and strength is written down in the royal records of the kings of Maday (Media) and Paras (Persia), as well as the complete account of the high position to which the king promoted Mordekai.
[Ester] [10]:[3] Mordekai the Yehudi (Jew) was second-in-command to the king Ahashverosh, and a leader among the Yehudim (Jews). He was popular with most of his own people, seeking good for them and teaching all his descendants how to live in peace.
[Iyov] [1]:[1] There was once a man called Iyov (Job) who lived in the Uts (Uz) region. He was blameless and righteous—both obeying God and avoiding evil.
[Iyov] [1]:[2] He had seven sons and three daughters,
[Iyov] [1]:[3] and he owned 7,000 sheep, 3,000 camels, 1,000 cattle, and 500 donkeys, as well as many slaves. Iyov was richer than anyone else who lived in the area east of the Yarden (Jordan) River.
[Iyov] [1]:[4] Iyov’s sons regularly held feasts in their homes, and whenever any of them held a feast, he would invite all his brothers and sisters to share the meal with him.
[Iyov] [1]:[5] Then once a feast was over, Iyov would send for his children and consecrate them—he got up early in the morning and offered burnt offerings for each of them, because Iyov said, “Perhaps my children have sinned and cursed God in their hearts.” It was Iyov’s regular habit to intercede for his children.
[Iyov] [1]:[6] It was the day that God’s sons came to present themselves to Yahweh, and the adversary (Satan) was also there among them.
[Iyov] [1]:[7] Yahweh asked him, “Where have you just come from?” “I have come from the earth, where I was travelling around to see what was going on.” Satan replied.
[Iyov] [1]:[8] “Have you noticed my servant Iyov (Job)?” Yahweh asked. “There’s no one else like him on the whole earth—a blameless and righteous man who obeys me God and avoids anything evil.”
[Iyov] [1]:[9] “Does Iyov get nothing back for respecting God?” Satan answered Yahweh.
[Iyov] [1]:[10] “Don’t you constantly protect him and his household and everything that’s his? You’ve blessed what he works on, and his livestock have multiplied prolifically.
[Iyov] [1]:[11] However, just stretch out your hand and ruin everything he has, then we’ll see that he’ll curse you to your face.”
[Iyov] [1]:[12] “Listen, I’ll cede you control over everything he has,” Yahweh replied. “Only just don’t do anything against Iyov himself.” So the adversary went away from Yahweh’s presence.
[Iyov] [1]:[13] So one day when Iyov’s (Job) sons and his daughters were eating and drinking wine in their eldest brother’s house,
[Iyov] [1]:[14] a messenger came to Iyov and reported, “While the oxen were ploughing and the donkeys were feeding nearby,
[Iyov] [1]:[15] raiders from Sheva attacked with their swords and stole them all. They killed all your slaves except that I managed to escape to tell you.”
[Iyov] [1]:[16] While he was still speaking, another messenger came and said, “The fire of God fell from the sky and burnt up the sheep and the shepherds. Only ashes are left, except that I alone escaped to tell you.”
[Iyov] [1]:[17] While he was still speaking, another one came and explained, “The Kasdim (Chaldeans) formed into three bands and raided the camels and took them, and they attacked the slaves with their swords, and I’m the only one who escaped to come and tell you.”
[Iyov] [1]:[18] While he was still speaking, another messenger came and said, “Your sons and daughters were eating and drinking wine in the house of their eldest brother
[Iyov] [1]:[19] when suddenly a freak wind came from across the desert and struck the house. It collapsed on the young people and killed them, and only I alone have escaped to tell you.”
[Iyov] [1]:[20] Then Iyov (Job) stood up and tore his robe and shaved his head. Then he knelt with his face to the ground and worshipped God,
[Iyov] [1]:[21] saying, “I came naked from my mother’s womb, and I will leave this life naked. Yahweh gave, and Yahweh has taken. May Yahweh’s reputation be blessed.”
[Iyov] [1]:[22] Through all of that, Iyov didn’t disobey God or accuse him of being evil.
[Iyov] [2]:[1] It was the day that God’s sons came to present themselves to Yahweh and the adversary (Satan) was also there among them.
[Iyov] [2]:[2] “Where have you come from?” Yahweh asked the adversary. “From wandering on the earth and going back and forth on it,” he answered.
[Iyov] [2]:[3] “Have you noticed my servant Iyov (Job)?” Yahweh asked Satan, “because there’s no one like him on the earth—a blameless and righteous man, striving to obey God and turning from evil. And he’s still holding firmly to his integrity, even though you incited me against him, to ruin him for nothing.”
[Iyov] [2]:[4] “Skin for skin,” replied the adversary, “actually, a person will give everything they have to save their life.
[Iyov] [2]:[5] However, just reach out and touch his flesh and bones, and see if he doesn’t curse you to your face.”
[Iyov] [2]:[6] “Listen,” Yahweh said to him, “I’ll give you power over him, but you must preserve his life.”
[Iyov] [2]:[7] So the adversary went away from Yahweh’s presence, and he infected Iyov with bad boils from the sole of his foot to the top of his head.
[Iyov] [2]:[8] Iyov picked up a piece of broken pottery to scratch himself with as he sat down in the middle of a pile of ashes.
[Iyov] [2]:[9] “Are you still holding tightly onto your integrity?” his wife asked him. “Just curse God and die.”
[Iyov] [2]:[10] “You’re talking like a foolish person,” Iyov replied. “Should we only accept good from God and not receive the bad?” In all of that, Iyov didn’t sin in what he said.
[Iyov] [2]:[11] When Iyov’s (Job) three friends heard about all the troubles that had happened to him, they each came from his place: Elifaz from Teyman, Bildad from Shuah, and Tsofar from Na’amah. They gathered together to come to console and comfort him.
[Iyov] [2]:[12] but when they saw him from a distance, they barely recognised him. They wailed loudly, and they ripped their own clothes, and they threw dust into the air so that it would fall on their heads. (All three of those were traditional signs of mourning.)
[Iyov] [2]:[13] Then they sat with him there on the ground for seven days and seven nights without saying a single word to Iyov because they had seen that his suffering was extreme.
[Iyov] [3]:[1] After that, Iyov (Job) spoke up and cursed the day of his conception.
[Iyov] [3]:[2] He said:
[Iyov] [3]:[3] May the day on which I was born perish, and the night that said, ‘A boy has been conceived.’
[Iyov] [3]:[4] May that day be dark. May God not search for it from above and may no light shine on it.
[Iyov] [3]:[5] May darkness and a dark shadow claim it. May a cloud remain over it. May the blacknesses of the day terrify it.
[Iyov] [3]:[6] May gloom take that night. May it not be happy among the days of the year. May it not enter into the number of months.
[Iyov] [3]:[7] Listen, may that night be barren. May a happy shout never enter it.
[Iyov] [3]:[8] May those who curse days, curse that one— yes, those people who are skillful enough to wake up the large sea monster.
[Iyov] [3]:[9] May the stars of its twilight be dark. May it stay waiting for the light that never arrives. May it not see the dawn breaking.
[Iyov] [3]:[10] Because it didn’t close the doors of my mother’s womb, to hide the sorrow from my eyes.
[Iyov] [3]:[11] Why didn’t I die at birth? Just come out then stop breathing?
[Iyov] [3]:[12] Why was I accepted onto her lap? And onto those breasts to suckle?
[Iyov] [3]:[13] Yes, I’d be peacefully lying down now. I would have slept and been at rest,
[Iyov] [3]:[14] along with kings and counsellors of the earth— yes, those who built monuments for themselves.
[Iyov] [3]:[15] Or been asleep with princes and their gold— those who filled their houses with silver.
[Iyov] [3]:[16] I might never have been—like a stillborn child. Like some infants who never see the light.
[Iyov] [3]:[17] Wicked people don’t cause any more trouble there. Those who’ve run out of strength rest there.
[Iyov] [3]:[18] Prisoners are able to relax together. They no longer hear the voice of their taskmaster.
[Iyov] [3]:[19] Ordinary and famous people are all alike there. And slaves there no longer have to obey their masters.
[Iyov] [3]:[20] Why is light given to those who are miserable? And why’s life given to those who are bitter inside?
[Iyov] [3]:[21] They wish for death but it won’t come. They dig for it more than for hidden treasure.
[Iyov] [3]:[22] Those who are happy for happiness sake, will celebrate when they find the grave.
[Iyov] [3]:[23] Why search for a path that’s hidden when God has hedged them in?
[Iyov] [3]:[24] Sighing has become more important than eating. My groans just pour out like water.
[Iyov] [3]:[25] I had my fears and they’ve come to pass. What I dreaded has come to me.
[Iyov] [3]:[26] I’m not relaxed or peaceful. I can’t rest because only trouble comes.
[Iyov] [4]:[1] Then Elifaz (from Teyman) replied:
[Iyov] [4]:[2] If someone tries to talk with you, will it wear you out? But who can resist answering?
[Iyov] [4]:[3] Listen, you’ve instructed many other people. And you’ve encouraged those who were weak.
[Iyov] [4]:[4] Your words have encouraged those who were stumbling. You’ve strengthened those whose knees were buckling.
[Iyov] [4]:[5] But now it’s you in trouble and you’re depressed. Troubles touch you and you’re discouraged.
[Iyov] [4]:[6] Doesn’t your faith give you confidence? What about your hope and your integrity?
[Iyov] [4]:[7] Remember: Who has ever perished when they were innocent? Or when were godly people ever destroyed?
[Iyov] [4]:[8] Just like I’ve seen those who plant evil and sow mischief harvest it back again,
[Iyov] [4]:[9] God’s breath causes them to perish, and with a snort of his nose they come to an end.
[Iyov] [4]:[10] The lion roars and the UNKNOWN-lion sounds his voice, AND the teeth of the young lions are broken.
[Iyov] [4]:[11] The UNKNOWN-lion starves to death because of a lack of prey, and the lionesses cubs are scattered.
[Iyov] [4]:[12] Now a message was brought secretly to me, and my ears caught a whisper of it.
[Iyov] [4]:[13] When troubled by thoughts from dreams in the night, when people have fallen into deep sleep,
[Iyov] [4]:[14] I was hit by fear and trembling— my bones were shaking with fright.
[Iyov] [4]:[15] A spirit passed over my face, and the hairs on my body stood on end.
[Iyov] [4]:[16] It stood still, but I didn’t recognise what it was. There was an image in front of my eyes. It was silent and then I heard a voice:
[Iyov] [4]:[17] ‘Can a mortal human be innocent before God? Can a person be more pure than the creator of people?’
[Iyov] [4]:[18] Listen, he doesn’t even trust his own servants, and he accuses his own messengers of making mistakes.
[Iyov] [4]:[19] How much less for those whose bodies were made from the clay, whose foundations were made from the dust. They’re crushed even easier than a moth is.
[Iyov] [4]:[20] They’re destroyed from morning to evening. They’re always dying even without anyone doing anything.
[Iyov] [4]:[21] Their tent cords are pulled out on them. They die and don’t even know why.
[Iyov] [5]:[1] Call out to God now. Does anyone answer? Which of the holy ones will you turn to?
[Iyov] [5]:[2] Resentment kills foolish people. Jealousy kills those who are simple-minded.
[Iyov] [5]:[3] I’ve seen foolish people taking root, then I’ve immediately cursed their homes.
[Iyov] [5]:[4] Their children are far from safety, and they are crushed in the gate, and no one saves them.
[Iyov] [5]:[5] Those who are hungry consume his harvest even getting it from among the thorns. Greedy people long for his wealth.
[Iyov] [5]:[6] Hardship doesn’t just grow up from the dust, and trouble doesn’t just spring up from the ground.
[Iyov] [5]:[7] Everyone is born into trouble— sparks tend to fly up high.
[Iyov] [5]:[8] But for myself, I’ll search for God and I’ll approach him with my case.
[Iyov] [5]:[9] He does incredible things, and performs wonders without number that are beyond our understanding.
[Iyov] [5]:[10] He’s the one giving rain all over the earth, and sending water onto the fields.
[Iyov] [5]:[11] God helps the humble to prosper, and he lifts those who are mourning to a safe place.
[Iyov] [5]:[12] He frustrates the schemes of the crafty, so their actions cannot succeed.
[Iyov] [5]:[13] He catches smart people in their craftiness, and he hurries along the plans of those who are deceptive.
[Iyov] [5]:[14] Even in the daytime, they remain in darkness. Even at midday, they feel their way around as if it’s nighttime.
[Iyov] [5]:[15] He saves the poor from the plans of those smart people, and from the actions of powerful people.
[Iyov] [5]:[16] So the poor have hope, and injustice is silenced.
[Iyov] [5]:[17] Listen, the person who’s corrected by God is blessed. Don’t despise chastening from God the provider.
[Iyov] [5]:[18] He wounds and he also bandages up. He strikes but his hands also heal.
[Iyov] [5]:[19] If you get in trouble six times, he’ll rescue you. Even seven times, he’ll prevent you from being harmed.
[Iyov] [5]:[20] During famines, he’ll rescue you from death, and in war, he’ll save you from slaughter.
[Iyov] [5]:[21] He’ll hide you away from hurting words, and when destruction comes, you won’t be afraid.
[Iyov] [5]:[22] You’ll laugh at destruction and at famine, and you won’t be afraid of wild animals,
[Iyov] [5]:[23] because you have an agreement with the stones in the fields for walls, and the wild animals will be at peace with you.
[Iyov] [5]:[24] You’ll know that your home is secure, and you’ll inspect your animal shelters and nothing will be missing.
[Iyov] [5]:[25] You’ll know that your descendants will be numerous, and your offspring like the grass on the land.
[Iyov] [5]:[26] You’ll reach an old age before you get to the grave, like grain that’s harvested at the right time.
[Iyov] [5]:[27] Listen to this: we’ve investigated and it’s true. Listen to it so you’ll know for yourself.
[Iyov] [6]:[1] Then Iyov (Job) responded:

[Iyov] [7]:[1] Aren’t people expected to work on earth? Aren’t a person’s days like the days of a hired labourer?
[Iyov] [7]:[2] He longs for the shade just like a slave does. He’s just like a hired man who waits eagerly for his wages.

[Iyov] [12]:[24] He removes the heart from the leaders of the people of the land, and makes them wander in wasteland where there’s no paths.
[Iyov] [12]:[25] They grope in the darkness without any light, and he makes them stagger around as if they’re drunk.
[Iyov] [13]:[1] Look here, my eyes have seen all that, my ears have heard it and understood.
[Iyov] [13]:[2] I also know everything that you know, I’m not way behind you.
[Iyov] [13]:[3] But I would like to talk to the provider, and I desire to plead with God.
[Iyov] [13]:[4] But you’re all smearers of lies, all of you are worthless healers.
[Iyov] [13]:[5] If only you all would remain silent, then you all might be considered wise.
[Iyov] [13]:[6] Please listen to my argument, and pay attention to the pleading of my lips.
[Iyov] [13]:[7] Will you all speak faithlessly on God’s behalf, and will you talk deceitfully for him?
[Iyov] [13]:[8] Will you show partiality to him, or argue the case for God?
[Iyov] [13]:[9] Is it good that he’ll examine you all, or will you deceive him like deceiving a person?
[Iyov] [13]:[10] He would certainly rebuke you all, if you were secretly showing partiality.
[Iyov] [13]:[11] Shouldn’t his majesty make you all afraid, and his dread fall on you all?
[Iyov] [13]:[12] Your traditional sayings are proverbs of ashes. Your defenses might as well be made of clay.
[Iyov] [13]:[13] Be silent in my presence and let me speak, and let come to me what may.
[Iyov] [13]:[14] Why should I bite my flesh with my own teeth, and take my life in my own hands?
[Iyov] [13]:[15] Even if he kills me, my hope will still be in him. I will certainly defend my behaviour to him in person.
[Iyov] [13]:[16] Even that would result in my salvation. A godless person wouldn’t enter his presence.
[Iyov] [13]:[17] Listen carefully to my words, and may my declaration be in the ears of you all.
[Iyov] [13]:[18] I’ve now arranged my case. I know that I’m in the right.
[Iyov] [13]:[19] Who will conduct my case? I’ll keep silent now and die.
[Iyov] [13]:[20] Just don’t do these two things to me, then I won’t hide myself from your presence:
[Iyov] [13]:[21] Don’t take your hand far away from me, and don’t terrify me with your dread.
[Iyov] [13]:[22] Then call me and I’ll answer, or let me speak and answer me.
[Iyov] [13]:[23] How many errors and sins do I have? Let me know how I disobeyed and sinned.
[Iyov] [13]:[24] Why are you keeping away from me, and treating me like an enemy?
[Iyov] [13]:[25] Would you terrify a leaf blown by the wind? Would you chase a dry stalk to punish it?
[Iyov] [13]:[26] You write bitter things against me, and even recall the errors of my youth.
[Iyov] [13]:[27] You lock my feet in stocks. You watch all my paths and mark the soles of my feet.
[Iyov] [13]:[28] He decays like something rotten. He’s like a garment that’s eaten by moths.
[Iyov] [14]:[1] Humans, born from women, live relatively short lives with lots of turmoil.
[Iyov] [14]:[2] People appear and then wither, just like the flowers. They don’t stay around, but rush away like shadows.
[Iyov] [14]:[3] Do you watch over even creatures like this? Do you bring me in to be judged?
[Iyov] [14]:[4] Who can make something innocent out of something impure? No one.
[Iyov] [14]:[5] Since a person’s lifespan is already determined, then you already know the number of months. You’ve set the limit and we won’t live past that.
[Iyov] [14]:[6] Stop watching us. Give us relief so we can take some pleasure in our daily work.
[Iyov] [14]:[7] There’s even hope for a tree that gets cut down. It will sprout again and its new shoots won’t fail.
[Iyov] [14]:[8] Even when its roots in the ground get old, and its base is rotting in the soil,
[Iyov] [14]:[9] when it detects water it’ll send up branches like a young plant.
[Iyov] [14]:[10] But a person dies and is laid out— a person breathes their last and now where are they?
[Iyov] [14]:[11] The water disappears from a lake, and the river level goes down then dries up.
[Iyov] [14]:[12] So too people lie down and don’t get up again. They won’t wake up until the sky no longer exists. For now they can’t be roused out of their sleep.
[Iyov] [14]:[13] If only you’d allow me to be hidden in the grave, that you’d conceal me until your anger is passed. but set a limit and then remember me.
[Iyov] [14]:[14] If a person dies, will they ever live again? I’ll keep doing my work here until I’m released from it.
[Iyov] [14]:[15] You’ll call me and I’ll answer you. You’ll desire the creature you’ve made.
[Iyov] [14]:[16] Now you’ll count my steps. You won’t keep watch on my sins.
[Iyov] [14]:[17] My disobedience would be sealed up in a bag, and you’d plaster over my wickedness.
[Iyov] [14]:[18] But mountains fall and crumble, and rocks move out of their places.
[Iyov] [14]:[19] Flowing water wears down stones, and its torrents wash away the soil. You destroy humankind’s hope.
[Iyov] [14]:[20] You’re forever overpowering us and we depart. You are changing the expression on our faces and sending us away.
[Iyov] [14]:[21] If our children achieved some honour, we wouldn’t even know it. Or if they’re put to shame, we wouldn’t be there to see it.
[Iyov] [14]:[22] Only our own bodies feel the pain. Only our inner selves mourn.
[Iyov] [15]:[1] Then Elifaz (from Teyman) replied:
[Iyov] [15]:[2] Do wise people just answer with knowledge full of wind? Do they just fill themselves with the east wind?
[Iyov] [15]:[3] Should a person argue against useless talk, or against words that have no value?
[Iyov] [15]:[4] You turn people from the fear of God, and discourage them from godly meditation.
[Iyov] [15]:[5] Thus your wickedness drives your words, and you choose the language of crafty people.
[Iyov] [15]:[6] It’s not me who condemns you, but it’s your own mouth. Your own lips testify against you.
[Iyov] [15]:[7] Were you the first person ever born? Were you created before the hills were made?
[Iyov] [15]:[8] Do you listen to God’s advice, or limit wisdom to your own experience?
[Iyov] [15]:[9] What do you know that we don’t? What do you understand that’s not clear to us?
[Iyov] [15]:[10] Both the grey-haired and the elderly are on our side, People who’ve lived longer than your father.
[Iyov] [15]:[11] Isn’t it enough when God comforts you? Aren’t his gentle words enough for you?
[Iyov] [15]:[12] Why do your emotions get carried away? Why do your eyes flash with anger?
[Iyov] [15]:[13] Are you turning your spirit against God as your words pour out of your mouth?
[Iyov] [15]:[14] What person could ever be pure, and how could someone born from a woman be righteous?
[Iyov] [15]:[15] He doesn’t even trust his holy ones, and the heavens aren’t pure from his viewpoint.
[Iyov] [15]:[16] Certainly not someone who’s corrupt and abhorrent, or a person who drinks wickedness like water.
[Iyov] [15]:[17] I’ll show you—listen to me— what I’ve seen and will tell everyone.
[Iyov] [15]:[18] What’s been told by wise people— that hasn’t been hidden from their ancestors.
[Iyov] [15]:[19] The land was given to them alone, and no stranger had come in among them.
[Iyov] [15]:[20] Wicked people squirm in pain for their entire lifetime. Those who oppress others have a number of years of pain stored up for them.
[Iyov] [15]:[21] Sounds of terrors are in their ears. The destroyer comes while they’re enjoying prosperity.
[Iyov] [15]:[22] They don’t believe that the darkness will ever end. They’re destined for the sword.
[Iyov] [15]:[23] They wander around searching for food that must be there. They know that dark days are ahead—already prepared.
[Iyov] [15]:[24] They’re terrified by distress and anguish. That dread overwhelms them like a king who’s ready for a battle.
[Iyov] [15]:[25] These things happen to wicked people because they oppose God. They’ve behaved arrogantly to the provider.
[Iyov] [15]:[26] They rush against him in defiance, trusting the thick reinforcing of their shields.
[Iyov] [15]:[27] Though their faces are round and fat, and their bodies have rolls on their hips,
[Iyov] [15]:[28] they’ll live in broken-down houses which people normally wouldn’t live in because they’re marked for demolition.
[Iyov] [15]:[29] They won’t be rich and their wealth won’t endure, and their herds and flocks won’t spread across the land.
[Iyov] [15]:[30] Wicked people will never escape the darkness. A flame will wither their branches, and with one breath of their mouths, they’ll be gone.
[Iyov] [15]:[31] Don’t let them trust in emptiness or they’ll be led astray, and worthlessness will be their only reward.
[Iyov] [15]:[32] They’ll be finished before their time, and their branches won’t flourish and produce leaves.
[Iyov] [15]:[33] They’ll be like grapevines that drop their grapes when they’re still unripe, and like olive trees that shed their blossoms.
[Iyov] [15]:[34] Yes, the company of godless people is worthless, and anything gained from bribery will be burnt up in the fire.
[Iyov] [15]:[35] They dream about trouble and encourage wickedness, and they give birth to deceitful plots.
[Iyov] [16]:[1] Then Iyov (Job) answered Elifaz:
[Iyov] [16]:[2] I’ve heard many things like that before. You come to comfort, but bring trouble instead.
[Iyov] [16]:[3] You need to limit your words full of wind. What makes you keep responding?
[Iyov] [16]:[4] I could also speak like you all if you were in my place. I could string words together against you all and shake my head at you.
[Iyov] [16]:[5] Alternatively, I could use my mouth to encourage you all. My lips could be used instead to bring relief.
[Iyov] [16]:[6] Even when I speak, it doesn’t take away my pain. But if I hold back, how will it go away?
[Iyov] [16]:[7] However, he’s now worn me out. My entire household has been devastated.
[Iyov] [16]:[8] You’ve made me lose so much weight that everyone can’t help notice it. My being so thin is used against me so people think from my face that I must be guilty.
[Iyov] [16]:[9] His anger has ripped my body open and in his hate he’s gnashed at me with his teeth. Even my enemy locks his eyes on me.
[Iyov] [16]:[10] People stare at me with their mouths wide open. They slap my cheek in contempt as they join together against me.
[Iyov] [16]:[11] God has handed me over to a YOUNG BOY and he throws me into the hands of wicked people.
[Iyov] [16]:[12] I was just living my life and he shattered me. He grabbed me by the neck and dashed me to pieces. He set me up as a his target.
[Iyov] [16]:[13] ≈Soldiers with bows and arrows surround me. He pierces my kidneys but doesn’t care. He splits my gallbladder and pours my bile out on the ground.
[Iyov] [16]:[14] He keeps breaking through my protective walls. He charges against me like a warrior.
[Iyov] [16]:[15] I’ve dressed in sackcloth to show I’m mourning. I’ve tossed my horn into the dust to show I’m defeated.
[Iyov] [16]:[16] My face is red from so much crying. My eyelids are surrounded by dark shadows.
[Iyov] [16]:[17] I haven’t committed any violence. My prayer is pure.
[Iyov] [16]:[18] Earth, don’t just cover over my blood. Don’t just become a hiding place for my cries.
[Iyov] [16]:[19] Even now, my witness is there in the heavens, and my advocate is up on high.
[Iyov] [16]:[20] My friends scorn me. The tears of my eyes are directed to God.
[Iyov] [16]:[21] May someone plead with God for a man, and a son of humanity plead for his friend.
[Iyov] [16]:[22] When a certain number of years have passed, I’ll go on a path that I won’t return from.
[Iyov] [17]:[1] My spirit is broken, my days are extinguished, only the grave is left.
[Iyov] [17]:[2] Surely there’s mockers with me. My eye is held by their provocations.
[Iyov] [17]:[3] Please give yourself to cover my bail. Who else would put up security for me?
[Iyov] [17]:[4] You’ve closed their minds from being able to understand, so therefore you won’t elevate them over me.
[Iyov] [17]:[5] People who’d denounce their friends for some gain, should expect their children to be selfish also.
[Iyov] [17]:[6] He’s made me into a local gossip point. Someone to spit at in the face.
[Iyov] [17]:[7] My eyes have become dark from my grief. Every one of my body parts is just like a shadow.
[Iyov] [17]:[8] Godly people are appalled by this, and innocent people are stirred up against those who are godless.
[Iyov] [17]:[9] But those who obey will be able to stay on the correct road, and those who haven’t done anything wrong will become stronger.
[Iyov] [17]:[10] But all of them and you all may return now and come, and I wouldn’t find a wise person among you all.
[Iyov] [17]:[11] My good days have passed. My plans are shattered, even my secret desires.
[Iyov] [17]:[12] They change night into day in their minds— making light seem near while staring into the darkness.
[Iyov] [17]:[13] If I wait for the grave to become my home, if I’ve spread out my blankets ready to sleep in the darkness,
[Iyov] [17]:[14] if I’ve called out and told the pit that it’s my father, and to the worm that it’s my mother and my sister,
[Iyov] [17]:[15] then where would my hope be placed? Who would know that I had any hope?
[Iyov] [17]:[16] Will they go down to the gates of the grave? Will we go down together into the ground?

[Iyov] [19]:[1] Iyov (Job) responded to Bildad and companions again:

[Iyov] [19]:[5] If you truly think that you’re better people than me, and use my disgrace to argue against me,

[Iyov] [19]:[7] There, I cry out that I’m being attacked, and get no answer. I call for help, but there’s no justice.
[Iyov] [19]:[8] He’s blocked my road so I can’t get past, and he places darkness over my paths.

[Iyov] [19]:[13] He’s moved my brothers far away from me, and my acquaintances have certainly kept out of my way.
[Iyov] [19]:[14] My relatives have deserted me, and my close friends have forgotten me.

[Iyov] [19]:[16] When I call my servant, he doesn’t answer. I try to persuade him with my words.
[Iyov] [19]:[17] My breath is repugnant to my wife, and abhorrent to my siblings.

[Iyov] [19]:[19] All my closest friends abhor me, and those I love have turned on me.
[Iyov] [19]:[20] My skin and flesh cling to my bones. I’ve escaped by the skin of my teeth.

[Iyov] [19]:[29] You should be afraid of the sword, because anger brings punishment by the sword, so that you will know that there is judgement.
[Iyov] [20]:[1] Then Tsofar (from Na’amah) responded to Iyov (Job):
[Iyov] [20]:[2] My anxious thoughts force me to answer, because of the turmoil that’s within me.
[Iyov] [20]:[3] I’ve heard your correction and it insults me, and a spirit beyond my understanding answers me.

[Iyov] [20]:[28] The contents of their houses will be removed— washed away in his severe anger.

[Iyov] [21]:[1] Then Iyov (Job) responded to Tsofar and the others:
[Iyov] [21]:[2] Listen carefully to my words, and let this be a consolation for you all.
[Iyov] [21]:[3] Bear with me while I speak, and after I’ve finished, you can continue mocking then.
[Iyov] [21]:[4] As for me, is my complaint against any person? If it was, then you might expect me to be impatient.

[Iyov] [21]:[6] When I remember what happened, I’m horrified, and my body starts shuddering.

[Iyov] [21]:[8] Their children become established around them, and their offspring become settled in front of them.

[Iyov] [21]:[31] Who will denounce their actions to their faces? Who will repay them for the evil they’ve done?
[Iyov] [21]:[32] They’ll be carried off to the cemetery, and someone will keep watch over their tombs.
[Iyov] [21]:[33] The clods of the riverbed will be sweet to them. Everyone will follow along behind them, and no one can count those who go in front of them.

[Iyov] [24]:[1] Why doesn’t the provider store up the times, and those who know him never see him age?

[Iyov] [41]:[31] It makes the deep ocean boil like a pot. It makes the sea swirl like a jar of ointment.
[Iyov] [41]:[32] It leaves a glistening wake behind it— you’d think that the deep water had white hair.
[Iyov] [41]:[33] There’s no equal to it on the earth— the creature that was made to have no fear.

[Iyov] [42]:[1] Then Iyov (Job) answered Yahweh:

[Iyov] [42]:[5] I’d heard you with my ears, but now I can see you with my eyes.
