[2 Maccabees] [12]:[16] Having taken the city by God’s will, they made unspeakable slaughter, so much that the adjoining lake, which was two furlongs broad, appeared to be filled with the deluge of blood.
[2 Maccabees] [12]:[17] When they’d gone seven hundred and fifty furlongs from there, they made their way to Karax, to the Yehudim (Jews) that are called Tubieni.
[2 Maccabees] [12]:[18] They didn’t find Timotheos in that district, for he had by then departed from the district without accomplishing anything, but had left behind a very strong garrison in one place.
[2 Maccabees] [12]:[19] But Dositheos and Sosipatros, who were captains under Makabi (Maccabaeus), went out and destroyed those who’d been left by Timotheos in the stronghold, more than ten thousand men.
[2 Maccabees] [12]:[20] Makabi, arranging his own army in divisions, set these two over the bands, and marched in haste against Timotheos, who had with him one hundred and twenty thousand infantry and two thousand and five hundred cavalry.
[2 Maccabees] [12]:[21] When Timotheos heard of the approach of Yehudah, he at once sent away the women and the children with the baggage into the fortress called Karnayim; for the place was hard to besiege and difficult of access because of the narrowness of the approaches on all sides.
[2 Maccabees] [12]:[22] When the band of Yehudah, who led the first division, appeared in sight, and when terror and fear came on the enemy, because the manifestation of him who sees all things came on them, they fled in every direction, carried this way and that, so that they were often injured by their own men, and pierced with the points of their own swords.
[2 Maccabees] [12]:[23] Yehudah continued the pursuit more vigorously, putting the wicked wretches to the sword, and he destroyed as many as thirty thousand men.
[2 Maccabees] [12]:[24] Timotheos himself, falling in with the company of Dositheos and Sosipatros, implored them with much crafty guile to let him go with his life, because he had in his power the parents of many of them and the kindred of some. “Otherwise, he said, little regard will be shown to these.”
[2 Maccabees] [12]:[25] So when he had with many words confirmed the agreement to restore them without harm, they let him go that they might save their kindred.
[2 Maccabees] [12]:[26] Then Yehudah, marching against Karnayim and Atergatis’ temple, killed twenty-five thousand people.
[2 Maccabees] [12]:[27] After he’d put these to flight and destroyed them, he marched against Efron also, a strong city, wherein were multitudes of people of all nations. Stalwart young men placed on the walls made a vigorous defence. There were great stores of war engines and darts there.
[2 Maccabees] [12]:[28] But calling on the Sovereign who with might shatters the strength of the enemy, they took the city into their hands, and killed as many as twenty-five thousand of those who were in it.
[2 Maccabees] [12]:[29] Setting out from there, they marched in haste against Beyt-Shean, which is six hundred furlongs away from Yerushalem (Jerusalem).
[2 Maccabees] [12]:[30] But when the Yehudim (Jews) who were settled there testified of the good will that the Scythopolitans had shown towards them, and of their kind treatment of them in the times of their misfortune,
[2 Maccabees] [12]:[31] they gave thanks, and further exhorted them to remain well disposed towards the race for the future. Then they went up to Yerushalem, the feast of weeks being close at hand.
[2 Maccabees] [12]:[32] But after the feast called Pentecost, they marched in haste against Gorgias Edom’s governor.
[2 Maccabees] [12]:[33] He came out with three thousand infantry and four hundred cavalry.
[2 Maccabees] [12]:[34] When they’d set themselves in array, it happened that a few of the Yehudim fell.
[2 Maccabees] [12]:[35] A certain Dositheos, one of Bacenor’s company, who was on horseback and was a strong man, pressed hard on Gorgias, and taking hold of his cloak dragged him along by main force. While he planned to take the accursed man alive, one of the Thracian cavalry bore down on him and disabled his shoulder, and so Gorgias escaped to Mareshah.
[2 Maccabees] [12]:[36] When those who were with Ezra had been fighting long and were weary, Yehudah (Judas) called on the master to show himself, fighting on their side and leading in the battle.
[2 Maccabees] [12]:[37] Then in the language of his ancestors he raised the battle cry joined with hymns. Then he rushed against Gorgias’ troops when they weren’t expecting it, and put them to flight.
[2 Maccabees] [12]:[38] Yehudah gathered his army and came to the city of Adulam. As the seventh day was coming on, they purified themselves according to the custom, and kept the Sabbath there.
[2 Maccabees] [12]:[39] On the following day, when it’d become necessary, Yehudah and his company came to take up the bodies of those who’d fallen, and in company with their kinsmen to bring them back to the sepulchres of their ancestors.
[2 Maccabees] [12]:[40] But under the clothes of each one of the dead they found consecrated tokens of the idols of Yavneh, which the law forbids the Yehudim to have anything to do with. It became clear to all that it was for this cause that they’d fallen.
[2 Maccabees] [12]:[41] All therefore, blessing the ways of the master, the righteous Judge, who makes manifest the things that are hidden,
[2 Maccabees] [12]:[42] turned themselves to supplication, praying that the sin committed might be wholly blotted out. The noble Yehudah exhorted the multitude to keep themselves from sin, for they’d seen with their own eyes what happened because of the sin of those who’d fallen.
[2 Maccabees] [12]:[43] When he’d made a collection man by man to the sum of two thousand drachmas of silver, he sent to Yerushalem (Jerusalem) to offer a sacrifice for sin, doing very well and honourably in this, in that he took thought for the resurrection.
[2 Maccabees] [12]:[44] Because if he wasn’t expecting that those who’d fallen would rise again, it’d be superfluous and idle to pray for the dead.
[2 Maccabees] [12]:[45] But if he was looking forward to an honourable memorial of gratitude laid up for those who die in godliness, then the thought was holy and godly. Therefore he made the atoning sacrifice for those who’d died, that they might be released from their sin.
[2 Maccabees] [13]:[1] In the one hundred and forty-ninth year, news was brought to Yehudah and his company that Antiokos (Antiochus) Eupator was coming with multitudes against Yehudah,
[2 Maccabees] [13]:[2] and with him Lusias his guardian and chancellor, each having a Greek force of one hundred and ten thousand infantry, five thousand and three hundred cavalry, twenty-two elephants, and three hundred chariots armed with scythes.
[2 Maccabees] [13]:[3] And Menelaos also joined himself with them, and with great hypocrisy encouraged Antiokos, not for the saving of his country, but because he thought that he’d be set over the government.
[2 Maccabees] [13]:[4] But the King of kings stirred up Antiokos’ anger against the wicked wretch. When Lusias informed him that this man was the cause of all the evils, the king commanded to bring him to Beroia, and to put him to death in the way customary in that place.
[2 Maccabees] [13]:[5] Now there’s in that place a tower that’s fifty cubits high, full of ashes, and it had all around it a circular rim sloping steeply on every side into the ashes.
[2 Maccabees] [13]:[6] Here one who’s guilty of sacrilege or notorious for other crimes is pushed down to destruction.
[2 Maccabees] [13]:[7] By such a fate it happened that the breaker of the law, Menelaos, died, without obtaining so much as a grave in the earth, and that justly;
[2 Maccabees] [13]:[8] for since he’d perpetrated many sins against the altar, whose fire and whose ashes were holy, he received his death in ashes.
[2 Maccabees] [13]:[9] Now the king, infuriated in spirit, was coming with intent to inflict on the Yehudim (Jews) the very worst of the sufferings that’d been done in his father’s time.
[2 Maccabees] [13]:[10] But when Yehudah heard of these things, he commanded the multitude to call on the master day and night, if ever at any other time, so now to help those who were at the point of being deprived of the law, their country, and the holy temple,
[2 Maccabees] [13]:[11] and not to allow the people who’d just begun to be revived to fall into the hands of those profane heathen.
[2 Maccabees] [13]:[12] So when they had all done the same thing together, begging the merciful master with weeping and fastings and prostration for three days without ceasing, Yehudah exhorted them and commanded they should join him.
[2 Maccabees] [13]:[13] Having consulted privately with the elders, he resolved that before the king’s army entered into Yehudah (Judea) and made themselves masters of the city, they should go out and decide the matter by the help of God.
[2 Maccabees] [13]:[14] And committing the decision to the master of the world, and exhorting those who were with him to contend nobly even to death for laws, temple, city, country, and way of life, he pitched his camp by Modi’in.
[2 Maccabees] [13]:[15] He gave out to his men the watchword, “VICTORY IS GOD’S”, with a chosen force of the bravest young men he attacked by the king’s pavilion by night, and killed of his army as many as two thousand men, and brought down the leading elephant with him who was in the tower on him.
[2 Maccabees] [13]:[16] At last they filled the army with terror and alarm, and departed with good success.
[2 Maccabees] [13]:[17] This had been accomplished when the day was just dawning, because of the master’s protection that gave Yehudah help.
[2 Maccabees] [13]:[18] But the king, having had a taste of the exceeding boldness of the Yehudim (Jews), made strategic attacks on their positions,
[2 Maccabees] [13]:[19] and on a strong fortress of the Yehudim at Beyt-Tsur. He advanced, was turned back, failed, and was defeated.
[2 Maccabees] [13]:[20] Yehudah sent the things that were necessary to those who were within.
[2 Maccabees] [13]:[21] But Rodokos, from the Jewish ranks, made secrets known to the enemy. He was sought out, arrested, and shut up in prison.
[2 Maccabees] [13]:[22] The king negotiated with them in Beyt-Tsur the second time, gave his hand, took theirs, departed, attacked the forces of Yehudah, was put to the worse,
[2 Maccabees] [13]:[23] heard that Filippos (Philip) who’d been left as chancellor in Antiokeia had become reckless, was confounded, made to the Yehudim an overture of peace, submitted himself and swore to acknowledge all their rights, came to terms with them and offered sacrifice, honoured the sanctuary and the place,
[2 Maccabees] [13]:[24] showed kindness and graciously received Makabi (Maccabaeus), left Hegemonides governor from Ptolemais even to the Gerrenians,
[2 Maccabees] [13]:[25] and came to Ptolemais. The men of Ptolemais were displeased at the treaty, for they had very great indignation against the Yehudim. They desired to annul the articles of the agreement.
[2 Maccabees] [13]:[26] Lusias came forward to speak, made the best defence that was possible, persuaded, pacified, gained their good will, and departed to Antiokeia. This was the issue of the attack and departure of the king.
[2 Maccabees] [14]:[1] Three years later, news was brought to Yehudah and his company that Demetrios the son of Seleukos (Seleucus), having sailed into the harbour of Tripolis with a mighty army and a fleet,
[2 Maccabees] [14]:[2] had taken possession of the country, having made away with Antiokos (Antiochus) and his guardian Lusias.
[2 Maccabees] [14]:[3] But one Alkimos, who’d formerly been high priest, and had wilfully polluted himself in the times when there was no mingling with the Gentiles, considering that there was no deliverance for him in any way, nor any more access to the holy altar,
[2 Maccabees] [14]:[4] came to King Demetrios in about the one hundred and fifty-first year, presenting to him a crown of gold and a palm, and beside these some of the festal olive boughs of the temple. Because that day, he held his peace;
[2 Maccabees] [14]:[5] but having gotten opportunity to further his own madness, being called by Demetrios into a meeting of his council, and asked how the Yehudim stood affected and what they intended, he answered:
[2 Maccabees] [14]:[6] “Those of the Yehudim called Hasidim, whose leader is Yehudah Makabi (Maccabaeus), keep up war and are seditious, not allowing the kingdom to find tranquillity.
[2 Maccabees] [14]:[7] Therefore, having laid aside my ancestral glory—I mean the high priesthood—I’ve now come here,
[2 Maccabees] [14]:[8] first for the genuine care I have for the things that concern the king, and secondly because I have regard also to my own fellow citizens. Because through the unadvised dealing of those of whom I spoke before, our whole race is in no small misfortune.
[2 Maccabees] [14]:[9] Oh king, having informed yourself of these things, take thought both for our country and for our race, which is surrounded by enemies, according to the gracious kindness with which you receive all.
[2 Maccabees] [14]:[10] Because as long as Yehudah remains alive, it’s impossible for the government to find peace.
[2 Maccabees] [14]:[11] When he’d spoken such words as these, at once the rest of the king’s friends, having ill will against Yehudah, inflamed Demetrios yet more.
[2 Maccabees] [14]:[12] He immediately appointed Nikanor, who’d been master of the elephants, and made him governor of Yehudah. He sent him out,
[2 Maccabees] [14]:[13] giving him written instructions to kill Yehudah himself and to scatter those who were with him, and to set up Alkimos as high priest of the great temple.
[2 Maccabees] [14]:[14] Those in Yehudah who had driven Yehudah into exile thronged to Nikanor in flocks, supposing that the misfortunes and calamities of the Yehudim would be successes to themselves.
[2 Maccabees] [14]:[15] But when the Yehudim heard of Nikanor’s advance and the assault of the heathen, they sprinkled dirt on their heads and made solemn prayers to him who’d established his own people forever, and who always, making manifest his presence, upholds those who are his own heritage.
[2 Maccabees] [14]:[16] When the leader had given orders, he immediately set out from there and joined battle with them at a village called Lessau.
[2 Maccabees] [14]:[17] But Shim’on (Simon), the brother of Yehudah, had encountered Nikanor, yet not till late, having been delayed because of the sudden consternation caused by his adversaries.
[2 Maccabees] [14]:[18] Nevertheless Nikanor, hearing of the valour of those who were with Yehudah, and their courage in fighting for their country, shrank from bringing the matter to the decision of the sword.
[2 Maccabees] [14]:[19] Therefore he sent Posidonios, Theodotos, and Matityah (Mattathias) to give and receive pledges of friendship.
[2 Maccabees] [14]:[20] So when these proposals had been long considered, and the leader had made the troops acquainted with them, and it appeared that they were all of like mind, they consented to the covenants.
[2 Maccabees] [14]:[21] They appointed a day on which to meet together by themselves. A chariot came forward from each army. They set up seats of honour.
[2 Maccabees] [14]:[22] Yehudah stationed armed men ready in convenient places, in case the enemy suddenly betrayed them. They held a conference as was appropriate.
[2 Maccabees] [14]:[23] Nikanor waited in Yerushalem (Jerusalem), and did nothing to cause disturbance, but dismissed the flocks of people that’d gathered together.
[2 Maccabees] [14]:[24] He kept Yehudah always in his presence. He’d gained a hearty affection for the man.
[2 Maccabees] [14]:[25] He urged him to marry and have children. He married, settled quietly, and took part in common life.
[2 Maccabees] [14]:[26] But Alkimos, perceiving the good will that was between them, and having taken possession of the covenants that’d been made, came to Demetrios and told him that Nikanor was disloyal to the government, for he’d appointed that conspirator against his kingdom, Yehudah, to be his successor.
[2 Maccabees] [14]:[27] The king, falling into a rage, and being exasperated by the false accusations of that most wicked man, wrote to Nikanor, signifying that he was displeased at the covenants, and commanding him to send Makabi (Maccabaeus) prisoner to Antiokeia in all haste.
[2 Maccabees] [14]:[28] When this message came to Nikanor, he was confounded, and was very troubled at the thought of annulling the articles that’d been agreed on, the man having done no wrong;
[2 Maccabees] [14]:[29] but because there was no opposing the king, he watched his time to execute this purpose by strategy.
[2 Maccabees] [14]:[30] But Makabi, when he perceived that Nikanor was behaving more harshly in his dealings with him, and that he’d become ruler in his customary bearing, understanding that this harshness came not of good, gathered together not a few of his men, and concealed himself from Nikanor.
[2 Maccabees] [14]:[31] But the other, when he became aware that he’d been bravely defeated by the strategy of Yehudah, came to the great and holy temple, while the priests were offering the usual sacrifices, and commanded them to hand over the man.
[2 Maccabees] [14]:[32] When they declared with oaths that they had no knowledge where the man was whom he sought,
[2 Maccabees] [14]:[33] he stretched out his right hand towards the sanctuary, and swore this oath: “If you won’t deliver up to me Yehudah as a prisoner, I’ll level this temple of God even with the ground, break down the altar, and I’ll erect here a temple to Dionusos for all to see.
[2 Maccabees] [14]:[34] And having said this, he departed. But the priests, stretching forth their hands towards heaven, called on him who always fights for our nation, in these words:
[2 Maccabees] [14]:[35] “You, Oh master of the universe, who in yourself have need of nothing, were well pleased that a sanctuary of your habitation should be set among us.
[2 Maccabees] [14]:[36] So now, Oh holy master of all holiness, keep undefiled forever this house that’s been recently cleansed.”
[2 Maccabees] [14]:[37] Now information was given to Nikanor against one Razis, an elder of Yerushalem (Jerusalem), who was a lover of his countrymen and a man of very good report, and one called Father of the Yehudim (Jews) for his good will.
[2 Maccabees] [14]:[38] Because in the former times when there was no mingling with the Gentiles, he’d been accused of following the Yehudim’ religion, and had risked body and life with all earnestness for the religion of the Yehudim.
[2 Maccabees] [14]:[39] Nikanor, wishing to make evident the ill will that he bore against the Yehudim, sent above five hundred soldiers to seize him;
[2 Maccabees] [14]:[40] for he thought by seizing him to inflict an injury on them.
[2 Maccabees] [14]:[41] But when the troops were at the point of taking the tower, and were forcing the courtyard door, and asked for fire to burn the doors, he, being surrounded on every side, fell onto his sword,
[2 Maccabees] [14]:[42] choosing rather to die nobly than to fall into the hands of the wicked wretches, and suffer outrage unworthy of his own nobleness.
[2 Maccabees] [14]:[43] But since he missed his stroke through the excitement of the struggle, and the crowds were now rushing within the door, he ran bravely up to the wall and threw himself down bravely among the crowds.
[2 Maccabees] [14]:[44] But as they quickly gave back, a space was made, and he fell on the middle of his side.
[2 Maccabees] [14]:[45] Still having breath within him, and being inflamed with anger, he rose up, and though his blood gushed out in streams and his wounds were grievous, he ran through the crowds, and standing on a steep rock,
[2 Maccabees] [14]:[46] when as his blood was now well near spent, he drew forth his bowels through the wound, and taking them in both his hands he shook them at the crowds. Calling on him who’s master of life and spirit to restore him these again, he died like this.
[2 Maccabees] [15]:[1] But Nikanor, hearing that Yehudah (Judas) and his company were in the region of Shomron (Samaria), resolved to attack them with complete safety on the day of rest.
[2 Maccabees] [15]:[2] When the Yehudim (Jews) who were compelled to follow him said, “Don’t destroy so savagely and barbarously, but give due glory to the day which he who sees all things has honoured and hallowed above other days.”
[2 Maccabees] [15]:[3] Then the thrice-accursed wretch asked if there were a Sovereign in heaven who’d commanded to keep the Sabbath day.
[2 Maccabees] [15]:[4] When they declared, “There’s the master, living himself as Sovereign in heaven, who told us observe the seventh day.”
[2 Maccabees] [15]:[5] He replied, “I also am a sovereign on the earth, who commands you to take up weapons and execute the king’s business.” Nevertheless he didn’t prevail to execute his cruel plan.
[2 Maccabees] [15]:[6] And Nikanor, in his utter boastfulness and arrogance, had determined to set up a monument of complete victory over Yehudah and all those who were with him.
[2 Maccabees] [15]:[7] But Makabi (Maccabaeus) still trusted unceasingly, with all hope that he should obtain help from the master.
[2 Maccabees] [15]:[8] He exhorted his company not to be fearful at the assault of the heathen, but keeping in mind the help which in former times they’d often received from heaven, so now also to look for the victory which would come to them from the Almighty,
[2 Maccabees] [15]:[9] and encouraging them out of the law and the prophets, and reminding them of the conflicts that they’d won, he made them more eager.
[2 Maccabees] [15]:[10] And when he’d aroused their courage, he gave them orders, at the same time pointing out the faithlessness of the heathen and their breach of their oaths.
[2 Maccabees] [15]:[11] Arming each one of them, not so much with the sure defence of shields and spears as with the encouragement of good words, and moreover relating to them a dream worthy to be believed, he made them all extremely glad.
[2 Maccabees] [15]:[12] The vision of that dream was this: Honyo (Onias), he who’d been high priest, a noble and good man, modest in bearing, yet gentle in manner and well-spoken, and trained from a child in all points of virtue, with outstretched hands invoking blessings on the whole body of the Yehudim (Jews).
[2 Maccabees] [15]:[13] Then he saw a man appear, of venerable age and exceeding glory, and the dignity around him was wonderful and most majestic.
[2 Maccabees] [15]:[14] Honyo replied, “This is the lover of the kindred, he who prays much for the people and the holy city: Yirmiyah (Jeremiah) God’s prophet.
[2 Maccabees] [15]:[15] Yirmiyah stretched out his right hand and delivered to Yehudah a gold sword, and in giving it addressed him thus:
[2 Maccabees] [15]:[16] “Take this holy sword, a gift from God, with which you’ll strike down the adversaries.”
[2 Maccabees] [15]:[17] Being encouraged by Yehudah’s (Judas) words, which were noble and effective, and able to incite to virtue and to stir the souls of the young to manly courage, they determined not to carry on a campaign, but nobly to bear down on the enemy, and fighting hand to hand with all courage bring the matter to a conclusion, because the city, the sanctuary, and the temple were in danger.
[2 Maccabees] [15]:[18] Because their fear for wives and children, and furthermore for family and relatives, was less important to them; but greatest and first was their fear for the consecrated sanctuary.
[2 Maccabees] [15]:[19] Also those who were shut up in the city were in no light distress, being troubled because of the encounter in the open country.
[2 Maccabees] [15]:[20] When all were now waiting for the decision of the issue, and the enemy had already joined battle, and the army had been set in array, and the elephants brought back to a convenient post, and the cavalry deployed on the flanks,
[2 Maccabees] [15]:[21] Makabi (Maccabaeus), perceiving the presence of the troops, and the various weapons with which they were equipped, and the savageness of the elephants, holding up his hands to heaven called on the master who works wonders, knowing that success comes not by weapons, but that, according to how the master judges, he gains the victory for those who are worthy.
[2 Maccabees] [15]:[22] And calling on God, he said this: “You, Oh Sovereign master, sent your angel in the time of King Hizkiyah (Hezekiah) of Yehudah, and he killed of the army of Sanheriv (Sennacherib) as many as one hundred and eighty-five thousand.
[2 Maccabees] [15]:[23] So now also, Oh Sovereign of the heavens, send a good angel before us to bring terror and trembling.
[2 Maccabees] [15]:[24] Through the greatness of your arm let them be stricken with dismay who with blasphemy have come here against your holy people.” As he finished these words,
[2 Maccabees] [15]:[25] Nikanor and his company advanced with trumpets and victory songs;
[2 Maccabees] [15]:[26] but Yehudah and his company joined battle with the enemy with invocation and prayers.
[2 Maccabees] [15]:[27] Fighting with their hands and praying to God with their hearts, they killed no less than thirty-five thousand men, being made extremely glad by the manifestation of God.
[2 Maccabees] [15]:[28] When the engagement was over and they were returning again with joy, they recognised Nikanor lying dead in full armour.
[2 Maccabees] [15]:[29] Then there was shouting and noise, and they blessed the Sovereign master in the language of their ancestors.
[2 Maccabees] [15]:[30] He who in all things was in body and soul the foremost champion of his fellow-citizens, he who kept through life the good will of his youth towards his countrymen, ordered that Nikanor’s head be cut off with his hand and arm, and that they be brought to Yerushalem (Jerusalem).
[2 Maccabees] [15]:[31] When he’d arrived there and had called his countrymen together and set the priests before the altar, he sent for those who were in the citadel.
[2 Maccabees] [15]:[32] Showing the head of the vile Nikanor and the hand of that profane man, which with proud brags he’d stretched out against the holy house of the Almighty,
[2 Maccabees] [15]:[33] and cutting out the tongue of the impious Nikanor, he said that he’d give it in pieces to the birds, and hang up these rewards of his folly near the sanctuary.
[2 Maccabees] [15]:[34] They all, looking up to heaven, blessed the master who’d manifested himself, saying, “Blessed is he who’s preserved his own place undefiled!”
[2 Maccabees] [15]:[35] He hung Nikanor’s head and shoulder from the citadel, a clear sign evident to all of the help of the master.
[2 Maccabees] [15]:[36] They all ordained with a common decree to in no way let this day pass undistinguished, but to mark with honour the thirteenth day of the twelfth month (it’s called Adar in the Arami (Syrian) language), the day before the day of Mordekai.
[2 Maccabees] [15]:[37] This then having been the account of the attempt of Nikanor, and the city having from those times been held by the Ivrim (Hebrews), I also will here make an end of my book.
[2 Maccabees] [15]:[38] If I’ve written well and to the point in my story, this is what I myself desired; but if it’s poorly done and mediocre, this is the best I could do.
[2 Maccabees] [15]:[39] Because as it’s distasteful to drink wine alone and likewise to drink water alone, while the mingling of wine with water at once gives full pleasantness to the flavour; so also the fashioning of the language delights the ears of those who read the story. Here is the end.
[3 Maccabees] [1]:[1] Now Filopator, on learning from those who came back that Antiokos (Antiochus) had made himself master of the places which belonged to himself, sent orders to all his infantry and cavalry, took with him his sister Arsinoe, and marched out as far as the parts of Rafiah, where Antiokos and his forces encamped.
[3 Maccabees] [1]:[2] And one Theodotos, intending to carry out his design, took with him the bravest of the armed men who’d been before committed to his trust by Ptolemaios (Ptolemy), and got through at night to Ptolemaios’ tent, to kill him on his own responsibility, and so to end the war.
[3 Maccabees] [1]:[3] But Dositheos, called the son of Drimulos, by birth a Yehudi (Jew), afterward a renegade from the laws and observances of his country, conveyed Ptolemaios away, and made an obscure person lie down in his stead in the tent. It turned out that this man received the fate which was meant for the other.
[3 Maccabees] [1]:[4] A fierce battle then took place. The men of Antiokos were prevailing. Arsinoe continually went up and down the ranks, and with dishevelled hair, with tears and entreaties, begged the soldiers to fight bravely for themselves, their children, and wives, and promised that if they proved conquerors, she’d give them each two minas of gold.
[3 Maccabees] [1]:[5] It thus fell out that their enemies were defeated in hand-to-hand encounter, and that many of them were taken prisoners.
[3 Maccabees] [1]:[6] Having vanquished this attempt, the king then decided to proceed to the neighbouring cities, and encourage them.
[3 Maccabees] [1]:[7] By doing this, and by making donations to their temples, he inspired his subjects with confidence.
[3 Maccabees] [1]:[8] The Yehudim (Jews) sent some of their council and of their elders to him. The greetings, welcoming gifts, and congratulations of the past, given by them, filled him with the greater eagerness to visit their city.
[3 Maccabees] [1]:[9] Having arrived at Yerushalem (Jerusalem), sacrificed, and offered thank offerings to the Greatest God, and done whatever else was suitable to the sanctity of the place, and entered the inner courtyard,
[3 Maccabees] [1]:[10] he was so impressed with the magnificence of the place, and so wondered at the orderly arrangements of the temple, that he considered entering the sanctuary itself.
[3 Maccabees] [1]:[11] When they told him that this wasn’t permissible, none of the nation, not even the priests in general, but only the supreme high priest of all, and he only once in a year, was allowed to go in, he’d by no means give way.
[3 Maccabees] [1]:[12] Then they read the law to him, but he persisted in intruding, exclaiming that he ought to be allowed. He said, “Even if they were deprived of this honour, I shouldn’t be.”
[3 Maccabees] [1]:[13] He asked why, when he entered all the other temples, did none of the priests who were present forbid him.
[3 Maccabees] [1]:[14] He was thoroughly answered by someone, that he did wrong to boast of this.
[3 Maccabees] [1]:[15] “Well, since I’ve done this,” he said, “be the cause what it may, won’t I enter with or without your consent?”
[3 Maccabees] [1]:[16] When the priests fell down in their sacred vestments imploring the Greatest God to come and help in time of need, and to avert the violence of the fierce aggressor, and when they filled the temple with lamentations and tears,
[3 Maccabees] [1]:[17] then those who’d been left behind in the city were scared, and rushed out, uncertain of the event.
[3 Maccabees] [1]:[18] Virgins, who’d been shut up within their chambers, came out with their mothers, scattering dust and ashes on their heads, and filling the streets with outcries.
[3 Maccabees] [1]:[19] Women who’d recently been arrayed for marriage left their bridal chambers, left the reserve that befitted them, and ran around the city in a disorderly manner.
[3 Maccabees] [1]:[20] New-born babes were deserted by the mothers or nurses who waited on them—some here, some there, in houses, or in fields; these now, with an ardour which couldn’t be checked, swarmed into the Most High temple.
[3 Maccabees] [1]:[21] Various prayers were offered up by those who assembled in this place because of the unholy attempt of the king.
[3 Maccabees] [1]:[22] Along with these there were some of the citizens who took courage and wouldn’t submit to his obstinacy and his intention of carrying out his purpose.
[3 Maccabees] [1]:[23] Calling out to arms, and to die bravely in defence of the law of their fathers, they created a great uproar in the place, and were with difficulty brought back by the aged and the elders to the station of prayer which they’d occupied before.
[3 Maccabees] [1]:[24] During this time, the multitude kept on praying.
[3 Maccabees] [1]:[25] The elders who surrounded the king tried in many ways to divert his arrogant mind from the design which he’d formed.
[3 Maccabees] [1]:[26] He, in his hardened mood, insensible to all persuasion, was going onward with the view of carrying out this design.
[3 Maccabees] [1]:[27] Yet even his own officers, when they saw this, joined the Yehudim (Jews) in an appeal to Him who has all power to aid in the present crisis, and not wink at such haughty lawlessness.
[3 Maccabees] [1]:[28] Such was the frequency and the vehemence of the cry of the assembled crowd, that an indescribable noise ensued.
[3 Maccabees] [1]:[29] Not the men only, but the very walls and floor seemed to sound out, all things preferring death rather than to see the place defiled.
[3 Maccabees] [2]:[1] Now it was that the high priest Shim’on (Simon) bowed his knees near the holy place, spread out his hands in reverent form, and uttered the following prayer:
[3 Maccabees] [2]:[2] “O master, master, King of the heavens, and Ruler of the whole creation, Holy among the holy, sole Governor, Almighty, give ear to us who are oppressed by a wicked and profane one, who celebrates in his confidence and strength.
[3 Maccabees] [2]:[3] It’s you, the Creator of all, the master of the universe, who are a righteous Governor, and judge all who act with pride and insolence.
[3 Maccabees] [2]:[4] It was you who destroyed the former workers of unrighteousness, among whom were the giants, who trusted in their strength and daring, by covering them with a measureless flood.
[3 Maccabees] [2]:[5] It was you who made the Sodomites, those workers of great wickedness, men notorious for their vices, an example to later generations, when you covered them with fire and brimstone.
[3 Maccabees] [2]:[6] You made known your power when you caused the bold Par’oh (Pharaoh), the enslaver of your people, to pass through the ordeal of many and diverse inflictions.
[3 Maccabees] [2]:[7] You rolled the depths of the sea over him when he pursued with chariots and with a multitude of followers, and gave a safe passage to those who put their trust in you, the master of the whole creation.
[3 Maccabees] [2]:[8] These saw and felt the works of your hands, and praised you, the Almighty.
[3 Maccabees] [2]:[9] You, Oh King, when you created the immeasurable and measureless earth, chose this city. You made this place sacred to your name, even though you need nothing. You glorified it with your illustrious presence, after constructing it to the glory of your great and honourable name.
[3 Maccabees] [2]:[10] You promised, out of love for Yisrael’s (Israel) people, that if we fall away from you, become afflicted, and then come to this house and pray, you’d hear our prayer.
[3 Maccabees] [2]:[11] Truly you’re faithful and true.
[3 Maccabees] [2]:[12] When you often aided our fathers when hard pressed and humiliated, and delivered them out of great dangers,
[3 Maccabees] [2]:[13] see now, holy King, how through our many and great sins we’re crushed and made subject to our enemies, and have become weak and powerless.
[3 Maccabees] [2]:[14] In our low condition, this bold and profane man seeks to dishonour this your holy place, consecrated out of the earth to the name of your Majesty.
[3 Maccabees] [2]:[15] Your dwelling place, the heaven of heavens, is indeed unapproachable to men.
[3 Maccabees] [2]:[16] But since it seemed good to you to exhibit your glory among your people Yisrael, you sanctified this place.
[3 Maccabees] [2]:[17] Don’t punish us by means of the uncleanness of their men, and don’t chastise us by means of their profanity, or those lawless people might boast in their rage, speak with excessive pride, and say,
[3 Maccabees] [2]:[18] ‘We’ve trampled on the holy house, as idolatrous houses are trampled on.’
[3 Maccabees] [2]:[19] Blot out our iniquities, do away with our errors, and show your compassion in this hour.
[3 Maccabees] [2]:[20] Let your mercies quickly go before us. Grant us peace, that the downcast and broken hearted may praise you with their mouth.”
[3 Maccabees] [2]:[21] At that time God, who sees all things, who’s beyond all Holy among the holy, heard that prayer, so suitable, and scourged the man who was greatly uplifted with scorn and insolence.
[3 Maccabees] [2]:[22] Shaking him back and forth as a reed is shaken with the wind, he threw him down on the pavement, powerless, with limbs paralysed, and by a righteous judgement deprived of the ability to speak.
[3 Maccabees] [2]:[23] His friends and bodyguards, seeing the swift recompense which had suddenly overtaken him, struck with exceeding terror, and fearing that he’d die, speedily removed him.
[3 Maccabees] [2]:[24] When in course of time he’d come to himself, this severe punishment caused no repentance within him, but he departed with bitter threatenings.
[3 Maccabees] [2]:[25] He proceeded to Mitsrayim (Egypt), grew worse in wickedness through his previously mentioned companions in wine, who were lost to all goodness,
[3 Maccabees] [2]:[26] and not satisfied with countless acts of impiety, his audacity so increased that he raised evil reports there, and many of his friends, watching his purpose attentively, joined in furthering his will.
[3 Maccabees] [2]:[27] His purpose was to inflict a public stigma on our race. Therefore he erected a stone pillar in the courtyard, and caused the following inscription to be engraved on it:
[3 Maccabees] [2]:[28] “Entrance to this temple is to be refused to all those who wouldn’t sacrifice. All the Yehudim (Jews) were to be registered among the slaves. Those who resisted are to be forcibly seized and put to death.
[3 Maccabees] [2]:[29] Those who are thus registered are to be marked on their persons by the ivy-leaf symbol of Dionusos, and to be reduced to these limited rights.”
[3 Maccabees] [2]:[30] To do away with the appearance of hating them all, he had it written underneath, that if any of them should elect to enter the community of those initiated in the rites, these should have equal rights with the Alexandrians.
[3 Maccabees] [2]:[31] Some of those who were over the city, therefore, abhorring any approach to the city of piety, unhesitatingly gave in to the king, and expected to derive some great honour from a future connection with him.
[3 Maccabees] [2]:[32] A nobler spirit, however, prompted the majority to cling to their religious observances, and by paying money that they might live unmolested, these sought to escape the registration,
[3 Maccabees] [2]:[33] cheerfully looking forward to future aid, they abhorred their own apostates, considering them to be national foes, and depriving them of common fellowship and mutual help.
[3 Maccabees] [3]:[1] On discovering this, so incensed was the wicked king, that he no longer confined his rage to the Yehudim in Alexandria. Laying his hand more heavily on those who lived in the country, he gave orders that they should be quickly collected into one place, and most cruelly deprived of their lives.
[3 Maccabees] [3]:[2] While this was going on, a hostile rumour was uttered abroad by men who’d banded together to injure the Jewish race. The pretext of their charge was that the Yehudim kept them away from the ordinances of the law.
[3 Maccabees] [3]:[3] Now the Yehudim always maintained a feeling of unwavering loyalty towards the kings,
[3 Maccabees] [3]:[4] yet, as they worshipped God and observed his law, they made certain distinctions, and avoided certain things. Hence they appeared hateful to some people,
[3 Maccabees] [3]:[5] although, as they adorned their conversation with works of righteousness, they’d established themselves in the good opinion of the world.
[3 Maccabees] [3]:[6] What all the rest of mankind said was, however, disregarded by the foreigners,
[3 Maccabees] [3]:[7] who said much of the exclusiveness of the Yehudim with regard to their worship and meats. They alleged that they were unsociable men, hostile to the king’s interests, refusing to associate with him or his troops. By this way of speaking, they brought much hatred on them.
[3 Maccabees] [3]:[8] This unexpected uproar and sudden gathering of people was observed by the Hellains (Greeks) who lived in the city, about men who’d never harmed them. Yet to aid them wasn’t in their power, since all was oppression around, but they encouraged them in their troubles, and expected a favourable turn of affairs.
[3 Maccabees] [3]:[9] He who knows all things won’t, they said, disregard so great a people.
[3 Maccabees] [3]:[10] Some of the neighbours, friends, and business associates of the Yehudim even called them secretly to an interview, pledged them their assistance, and promised to do their very utmost for them.
[3 Maccabees] [3]:[11] Now the king, elated with his prosperous fortune, and not regarding the superior power of God, but thinking to persevere in his present purpose, wrote the following letter to the prejudice of the Yehudim:
[3 Maccabees] [3]:[12] “King Ptolemaios (Ptolemy) Filopator, to the commanders and soldiers in Mitsrayim (Egypt), and in all places, health and happiness!
[3 Maccabees] [3]:[13] I’m doing well, and so, too, are my affairs.
[3 Maccabees] [3]:[14] Since our Asiatic campaign, the particulars of which you know, and which by the aid of the gods, not lightly given, and by our own vigour, has been brought to a successful conclusion according to our expectation,
[3 Maccabees] [3]:[15] we resolved, not with strength of spear, but with gentleness and much humanity, as it were to nurse the inhabitants of Coele-Syria and Foinikai, and to be their willing benefactors.
[3 Maccabees] [3]:[16] So, having bestowed considerable sums of money on the temples of the several cities, we proceeded even as far as Yerushalem (Jerusalem), and went up to honour the temple of these wretched beings who never cease from their folly.
[3 Maccabees] [3]:[17] To outward appearance they received us willingly, but belied that appearance by their actions. When we were eager to enter their temple, and to honour it with the most beautiful and exquisite gifts,
[3 Maccabees] [3]:[18] they were so carried away by their old arrogance as to forbid us the entrance, while we, out of our forbearance towards all men, refrained from exercising our power on them.
[3 Maccabees] [3]:[19] Thus, exhibiting their enmity against us, they alone among the nations lift up their heads against kings and benefactors, as men unwilling to submit to any reasonable thing.
[3 Maccabees] [3]:[20] We then, having endeavoured to make allowance for the madness of these people, and on our victorious return treating all people in Mitsrayim courteously, acted in a manner which was befitting.
[3 Maccabees] [3]:[21] Accordingly, bearing no ill will against their kinsmen, but rather remembering our connection with them, and the numerous matters with sincere heart from a remote period entrusted to them, we wished to venture a total alteration of their state, by giving them the rights of citizens of Alexandria, and to admit them to the eternal rites of our solemnities.
[3 Maccabees] [3]:[22] All this, however, they’ve taken in a very different spirit. With their innate malignity, they’ve spurned the fair offer, and constantly inclining to evil,
[3 Maccabees] [3]:[23] have rejected the inestimable rights. Not only so, but by using speech, and by refraining from speech, they abhor the few among them who are heartily disposed towards us, ever deeming that their infamous way of life will force us to do away with our reform.
[3 Maccabees] [3]:[24] Having then received certain proofs that these Yehudim (Jews) bear us every sort of ill will, we must look forward to the possibility of some sudden tumult among ourselves when these impious men may turn traitors and barbarous enemies.
[3 Maccabees] [3]:[25] Therefore, as soon as the contents of this letter become known to you, in that same hour we order those Yehudim who live among you, with wives and children, to be sent to us, vilified and abused, in chains of iron, to undergo a cruel and shameful death, suitable to enemies.
[3 Maccabees] [3]:[26] Because by the punishment of them in one body we perceive that we’ve found the only means of establishing our affairs for the future on a firm and satisfactory basis.
[3 Maccabees] [3]:[27] Anyone who protects a Yehudi (Jew), whether it be old man, child, or nursing baby, will with his whole house be tortured to death.
[3 Maccabees] [3]:[28] Anyone who informs against the Yehudim, besides receiving the property of the person charged, will be presented with two thousand drachmas from the royal treasury, will be made free, and will be crowned.
[3 Maccabees] [3]:[29] Whatever place shelters a Yehudi will be made unapproachable and will be put under the ban of fire, and be forever rendered useless to every living being for all time to come.”
[3 Maccabees] [3]:[30] The king’s letter was written in the above form.
[3 Maccabees] [4]:[1] Wherever this decree was received, the people kept up a revelry of joy and shouting, as if their long-pent-up, hardened hatred would now show itself openly.
[3 Maccabees] [4]:[2] The Yehudim suffered great throes of sorrow and wept much, while their hearts, all things around being lamentable, were set on fire as they bewailed the sudden destruction which was decreed against them.
[3 Maccabees] [4]:[3] What home, or city, or any inhabited place, or what streets were there, which their condition didn’t fill with wailing and lamentation?
[3 Maccabees] [4]:[4] They were sent out unanimously by the generals in various cities, with such stern and pitiless feeling that the exceptional nature of the infliction moved even some of their enemies. These, influenced by sentiments of common humanity, and reflecting on the uncertain issue of life, shed tears at their miserable expulsion.
[3 Maccabees] [4]:[5] A multitude of aged hoary-haired old men were driven along with halting bending feet, urged onward by the impulse of a violent, shameless force to quick speed.
[3 Maccabees] [4]:[6] Girls who’d entered the bridal chamber quite lately, to enjoy the partnership of marriage, exchanged pleasure for misery; and with dust scattered on their myrrh-anointed heads, were hurried along unveiled; and, in the middle of outlandish insults, set up with one accord a lamentable cry instead of the marriage hymn.
[3 Maccabees] [4]:[7] Bound and exposed to public gaze, they were hurried violently on board ship.
[3 Maccabees] [4]:[8] The husbands of these, in the prime of their youthful vigour, instead of crowns, wore ropes round their necks. Instead of feasting and youthful celebration, they spent the rest of their nuptial days in wailing, and saw only the grave at hand.
[3 Maccabees] [4]:[9] They were dragged along by unyielding chains, like wild animals. Of these, some had their necks thrust into the benches of the rowers, while the feet of others were enclosed in hard fetters.
[3 Maccabees] [4]:[10] The planks of the deck above them blocked out the light and shut out the day on every side, so that they might be treated like traitors during the whole voyage.
[3 Maccabees] [4]:[11] They were carried like this in this vessel, and at the end of it arrived at Schedia. The king had ordered them to be thrown into the vast hippodrome, which was built in front of the city. This place was well adapted by its situation to expose them to the gaze of all comers into the city, and of those who went from the city into the country. Thus they could hold no communication with his forces. They weren’t deemed worthy of any civilized accommodation.
[3 Maccabees] [4]:[12] When this was done, the king, hearing that their kindred in the city often went out and lamented the melancholy distress of these victims,
[3 Maccabees] [4]:[13] was full of rage, and commanded that they should be carefully subjected to the same—and not one bit milder—treatment.
[3 Maccabees] [4]:[14] The whole nation was now to be registered. Every individual was to be specified by name, not for that hard servitude of labour which we have a little before mentioned, but that he might expose them to the before-mentioned tortures; and finally, in the short space of a day, might exterminate them by his cruelties.
[3 Maccabees] [4]:[15] The registering of these men was carried on cruelly, zealously, assiduously, from the rising of the sun to its going down, and wasn’t brought to an end in forty days.
[3 Maccabees] [4]:[16] The king was filled with great and constant joy, and celebrated banquets before the temple idols. His erring heart, far from the truth, and his profane mouth gave glory to idols, deaf and incapable of speaking or aiding, and uttered unworthy speech against the Greatest God.
[3 Maccabees] [4]:[17] At the end of the above-mentioned interval of time, the registrars brought word to the king that the multitude of the Yehudim (Jews) was too great for registration,
[3 Maccabees] [4]:[18] since there were many still left in the land, of whom some were in inhabited houses, and others were scattered about in various places, so that all the commanders in Mitsrayim (Egypt) were insufficient for the work.
[3 Maccabees] [4]:[19] The king threatened them, and charged them with taking bribes, in order to contrive the escape of the Yehudim, but was clearly convinced of the truth of what had been said.
[3 Maccabees] [4]:[20] They said, and proved, that paper and pens had failed them for the carrying out of their purpose.
[3 Maccabees] [4]:[21] Now this was an active interference of the unconquerable Providence which assisted the Yehudim from heaven.
[3 Maccabees] [5]:[1] Then he called Hermon, who had charge of the elephants. Full of rage, altogether fixed in his furious design,
[3 Maccabees] [5]:[2] he commanded him, with a quantity of unmixed wine with handfuls of incense infused, to drug the elephants early on the following day. These five hundred elephants were, when infuriated by the copious drinks of frankincense, to be led up to the execution of death on the Yehudim.
[3 Maccabees] [5]:[3] The king, after issuing these orders, went to his feasting, and gathered together all those of his friends and of the army who hated the Yehudim the most.
[3 Maccabees] [5]:[4] The master of the elephants, Hermon, fulfilled his commission punctually.
[3 Maccabees] [5]:[5] The servants appointed for the purpose went out about evening and bound the hands of the miserable victims, and took other precautions for their security at night, thinking that the whole race would perish together.
[3 Maccabees] [5]:[6] The heathen believed the Yehudim to be destitute of all protection, for chains bound them.
[3 Maccabees] [5]:[7] They invoked the Almighty master, and ceaselessly implored with tears their merciful God and Father, Ruler of all, master of every power,
[3 Maccabees] [5]:[8] to overthrow the evil purpose which had gone out against them, and to deliver them by extraordinary manifestation from that death which was in store for them.
[3 Maccabees] [5]:[9] Their earnest entreaty went up to heaven.
[3 Maccabees] [5]:[10] Then Hermon, who’d filled his merciless elephants with copious drinks of mixed wine and frankincense, came early to the palace to report on these preparations.
[3 Maccabees] [5]:[11] He, however, who’s sent his good creature sleep from all time by night or by day thus gratifying whom he wills, diffused a portion of it now on the king.
[3 Maccabees] [5]:[12] By this sweet and profound influence of the master, he was held fast, and thus his unjust purpose was quite frustrated, and his unflinching resolve greatly falsified.
[3 Maccabees] [5]:[13] But the Yehudim, having escaped the hour which had been fixed, praised their holy God, and again prayed him who’s easily reconciled to display the power of his powerful hand to the arrogant Gentiles.
[3 Maccabees] [5]:[14] The middle of the tenth hour had nearly arrived, when the person who sent invitations, seeing the guests who were invited present, came and shook the king.
[3 Maccabees] [5]:[15] He gained his attention with difficulty, and hinting that the mealtime was getting past, talked the matter over with him.
[3 Maccabees] [5]:[16] The king listened to this, and then turning aside to his drinking, commanded the guests to sit down before him.
[3 Maccabees] [5]:[17] This done, he asked them to enjoy themselves, and to indulge in mirth at this somewhat late hour of the banquet.
[3 Maccabees] [5]:[18] Conversation grew on, and the king sent for Hermon, and enquired of him, with fierce denunciations, why the Yehudim had been allowed to outlive that day.
[3 Maccabees] [5]:[19] Hermon explained that he’d done his bidding over night; and in this he was confirmed by his friends.
[3 Maccabees] [5]:[20] The king, then, with a barbarity exceeding that of Falaris, said, “They might thank his sleep of that day. Lose no time, and get ready the elephants against tomorrow, as you did before, for the destruction of these accursed Yehudim.”
[3 Maccabees] [5]:[21] When the king said this, the company present were glad, and approved. Then each man went to his own home.
[3 Maccabees] [5]:[22] They didn’t employ the night in sleep, but in contriving cruel mockeries for those deemed miserable.
[3 Maccabees] [5]:[23] The morning cock had just crowed, and Hermon, having harnessed the brutes, was stimulating them in the great colonnade.
[3 Maccabees] [5]:[24] The city crowds were collected together to see the hideous spectacle, and waited impatiently for the dawn.
[3 Maccabees] [5]:[25] The Yehudim, breathless with momentary suspense, stretched out their hands and prayed the Greatest God, in mournful strains, again to help them speedily.
[3 Maccabees] [5]:[26] The sun’s rays weren’t yet shining and the king was waiting for his friends when Hermon came to him, calling him out, and saying that his desires could now be realised.
[3 Maccabees] [5]:[27] The king, receiving him, was astonished at his unusual invitation. Overwhelmed with a spirit of oblivion about everything, enquired about the object of this earnest preparation.
[3 Maccabees] [5]:[28] But this was the working of that Almighty God who’d made him forget all his purpose.
[3 Maccabees] [5]:[29] Hermon and all his friends pointed out the preparation of the animals. They’re ready, Oh king, according to your own strict injunction.
[3 Maccabees] [5]:[30] The king was filled with fierce anger at these words, for, by the Providence of God regarding these things, his mind had become entirely confused. He looked hard at Hermon, and threatened him as follows:
[3 Maccabees] [5]:[31] “Your parents, or your children, were they here, would have given a large meal to these wild animals, not these innocent Yehudim, who’ve loyally served me and my forefathers.
[3 Maccabees] [5]:[32] Had it not been for familiar friendship, and the claims of your office, your life should have gone for theirs.”
[3 Maccabees] [5]:[33] Hermon, being threatened in this unexpected and alarming manner, was troubled in his eyes, and his face fell.
[3 Maccabees] [5]:[34] The friends, too, stole out one by one, and dismissed the assembled multitudes to their respective occupations.
[3 Maccabees] [5]:[35] The Yehudim, having heard of these events, praised the glorious God and King of kings, because they’d obtained this help, too, from him.
[3 Maccabees] [5]:[36] Now the king arranged another banquet in the same way, and proclaimed an invitation to mirth.
[3 Maccabees] [5]:[37] He summoned Hermon to his presence, and said, with threats, “How often, Oh wretch, must I repeat my orders to you about these same persons?
[3 Maccabees] [5]:[38] Once more, arm the elephants for the extermination of the Yehudim tomorrow!”
[3 Maccabees] [5]:[39] His kinsmen, who were reclining with him, wondered at his instability, and thus expressed themselves:
[3 Maccabees] [5]:[40] “O king, how long do you test us, as of men bereft of reason? This is the third time that you’ve ordered their destruction. When the thing is to be done, you change your mind, and recall your instructions.
[3 Maccabees] [5]:[41] Because of this, the feeling of expectation causes tumult in the city. It swarms with factions, and is continually on the point of being plundered.”
[3 Maccabees] [5]:[42] The king, just like another Falaris, a prey to thoughtlessness, made no account of the changes which his own mind had undergone, issuing in the deliverance of the Yehudim. He swore a fruitless oath, and determined immediately to send them to hades, crushed by the knees and feet of the elephants.
[3 Maccabees] [5]:[43] He’d also invade Yehudah (Judea), level its towns with fire and the sword, destroy that temple which the heathen might not enter, and prevent sacrifices ever after being offered up there.
[3 Maccabees] [5]:[44] Joyfully his friends broke up, together with his kinsmen; and, trusting in his determination, arranged their forces in guard at the most convenient places of the city.
[3 Maccabees] [5]:[45] The master of the elephants urged the animals into an almost maniacal state, drenched them with incense and wine, and decked them with frightful devices.
[3 Maccabees] [5]:[46] About early morning, when the city was filled with an immense number of people at the hippodrome, he entered the palace and called the king to the business in hand.
[3 Maccabees] [5]:[47] The king’s heart teemed with impious rage; and he rushed forth with the mass, along with the elephants. With unsoftened feelings and pitiless eyes, he longed to gaze at the hard and wretched doom of the previously mentioned Yehudim.
[3 Maccabees] [5]:[48] But the Yehudim, when the elephants went out at the gate, followed by the armed force. When they saw the dust raised by the throng, and heard the loud cries of the crowd,
[3 Maccabees] [5]:[49] thought that they’d come to the last moment of their lives, to the end of what they’d tremblingly expected. They gave way, therefore, to lamentations and moans. They kissed each other. Those nearest of kin to each other hung around one another’s necks—fathers hugging their sons and mothers their daughters. Other women held their infants to their breasts, which drew what seemed their last milk.
[3 Maccabees] [5]:[50] Nevertheless, when they reflected on the help previously granted them from heaven, they prostrated themselves with one accord, removed even the sucking children from the breasts, and
[3 Maccabees] [5]:[51] sent up a very great cry asking the master of all power to reveal himself, and have mercy on those who now lay at the gates of hades.
[3 Maccabees] [6]:[1] Then Eleazar, an illustrious priest of the country, who’d attained to length of days, and whose life had been adorned with virtue, caused the elders who were around him to cease to cry out to the holy God, and prayed this:
[3 Maccabees] [6]:[2] “O king, mighty in power, most high, Almighty God, who regulates the whole creation with your tender mercy,
[3 Maccabees] [6]:[3] look at the seed of Avraham, at the children of the sanctified Ya’akov (Jacob), your sanctified inheritance, Oh Father, now being wrongfully destroyed as foreigners in a foreign land.
[3 Maccabees] [6]:[4] You destroyed Par’oh (Pharaoh) with his army of chariots when that lord of this same Mitsrayim (Egypt) was uplifted with lawless daring and loud-sounding tongue. Shedding the beams of your mercy on the race of Yisrael (Israel), you overwhelmed him and his proud army.
[3 Maccabees] [6]:[5] When Sanheriv (Sennacherib), the grievous king of the Assyrians, exulting in his countless army, had subdued the whole land with his spear and was lifting himself against your holy city with boastings grievous to be endured, you, Oh master, demolished him and displayed your might to many nations.
[3 Maccabees] [6]:[6] When the three friends in the land of Bavel (Babylon) of their own will exposed their lives to the fire rather than serve vain things, you sent a moist coolness through the fiery furnace, and brought the fire on all their adversaries.
[3 Maccabees] [6]:[7] It was you who, when Daniyel was hurled, through slander and envy, as a prey to lions down below, brought him back again unharmed to light.
[3 Maccabees] [6]:[8] When Yonah (Jonah) was pining away in the belly of the sea-born monster, you looked at him, Oh Father, and recovered him to the sight of his own.
[3 Maccabees] [6]:[9] Now, you who hate insolence, you who abound in mercy, you who are the protector of all things, appear quickly to those of the race of Yisrael, who are insulted by abhorred, lawless gentiles.
[3 Maccabees] [6]:[10] If our life during our exile has been stained with iniquity, deliver us from the hand of the enemy, and destroy us, Oh master, by the death which you prefer.
[3 Maccabees] [6]:[11] Don’t let the vain-minded congratulate vain idols at the destruction of your beloved, saying, ‘Their god didn’t deliver them.’
[3 Maccabees] [6]:[12] You who are All-powerful and Almighty, Oh Eternal One, look! Have mercy on us who are being withdrawn from life, like traitors, by the unreasoning insolence of lawless men.
[3 Maccabees] [6]:[13] Let the heathen cower before your invincible might today, Oh glorious One, who have all power to save the race of Ya’akov (Jacob).
[3 Maccabees] [6]:[14] The whole band of infants and their parents ask you with tears.
[3 Maccabees] [6]:[15] Let it be shown to all the nations that you’re with us, Oh master, and haven’t turned your face away from us, but as you said that you wouldn’t forget them even in the land of their enemies, so fulfil this saying, Oh master.”
[3 Maccabees] [6]:[16] Now, at the time that Eleazar had ended his prayer, the king came along to the hippodrome with the wild animals, and with his tumultuous power.
[3 Maccabees] [6]:[17] When the Yehudim saw this, they uttered a loud cry to heaven so that the adjacent valleys resounded and caused an irrepressible lamentation throughout the army.
[3 Maccabees] [6]:[18] Then the all-glorious, all-powerful, and true God, displayed his holy face, and opened the gates of heaven, from which two angels, dreadful of form, came down and were visible to all but the Yehudim.
[3 Maccabees] [6]:[19] They stood opposite, and filled the enemies’ army with confusion and cowardice, and bound them with immoveable shackles.
[3 Maccabees] [6]:[20] A cold shudder came over the person of the king, and oblivion paralysed the vehemence of his spirit.
[3 Maccabees] [6]:[21] They turned back the animals on the armed forces who followed them; and the animals trampled them and destroyed them.
[3 Maccabees] [6]:[22] The king’s anger was converted into compassion; and he wept at the things he’d devised.
[3 Maccabees] [6]:[23] Because when he heard the cry, and saw them all on the verge of destruction, with tears he angrily threatened his friends, saying,
[3 Maccabees] [6]:[24] “You’ve governed badly, and have exceeded tyrants in cruelty. You’ve laboured to deprive me, your benefactor, at once of my dominion and my life, by secretly devising measures injurious to the kingdom.
[3 Maccabees] [6]:[25] Who’s gathered here, unreasonably removing each from his home, those who, in fidelity to us, had held the fortresses of the country?
[3 Maccabees] [6]:[26] Who’s consigned to unmerited punishments those who in good will towards us from the beginning have in all things surpassed all nations, and who often have engaged in the most dangerous undertakings?
[3 Maccabees] [6]:[27] Loose, loose the unjust bonds! Send them to their homes in peace, begging pardon for what’s been done.
[3 Maccabees] [6]:[28] Release the sons of the almighty living god of heaven, who from our ancestors’ times until now has granted a glorious and uninterrupted prosperity to our affairs.”
[3 Maccabees] [6]:[29] He said these things, and they, released the same moment, having now escaped death, praised God their holy Saviour.
[3 Maccabees] [6]:[30] The king then departed to the city, and called his financier to himself, and asked him provide a seven days’ quantity of wine and other materials for feasting for the Yehudim (Jews). He decided that they should keep a cheerful festival of deliverance in the very place in which they expected to meet with their destruction.
[3 Maccabees] [6]:[31] Then they who were before despised and near to hades, yes, rather advanced into it, partook of the cup of salvation, instead of a grievous and lamentable death. Full of exultation, they apportioned the place intended for their fall and burial into banqueting booths.
[3 Maccabees] [6]:[32] Ceasing their miserable strain of woe, they took up the subject of their fatherland, singing in praise to God their wonder-working Saviour. All groans and all wailing were laid aside. They formed dances as a sign of peaceful joy.
[3 Maccabees] [6]:[33] So the king also collected a number of guests for the occasion, and returned unceasing thanks with much magnificence for the unexpected deliverance afforded him.
[3 Maccabees] [6]:[34] Those who’d marked them out as for death and for carrion, and had registered them with joy, howled aloud, and were clothed with shame, and had the fire of their rage ingloriously put out.
[3 Maccabees] [6]:[35] But the Yehudim, as we just said, instituted a dance, and then gave themselves up to feasting, glad thanksgiving, and psalms.
[3 Maccabees] [6]:[36] They made a public ordinance to commemorate these things for generations to come, as long as they should be sojourners. They thus established these days as days of mirth, not for the purpose of drinking or luxury, but because God had saved them.
[3 Maccabees] [6]:[37] They requested the king to send them back to their homes.
[3 Maccabees] [6]:[38] They were being enrolled from the twenty-fifth of Pachon to the fourth of Epifi, a period of forty days. The measures taken for their destruction lasted from the fifth of Epifi till the seventh, that is, three days.
[3 Maccabees] [6]:[39] The Ruler over all during this time manifested his mercy gloriously, and delivered them all together unharmed.
[3 Maccabees] [6]:[40] They feasted on the king’s provision up to the fourteenth day, then asked to be sent away.
[3 Maccabees] [6]:[41] The king commended them, and wrote the following letter, of magnanimous import for them, to the commanders of every city:
[3 Maccabees] [7]:[1] “King Ptolemaios (Ptolemy) Filopator to the commanders throughout Mitsrayim (Egypt), and to all who are set over affairs, joy and strength.
[3 Maccabees] [7]:[2] We, too, and our children are well. God has directed our affairs as we wish.
[3 Maccabees] [7]:[3] Certain of our friends out of malice vehemently urged us to punish the Yehudim (Jews) of our realm in a body, with the infliction of a monstrous punishment.
[3 Maccabees] [7]:[4] They pretended that our affairs would never be in a good state till this took place. Such, they said, was the hatred borne by the Yehudim to all other people.
[3 Maccabees] [7]:[5] They brought them fettered in grievous chains as slaves, no, as traitors. Without enquiry or examination they endeavoured to annihilate them. They buckled themselves with a savage cruelty, worse than Skuthais custom.
[3 Maccabees] [7]:[6] Because this cause we severely threatened them; yet, with the clemency which we usually extend to all men, we at length permitted them to live. Finding that the god of heaven threw a shield of protection over the Yehudim so as to preserve them, and that he fought for them as a father always fights for his sons,
[3 Maccabees] [7]:[7] and taking into consideration their constancy and fidelity towards us and towards our ancestors, we have, as we ought, acquitted them of every sort of charge.
[3 Maccabees] [7]:[8] We’ve dismissed them to their several homes, telling all men everywhere to do them no wrong, or unrighteously revile them about the past.
[3 Maccabees] [7]:[9] Because know this, that should we conceive any evil design, or in any way aggrieve them, we’ll ever have as our adversary, not man, but the highest God, the ruler of all might. From Him there’ll be no escape, as the avenger of such actions. Farewell.”
[3 Maccabees] [7]:[10] When they’d received this letter, they didn’t hurry to depart immediately. They petitioned the king to be allowed to inflict fitting punishment on those of their race who’d willingly transgressed the holy god, and God’s law.
[3 Maccabees] [7]:[11] They alleged that men who had for their bellies’ sake transgressed the ordinances of God, would never be faithful to the interests of the king.
[3 Maccabees] [7]:[12] The king admitted the truth of this reasoning, and commended them. Full power was given them, without warrant or special commission, to destroy those who’d transgressed God’s law boldly in every part of the king’s dominions.
[3 Maccabees] [7]:[13] Their priests, then, as it was appropriate, saluted him with good wishes, and all the people echoed with the “Hallelujah!” Then they joyfully departed.
[3 Maccabees] [7]:[14] Then they punished and shamefully destroyed every polluted Yehudi (Jew) that fell in their way,
[3 Maccabees] [7]:[15] slaying this way, in that day, more than three hundred men, and esteeming this destruction of the wicked a season of joy.
[3 Maccabees] [7]:[16] They themselves having held closely to their god to death, and having enjoyed a full deliverance, departed from the city garlanded with sweet-flowered wreaths of every kind. Uttering exclamations of joy, with songs of praise, and melodious hymns, they thanked the god of their fathers, the eternal Saviour of Yisrael (Israel).
[3 Maccabees] [7]:[17] Having arrived at Ptolemais, called from the specialty of that district “Rose-bearing”, where the fleet, in accordance with the general wish, waited for them seven days,
[3 Maccabees] [7]:[18] they partook of a banquet of deliverance, for the king generously granted them all the means of securing a return home.
[3 Maccabees] [7]:[19] They were accordingly brought back in peace, while they gave utterance to appropriate thanks; and they determined to observe these days during their sojourn as days of joyfulness.
[3 Maccabees] [7]:[20] These they registered as sacred on a pillar, when they’d dedicated the place of their festivity to be one of prayer. They departed unharmed, free, abundant in joy, preserved by the king’s command, by land, by sea, and by river, each to his own home.
[3 Maccabees] [7]:[21] They had more weight than before among their enemies, and were honoured and feared. No one in any way robbed them of their goods.
[3 Maccabees] [7]:[22] Every man received back his own, according to inventory, those who’d obtained their goods, giving them up with the greatest terror. Because the greatest God made perfect wonders for their salvation.
[3 Maccabees] [7]:[23] Blessed be the Redeemer of Yisrael forever! Amen.
[4 Maccabees] [1]:[1] As I’m going to demonstrate a most philosophical proposition, namely, that religious reasoning is absolute master of the emotions. I’d willingly advise you to give the utmost heed to philosophy.
[4 Maccabees] [1]:[2] Because reason is necessary to everyone as a step to science. In addition, it embraces the praise of self-control, the highest virtue.
[4 Maccabees] [1]:[3] If, then, reasoning appears to hold the mastery over the emotions which stand in the way of temperance, such as gluttony and lust,
[4 Maccabees] [1]:[4] it surely also and manifestly rules over the affections which are contrary to justice, such as malice, and of those which are hindrances to courage, such as anger, pain, and fear.
[4 Maccabees] [1]:[5] Perhaps some may ask, “How is it, then, that reasoning, if it rules the emotions, isn’t also master of forgetfulness and ignorance?” They attempt a ridiculous argument.
[4 Maccabees] [1]:[6] Because reasoning doesn’t rule over its own emotions, but over those that are contrary to justice, courage, temperance, and self-control; and yet over these, so as to withstand, without destroying them.
[4 Maccabees] [1]:[7] I might prove to you from many other considerations, that religious reasoning is sole master of the emotions;
[4 Maccabees] [1]:[8] but I’ll prove it with the greatest force from the fortitude of Eleazar, and seven kindred, and their mother, who suffered death in defence of virtue.
[4 Maccabees] [1]:[9] Because all these, treating pains with contempt even to death, by this contempt, demonstrated that reasoning has command over the emotions.
[4 Maccabees] [1]:[10] Because their virtues, then, it’s right that I should commend those men who died with their mother at this time on behalf of nobility and goodness; and for their honours, I may count them blessed.
[4 Maccabees] [1]:[11] Because they, winning admiration not only from men in general, but even from the persecutors, for their courage and endurance, became the means of the destruction of the tyranny against their nation, having conquered the tyrant by their endurance, so that by them their country was purified.
[4 Maccabees] [1]:[12] But we may now at once enter on the question, having commenced, as is our custom, with laying down the doctrine, and so proceed to the account of these people, giving glory to the all-wise God.
[4 Maccabees] [1]:[13] Therefore the question whether reasoning is absolute master of the emotions.
[4 Maccabees] [1]:[14] Let’s determine, then, what reasoning is and what emotion is, and how many forms of emotion there are, and whether reasoning rules over all of these.
[4 Maccabees] [1]:[15] Reasoning is intellect accompanied by a life of righteousness, putting foremost the consideration of wisdom.
[4 Maccabees] [1]:[16] Wisdom is a knowledge of divine and human things, and of their causes.
[4 Maccabees] [1]:[17] This is contained in the education of the law, by means of which we learn divine things reverently and human things profitably.
[4 Maccabees] [1]:[18] The forms of wisdom are self-control, justice, courage, and temperance.
[4 Maccabees] [1]:[19] The leading one of these is self-control, by whose means, indeed, it’s that reasoning rules over the emotions.
[4 Maccabees] [1]:[20] Of the emotions, pleasure and pain are the two most comprehensive; and they also by nature refer to the soul.
[4 Maccabees] [1]:[21] There are many attendant affections surrounding pleasure and pain.
[4 Maccabees] [1]:[22] Before pleasure is lust; and after pleasure, joy.
[4 Maccabees] [1]:[23] Before pain is fear; and after pain is sorrow.
[4 Maccabees] [1]:[24] Anger is an affection, common to pleasure and to pain, if any one will pay attention when it comes on him.
[4 Maccabees] [1]:[25] There exists in pleasure a malicious disposition, which is the most complex of all the affections.
[4 Maccabees] [1]:[26] In the soul, it’s arrogance, love of money, thirst for honour, contention, faithlessness, and the evil eye.
[4 Maccabees] [1]:[27] In the body, it’s greediness, indiscriminate eating, and solitary gluttony.
[4 Maccabees] [1]:[28] As pleasure and pain are, therefore, two growths out of the body and the soul, so there are many offshoots of these emotions.
[4 Maccabees] [1]:[29] Reasoning, the universal farmer, purging and pruning each of these, tying up, watering, and transplanting, in every way improves the materials of the morals and affections.
[4 Maccabees] [1]:[30] Because reasoning is the leader of the virtues, but it’s the sole ruler of the emotions. Observe then first, through the very things which stand in the way of temperance, that reasoning is absolute ruler of the emotions.
[4 Maccabees] [1]:[31] Now temperance consists of a command over the lusts.
[4 Maccabees] [1]:[32] But of the lusts, some belong to the soul and others to the body. Reasoning appears to rule over both.
[4 Maccabees] [1]:[33] Otherwise, how is it that when urged on to forbidden meats, we reject the gratification which would come from them? Isn’t it because reasoning is able to command the appetites? I believe so.
[4 Maccabees] [1]:[34] Hence it is, then, that when craving seafood, birds, four-footed animals, and all kinds of food which are forbidden to us by the law, we withhold ourselves through the mastery of reasoning.
[4 Maccabees] [1]:[35] Because the affections of our appetites are resisted by the temperate understanding, and bent back again, and all the impulses of the body are reined in by reasoning.
[4 Maccabees] [2]:[1] Is it any wonder? If the lusts of the soul, after participation with what’s beautiful, are frustrated,
[4 Maccabees] [2]:[2] on this ground, therefore, the temperate Yosef (Joseph) is praised in that by reasoning, he subdued, on reflection, the indulgence of the senses.
[4 Maccabees] [2]:[3] Because, although young, and ripe for sexual intercourse, he nullified by reasoning the stimulus of his emotions.
[4 Maccabees] [2]:[4] It isn’t merely the stimulus of sensual indulgence, but that of every desire, that reasoning is able to master.
[4 Maccabees] [2]:[5] For example, the law says, “You mustn’t desire your neighbour’s wife, nor anything that belongs to your neighbour.”
[4 Maccabees] [2]:[6] Now, then, since it’s the law which has forbidden us to desire, I’ll much the more easily persuade you, that reasoning is able to govern our lusts, just as it does the affections which are impediments to justice.
[4 Maccabees] [2]:[7] Since in what way is a solitary eater, a glutton, and a drunkard reclaimed, unless it’s clear that reasoning is lord of the emotions?
[4 Maccabees] [2]:[8] Therefore, a man who regulates his course by the law, even if he’s a lover of money, immediately puts pressure on his own disposition by lending to the needy without interest, and cancelling the debt on the seventh year.
[4 Maccabees] [2]:[9] If a man is greedy, he’s ruled by the law acting through reasoning, so that he doesn’t glean his harvest crops or vintage. In reference to other points we may perceive that it’s reasoning that conquers his emotions.
[4 Maccabees] [2]:[10] Because the law conquers even affection towards parents, not surrendering virtue on their account.
[4 Maccabees] [2]:[11] It prevails over love for one’s wife, rebuking her when she breaks the law.
[4 Maccabees] [2]:[12] It lords it over the love of parents towards their children, for they punish them for vice. It domineers over the intimacy of friends, reproving them when wicked.
[4 Maccabees] [2]:[13] Don’t think it’s a strange assertion that reasoning can on behalf of the law conquer even enmity.
[4 Maccabees] [2]:[14] It doesn’t allow cutting down the fruit trees of an enemy, but preserves them from the destroyers, and collects their fallen ruins.
[4 Maccabees] [2]:[15] Reason appears to be master of the more violent emotions, like love of empire, empty boasting, and slander.
[4 Maccabees] [2]:[16] Because the temperate understanding repels all these malignant emotions, as it does anger; for it masters even this.
[4 Maccabees] [2]:[17] Thus Mosheh (Moses), when angered against Datan and Aviram, did nothing to them in anger, but regulated his anger by reasoning.
[4 Maccabees] [2]:[18] Because the temperate mind is able, as I said, to be superior to the emotions, and to correct some and destroy others.
[4 Maccabees] [2]:[19] Because why else did our most wise father Ya’akov (Jacob) blame Shim’on (Simeon) and Levi for having irrationally slain the whole race of the Shechemites, saying, “Cursed be their anger!”?
