[Acts] [11]:[12] and the spirit told me to go with them without questioning anything they said. These six other believers went with me, and we arrived at the house of the man who had sent the three.
[Acts] [11]:[13] He told us how he’d seen one of God’s messengers standing there in his house and who’d told him, ‘Send someone to Yafo to fetch Shim’on (Simon), the one called Kefa,
[Acts] [11]:[14] and he will explain to you how you and all your household can be saved.’
[Acts] [11]:[15] Then when I started speaking to them, the holy spirit came down on them just like it had happened to us previously.
[Acts] [11]:[16] That reminded me of the words of the master when he told us, ‘Yohan (John; Grk. Yoannes) immersed people in water, but you all will be immersed in the holy spirit.
[Acts] [11]:[17] Therefore if God gave the same gift to them that he’d given to us when we’d believed in the master Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) the messiah, what authority did I have to contradict God?’ ”
[Acts] [11]:[18] When the group heard all this, they had no objections and they praised God, saying, “It seems that God has also allowed the pagans to repent and live.”
[Acts] [11]:[19] Over time, due to the persecution that began with Stefanos’s killing, the ones who had moved away went as far as Foinikai, Kupros (Cyprus), and Antiokeia, but they only shared Yeshua’s (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) teaching with other Yehudim (Jews).
[Acts] [11]:[20] However, some of the believers were from Kupros and Kurainai (Cyrene), and when they got to Antiokeia they proclaimed the good news from the master Yeshua to the Hellains (Greeks).
[Acts] [11]:[21] Yahweh caused their efforts to prosper, so a large number of Hellains believed and decided to follow the master.
[Acts] [11]:[22] News about this reached the assembly in Yerushalem (Jerusalem), so they sent Barnabas to Antiokeia.
[Acts] [11]:[23] When he arrived and saw how God’s grace was spreading, he was elated and encouraged them all to earnestly continue to follow the master.
[Acts] [11]:[24] Barnabas was good man and full of the holy spirit and full of faith in God, and a large number of people decided to follow Yeshua.
[Acts] [11]:[25] So Barnabas went to Tarsos to look for Sha’ul (Saul; Grk. Saulos/Saul),
[Acts] [11]:[26] and when he found him, he brought him back to Antiokeia. Then for a whole year they met with the assembly and regularly taught a large crowd. It was there in Antiokeia that the believers were first called Christians.
[Acts] [11]:[27] In those days, some prophets from Yerushalem went to Antiokeia,
[Acts] [11]:[28] and one of them named Agabos when he was prompted by the spirit, stood up and predicted that the world would experience a severe famine (and this happened later during the reign of Klaudios).
[Acts] [11]:[29] The believers decided to send assistance to their fellow believers who lived in Yehudah (Judea)—each one according to his means—
[Acts] [11]:[30] and so they did, sending their contributions with Barnabas and Sha’ul to take to the elders.
[Acts] [12]:[1] Around that time, King Herodes (Herod) Agrippas used his power to mistreat some of the believers from the assembly,
[Acts] [12]:[2] and he had Ya’akov (James; Grk. Yakobos), the brother of Yohan (John; Grk. Yoannes), executed by the sword.
[Acts] [12]:[3] Then when he saw that it pleased the Jewish religious leaders, he went on to seize Kefa (Peter; Grk. Petros) during the Flat Bread Celebration.
[Acts] [12]:[4] After being arrested, Kefa was put in prison where he was guarded by four squads of four soldiers each. After the Passover Feast, Herodes planned to display Kefa to the people,
[Acts] [12]:[5] but while he was being held in prison, those in the assembly were earnestly asking God to help him.
[Acts] [12]:[6] Herodes (Herod) planned to send for Kefa (Peter; Grk. Petros) later that evening, but meanwhile Kefa had fallen asleep chained with two chains between two soldiers. There were also prison guards at the door
[Acts] [12]:[7] but one of Yahweh’s messengers suddenly appeared standing by Kefa and light radiated through the prison cell. The messenger poked Kefa in the side to wake him up, saying, “Quickly, get up!” The chains fell off his wrists
[Acts] [12]:[8] and the messenger said, “Get dressed and put on your sandals,” so he did. Then the messenger said, “Now put on your coat and follow me.”
[Acts] [12]:[9] So Kefa followed the messenger out of the cell, not really knowing if it was real or if he was still dreaming.
[Acts] [12]:[10] They went past the first guard and then the second, and then came to the iron gate which led out of the prison into the city. The gate opened by itself and they went out onto the street, then at the end of the street the messenger suddenly left him.
[Acts] [12]:[11] By now Kefa was fully awake and said to himself, “Now I know that the master really did send his messenger to rescue me from Herodes and from the plans of the Jewish leaders.”
[Acts] [12]:[12] Now that he realised this, he went to Miryam’s (Grk. Maria/Mariam) house (the mother of Yohan (John; Grk. Yoannes) Markos / John Mark) where many believers had met to pray.
[Acts] [12]:[13] He knocked at the door in the fence and a servant girl named Rode came out to see who it was.
[Acts] [12]:[14] But when she recognised Kefa’s voice, she was so excited that she forgot about opening the door, but ran back inside to tell everyone that Kefa was standing out there.
[Acts] [12]:[15] They told her that she must be raving mad, but she insisted it was true, but they said that it must be his messenger.
[Acts] [12]:[16] Meanwhile Kefa continued knocking, and when they eventually opened the outer door, they saw that it was him and they were amazed.
[Acts] [12]:[17] But Kefa signalled them with his hand to be quiet, and then he explained how the master had led him out of the prison, and instructed them, “Tell this to Ya’akov (James; Grk. Yakobos) and the brothers.” Then he left and went off to another place.
[Acts] [12]:[18] Once daylight came, there was pandemonium among the soldiers in the prison as they tried to figure out what had happened to Kefa.
[Acts] [12]:[19] Then when King Herodes sent for Kefa and he wasn’t there, the prison guards were interrogated and then taken away to be executed. After that, Herodes (Herod) left Yehudah (Judea) and went up to Kaisareia to stay.
[Acts] [12]:[20] Now King Herodes (Herod) was disputing with the people of Tsor (Tyre) and Tsidon (Sidon), and so they got together and persuaded Blastos, a close personal servant of the king, to be their spokesman in asking for peace because they were dependent on food from the king’s provinces.
[Acts] [12]:[21] On the agreed day, Herodes, dressed in his royal garments and seated on his throne, started to address them.
[Acts] [12]:[22] The crowd shouted out, “This is the voice of a god, not of a man.”
[Acts] [12]:[23] Because he didn’t attribute the honour to God, one of the Yahweh’s messengers immediately struck him down and he stopped breathing as a result of a worm infestation.
[Acts] [12]:[24] Meanwhile God’s message continued to spread and multiply.
[Acts] [12]:[25] By then Barnabas and Sha’ul (Saul; Grk. Saulos/Saul) had completed their ministry and returned to Yerushalem (Jerusalem) taking Yohan (John; Grk. Yoannes) Markos (Yohan Markos) along with them.
[Acts] [13]:[1] In the assembly at Antiokeia there were some prophets and teachers: Barnabas, Shim’on (Simeon; Grk. Sumeon) (called Niger), Lukios from Kurainai (Cyrene), Menahem (Grk. Manaen) (who grew up with Herodes (Herod) the tetrarch), and Sha’ul (Saul; Grk. Saulos/Saul).
[Acts] [13]:[2] One day when they were ministering to the master and fasting, the holy spirit said, Appoint Barnabas and Sha’ul to serve me and do the work that I have called them to.”
[Acts] [13]:[3] So they fasted and prayed and placed their hands on the two, and then sent them off.
[Acts] [13]:[4] So Barnabas and Sha’ul (Saul; Grk. Saulos/Saul), having been sent by the holy spirit, went down to Seleukeia at the coast and from there sailed on to the island of Kupros (Cyprus).
[Acts] [13]:[5] When they arrived in the town of Salamis, they proclaimed God’s message in the Jewish meeting halls. They also had Yohan (John; Grk. Yoannes) as their assistant.
[Acts] [13]:[6] They travelled around the island and when they got to Pafos, they met a Jewish man named Bar-Yeshua (Grk. Bariesus). He was a sorcerer and false prophet
[Acts] [13]:[7] who was with Sergios Paulos the proconsul, an intelligent man. Sergios sent for Barnabas and Sha’ul (Saul; Grk. Saulos/Saul) because he wanted to hear God’s message from them,
[Acts] [13]:[8] but the sorcerer opposed them and tried to prevent Sergios from believing.
[Acts] [13]:[9] So then Sha’ul (the Romaios form of his name was Paulos), filled with the holy spirit looked intently at Bar-Yeshua
[Acts] [13]:[10] and said, “You’re full of all kinds of deceit and fraud you child of the devil. Will you never stop twisting the truth about following the master?
[Acts] [13]:[11] Well, look here! Yahweh will extend his power against you and blind you—you’ll go a season without seeing the sun!” And immediately he could only see fog and darkness, and needed someone to guide him around by the hand.
[Acts] [13]:[12] The proconsul believed when he saw what had happened, and was amazed as he learnt about the master.
[Acts] [13]:[13] After that, Paulos and his companions sailed from Pafos to Pergai in Pamfulia, but Yohan (John; Grk. Yoannes) Markos (John Mark) left them and returned to Yerushalem (Jerusalem).
[Acts] [13]:[14] Paulos and his companions, went on from Pergai to Pisidian Antiokeia, where they entered the Jewish meeting hall on the Rest Day and sat down with the congregation.
[Acts] [13]:[15] After the readings from the Law and from the Prophets, the leaders sent a messenger over to them to ask, “Men, brothers, if you bring any message of encouragement for the congregation, please share it.”
[Acts] [13]:[16] So Paulos stood up and, motioning with his hand, started speaking, “Fellow Israelis and everyone who reveres God, listen to me.
[Acts] [13]:[17] The God of the people of Yisrael (Israel) chose our ancestors and helped the people to prosper when they were staying in Mitsrayim (Egypt). Then later he showed his power as he led them out
[Acts] [13]:[18] and endured them in the wilderness for around forty years.
[Acts] [13]:[19] Then having overthrown seven nations in Kena’an (Canaan), he passed on that land as an inheritance
[Acts] [13]:[20] after around 450 years. “Then he gave them judges through until the time of the prophet Shmuel (Samuel)
[Acts] [13]:[21] when they requested a king, and God gave them Sha’ul (Saul; Grk. Saulos/Saul), the son of Kish from the tribe of Benyamin to reign for forty years.
[Acts] [13]:[22] After Sha’ul was removed, God chose David to be their king—the man of whom he said, ‘I found David the son of Yishay (Jesse), a man who wants to obey me and do everything I ask.’
[Acts] [13]:[23] Then eventually a descendant of David arrived in Yisrael as promised—the saviour Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus).
[Acts] [13]:[24] Before he arrived Yohan-the-immerser had publicly preached to all the people of Yisrael about being immersed as a sign of repentance.
[Acts] [13]:[25] As Yohan’s (John; Grk. Yoannes) ministry was nearing an end, he asked, ‘Who do you suspect I am? I’m not the messiah, but he will come after me, and I’m not even worthy to undo his sandals.’
[Acts] [13]:[26] “Men, brothers, descendants of Avraham and others here who revere God, the teaching about this salvation has been sent to us.
[Acts] [13]:[27] The people of Yerushalem (Jerusalem) and their religious leaders didn’t recognise this Yeshua, but by their judgement of him they fulfilled the words of the prophets that are read every Rest Day.
[Acts] [13]:[28] Despite not finding even one charge against him worthy of death, they requested Pilatos (Pilate) to execute him
[Acts] [13]:[29] and when they’d done all the things that the prophets had written about him, they took his body down from the post he’d been nailed to and placed it in a burial chamber.
[Acts] [13]:[30] But God brought him back to life
[Acts] [13]:[31] and his followers who had come to Yerushalem from Galil saw him for several days and now testify about this to the people.
[Acts] [13]:[32] So now we’re preaching this good message to you that what God promised to our ancestors
[Acts] [13]:[33] has now been fulfilled for our descendants, now that God brought Yeshua back to life just like it’s written in the second psalm: ‘You are my son; today I have borne you.’
[Acts] [13]:[34] God brought him back to life, and he’s never going to return to the grave to decay. As God said, ‘I will give David’s faithful devout things??? to you all.’
[Acts] [13]:[35] So in another psalm God said, ‘You won’t allow your devout one to experience decay.’
[Acts] [13]:[36] This can’t be David, because after he’d served his own generation as God led him, he indeed died and was buried with his ancestors and his body decayed.
[Acts] [13]:[37] On the contrary, the one who God raised from the dead never experienced decay.
[Acts] [13]:[38] So brothers, let it be known to you all that your sins can now be forgiven through this Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus)—the law of Mosheh (Moses) was never able to offer you that.
[Acts] [13]:[39] Everyone who puts their trust in Yeshua is able to receive a clean record.
[Acts] [13]:[40] But keep your eyes open in case something else the prophets wrote might come true:
[Acts] [13]:[41] ‘Watch you scoffers, and be amazed and die because I’m doing something special during your time. Even if someone described it clearly to you all, you still might not believe it.’ ”
[Acts] [13]:[42] As they left the meeting hall after the service, the people invited them to speak again the following Rest Day.
[Acts] [13]:[43] But when they started walking away, many people followed after Paulos and Barnabas, who then addressed them and encouraged them to continue trusting in God’s grace.
[Acts] [13]:[44] So on the following Rest Day, nearly everyone in the city had gathered there to hear the message from God.
[Acts] [13]:[45] But the Jewish religious leaders became very jealous when they saw the crowds and claimed that Paulos’s words had slandered God.
[Acts] [13]:[46] But Paulos and Barnabas responded boldly, “It was necessary for God’s message to be explained in the meeting hall to all of the Yehudim (Jews) first. But since you are rejecting that teaching, you are all judging yourselves to be unworthy of living forever, so instead, we will now share it with the non-Jews.
[Acts] [13]:[47] Because this is what the master commanded us: ‘I have chosen you to be a light for the pagans; You will take salvation to the end of the earth.’
[Acts] [13]:[48] When the non-Jews heard that, they were very happy and were praising the master’s message, and as many as were appointed to receive eternal life believed it.
[Acts] [13]:[49] So from there, the master’s message spread throughout the entire region.
[Acts] [13]:[50] But the Jewish religious leaders incited some prominent women from the meeting halls and some from the local city government, and they then stirred up persecution against Paulos and Barnabas and had them expelled out of their region.
[Acts] [13]:[51] So Paulos and Barnabas just left that place to face their own consequences, and continued on to Ikonion.
[Acts] [13]:[52] Meanwhile the believers back in Pisidian Antiokeia were full of happiness and of the holy spirit.
[Acts] [14]:[1] A similar thing happened in Ikonion. Paulos and Barnabas went into the Jewish meeting hall and spoke in such a way that a lot of both Yehudim (Jews) and Hellains (Greeks) believed.
[Acts] [14]:[2] But those Yehudim who didn’t believe got the non-Jews emotionally stirred up to oppose the believers.
[Acts] [14]:[3] So Paulos and Barnabas ended up staying there for quite a while, and as they spoke boldly for the master, he himself confirmed his grace by enabling the two of them to be able to do miracles and amazing things.
[Acts] [14]:[4] Nevertheless, the people of the city were divided—some agreeing with the strict Yehudim, and others supporting the missionaries.
[Acts] [14]:[5] At one point, both the non-Jews and the strict Yehudim and their leaders got worked up enough to come in order to attack them and throw rocks to kill them.
[Acts] [14]:[6] However, Paulos and Barnabas found out about it and escaped to the Lukaonios cities of Lustra and Derbai and the surrounding region
[Acts] [14]:[7] and preached the good message there.
[Acts] [14]:[8] In Lustra there was a man sitting there who had been unable to use his legs since birth.
[Acts] [14]:[9] He was listening to Paulos speaking, when Paulos looked straight at him and realised that the man had the faith to be healed.
[Acts] [14]:[10] So in a loud voice, Paulos said, “Stand upright on your feet.” And the man sprang up and was walking around.
[Acts] [14]:[11] The crowd of people who saw what Paulos had done began to shout out in Lukaonios, “These two look like men, but they’re really gods who have come down to us!”
[Acts] [14]:[12] They called Barnabas ‘Zeus’ and called Paulos ‘Hermas’ since he was the main speaker.
[Acts] [14]:[13] And the priest of Zeus wanted to sacrifice with the crowds, so he brought bulls and garlands of flowers to the city gates from the temple on the path to the city.
[Acts] [14]:[14] But when the missionaries Barnabas and Paulos heard what was going on, they tore their clothes in dismay as they rushed out into the crowd
[Acts] [14]:[15] shouting, “Men, why are you doing all these things? We are only humans just like all of you. We were bringing you the good message about abandoning these useless sacrifices and turning to the living God who made heaven and the earth and the sea and everything in them.
[Acts] [14]:[16] In previous generations he allowed all the nations to go their own different ways,
[Acts] [14]:[17] but he never left himself without evidence of himself—sending good rains from heaven to give you all fruitful seasons with food to fill your stomachs and happiness to fill your hearts.”
[Acts] [14]:[18] By saying these things, they were eventually just able to restrain the people from sacrificing to them.
[Acts] [14]:[19] But some strict Yehudim (Jews) came over from Pisidian Antiokeia and Ikonion and were able to persuade the crowds. They threw rocks at Paulos to kill him and dragged his body outside the city gates thinking that he was dead.
[Acts] [14]:[20] But as the believers were standing around him, Paulos got up and went back into the city, but he left again with Barnabas the next day and went to Derbai.
[Acts] [14]:[21] They preached the good message in Derbai, and after giving further training to many of them, they returned to Lustra and Ikonion and Antiokeia.
[Acts] [14]:[22] There they strengthened the faith of the believers—encouraging them to continue believing and to expect that it’s normal to endure a lot of suffering on the path to God’s kingdom.
[Acts] [14]:[23] They appointed some elders for each assembly, then they fasted and prayed for the elders—asking the master that they believed in to look after them.
[Acts] [14]:[24] After passing through Pisidia, they arrived at Pamfulia
[Acts] [14]:[25] and after teaching the master’s message in Pergai, they went down to the coastal city of Atalia.
[Acts] [14]:[26] From there, they sailed back to Arami (Syrian) Antiokeia where the congregation had prayed for God’s grace to be with them for the work they had just fulfilled.
[Acts] [14]:[27] So when they arrived, they gathered the assembly together there and shared about what God had done with them and how he had opened up the door of faith to the non-Jews.
[Acts] [14]:[28] Then they stayed on with them there for quite a while.
[Acts] [15]:[1] Then some people came to Antiokeia from Yehudah (Judea) and were teaching the believers that according to Mosheh’s (Moses) teachings, you can’t be saved unless you’ve been circumcised.
[Acts] [15]:[2] This led to no end of argument and debate between them and Paulos and Barnabas until it was decided that the two of them and some other believers should go to Yerushalem (Jerusalem) to ask the missionaries and the elders there about this issue.
[Acts] [15]:[3] So indeed the assembly sent the group on their way, and as they passed through Foinikai and Shomron (Samaria), they described how non-Jews had become believers and this news made the believers there very happy.
[Acts] [15]:[4] When they arrived in Yerushalem, they were welcomed by the assembly and the missionaries and the elders, and they explained how God had used them.
[Acts] [15]:[5] But some of the believers who were also members of the Farisaios party stood up and said, “It’s quite proper for them to be circumcised and to be commanded to keep the Jewish religious laws.”
[Acts] [15]:[6] So the missionaries and the elders met separately in order to consider the matter further.
[Acts] [15]:[7] After a lot of debate, Kefa (Peter; Grk. Petros) stood up and said, “Men, brothers, all of you here know that some time back, God chose me to be a mouthpiece so that the non-Jews could hear the good message and believe.
[Acts] [15]:[8] And God who knows even people’s inner thoughts, gave them the same holy spirit that he gave us,
[Acts] [15]:[9] and when he purified their minds by the faith, he didn’t do anything different for them than he did for us.
[Acts] [15]:[10] So why are you all provoking God by putting a load on the shoulders of these believers that neither we, nor our ancestors, were ever able to bear?
[Acts] [15]:[11] But we ourselves have believed thanks to the grace of Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) the master, and they can be saved in just the same way.”
[Acts] [15]:[12] The whole group sat in silence, and then they listened to Barnabas and Paulos as they described everything that God had done among the non-Jews through them, including miracles and amazing things.
[Acts] [15]:[13] Then while they were still silent, Ya’akov (James; Grk. Yakobos) responded, “Men, brothers, listen to me.
[Acts] [15]:[14] Shim’on (Simon) Kefa has told us how God first intervened in order to select a people for himself from among the non-Jews.
[Acts] [15]:[15] And this actually agrees with the message that the prophets recorded,
[Acts] [15]:[16] ‘After these things have happened I will return, and I will rebuild the worship tent from David’s time that has collapsed, Although it was overturned, I will rebuild and restore it,
[Acts] [15]:[17] so that the remaining people will want to find the master, and also the non-Jews who cried out to me. Yahweh who’s doing these things is saying this,
[Acts] [15]:[18] and planned it this way from eternity.’
[Acts] [15]:[19] Because of this, my ruling is not to be troubling the non-Jews who are turning back to God,
[Acts] [15]:[20] but to write to them to keep away from anything polluted by idols, from sexual immorality, and from strangled animals and eating or drinking blood.
[Acts] [15]:[21] Mosheh’s (Moses) writings have been preached in every city and are read in our meeting halls on every Rest Day.
[Acts] [15]:[22] So the missionaries and elders with all the assembly decided to choose some men to accompany Paulos and Barnabas to Antiokeia, so they chose Yehudah (Judas; Grk. Yudas) (nicknamed Bar-Saba) and Silas who were leaders among the believers,
[Acts] [15]:[23] This is what they wrote: This letter is from the missionaries and elders, your brothers here in Yerushalem (Jerusalem) to our non-Jewish fellow believers in Antiokeia and Aram (Syria) and Kilikia.
[Acts] [15]:[24] Since we heard that some people who weren’t sent by us came from here and disturbed you all with their upsetting messages,
[Acts] [15]:[25] we unanimously agreed to select some men to accompany our dear friends Barnabas and Paulos back.
[Acts] [15]:[26] These are men who have dedicated their lives to our master, Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) the messiah.
[Acts] [15]:[27] So we’ve sent Yehudah and Silas and they’ll confirm in person what we are writing.
[Acts] [15]:[28] It seemed right to the holy spirit and to us to not burden you all with anything more than the following commands:
[Acts] [15]:[29] you all must keep away from anything sacrificed to idols, from eating or drinking blood or strangled animals, and from sexual immorality. You will do well if you avoid these things. Farewell.
[Acts] [15]:[30] So they were sent off and when they arrived at Antiokeia, they gathered the believers and handed across the letter,
[Acts] [15]:[31] and when they read it, they were very happy with the encouraging contents.
[Acts] [15]:[32] Yehudah and Barnabas were both prophets, and said a lot to encourage them and strengthen their faith.
[Acts] [15]:[33] After they’d stayed there for a while, the believers sent them home carrying greetings from them to the assembly back in Yerushalem (Jerusalem).
[Acts] [15]:[34] ◘
[Acts] [15]:[35] But Paulos and Barnabas stayed on there in Antiokeia, teaching them and preaching the good message along with many others.
[Acts] [15]:[36] After a few days, Paulos suggested to Barnabas, “Let’s go back and visit the believers in each city where we proclaimed the master’s message, and see how they’re doing.”
[Acts] [15]:[37] Barnabas agreed and wanted to take Yohan (John; Grk. Yoannes) Markos (John Mark) along with them as well,
[Acts] [15]:[38] but Paulos didn’t want to take him because he had left them in Pamfulia instead of continuing with them in their work.
[Acts] [15]:[39] And so it turned into such a disagreement that the two of them each went their different ways. Barnabas took Yohan Markos with him and sailed to Kupros (Cyprus)
[Acts] [15]:[40] while Paulos chose Silas and they left after being entrusted to the master’s grace by the believers.
[Acts] [15]:[41] They went through Aram (Syria) and Kilikia, strengthening the assemblies there.
[Acts] [16]:[1] Then Paulos went to Derbai and then on to Lustra where a believer named Timotheos lived. His mother was a Jewish believer, but his father was Greek.
[Acts] [16]:[2] The believers in Lustra and Ikonion spoke well of Timotheos
[Acts] [16]:[3] and Paulos wanted him to accompany them on his trip so he circumcised him in advance because of the Yehudim (Jews) in that region—everyone knew that his father was a Greek.
[Acts] [16]:[4] As they passed through various towns, they explained the decision of the missionaries and elders in Yerushalem (Jerusalem) about which commands they must adhere to.
[Acts] [16]:[5] So the assemblies were strengthened in this way and their numbers were increasing each day.
[Acts] [16]:[6] From there, they travelled through Frugia and the Galatia region, after the holy spirit prevented them from proclaiming the message in Asia Minor.
[Acts] [16]:[7] When they got to Musia, they planned to go on into Bithunia, but Yeshua’s (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) spirit didn’t let them,
[Acts] [16]:[8] so after leaving Musia they went to Troias.
[Acts] [16]:[9] During the night, Paulos had a vision of a Makedonian man standing there and imploring him, “Come on to Makedonia and help us here.”
[Acts] [16]:[10] So as a result of the vision, we decided to go straight to Makedonia, concluding that God had called us to share the good message with them.
[Acts] [16]:[11] From Troias we sailed directly to Samothrakai, and then on to Neapolis the following day.
[Acts] [16]:[12] From there we continued on to Filippou (Philippi) which is a Romaios colony and the capital city of the Makedonia district where we stayed for several days.
[Acts] [16]:[13] On the Rest Days, we went down to the river outside the city gate where we thought people might be praying, and we spoke to the women who had met there.
[Acts] [16]:[14] One of them was Ludia from Thuateira who was a seller of purple goods and although she already worshipped God, the master opened her mind and she readily accepted what Paulos was saying.
[Acts] [16]:[15] So then Ludia and her household were all ceremonially immersed, and then she requested, “If you all consider me to be faithful to the master, come and stay at my place.” So she persuaded us.
[Acts] [16]:[16] One time as we were walking to the prayer meeting, we met a female slave who was possessed by a spirit that enabled her to tell fortunes, and thanks to that, to earn a lot of money for her masters.
[Acts] [16]:[17] She walked along behind us and shouted out, “These men are slaves of the highest god and they will be telling you all how to be saved.”
[Acts] [16]:[18] After she’d done this for several days, Paulos was so frustrated that he turned around and spoke to the spirit in her, “I command you by the authority of Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) the messiah to leave her.”
[Acts] [16]:[19] But when her masters realised that their profitable business was about to come to an end, they grabbed Paulos and Silas and dragged them to the authorities at the marketplace.
[Acts] [16]:[20] They brought them forward to face the magistrates and said, “These Yehudim (Jews) are disturbing the peace in our city
[Acts] [16]:[21] and teaching behaviour that we as Romaios can neither accept nor practice.”
[Acts] [16]:[22] An angry crowd gathered around and the magistrates ordered for Paulos and Silas to have their robes torn off and then to be beaten with rods.
[Acts] [16]:[23] They were severely beaten and then thrown into prison where the officer was commanded to keep them secure.
[Acts] [16]:[24] Because of that, he threw them into the inner cell and locked their feet in stocks.
[Acts] [16]:[25] Around midnight Paulos and Silas were praying and singing praises to God, and the other prisoners were listening to them.
[Acts] [16]:[26] Suddenly there was a strong earthquake that shook even the foundations of the prison, and immediately all the prison doors opened up and the chains of all the prisoners came loose.
[Acts] [16]:[27] The prison officer woke up, and when he saw that all the prison doors were open, he drew his sword to take his own life as he figured that all the prisoners must have escaped.
[Acts] [16]:[28] But Paulos shouted out, “Don’t harm yourself! We’re all still here!”
[Acts] [16]:[29] The officer called for torches, then rushed in and knelt down trembling in front of Paulos and Silas.
[Acts] [16]:[30] Then he escorted them out and asked, “Masters, what do I need to do to be saved?”
[Acts] [16]:[31] “Believe in the master Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus),” they replied, “then you and your household can all be saved.”
[Acts] [16]:[32] Then they explained the message about the master to him and all those in his household.
[Acts] [16]:[33] Even though it was still the middle of the night, he sponged their wounds, and then him and his household were all immersed straight away.
[Acts] [16]:[34] He took Paulos and Silas up into his house and gave them a meal, and his whole household were happy because they now believed in God.
[Acts] [16]:[35] The next day the magistrates sent officials to tell the jailer to release Paulos and Silas.
[Acts] [16]:[36] So the officer told Paulos, “The magistrates sent these officials to order that you two be released.”
[Acts] [16]:[37] But Paulos responded, “You mean that after publicly beating us Romaios men without a trial, they threw us into prison and now they want to just quietly release us.”
[Acts] [16]:[38] So the officials reported this back to the magistrates, and they were quite afraid when they heard that Paulos and Silas were Romaios citizens.
[Acts] [16]:[39] So now they came to the prison in person, and appealed to them, and escorting them out of prison themselves, asked them to please leave the city.
[Acts] [16]:[40] So after Paulos and Silas left the prison, they went to see Ludia and after encouraging the believers there, they left.
[Acts] [17]:[1] After travelling through Amfipolis and Apollonia, Paulos and Silas went to Thessalonikai where there was a Jewish meeting hall.
[Acts] [17]:[2] Paulos’s custom was to attend at the local meeting hall on the Rest Day, so he did that, and for three weekends in a row he discussed the scriptures with them,
[Acts] [17]:[3] showing them how that it had been written that the messiah would suffer and be killed and come back to life, and then explaining, “This Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) that I’ve been telling you about is the messiah.”
[Acts] [17]:[4] Some of them were persuaded and joined with Paulos and Silas, along with a big group of godly Hellains (Greeks) and quite a few prominent women.
[Acts] [17]:[5] But some of the other Yehudim (Jews) were envious of them, and enlisted some of the troublemakers from the marketplaces to form a mob. They stirred up all the people, and looking for Paulos and Silas so they could bring them out, arrived at the house of a man named Yason.
[Acts] [17]:[6] But when they realised that Paulos and Silas weren’t there, they dragged Yason and some other believers off to the city leaders, shouting, “Those two men who’ve gone around upsetting the whole world have now come here as well
[Acts] [17]:[7] and Yason has welcomed them into his house. They rebel against Kaisar’s decrees and claim that Yeshua is a rival king.”
[Acts] [17]:[8] They stirred up the crowd and the city leaders with these accusations,
[Acts] [17]:[9] so the leaders collected a heavy fine from Yason and the others, and then released them.
[Acts] [17]:[10] So the believers immediately sent Paulos and Silas off during the night to go to Beroia. In Beroia they also attended at the Jewish meeting hall
[Acts] [17]:[11] and this group were more upper-class than the congregation in Thessalonikai. They eagerly accepted the message and examined the scriptures every day to check if what was being taught matched what was written there.
[Acts] [17]:[12] Because it did, many of the people believed including quite a few of the prominent Hellains (Greeks).
[Acts] [17]:[13] But when the Yehudim (Jews) from Thessalonikai found out that God’s message was also being proclaimed by Paulos there in Beroia, they soon turned up to agitate and stir the crowds.
[Acts] [17]:[14] So the believers immediately sent Paulos off to the coast, but Silas and Timotheos both stayed.
[Acts] [17]:[15] The ones guiding Paulos took him to Athainai before they headed back with his instructions for Silas and Timotheos to come and join him again as soon as possible.
[Acts] [17]:[16] While Paulos stayed in Athainai waiting for them, he was upset in his spirit as he observed how idolatrous the people were.
[Acts] [17]:[17] So while he stayed busy having discussions with the Yehudim (Jews) and other worshippers from the meeting hall, he also spent time every day with anyone who just happened to be around in the marketplace.
[Acts] [17]:[18] Some of the Epikoureios and Stoikos philosophers enjoyed discussing things with him, but others just mocked him, “What does this babbler want to talk about now?” But others said, “Seems that he’s talking about strange demons,” because he was preaching the good message about Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) and coming back to life.
[Acts] [17]:[19] So they grabbed him and brought him to the Areios Hill where the council sat and asked, “Are we allowed to know what this new teaching that you’re bringing is about?
[Acts] [17]:[20] It seems that you have some surprising ideas for our ears, so we want to hear what it’s all about.”
[Acts] [17]:[21] (Everyone in Athainai and even visitors often took the opportunity either to explain or to listen to any new things.)
[Acts] [17]:[22] So Paulos stood up in the middle of the gathering on the hill and spoke, “Men of Athainai, I’ve noticed how you all are very religious,
[Acts] [17]:[23] because as I was looking around and observing your objects of worship, I even discovered an altar that was inscribed, ‘To the unknown god.’ So without knowing it, you already worship this God that I’m going to tell you about.
[Acts] [17]:[24] This God who created the earth and everything in it is Yahweh who’s over heaven and earth. He doesn’t live in man-made temples
[Acts] [17]:[25] nor can he be repaired by any human hands and he doesn’t need to be fed. On the contrary, he’s the one who gives life and breath and who gives us everything that we need.
[Acts] [17]:[26] From one man he made every nationality that lives across all the earth and designated their boundaries and their futures.
[Acts] [17]:[27] He made them so that they would try to discover God, and if they did search for him they might find him as he’s not far from any one of us
[Acts] [17]:[28] because ‘We live in him and are moved by him and exist through him.’ Even some of your own poets wrote, ‘We are all descended from just one.’
[Acts] [17]:[29] So since we are God’s offspring, we shouldn’t be putting gold or silver or stone craftsmanship in the same class as the divine.
[Acts] [17]:[30] In fact God overlooked times of such ignorance in the past, but now he’s informing everyone and requiring them to repent
[Acts] [17]:[31] because he’s set a date for when he’s going to be fairly judging the world. He’s already appointed the judge who everyone can have faith in because he brought him back to life from the dead.
[Acts] [17]:[32] When they heard about a dead person coming back to life, some started mocking but others said, “We’d like to hear more about this from you another time.”
[Acts] [17]:[33] So Paulos left at that stage
[Acts] [17]:[34] but some people joined with him and believed, including Dionusios who was a council member, a woman named Damaris, and others as well.
[Acts] [18]:[1] After this, Paulos left Athainai and travelled to Korinthos.
[Acts] [18]:[2] There he came across a Yehudi (Jew) named Akulas (Aquila) who had been born in Pontos but who had recently moved from Italia along with his wife Priskilla because Emperor Klaudios had ordered all Yehudim (Jews) to leave Romai. So Paulos approached them,
[Acts] [18]:[3] and since they worked in the same trade, he ended up staying with them and they worked together in their craft of tent-making.
[Acts] [18]:[4] On every Rest Day, Paulos debated in the Jewish meeting hall, and was persuading both Yehudim and Hellains (Greeks).
[Acts] [18]:[5] However when Silas and Timotheos arrived from Makedonia, Paulos was able to devote his full time to the message—demonstrating to the Yehudim that Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) is the promised messiah.
[Acts] [18]:[6] But when they opposed the message and made false accusations, he publicly brushed the dust off his clothes and said, “Your future deaths are your own problem. I’m innocent of your guilt. From now on, I’ll going to the non-Jews.”
[Acts] [18]:[7] So Paulos left there, and went to stay at the house of a man named Titos Yustos who worshipped God and whose house was next-door to the meeting hall.
[Acts] [18]:[8] Krispos the meeting hall leader and all his household decided to follow the master, and many of the Korinthios believed after they heard the message and were immersed.
[Acts] [18]:[9] Then the master spoke to Paulos one night in a vision, “Don’t be afraid and stay silent, but keep speaking out
[Acts] [18]:[10] because I am with you and no one can mistreat you here because there are many of my people in this city.”
[Acts] [18]:[11] So Paulos stayed on for eighteen months, teaching God’s message to the people there.
[Acts] [18]:[12] Then at the time when Gallion was the proconsul of Akaia, the Yehudim united against Paulos and brought a case to the tribunal against him
[Acts] [18]:[13] saying, “This man is going against the law by persuading people to be worshipping his God.”
[Acts] [18]:[14] But as Paulos opened his mouth to speak, Gallion said to the Yehudim, “I would have accepted this charge if it was a serious wrong or evil crime and would have listened to you Yehudim.
[Acts] [18]:[15] However, since it’s a question about a message and names and your own law, you all can see to it yourselves because I don’t want to get involved in judging things like that.”
[Acts] [18]:[16] So he sent them away from the tribunal,
[Acts] [18]:[17] but they grabbed Sosthenes, the leader from the meeting hall, and beat him up right there in front of the tribunal. But Gallion took action to stop them.
[Acts] [18]:[18] Paulos stayed on for quite a few days after that, then he farewelled the believers and went to Kegkreai where he had his hair cut as was the custom for someone making a vow. Then taking Priskilla and Akulas (Aquila) with him, he sailed towards Aram (Syria).
[Acts] [18]:[19] When they arrived at Efesos, he left the other two there while he went into the Jewish meeting hall and had a discussion with the Yehudim (Jews) there.
[Acts] [18]:[20] They asked him to remain longer, but he turned them down
[Acts] [18]:[21] although as he gave his farewells, he said, “I’ll come back here again if God wills it,” then he sailed on from Efesos.
[Acts] [18]:[22] When he landed at Kaisareia, he went to Yerushalem (Jerusalem) and greeted the assembly there before continuing on to Antiokeia.
[Acts] [18]:[23] He stayed there for some time before travelling through the regions of Galatia and Frugia strengthening the faith of the believers through his teaching.
[Acts] [18]:[24] Meanwhile a Jewish man named Apollos (who had been born in the city of Alexandria) arrived in Efesos. He knew the Hebrew scriptures well
[Acts] [18]:[25] and had been taught about the master’s way. Being a very enthusiastic person, he started teaching about Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus), even though he didn’t know about being filled with the spirit.
[Acts] [18]:[26] So Apollos started speaking out boldly in the Jewish meeting hall. Priskilla and Akulas (Aquila) listened to him, then asked to speak with him privately and explained God’s way more accurately.
[Acts] [18]:[27] Now Apollos wanted to go to Akaia, so the believers encouraged him and sent a letter ahead of him to tell the believers there to welcome him, so when he arrived there, he was able to contribute a lot to those who through God’s grace had also become believers.
[Acts] [18]:[28] Apollos was also able to thoroughly refute the arguments of the Yehudim (Jews) and used the scriptures to show that Yeshua is the messiah.
[Acts] [19]:[1] So then while Apollos was at Korinthos, Paulos travelled through the interior regions before arriving at Efesos. He found some followers there,
[Acts] [19]:[2] and asked them if they had received the holy spirit when they had first believed in Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus). They replied, “We hadn’t even heard that there’s a holy spirit.”
[Acts] [19]:[3] “So then what were you immersed into?” asked Paulos. “With Yohan’s (John; Grk. Yoannes) immersion,” they answered.
[Acts] [19]:[4] Then Paulos said, “Yohan immersed people in water with an immersion that went with repentance from their sins, but he told them to believe in the one who would follow him, that is to believe in Yeshua.”
[Acts] [19]:[5] When the followers heard this, they were immersed in water again, this time proclaiming their faith in Yeshua the master.
[Acts] [19]:[6] Then Paulos placed his hands on them and prayed and the holy spirit came down onto them and they started speaking in other languages and speaking messages from God.
[Acts] [19]:[7] There were about twelve men in the group.
[Acts] [19]:[8] So Paulos started going to the Jewish meeting hall and for the next three months he boldly discussed and persuaded them about God’s kingdom.
[Acts] [19]:[9] But as some of them refused to believe and became hardened against his teaching and started telling everyone that the Yeshua way was evil, Paulos stopped teaching in the meeting hall and taught the followers at Turannos’ school instead.
[Acts] [19]:[10] This went on for two years to the point that everyone in Asia Minor, whether Yehudim (Jews) or Hellains (Greeks), heard the message about Yeshua.
[Acts] [19]:[11] And God was doing incredible miracles through Paulos
[Acts] [19]:[12] such that even if handkerchiefs or aprons that had touched his skin were placed on top of any person who was sick or troubled with demons, then they would recover and the evil spirits would leave them.
[Acts] [19]:[13] But some of the Jewish exorcists going around attempted to use the name of Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) to drive out evil spirits by telling them, “I am imploring you all by Yeshua that Paulos preaches about.”
[Acts] [19]:[14] Seven sons of the Jewish chief priest, Skeuas were doing this.
[Acts] [19]:[15] But the evil spirit would answer them saying, “I know Yeshua and I recognise Paulos, but who are you?”
[Acts] [19]:[16] Then the man who had the evil spirit would jump on them and beat them up so they’d end up escaping out of the house naked and wounded.
[Acts] [19]:[17] When everyone in Efesos heard about this, both Yehudim (Jews) and Hellains (Greeks) were frightened, and the name of Yeshua the master was being honoured.
[Acts] [19]:[18] Many of the people who believed in Yeshua came and confessed their sins and wrong practices.
[Acts] [19]:[19] Lots of the people who’d practiced magic brought their scrolls and burnt them in front of the others. When the values of all of these were added up, it was huge—worth around 50,000 silver coins.
[Acts] [19]:[20] So that was how the master’s message had a powerful effect and won over many people.
[Acts] [19]:[21] After all of this, Paulos decided in his spirit that he would need to travel through Makedonia and Akaia enroute to Yerushalem (Jerusalem), saying, “After I’ve been there a while, I will also need to go to Romai.”
[Acts] [19]:[22] He sent two of his workers, Timotheos and Erastos, to Makedonia while he stayed on a bit longer in Asia Minor.
[Acts] [19]:[23] But while he was still there, a major disturbance hit the Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) followers.
[Acts] [19]:[24] A silversmith named Demetrios made little silver shrines of Artemis and this business brought a tidy profit to the local craftsmen.
[Acts] [19]:[25] Demetrios gathered all the workers together and told them, “Men, you all know that our prosperity comes from this business of ours.
[Acts] [19]:[26] But you’ve seen yourselves and heard from others that not only Efesos, but almost our entire province of Asia Minor has become persuaded by this Paulos fellow, and now the crowds are saying that what we make are not real gods.
[Acts] [19]:[27] However it’s not only us and our trade that is coming into disrepute, but the temple of the great goddess Artemis is considered to be useless. This could result in a loss of power for the great Artemis that all of Asia Minor and the inhabited world have been worshipping.”
[Acts] [19]:[28] When the gathering heard this, they became very angry and yelled out, “Artemis of the people from Efesos is great!”
[Acts] [19]:[29] Then the whole city was filled with confusion and the people rushed to the theatre and grabbed Gaios and Aristarkos from Makedonia—travelling companions of Paulos’s.
[Acts] [19]:[30] Now Paulos wanted to go there and speak to the crowd, but the believers wouldn’t let him go.
[Acts] [19]:[31] Also some of the leaders from Asia Minor who were friendly towards him, sent messengers to him to implore him not to go to the theatre.
[Acts] [19]:[32] Some of the people gathered there were yelling out something, but overall it was just confusion, and the majority of the people couldn’t even tell you the reason why they were there.
[Acts] [19]:[33] Some people in the crowd selected Alexandros (Alexander) the Yehudi (Jew) and sent him forward to speak, so he motioned with his hand ready to explain the situation to the people.
[Acts] [19]:[34] But as soon as they recognised that he was a Yehudi, people started yelling, “Artemis of the people from Efesos is great,” and this continued for over two hours.
[Acts] [19]:[35] Eventually the city administrator was able to calm the crowd and tell them, “Men, fellow people from Efesos, what person from around here doesn’t know that it’s Efesos that’s the temple keeper of the great Artemis and of this image that fell down from Zeus?
[Acts] [19]:[36] Since all of this is unquestionable, it makes sense for everyone to calm down and not do anything reckless.
[Acts] [19]:[37] These men that you presented here haven’t stolen anything from the temple, nor have they slandered our goddess.
[Acts] [19]:[38] So if Demetrios and the silver craftsmen with him have a case against anyone, they should bring it to the courts and the proconsuls and register the charges.
[Acts] [19]:[39] But for the rest of you, if you have a grievance against others, it needs to be settled in a lawful assembly
[Acts] [19]:[40] because we’re in danger of being charged with insurrection about what happened today. And we would have no defence that we could respond with concerning this disorderly gathering.”
[Acts] [19]:[41] Then he told them all to go home.
[Acts] [20]:[1] After all the commotion had died down, Paulos sent for the believers, and after greeting and encouraging them, he left Efesos to go to Makedonia.
[Acts] [20]:[2] As he travelled through the districts, he challenged the people there with a lot of messages, until he eventually arrived in Yavan (Greece).
[Acts] [20]:[3] He’d been there about three months when he heard about a plot by some Yehudim (Jews) to waylay him as he boarded a ship to return to Aram (Syria), so instead he decided to return through Makedonia
[Acts] [20]:[4] with Sopatros son of Puros from Beroia, Aristarkos and Sekundos from Thessalonikai, Gaios from Derbai, Tukikos and Trofimos from the province of Asia Minor, and Timotheos all accompanying him.
[Acts] [20]:[5] They went ahead and waited for us at Troias.
[Acts] [20]:[6] So we sailed out from Filippou (Philippi) after the Flat Bread Celebration. We arrived and meet the others there at Troias after a five-day trip, and then stayed on there for seven days.
[Acts] [20]:[7] On the Sunday we had gathered together to break bread together and Paulos was discussing many things with them. As he was scheduled to leave the next day, the meeting went on towards midnight
[Acts] [20]:[8] and there were many lamps in the upper room where we had all gathered.
[Acts] [20]:[9] Now there was a young man named Eutukos who was sitting on the window sill, and as Paulos went on, he fell asleep and toppled down from the third storey. The ones who reached him first thought he was dead,
[Acts] [20]:[10] but Paulos had come downstairs and bent over Eutukos and held him in his arms and said to the crowd, “Don’t worry, he’s still alive.”
[Acts] [20]:[11] Then Paulos went back up and broke the bread with the others, eating a little and continuing to talk with them until leaving at daybreak.
[Acts] [20]:[12] The locals took the young man home and were very relieved that he was alive.
[Acts] [20]:[13] We went ahead to the ship and departed for Assos where it had been arranged that we’d pick up Paulos because he wanted to walk there.
[Acts] [20]:[14] So when we met him at Assos, he boarded the ship and we all sailed on to Mitulainai.
[Acts] [20]:[15] After we left Mitulainai, we were out from Kios the next day, in Samos the day after that, and then the following day we arrived at Milaitos.
[Acts] [20]:[16] Paulos had decided to sail past Efesos because he was hurrying to try to get to Yerushalem (Jerusalem) for the Day of Pentecost so he didn’t want to spend time in Asia Minor.
[Acts] [20]:[17] So while we were at Milaitos, he sent a message to Efesos for the elders of the assembly to come to him.
[Acts] [20]:[18] When they arrived, he told them, “You all know that from the very first day that I set foot in Asia Minor and for the entire time that I was there
[Acts] [20]:[19] I humbly served the master even through tears and trials when the Yehudim (Jews) plotted to destroy me.
[Acts] [20]:[20] But I didn’t shrink back from teaching you everything that would help you, whether I was teaching in public or in individual homes.
[Acts] [20]:[21] I explained to both Yehudim and Hellains (Greeks) how they needed to turn their backs on their sins and towards God with faith in our master Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) the messiah.
[Acts] [20]:[22] However the spirit is now forcing me towards Yerushalem (Jerusalem) even though I don’t know what will happen to me there.
[Acts] [20]:[23] I just know that recently in every city, the holy spirit tells me that chains and hardships are waiting for me.
[Acts] [20]:[24] But I’ve never regarded my own life as being valuable—I only want to reach the end of my life having served in the way that the master Yeshua instructed me to speak out the good message about God’s grace.
[Acts] [20]:[25] So you see, I know that all of you from here where I passed through proclaiming God’s kingdom, you will never see me again.
[Acts] [20]:[26] That’s why I’m declaring to all of you today that I’m not guilty of your judgement
[Acts] [20]:[27] because I didn’t avoid telling you anything that I had from God.
[Acts] [20]:[28] So now you elders look after your own lives and those of your flock because the holy spirit chose you as overseers to shepherd the assembly of God’s people who he paid for with his very own blood.
[Acts] [20]:[29] I’m aware that after I leave, vicious wolves will come in amongst you and trying to steal the flock.
[Acts] [20]:[30] Even some of you will rise up and teach a message that’s warped but which will draw some of the believers away to follow it,
[Acts] [20]:[31] so take great care. Remember that for three years, I never stopped warning each of you along with my tears
[Acts] [20]:[32] so now I’m leaving you all in God’s hands and with the message of his grace which is quite capable of helping you grow to receive the inheritance that’s for all those who’ve been purified.
[Acts] [20]:[33] I never envied anyone’s gold or silver or fancy clothes
[Acts] [20]:[34] and you yourselves know that I laboured with my own hands to cover my expenses and for those with me.
[Acts] [20]:[35] Yes, I showed you all that it’s good to work and to take care of the weaker ones and to remember the message of the master Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) when he said that it’s better to be a giver than a taker.”
[Acts] [20]:[36] When he’d finished speaking, Paulos knelt down and prayed with them all.
[Acts] [20]:[37] Everyone was sobbing as they hugged and kissed him
[Acts] [20]:[38] because what he’d said about never seeing him again had really distressed them. Then they accompanied him to his ship.
[Acts] [21]:[1] When it was time for us to sail, we left them and sailed directly across to Kos before going on to Rodos the next day and then on to Patara.
[Acts] [21]:[2] From there we found a ship heading to Foinikai, so we boarded that and set off.
[Acts] [21]:[3] After sighting Kupros (Cyprus) and then leaving it behind on our left, we sailed on to Aram (Syria) and docked there at the port of Tsor (Tyre) where the ship had cargo to be unloaded.
[Acts] [21]:[4] We searched for the believers there and then stayed on with them for seven days. They were inspired by the spirit to tell Paulos not to go to Yerushalem (Jerusalem).
[Acts] [21]:[5] Once our time was up there and everyone knew that we were leaving, even the wives and children accompanied us out of the city to the port. We all knelt on the beach and prayed
[Acts] [21]:[6] before we continued on and boarded our ship and they went back to their own homes.
[Acts] [21]:[7] So we sailed from Tsor down to Ptolemais where we were able to greet the brothers and sisters and stay overnight with them.
[Acts] [21]:[8] The next day we continued on to Kaisareia and ended up in Filippos’s (Philip) house. He was one of the original seven men who had been given the responsibility of distributing aid—a preacher of the good message, and we stayed with him.
[Acts] [21]:[9] Filippos had four unmarried daughters still at home, and they shared messages from God.
[Acts] [21]:[10] Several days later a man named Agabos came from Yehudah (Judea). He too shared messages from God
[Acts] [21]:[11] and when he arrived, he picked up Paulos’s belt and tied it around his own feet and hands, telling them that the holy spirit had told him that this is how the owner of the belt would be treated by the Jewish leaders in Yerushalem before they would then hand him over to the non-Jews to be dealt with.
[Acts] [21]:[12] When we heard this described, both we and the locals begged Paulos not to go to Yerushalem
[Acts] [21]:[13] but he answered, “Oh come on, what’s all this weeping and carrying on that’s breaking my heart? Actually I’m quite ready not only to be tied up, but even to be killed in Yerushalem as a testimony to the master Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus).”
[Acts] [21]:[14] When we saw that we couldn’t change his mind, we didn’t say anything else, figuring out that whatever the master wills for the situation would happen,
[Acts] [21]:[15] and so after these several days, we had gotten everything ready and started off for Yerushalem.
[Acts] [21]:[16] Some of the believers from Kaisareia accompanied us and led us to the home of a man named Mnason to stay—he was an older believer from Kupros (Cyprus).
[Acts] [21]:[17] When we arrived at Yerushalem (Jerusalem), the brothers and sisters there happily welcomed us,
[Acts] [21]:[18] and the next day, we accompanied Paulos to go and see Ya’akov (James; Grk. Yakobos) and the elders of the assembly there.
[Acts] [21]:[19] After greeting them, Paulos then described all the things that God had done among the non-Jews as he had served among them,
[Acts] [21]:[20] and when they’d heard all that they praised God and told Paulos, “Brother, you’ve noticed how many thousands of Yehudim (Jews) have believed in the messiah but they still strive to observe Mosheh’s (Moses) laws.
[Acts] [21]:[21] But they’ve heard reports that you’ve been teaching the Yehudim that live outside our country that they don’t have to obey what Mosheh wrote—telling them that they don’t have to have their children circumcised and that they don’t have to follow our Jewish customs.
[Acts] [21]:[22] What will happen now, because the leaders here will certainly hear that you have arrived?
[Acts] [21]:[23] So here’s what we suggest that you do: Four of our men are making a public vow.
[Acts] [21]:[24] Why don’t you join these four and join them in the purification ceremony at the temple and pay their expenses in getting your heads shaved. Then everyone will be able to see that it’s false what they’ve heard about you, because you clearly still comply with Mosheh’s instructions.
[Acts] [21]:[25] And as for the believers who are non-Jews, we’ve informed them of our recommendation that they should avoid anything that’s been offered to an idol, avoid consuming blood and meat from strangled animals and birds, and avoid sexual immorality.”
[Acts] [21]:[26] So the next day Paulos took the four men for the purification ceremony in the temple and there they announced the date when their vows would be fulfilled and their sacrifices made.
[Acts] [21]:[27] When the seven days of the vow were almost over, some Yehudim (Jews) from the province of Asia Minor noticed Paulos in the temple. They stirred up the crowd and grabbed hold of him,
[Acts] [21]:[28] yelling out, “Men of Yisrael (Israel). Help us here. This is the man who’s been teaching all around the world against Yisrael and against Mosheh’s (Moses) law and against this temple. What’s more he brought non-Jews here into the temple and so has defiled this holy place.”
[Acts] [21]:[29] (They said this because they had previously seen Trofimos from Efesos in the city with Paulos and had assumed that he had brought him into the temple.)
[Acts] [21]:[30] So now the whole city was in an uproar, and the crowds rushed in, grabbed Paulos, and dragged him out of the temple and hurriedly closed the temple gates.
[Acts] [21]:[31] They were ready to kill Paulos, but the commander of the Romaios soldiers had heard that all Yerushalem (Jerusalem) was in an uproar.
[Acts] [21]:[32] Taking some soldiers and officers, he immediately ran down to the temple, and when the crowd saw the commander and the soldiers they stopped beating Paulos.
[Acts] [21]:[33] The commander came close and took hold of Paulos and ordered that he be tied up with a pair of chains while he tried to find out who he was and what he’d done wrong.
[Acts] [21]:[34] Various people in the crowd were shouting out different things, and not being able to make any sense of it because of all the commotion, the commander ordered that Paulos be taken into the barracks.
[Acts] [21]:[35] When they got to the stairs, the soldiers had to lift him up above their heads because of the frenzy of the crowd,
[Acts] [21]:[36] because most of the people were following and shouting out, “Do away with him!”
[Acts] [21]:[37] As they were able to carry him into the fortress, Paulos called down to the commander, “Can I say something to you?” “You speak Greek!”, replied the commander.
[Acts] [21]:[38] “Aren’t you the Mitsri (Egyptian) who stirred up a group of assassins a while back and led them out into the wilderness?”
[Acts] [21]:[39] “No, I’m a Yehudi (Jew) from Tarsos in Kilikia—a citizen of an important city,” said Paulos. “But please, let me speak to these people.”
[Acts] [21]:[40] The commander nodded, so the soldiers stood Paulos on the stairs where he gestured to the people. The crowd quietened down, and so Paulos spoke loudly in his Hebrew language:
[Acts] [22]:[1] “Men, brothers, and fathers, listen to what I have to say for myself.”
[Acts] [22]:[2] When they heard him speaking Hebrew, they became even more quiet as he continued,
[Acts] [22]:[3] “I am a Yehudi who grew up in this very city to study under Gamliel. I’ve been raised according to every part of our ancestral law, working hard to obey God like all of you here today.
[Acts] [22]:[4] I used to persecute the followers of ‘The Path’ even to death—tying up both men and women and handing them over to the prisons
[Acts] [22]:[5] as the Chief Priest and all the council of elders can tell you. I took letters from them to our Jewish brothers in Damesek (Damascus) when I went so that I could arrest the ones there and bring them back here to Yerushalem (Jerusalem) to be punished.
[Acts] [22]:[6] “But one time as I was travelling and getting close to Damesek (Damascus) by the middle of the day, suddenly a bright light from the sky began to flash around me
[Acts] [22]:[7] and I fell to the ground. I heard a voice asking me, ‘Sha’ul (Saul; Grk. Saulos/Saul), Sha’ul, why are you persecuting me?’
[Acts] [22]:[8] ‘Who are you, master?’ I answered. And the voice said, ‘I am Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus)—the one from Nazaret that you are persecuting.’
[Acts] [22]:[9] The other people with me saw the light but didn’t hear the voice that spoke to me.
[Acts] [22]:[10] Then I asked, ‘What do I need to do, master?’ ‘Get up and continue into Damesek,’ the master said. ‘When you get there, you’ll be told everything that you’ve been assigned to do.’
[Acts] [22]:[11] But I couldn’t see anything because the brightness of the light had affected my eyes, so my companions had to lead me by hand into Damesek.
[Acts] [22]:[12] “In Damesek there was a man named Hananyah (Ananias; Grk. Hananias)—a non-Jew but who was respected by the Yehudim (Jews) there because he strove to obey Mosheh’s (Moses) instructions about living.
[Acts] [22]:[13] Hananyah came to where I was and standing by me said, “Brother Sha’ul, receive your sight!” That very hour I was able to see again and look at him
[Acts] [22]:[14] and he said, ‘The god of our ancestors has decided in advance to reveal his plans to you, and for you to see the sinless one—to hear him speaking
[Acts] [22]:[15] because he wants you to inform people everywhere what you’ve seen and heard.
[Acts] [22]:[16] So what else are you waiting for? Get up and wash away your sins by getting immersed in water as you request his forgiveness.’
[Acts] [22]:[17] “Then when I returned to Yerushalem (Jerusalem) and was praying in the temple, I fell into a trance
[Acts] [22]:[18] and saw the master telling me, ‘Get out of Yerushalem in a hurry because they won’t accept what you’re teaching them about me.’
[Acts] [22]:[19] ‘Master,’ I replied, ‘they know that previously I was the one imprisoning and beating the people who believed in you,
[Acts] [22]:[20] and when Stefanos was killed after teaching about you, it was me standing there and cheering on the ones executing him as I held their coats for them.’
[Acts] [22]:[21] Then the master told me, ‘Get going now because I’m sending you away to the non-Jews.’ ”
[Acts] [22]:[22] Until this point in his message, the crowd had been listening to Paulos, but now they started shouting, “Do away with this man! He doesn’t deserve to live in this world!”
[Acts] [22]:[23] Then they yelled and threw some of their clothes down onto the ground and threw dust up into the air.
[Acts] [22]:[24] So the commander ordered Paulos to be brought inside into barracks and ordered that he be flogged and interrogated to determine what he’d done that would make the crowd react like that.
[Acts] [22]:[25] But as they strapped him down and stretched him out for the flogging, Paulos asked the centurion standing there, “It is legal for you to flog a Romaios citizen who hasn’t even been tried?”
[Acts] [22]:[26] When he heard that, the centurion went to the commander and reported, “How are we going to handle this, because this man is a Romaios citizen?”
[Acts] [22]:[27] So the commander went in to where Paulos was and asked him, “Tell me the truth. Are you a Romaios citizen?” “Yes I am,” said Paulos.
[Acts] [22]:[28] “Yeah, and I paid a lot for mine as well,” mocked the commander. “Actually mine is through birth,” Paulos responded.
[Acts] [22]:[29] At this point, the soldiers who were about to interrogate Paulos left the room, and even the commander was now afraid after learning that he’d had a Romaios citizen tied down to be flogged.
[Acts] [22]:[30] The next day, the Romaios commander still wanted to know what was behind the anger of the Yehudim (Jews), so he had Paulos released from the cell, but brought him down to a room where he’d ordered the chief priests and the Jewish council to convene. Paulos was given a seat
[Acts] [23]:[1] and looking directly at the council members said, “Men, brothers, all my life I have lived before God as a good citizen and with a clean conscience.”
[Acts] [23]:[2] But Hananyah (Ananias; Grk. Hananias) the chief priest commanded one of his companions to whack Paulos on the mouth.
[Acts] [23]:[3] “God will strike you,” said Paulos, “you grand show-off. You’ve been brought here to judge me as someone who knows the law and yet you violate the law by commanding that I be hit in the face.”
[Acts] [23]:[4] But the others standing there said, “Are you insulting God’s chief priest?”
[Acts] [23]:[5] “Brothers,” said Paulos, “I didn’t realise that he’s the chief priest, because the scriptures teach us not to speak wrongly of our leaders.”
[Acts] [23]:[6] But then, knowing that the council consisted of some from the sect of the Saddoukaios (Sadducees) and some from the Farisaios’ party, Paulos continued loudly, “Men, brothers, like my father, I’m a member of the Farisaios and I’m being tried today concerning the hope and the resurrection of the dead!”
[Acts] [23]:[7] Well, as soon as he said this, the council was split as the Farisaios and the Saddoukaios started arguing.
[Acts] [23]:[8] (Saddoukaios say that the dead don’t come back to life, and there’s no messengers and no spirits, but the Farisaios believe there is.)
[Acts] [23]:[9] So then there was a big kerfuffle because some of the teachers of the law spoke up for the Farisaios saying, “We don’t see anything wrong with this man. Maybe it was a spirit or one of God’s messengers that spoke to him.”
[Acts] [23]:[10] But the Romaios commander was afraid that they might tear Paulos apart in the big argument, so he called for his soldiers to come down to uplift Paulos and return him to the barracks.
[Acts] [23]:[11] The following night, the master appeared to Paulos and told him, “Be brave because just like you testified about me here in Yerushalem (Jerusalem), so too you’ll tell them about me in Romai.”
[Acts] [23]:[12] The next day, some of the Yehudim (Jews) gathered informally and pledged not to eat or drink until they’d killed Paulos.
[Acts] [23]:[13] There were more than forty of them in this conspiracy,
[Acts] [23]:[14] and they approached the chief priests and elders and told them, “We’ve made an oath to taste nothing until we’ve killed Paulos, otherwise we’ll bring a curse on ourselves.
[Acts] [23]:[15] So you guys assemble the council and report to the commander so that he’ll bring him down to you all as if you need more information about his actions, and then we’ll have an opportunity to kill before he gets here.
[Acts] [23]:[16] But a nephew of Paulos had heard about this ambush and went in to the barracks to inform Paulos.
[Acts] [23]:[17] Paulos then called one of the Romaios centurions and told him to take the young man to the commander because he had something to tell him.
[Acts] [23]:[18] So the centurion took him to the commander, explaining, “The prisoner Paulos, called me and asked me to bring this young man to you because he has something to report to you.”
[Acts] [23]:[19] The commander took the young man by the hand and led him into his private office and asked, “What do you have to tell me?”
[Acts] [23]:[20] “The Yehudim (Jews) have decided to ask you,” he said, “that tomorrow you bring Paulos down to the council as if they wanted to question him further.
[Acts] [23]:[21] But don’t listen to them because over forty of their men will be lying in wait for him, and they’ve sworn not to eat or drink until they’ve killed him. In fact, they’re all set up already, just waiting for your consent.”
[Acts] [23]:[22] The commander told the young man not to tell anyone else about the ambush and dismissed him.
[Acts] [23]:[23] Then the commander called in two of his centurions and ordered them to prepare two-hundred soldiers to travel as far as Kaisareia, supported by seventy mounted soldiers and two-hundred more with spears. They were to be ready to leave by 9pm,
[Acts] [23]:[24] along with a horse for Paulos to ride, and were to get him safely to Governor Felix.
[Acts] [23]:[25] Then the commander wrote a letter ready to take:
[Acts] [23]:[26] “Greetings to the most excellent Governor Felix from Klaudios Lusias.
[Acts] [23]:[27] I’m writing to you about this man who had been captured by the Yehudim (Jews) here and they were about to kill him when I moved in with my soldiers because he is a Romaios citizen.
[Acts] [23]:[28] I wanted to know what they were accusing him of, so I took him down to their council meeting,
[Acts] [23]:[29] but I discovered that it was just some detail about their Jewish law and nothing that should result in death or imprisonment.
[Acts] [23]:[30] Then when I learnt that they have a plot to try to ambush and kill him, I sent him immediately to you, and I’ll order his accusers to bring their case before you.”
[Acts] [23]:[31] So the soldiers carried out their instructions and took Paulos as far as Antipatris during the night.
[Acts] [23]:[32] The next morning the foot soldiers returned to the barracks, leaving the mounted soldiers to take him on
[Acts] [23]:[33] to Kaisareia, where they presented Paulos to the governor along with the letter.
[Acts] [23]:[34] After reading the letter the governor asked Paulos what province that he’s from and found out that he was from Kilikia.
[Acts] [23]:[35] Then he ordered Paulos to be kept under guard in the prison in Herodes’s (Herod) palace until he would hear from him in the future once his accusers got there.
[Acts] [24]:[1] Five days later, Hananyah (Ananias; Grk. Hananias) the chief priest arrived along with some elders and an attorney named Tertullos, to bring the charges against Paulos before Governor Felix.
[Acts] [24]:[2] Once he was called to speak, Tertullos began his accusation of Paulos: “We have seen peace under your rule and the helpful reforms that this nation has experienced through your provision,
[Acts] [24]:[3] most excellent Felix, and we gratefully welcome everything you’ve done and everywhere you’ve done it.
[Acts] [24]:[4] But in order not to oblige you longer than necessary, in your gentleness we request you to listen to our brief statement.
[Acts] [24]:[5] This man here has been found to be a troublemaker, stirring up riots among the Yehudim (Jews) throughout the inhabited world, and as a ring-leader of the Nazoraios sect
[Acts] [24]:[6] he even attempted to profane the temple where we were able to arrest him.
[Acts] [24]:[7] ◘
[Acts] [24]:[8] When you examine him yourself you’ll discover all these things that we’re accusing him of.”
[Acts] [24]:[9] The Yehudim who had come also affirmed all the accusations.
[Acts] [24]:[10] So the governor nodded for Paulos to speak and he started, “I happily defend myself today knowing that you have many years of experience ruling in this region.
[Acts] [24]:[11] You can quickly establish that it was less than twelve days ago that I arrived in Yerushalem (Jerusalem) to worship there.
[Acts] [24]:[12] They never found me in the temple arguing with anyone or stirring up the crowd, and nor was I doing that in the Jewish meeting halls or anywhere in the city
[Acts] [24]:[13] and so they can’t provide evidence to you to support any of their accusations.
[Acts] [24]:[14] However, I must confess that I follow ‘The Path’ that they call a sect which serves the God of our ancestors and believes everything in Mosheh’s (Moses) law as well as the writings of the prophets.
[Acts] [24]:[15] We put our trust in the same God that they themselves follow, and we all anticipate a resurrection of those who serve God and those who don’t.
[Acts] [24]:[16] Because of this, I also strive to maintain a clean conscience in everything, before God and the people.
[Acts] [24]:[17] After several years away, I arrived in Yerushalem bringing offerings to help my own people and before God.
[Acts] [24]:[18] That was when they found me in the temple after going through the purification ceremony, and without either a crowd or a commotion around me.
[Acts] [24]:[19] But there were some Yehudim (Jews) from the province of Asia Minor who are the ones who should be appearing here before you, and they should be the ones accusing me if they could find anything against me.
[Acts] [24]:[20] Even these ones here now should explain what their council found me guilty of,
[Acts] [24]:[21] other than my calling out that I was being judged because I believe in the resurrection of the dead.
[Acts] [24]:[22] But Felix who was already familiar with followers of ‘The Path’, announced that the trial would be adjourned until Commander Lusias arrived when he would investigate further.
[Acts] [24]:[23] He ordered the centurion to keep Paulos confined, but under relaxed conditions and allowing any of his friends to bring him anything he needed.
[Acts] [24]:[24] However, several days later Felix returned there, this time with his wife Drusilla who was Jewish. He sent for Paulos and listened to him explain about faith in the messiah.
[Acts] [24]:[25] But when the subject turned to righteousness and self-control and the coming judgement, Felix became very uncomfortable and told him, “That’s enough for now. If I have time in the future, I’ll send for you.”
[Acts] [24]:[26] However he was also hoping that Paulos would give him money, so he often sent for him and spoke with him.
[Acts] [24]:[27] This went on for two years, until Felix was replaced as governor by Porkios Festos, but wanting to stay in the good books of the Yehudim (Jews), Felix left Paulos confined.
[Acts] [25]:[1] After Festos had been in the area for three days, he made the uphill trip from Kaisareia to Yerushalem (Jerusalem).
[Acts] [25]:[2] There the chief priests and the Jewish leaders repeated their case against Paulos, and they implored Festos,
[Acts] [25]:[3] asking as a special favour, that he would order Paulos to be sent to Yerushalem (because they wanted to ambush and kill him on the way).
[Acts] [25]:[4] But Festos replied that he’d keep Paulos in Kaisareia and he was heading back there soon,
[Acts] [25]:[5] so he told them, “Some of your leaders can go there with me, and if the man has done anything wrong, they can explain their accusations there.”
[Acts] [25]:[6] After staying seven or eight days in Yerushalem, Festos and company travelled back to Kaisareia, and the next day he sat at the judge’s bench and ordered that Paulos be brought in.
[Acts] [25]:[7] When he arrived, the Yehudim (Jews) who’d come from Yerushalem stood facing Paulos and presented many heavy charges which they weren’t able to prove.
[Acts] [25]:[8] Paulos defended himself, stating that he hadn’t sinned against any Jewish law or against the temple, nor against any Romaios law.
[Acts] [25]:[9] However, Festos wanted to be able to grant a favour to the Yehudim, so in response to Paulos he asked, “Are you willing to be returned to Yerushalem so that I can judge you about these things there?”
[Acts] [25]:[10] “I’m here facing Kaisar’s representative,” Paulos replied. “and it’s quite appropriate for me to be judged here. I’ve done nothing wrong to these Yehudim as you can no doubt see for yourself.
[Acts] [25]:[11] If I had done anything wrong, anything worthy of the death sentence, then I’m ready to accept death. On the other hand, if none of their accusations are true, no one can hand me over to them. I appeal to Kaisar.”
[Acts] [25]:[12] So Festos conferred with his legal counsel and answered, “Well, you’ve appealed to Kaisar so you’ll go to Kaisar!”
[Acts] [25]:[13] Several days later, King Agrippas and his sister Bernike arrived in Kaisareia to meet Festos.
[Acts] [25]:[14] As they had planned to stay on for a few days, Festos mentioned about Paulos to the king, telling him, “There’s a prisoner here that Felix left behind.
[Acts] [25]:[15] When I was in Yerushalem (Jerusalem), the chief priests and Jewish elders reported to me, wanting a conviction of this man.
[Acts] [25]:[16] I told them that it’s not the Romaios way to convict someone until they’ve been able to face their accusers and make their defence against the accusations.
[Acts] [25]:[17] So as soon as they arrived here, on the very next day I sat on the judge’s bench and ordered the man to be brought in
[Acts] [25]:[18] that they were accusing, but they didn’t raise even one of the charges that I expected.
[Acts] [25]:[19] Instead they raised some issues about their own beliefs and about some dead person called Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) that Paulos reckoned was still living.
[Acts] [25]:[20] I was puzzled about this debate and asked him if he wanted to be judged about these things in Yerushalem.
[Acts] [25]:[21] But Paulos appealed to be kept safe from them until he could face the emperor, so I ordered him to be kept in prison until I can send him to Romai.”
[Acts] [25]:[22] “I’d quite like to hear him myself,” Agrippas said. “Well, tomorrow,” replied Festos, “you’ll be able to hear from him.”
[Acts] [25]:[23] So the next day, King Agrippas and Bernike formally arrived with all their attendants and entered the auditorium to greet the commanders and the prominent men of the city, and then Festos ordered for Paulos to be brought in.
[Acts] [25]:[24] Festos started, “King Agrippas and everyone present, observe the prisoner who a multitude of Yehudim (Jews) pleaded with me about both in Yerushalem and here, that he doesn’t deserve to still be alive.
